# Changelog

All notable changes to this project will be documented in this file.

The format is based on [Keep a Changelog](https://keepachangelog.com/en/1.1.0/),
and this project adheres to [Semantic Versioning](https://semver.org/spec/v2.0.0.html).

## [Unreleased]

## [0.49.0] - 2026-08-22

### Added

- **An `actionlint` validator for `.github/workflows/*.{yml,yaml}`** ([#1798](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1798)). Nothing checked whether GitHub would accept this repo's own workflow files or whether a job did what it says — two hand-rolled greps (`test_coverage_gate_workdir_877.py`, `test_ci_job_timeouts_722.py`) stood in for that as a schema check, which is the shape of a missing validator. The new adapter wraps `actionlint -no-color -oneline`, mapping its `file:line:col: message [rule]` output onto the shared error shape the other adapters emit. `actionlint` is not installed on the machine this was written on, so the absent-tool path was written and tested first: `skipped` with an install hint (`brew install actionlint`), never a fabricated `ok: true` about a workflow nothing checked — the same failure #1202 fixed across ten other adapters, and now pinned generally for this one too via `tests/test_validators_absent_tool_third_state_1202.py`. Registered in `.supertool.example.json`; the intentionally-hard `glab ci lint` half stays out, split off as #1797.

- **A test can now ask for a preset-derived op instead of rediscovering why it is missing** ([#1812](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1812)). `tests/conftest.py`s autouse `_disable_rtk_and_config` hands every test `_CONFIG = {}` — deliberately, because `_load_config()` walks up from the cwd and an unreset config would make a test behave differently depending on which checkout it ran from. The cost was that every op routed through a preset manifest rather than the builtin table did not exist in any test: `git-commit`, `git-push`, the whole `gh-*` family, never intermittently and never only locally.

  `with_preset_op(*names, payload_route=False)` is the opt-in. It reads the entries off the shipped manifests through the real loader, installs only the ops named, and returns them. **It fails rather than skips**, in all three refusals: no shipped config declares the name, the entry declares a payload route in its `syntax` that derives no field names ([#770](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/770)), or a route was demanded of an op that has none. A preset manifest that cannot answer is a broken checkout, not an under-equipped machine — so there is no environment in which a skip would be the honest answer, and a fixture that skipped would reproduce one layer up the defect it exists to remove.

  On [#1776](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1776) a test asserting that the `@-` guard refuses `git-commit` — the most destructive op the guard covers — armed a skip on the absent route and took it on every invocation, reporting `git-commit has no payload route in this environment`. A well-written message that reads as a local quirk, for an assertion that had never executed anywhere. That fixture is now three lines over `with_preset_op`, and the argument is made once for the suite rather than per file.

  A census over the whole suite says how big this was: **0 of 90 skips in a full run are attributable to the reset**, and no surviving assertion was found covering nothing because of it — a papercut on that axis, which is the answer the issue asked for and did not assume. What the census did find is duplication: **43 test files carry a hand-rolled opt-out**, in three distinct idioms, each rediscovering the mechanism from scratch.

- **A test can now ask for the whole shipped registry, not just one route of it** ([#1829](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1829)). `with_preset_op` ([#1812](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1812)) installs a **subset**, deliberately: a test asking for `git-commit` must not silently acquire `gh-pr` as well, or every other op's presence in that test becomes an accident of the fixture. Eight test files wanted the other thing — this repo's own `.supertool.json` with every preset resolved, because the thing they assert about *is* the whole registry — and each of the eight had rediscovered `_merge_presets` from scratch. Six of them already spelled it `shipped_config`.

  `shipped_config` is that second fixture. It reads the tracked manifests through the real loader, installs the result as `_CONFIG` for one test, and hands back a private deep copy so a consumer that mutates what it was given cannot poison the process-wide cache for the next test. The two fixtures share the loader and nothing else — `with_preset_op` still installs only the entries it was asked for, and that is pinned as a behaviour rather than left to a comment.

  **It fails rather than skips**, on the same argument: `presets/*.json` are tracked files one directory from `conftest.py`, so a checkout that cannot read them is broken rather than under-provisioned, and a skip would report an environment quirk for a suite that had quietly stopped exercising the shipped registry.

  The guard for that is not the one the obvious implementation writes, and this is the part worth knowing. `.supertool.json` declares eight ops **directly**, so `assert config["ops"]` stays true with every single preset manifest deleted — a guard reporting a healthy registry for a checkout that resolved none of it, which is this repository's own defect class sitting inside the guard against it. It refuses on three separate conditions instead: a `_preset_warnings` entry, an empty `ops`, and a declared preset that contributed no op to the registry. That last one is asked per preset against the provenance the loader stamps as it merges (`_op_sources`), not by counting the op names the merge added — counting names cannot see a preset whose whole contribution collides by key with an op the project also declares, and this repo's eight direct `ops` entries are exactly the keys `git`, `watch` and `dashboard` ship. Each condition was checked by neutering it on its own; each reddens exactly one test and no other.

  One conversion changed behaviour rather than only shape. `test_ops_underreports_dispatchable_ops_1124.py`'s hand-rolled fixture loaded `.supertool.json` and **never called `_merge_presets`**, so a file about what the tool can do had been asserting against a config with no preset-derived op in it at all. It now sees the resolved registry, and its assertions hold.

- **The version sites are now guarded as a set, not one test per site** ([#1854](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1854)). `tests/test_version_sites_agree_1854.py` derives the five sites from `.oss.json`'s `version_sites` — the repository's own declared list, previously read by nothing in this tree — and asserts they all agree with `supertool.VERSION`. Declaring a **sixth** site now reds the suite until somebody says how to read a version out of it, which is the case `CLAUDE.md` named as the hand-sweep's real value and left to whoever remembered to run it.

  **The premise the issue was filed on was already false, and that is the more useful finding.** #1854 says the `README.md` badge is guarded by nothing; `test_readme_version_badge_matches_code` has pinned it since the badge was caught fifteen releases stale. What was actually unguarded was the *set*: five hand-written tests across four files covering five hand-written paths, with nothing tying them to the list. `CLAUDE.md` and `.claude/jit-context/paths/00-manual/version-sites.md` both said "only four are guarded" and are corrected here — the sentence is what produced the issue.

  The control is the point: a fixture freezes one site at an older version while the other four agree, parametrised over all five, and asserts exactly one disagreement is reported. A checker that reads four of five returns `[]` against a frozen fifth site — measured — so without that control the guard would pass exactly as the repository did while the badge rotted. An unreadable site and a site with no reader are findings in their own words, never folded into agreement.

  No new gate was needed for the release path. The suite runs on every pull request and `.githooks/pre-push` runs it again for a push whose destination is `master`, which is the path release commits actually take.

- **`SUPERTOOL_GIT_TIMEOUT`'s three defaults are now guarded against the prose that documents them** ([#1903](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1903)). #1886 fixed `docs/validators.md` and `validators/git-status/README.md` to state all three defaults (5s in `presets/git/status.py`, 10s in `presets/git/_git_common.py`, 15s in the `git-status` validator) instead of one — but nothing joined that prose to the code, so the next time any of the three numbers moved, the docs would go stale silently again. `tests/test_git_timeout_defaults_agree_1903.py` imports each module's own constant and regex-extracts each doc site's claimed number, failing loudly when a default moves without its prose, when a doc site's wording no longer matches the extractor, or when either doc site claims a fourth site the test does not know about. Same shape as `.oss.json`'s `version_sites` / `test_version_sites_agree_1854.py`, one variable over.

### Changed

- **`op_vim`'s `:r` failure receipt now names which of two shapes an ENOENT is** ([#1763](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1763)). `test_log_pattern_Nr_read_file_after_line` went red once on `windows-latest 3.9` with `[Errno 2] No such file or directory` on a path `tempfile.mkstemp` had created three statements earlier -- other interpreters green on the same commit, a rerun passed, never reproduced. Bare ENOENT could not tell "the path never resolved" from "something was there and is now gone", so the next occurrence would have cost the same log read and status calls this one did. The receipt on a missing-file `:r` now appends whether the parent directory exists: `(parent directory does not exist)` when the path never resolved at all, `(parent directory exists; the file itself does not)` when it did and no longer does -- the shape a reap-after-close would leave. Fires only for `FileNotFoundError`; a permission error or `:r`-ing a directory keeps its old one-line message, so the ordinary typo'd-path case does not grow a diagnostic block it has no use for.

- **The pre-push hook stops running the suite for a caller that is not git, and keeps running it for a push to `master`** ([#1802](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1802)). The issue proposed removing the suite run entirely, resting on the claim that "almost nothing reaches master by direct push". That claim was checked rather than taken, and it does not hold: measured 2026-08-20 over the last 400 commits on `origin/master`, **30 arrived by direct push and 15 of those touch `.py` or `presets/`**, the most recent two days before the issue was worked. The squash-merge path commits as `GitHub <noreply@github.com>`, so the two are separable without guessing. Thirteen of the fifteen are release commits — the one path that never passes through a PR, and the one where the four tested version sites are all that stands between a typo and a published artifact. So the master arm is live rather than vestigial and keeps its job; the smaller half of the issue was taken instead.

  **The arm that went is the not-git fallback, and its reasoning had the odds backwards.** It ran the suite whenever the hook was invoked with no ref lines *and* no argv, on the stated trade "being wrong that way costs three minutes and being wrong the other way costs master". But it fires exactly when the destination is **unknown**, and a push in this repo is overwhelmingly to a feature branch — which the hook has declined to gate since #893. It was therefore buying a macOS-only verdict, serially, on the author's machine, in a suite that rewrites the index of the live worktree it runs in, for a push it had no reason to believe was going anywhere shared. CI gates the commit on all three platforms either way.

  **Four states still, and they are still told apart.** Only the verdict of the fourth moved: it now skips and says *the destination was never established*, which is neither "there is nothing to push" nor "this is a feature branch". #1242 split those apart and that split stands. `PREPUSH_FULL=1` still forces the run in every skipping state, and the override is asked **inside** each state rather than ahead of all of them — hoisting it would print one banner for two states and rebuild #1242's conflation one layer up. That was caught in review of this change's own first draft, which had hoisted it.

  **The git env scrub stays, and that was a decision rather than an omission.** The scrub exists because the suite runs inside the hook, so the issue put its fate in scope. The suite still runs inside the hook on the master arm, so the scrub still has a reason to exist and `tests/test_git_env_scrub_692.py` is untouched.

  **The retired arm turned out to be load-bearing for eleven tests that were not about it.** `tests/test_pre_push_interpreter_572.py` and `tests/test_git_env_leak_416.py` both invoke the hook with no argv and no stdin, and reached pytest through the fallback — an incidental dependency that made interpreter-resolution and env-scrub tests fail on a change to a question neither asks. Both now pass `PREPUSH_FULL=1`, stating the dependency instead of inheriting whatever the zero-ref default happens to be.

- **A doubled-backslash refusal now locates every occurrence, with a payload line, a column and a caret** ([#1814](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1814), [#1808](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1808), [#1819](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1819)). The gate was never the problem — every reported refusal was correct and at least two caught real payload bugs. The cost of *answering* one was: the retry on this route is the whole payload, and a refusal that named the first of three offences bought three full re-sends of a file the scanner had already parsed in full. Measured at four re-sends in one agent run, on payloads up to 14 KB. Within a field the scan walked every pair to produce its count and then discarded every position but the first; `search` became `finditer` and the positions are now reported. Each is rendered as `N/M at payload line L, column C` with an excerpt of the caller's own line **centred on the pair** rather than up to 48 characters of the head of whatever line it sat on — on the reported 9 KB payload with 93 pairs, the head of the line did not contain the offending bytes at all, because a shell `printf` format is frequently 200 characters in. The message also says the two fixes are **opposite** and that nothing in the tool can tell which was meant: *needs `literal_backslashes = true`* and *has doubled backslashes that wanted to be single* are decided per occurrence and used to read identically. Beyond four occurrences in a field, and beyond three fields, the remainder is **named by payload line, never merely counted**. Where the excerpt must be flattened (a `U+2028` in the value, #1583) the caret is declined with a reason rather than drawn on offsets the flattening has shifted — the line and column are measured on the raw payload and stay exact.

- **Census: no other `validators/*` adapter treats an `OSError` from `communicate()` as a dead child** ([#1888](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1888)). PR [#1883](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/pull/1883) fixed that shape in `git-status.py` — a broken pipe under a live child is not the same event as a dead one, and the first `_stop()` conflated them, leaking a process that could still hold `.git/index.lock`. Every other adapter that spawns a subprocess does so through a single `subprocess.run(..., timeout=...)` call rather than its own `Popen`/`communicate()`/kill path, so there is no site outside `git-status.py` where an adapter's own code makes that read. `tests/test_communicate_oserror_census_1888.py` pins the population so a future adapter growing its own manual teardown does not pass this census unexamined. A residual instance of the same shape was found inside `git-status.py` itself — its outer `run()` catches `TimeoutExpired` around its first `communicate()` call but not `OSError`, so that call can still leak a live child on a broken pipe outside the already-fixed `_stop()` path — and is filed rather than fixed here, since `git-status.py` is this issue's reference implementation, not a site this diff touches.

### Fixed

- **Four printed remedies that hardcoded `./supertool` — wrong the moment they are read from a linked worktree, which is where this repo says agents work — now route through a new shared helper, `presets/_st_hint.py::st_hint`, that picks the invocation the environment it is running in can actually run** ([#905](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/905)). The issue's own filed count was seven; measured on this tree, 71 line matches across 22 files, of which 63 remain — this fix routes the four sites the issue named (`_branch_locale.py`'s `MISMATCH` remedy, `_repo_target.py`'s two `no_repo_error` messages, three sites in `presets/gitlab/job.py`, four in `presets/github/check.py`) and leaves the rest as tracked debt rather than doubling the diff into modules #905 never asked for.

  **`_st_hint.st_hint` is new, not a re-export of `presets/git/_git_common.py::st_hint`.** The two duplicate the same three states — a `./supertool` wrapper, `sys.executable supertool.py`, or neither — because `test_printed_invocation_worktree_1012.py` pins `_git_common.st_hint`'s globals identity (`conflicts.st_hint.__globals__ is vars(git_common)`) and several tests monkeypatch `_git_common.install_dir` and read the effect back through `_git_common.st_hint`; a re-export from a different module would answer to neither. The new helper is also variadic (`st_hint(*args)`), because `_repo_target.py`'s message chains two ops in one call (`repo:OWNER/NAME` ahead of the op it scopes) and that is one invocation, not two hints with no shared route between them.

  **A build gate, not only a paragraph.** `tests/test_supertool_hint_register_905.py` AST-scans every `presets/**/*.py` string constant naming `./supertool`, classifies each as `DEFINITION` (the two functions whose job is deciding the spelling), `PROSE` (docstring history, never printed) or `REMEDY-DEBT` (an actual hardcoded remedy, not yet fixed), and refuses an unregistered site or a `REMEDY-DEBT` count above the pinned ceiling — so a new hardcoded `./supertool` fails CI on the PR that adds it, the same way #905 itself would have failed had this existed in 2026-08-05. A second, non-AST test census-checks the whole `presets/` tree by plain substring count, so a comment, a JSON description field or a README code block — none of them `ast.Constant` nodes — cannot drift unnoticed either.

  **Putting `sys.executable` in a printed message made one existing assertion a measurement of the host, and #1917 found it on seven CI legs.** `tests/test_repo_target_no_repo_error_1789.py::test_a_very_long_reason_is_capped` asserted `len(msg) < 600` on the whole message; the total is `545 + len(sys.executable)`, so every ubuntu leg passed at 594 and macOS (61-char framework path, 606) and Windows (55-char hostedtoolcache path, **exactly 600**) did not. The Windows leg reads as an off-by-one — `600 < 600` against a cap that clamps at 600 — and is not one: the only clamp in `no_repo_error` is `_DETAIL_CAP`, it is 200, and it applies to gh's stderr. Nothing produces 600; that runner's interpreter path is 55 characters and `545 + 55` is 600. `<=` would pass it and fail the next runner at 56. So the assertion now measures the message **minus the invocation it contains** — 498 on every host, against 5307 with the cap removed — and the hint is left whole, because a shortened one no longer runs, which is the defect #905 exists to fix. Two new tests pin it: one drives a 226-character interpreter path through a `tmp_path` install with no wrapper (so the interpreter arm fires on every host rather than vacuously passing on one with a `./supertool` symlink), and one runs all three real runner paths and asserts they differ by exactly the spread of the paths themselves.

  **`presets/watch/README.md`'s ten occurrences and `README.md`'s own stale example transcripts (the `no_repo_error` messages this fix changed, quoted verbatim at two places) are reported, not edited** — both files are held by other work in flight at the time of this fix.

- **`git-status` flattened an MR/MR target branch and then built a git ref from the flattened name** ([#977](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/977)). `presets/git/status.py` ran `mr_target = _untrusted.flat(str(mr.get("target_branch", "?")))` and then built `f"origin/{mr_target}"` for `git diff --shortstat`. `flat()` discloses U+2028/U+2029 as `[U+2028]`/`[U+2029]` rather than passing them through, and `git check-ref-format` accepts both in a refname (#1654), so a target branch carrying one built a ref (with literal `[`/`]` in it) that does not exist — the diff call failed silently and the `(+a -d)` figure vanished with no error shown anywhere. The fix keeps the raw name for the ref and flattens only at the print, the same split `presets/github/job.py` already uses for `pr_branch`/`_local_branch_check`. The GitHub sibling (`pr_target` in the same file) was checked and is display-only, so it needed no change.
- **`per=²` crashing the refusal instead of refusing it was already fixed** ([#977](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/977)). The issue was filed against v0.26.0; #1727 (then #1748/#1764/#1765) replaced the `str.isdigit()`-then-`int()` shape across every preset guard, including `presets/_filter_tokens.py::bad_values`, with `presets/_digits.is_ascii_int` — an anchored ASCII-only `^[0-9]+\Z`. `²` and `٢` are both refused cleanly today; no code change was needed for this half.

- **The edit-miss diagnostic now names a doubled-backslash mismatch in either direction, not just one** ([#985](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/985)). #380/#1027 already named the case where a payload's `old` carried two literal backslashes and the file held one -- TOML literal blocks process no escapes, so the two can never match. The reverse direction -- a file holding two literal backslashes (written earlier with `literal_backslashes = true`, or by hand) and an `old` carrying one -- fell through to a bare percentage-and-line nearest-match hint with no mention of backslashes at all, which is the "fails quietly" half #985 was re-scoped to after #1027 shipped the `new`-side warning.

  `_edit_miss_diagnostic`'s doubled-backslash check now runs both directions: `old` doubled against a single-backslash file (existing), and `old` single against a doubled-backslash file (new), each naming which count the file actually holds. A no-match whose only difference is backslash escaping now says so regardless of which side carries the extra pair.

- **A second op that declares a project-config key already claimed by another op now refuses at the point it would run, instead of silently sharing one env var with it** ([#1009](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1009)). `ops.<op>.<key>` in `.supertool.json` has always reached that op's own subprocess as `SUPERTOOL_<KEY>` -- the key alone, never namespaced by the op that declared it. Nothing stopped a second op from picking the same key name for something unrelated; a live instance shipped as `hashnode_react.auto_force` / `hashnode_comment.auto_force`, two separately documented opt-ins, both landing on `SUPERTOOL_AUTO_FORCE`.

  Refusal, not renaming: `SUPERTOOL_<OP>_<KEY>` would break every project's `.supertool.json` and every preset reading the existing flat names, for a defect that -- measured against this repository's own config -- costs nothing to catch instead. The check is scoped to a project's own `ops` section and to genuinely *differing* values; a preset's shipped vocabulary shared across many ops on purpose (`REPO_TARGET`, `DEFAULT_LIMIT`, this repository's own `watch_name` repeated across the whole `watch` family) is untouched, because flagging it would have refused this repository's own config the moment the fix landed.

- **Both ASCII-digit recurrence scans matched `.isdigit(` and `.isnumeric(` but not `.isdecimal(`, which is the spelling that produces the defect they guard** ([#1764](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1764)). `str.isdecimal()` is True for `٢` (U+0662 ARABIC-INDIC DIGIT TWO) and `int()` converts it, so it is the *silent* half of the two classes both guard files document at their top — the half where an op proceeds against a number the caller never typed and renders it back in a receipt. Neither reader could see it: driving the module's own scan gave `scan sees isdecimal line? -> []` against `scan sees isdigit line? -> ['1: if x.isdigit():']`. So `if x.isdecimal(): int(x)` at any of the 36 core sites or 11 guarded preset files reintroduced [#1727](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1727)/[#1748](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1748) with both legs green — a scan whose green is a claim about a population it cannot fully see. Both readers now match all three spellings. **No allowlist was needed, and that is a measurement rather than a preference**: the issue expected `presets/watch/tiers/_snapshot.py:145`, which uses `isdecimal` deliberately as a documented sort key, to force one. It does not, because neither scan sweeps the tree — the core reader reads `_supertool.py` alone and the preset reader an 11-entry `GUARDED` tuple, and `_snapshot.py` is in neither. Widening was measured clean over both populations before it was made. The one in-population occurrence, `presets/_filter_tokens.py:393`, is a backticked comment and was already double-skipped by the reader's own prose filter. Each scan's positive control now carries one case per spelling and a must-not-match trio, because the real assertion is `offenders == []`, which a reader returning nothing satisfies just as well as a working one.

- **The core said `presets/_digits.py` holds the identical digit predicate and nothing compared them** ([#1765](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1765)). `_supertool.py`'s comment states that the preset module "holds the identical pair" and is deliberately not imported — presets run as standalone subprocesses with only `presets/` on their own path, so sharing one module would mean shipping the core into every preset. The duplication is right and stays; the claim was simply unpinned. Both are `^[0-9]+\Z` today, so this is drift exposure rather than a live disagreement: if they part, the core and a preset disagree about what a number is at two layers of one call and no leg goes red. The pin mirrors `tests/test_mcp_autospawn_honoured_1743.py`, which pins the one other core/preset pair claimed by a comment in the same delta — and the asymmetry was the reason this was worth an issue rather than a drive-by, because a reader had no way to tell the pinned pair from the merely-claimed one. `pattern` and `flags` are compared as live objects rather than against a literal written twice, since a third copy would be one more thing to keep in step. Two identically-wrong regexes would satisfy an equality assertion on its own, so the test also pins both sides to the ASCII behaviour: `2` and `1764` match, and `٢`, `²`, `2 `, a trailing newline, the empty string and `1.0` do not. Proved by mutating one side to `^[0-9]+$` — the exact [#1188](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1188) regression, where Python's `$` also matches before a final newline — and watching the comparison fail.

- **Two of #1708's three flattening sites had no positive control** ([#1766](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1766)). `_list_conflicts` has read `-z` since #1708, so a conflicted path arrives as its real bytes and can carry LF, CR or U+2028 into the `## ...` heading `git-conflicts` and `git-merge` print at column 0 — both already flatten it with `_untrusted.flat(path, disclose_newline=True)`, but nothing noticed if that stopped: restoring the pre-#1708 raw interpolation at both sites and running the full suite twice, mutated and restored, produced the identical `21 failed, 13934 passed, 56 skipped`. `resolve.py`'s third flattening site already had one (`tests/test_list_conflicts_quotepath_1708.py`); `tests/test_conflict_merge_heading_flatten_1766_positive_control.py` adds the same shape for the other two, mutation-tested — both assertions go red against the restored raw interpolation and green against the shipped flattening. Per-site rather than a register: `_list_conflicts` has exactly three callers, and the one register precedent in this tree for "survives a fourth site" (`tests/test_preset_git_splitlines_register_1130.py`) answers a different, static question, whose own published deciding rule #1654 measured as correct for only 3 of its 27 entries — a warning against forcing an AST-verified shape onto a question that only running the render actually answers.

- **A truncated delegated `grep` said how truncated it was not, and now says how many matches there are** ([#1771](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1771)). `(10 results in 1 files, scanned ? files — delegated to rtk, limit 10 — TRUNCATED, more matches exist (total not counted))` told the caller the answer was partial and not *how* partial, over a denominator that was unknown too — an unquantified numerator over an unquantified denominator, which is this repo's own defect class with both halves missing at once. It matters more on this op than on an ordinary grep: a rule shipped in `claude-jit-context` refuses the harness `Grep` tool and names `grep` as the replacement, so every completeness sweep an agent runs lands on this path, including the ones whose whole purpose is completeness.

  **The count was obtainable, and cheaply.** #414 declined it on the grounds that computing the denominator meant walking the tree in Python, which is what delegation exists to avoid — true, and it hid a third option. `grep -rc` is not that walk: same C engine, same tree, and `-rc` names *every* file it scanned, zero-match ones included, so one extra call answers the numerator and the denominator together. A truncated delegated grep now reads `(10 results in 3 files, scanned 1154 files — delegated to rtk, limit 10 — TRUNCATED, 47 matches total)`, in the native walker's own vocabulary. The total is **exact** rather than the walker's `N+ … (count capped at N)`: that spelling exists because a Python walk has to stop counting somewhere, and this one does not.

  **The second pass is bought only where it buys something.** It runs on truncation and never on a complete result, which needs no total and keeps the single call it has always had. Measured on this repository (1,159 files, dense pattern): 0.47s for the `-m`-capped match pass, 0.65s for the census. `builtin-ops.grep.count_truncated: 0` (or `SUPERTOOL_GREP_COUNT_TRUNCATED=0`) declines it for a tree where that trade is wrong.

  **The uncounted state survives, named rather than filed as an aside — and it says which way it declined.** rtk absent, failing or timing out, `-rc` output that is not `path:N`, a non-ASCII decimal `int()` would silently have converted, or the switch above turned off: no total came back, and the report reads `total unknown (the delegated count pass returned no total)`. A census that answered and was **refused** — its total at or below the number of rows printed under it, the two passes being separate reads of a tree that can change between them — gets its own sentence naming both numbers. One sentence for both would have been a receipt misreporting its own mechanism, in the change that exists to stop receipts doing that; the audit of this commit's first version is where that turned up. Either way no number is printed, because a guessed total is worse than an admitted gap: nothing downstream knows to distrust it.

  **Excluded files are subtracted from both numbers.** The default exclude list carries negations, which system grep cannot express, so `_grep_exclude_flags` withholds every wildcard entry and a `server.pem` really is read by the census pass — counting it would have put matches in the total that the caller was told were not there, and a file in the denominator that nobody searched. The census applies the same `_is_excluded` the native walker does.

  **Two of the issue's four questions are deliberately left open**, and both need a decision this change was not the place to make. Whether the default limit of 10 should still cap a sweep is a repo-wide default with `all` and an explicit `LIMIT` already answering it. Whether a truncated result should exit non-zero is a change to `main()`, which returns one batch-level `1 if any_failure else 0` — a per-op truncation code needs a composition rule for a batch where one op truncates and another fails, and that belongs in the dispatcher rather than in `grep`. The `?` denominator on a *complete* delegated result also stays: with no `TRUNCATED` marker every match is on the screen, which is the only thing a breadth question needed the denominator for.

- **Three stale claims in `docs/operations/meta.md` corrected, and the figures pinned to the renders they describe** ([#1783](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1783)). A quoted `ops:gh-labels` transcript still ended `Every entry: 'ops'.`, a line the refusal stopped printing when it grew a third mode; the file gave `ops:roster` two different sizes four lines apart, both stale; and the sentence describing #1781's own correction repeated the error it corrected, saying the `ops` footer reports what the descriptions cost when it reports the whole `ops:full` render.

  **The transcript was re-run rather than reasoned about, and that mattered.** #1783 proposed a replacement last line for the fence and the proposal was itself wrong. The op actually prints `Every name plus its safety class: 'ops:roster'. Every signature: 'ops'. Every description: 'ops:full'.` — three clauses, not two. Editing a quoted transcript to what it ought to say is how it rots in the first place, so `tests/test_meta_doc_figures_1783.py` now executes the fence's own command and compares, and a transcript that drifts reds in the PR that drifts it.

  **Every render in that file carries the absolute path of the config it read, so its size is a fact about the reader's filesystem.** The same tree at `.../claude-supertool` (46 characters) and at `.../st-wt/1783` (40) renders `ops:roster` at 1,969 and 1,963 bytes — the six-character difference exactly, and the same six bytes in `ops`, `ops:full` and `ops-compact`. Three of #1783's four figures were therefore not stale at all: they were measured in the clone and correct there. Only `ops:full` had genuinely moved, 74,838 to 72,715. `tests/test_ops_roster_1231.py` had already written this down as policy for the roster; the file now states how large the effect is, so the next reader who measures a few tens of bytes out does not go looking for a change that never happened.

  **One exact number in that file is stable, and it is the one the corrected sentence needed.** `ops:full` minus `ops` cancels the disclosure each carries once, giving 68,988 bytes of description at either path. The new tests assert both halves of the claim — that the footer really does carry the whole-render number and not the difference, and that the doc really does quote the difference — because either alone would let the sentence be wrong in the other direction.

  **The same species survives in four files this change does not touch**, all outside the lane it was scoped to: `README.md` (`ops:full` 74,838, roster ~1.7KB), `docs/operations/index.md` (roster ~1.4KB), `hooks/session-start.sh` (~1.7KB and a ~2.7KB hook payload, now ~2.9KB) and `docs/contributing.md` (74,838). Recorded rather than fixed, because a figure corrected in one file and left in four reads as a file nobody swept.

- **`_repo_target`'s marker tuples are documented as narrower than the call sites, because they are** ([#1807](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1807)). `_ABSENT_CWD` and `_ABSENT_TARGET` claimed to hold *the same phrases the twelve classifying call sites already match on*. They hold strict refinements of those phrases: `no git remotes` and `git remotes found` for the call sites' bare `git remotes`, `could not determine base repository` for their `could not determine`, and no counterpart at all for their broadest marker, `not found`.

  The narrowing is deliberate, and the comment now says why rather than claiming the two lists are one. A call site is an ordered if-chain over a single lookup: its `repo` arm is tried before `notfound`, `auth` and `ratelimit`, and only after the caller has turned a missing binary and a timeout into their own messages. `classify_detail` is a standalone two-way classifier with no ordering and nothing filtered out ahead of it, so the same words carry a different risk — widening it to the call sites' vocabulary would classify `gh not found - install from ...` as *absent*, which is [#1789](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1789) reintroduced in the module written to fix it.

  The cost of staying narrow is stated too: a future `gh` rewording that satisfies only a broad marker lands on `unknown` here and `absent` at a call site. That is a real divergence, in the direction that asserts nothing false about the reader's machine.

  `tests/test_repo_target_marker_vocabulary_1807.py` derives both vocabularies from the tree with an AST register rather than retyping them, and fails if the tuples grow a spelling no call site matches, if the strict pairs stop being strict, or if the comment goes back to claiming the lists are the same. No behaviour changed.

- The raw-command guard's refusal now names the op's `@payload` route on its own line, above the quoted description
  ([#1815](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1815)). The description is cut at 320
  characters by position, so `git commit -F -` — the one raw spelling that takes a multi-line message — was refused,
  pointed at `git-commit`, and shown a contract whose visible half did not contain `git-commit:@-`, costing a
  `help:git-commit` round-trip to recover the sentence the refusal was already trying to deliver. The line is rendered
  from the registry that drives the route rather than typed, so it cannot advertise a route a `syntax` reword deleted,
  and an op with no route prints no line. Where the message runs out of room for a route, or the registry cannot
  answer for one, that is counted and said rather than rendered as the same silence an op with no route produces —
  three states, which the audit of this change found the first draft collapsing into one empty string.

- The guard can now read an exclusion flag standing behind another flag on the git subcommands it gates, so
  `git commit --no-verify --amend` is un-claimed silently instead of allowed with "the guard did not run"
  ([#1816](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1816)). `_GUARD_VALUELESS_FLAGS` carries
  which flags consume no separate value for `git commit`, `git push`, `git status` and `git worktree list`, measured
  from `git <sub> -h` on git 2.46.2. Only that half is tabled: a flag absent from it stays ambiguous, allowed and
  disclosed, and both ways the table can age land on allowing more rather than on manufacturing a block. gh is
  deliberately not in it. The allow decision is unchanged for every command.
- When the guard still cannot read a flag, the note now names **which op's claim went unevaluated** and what a
  readable re-issue would be, rather than reporting only that a check was skipped
  ([#1816](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1816)).

- **A `read` window that came back whole and one that was cut short rendered the same line** ([#1820](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1820)). `read:PATH:40-72` on a 1,974-line file printed `stopping at line 72: the limit was reached` — the sentence a *truncated* read prints too. The clause named which bound closed the window; nothing said whether that bound had cost anything, so telling a satisfied read from a truncated one meant reading again, wider, and comparing. That is one extra read of the reporter's file spent to learn the first had already answered, and it is this repo's own defect class pointed at the op's own message.

  **A window that ended at the bound the caller set now says so**: `— the window ends here because it was asked to, nothing was cut`. The clause is absent from the other three states and each absence is a fact rather than an oversight — EOF already settles it in its own words (`nothing follows line N`, [#1342](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1342)) and a second verdict beside it would be two speakers on one question; a genuine cap cut is the state this distinguishes *from*; and the `read.max_lines` default was never asked for, so nothing about it ends where it was asked to.

  **"Limit" was one word for two different bounds, and they want opposite responses.** `read:PATH:10:20` ends at a window the caller closed themselves and needs no action. `read:PATH:10` ends at `read.max_lines` — the op's own cap on output, standing in for a bound nobody named, and the one that hides the rest of the file. Both said `the limit was reached`. The second now names the setting and counts what is below it: `the read.max_lines default of 300 lines was reached — you named no LIMIT, so this bound is the op's and 690 lines of the file are below it`. `op_read` resolves that default before `render_file` is called, so the fact is recorded where the two are still distinguishable and passed rather than re-derived, the same shape as the `grep=` case one argument over ([#1052](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1052)).

  Found building this, not by the issue: the first cut fired the satisfied verdict on the defaulted case too, so the note read `you named no LIMIT, so this bound is the op's — the window ends here because it was asked to`. Nobody asked. It is pinned by its own test.

  **The window note is emitted only for a non-zero OFFSET, and a range starting at line 1 has an offset of zero** — so the whole fix above missed `read:PATH:1-50`, which is the shape the issue is most likely to be asked about. That call and a plain `read:PATH` cut short by `read.max_lines` both closed with a bare `... (150 more lines)`, byte for byte, one having delivered exactly what was asked and the other missing 150 lines to a bound the caller never set. The footer now carries the same two verdicts the note does. Found by the audit of this change's own first commit, which is why it is a second hunk; the tests that reach the note all use a non-zero offset, so nothing in the suite would have caught it.

  Under compact mode that footer drops the `nothing was cut` half: blanks and comments really were dropped, and unlike the window note the footer has no `held` clause beside it to say so. Trading a silent truncation for a confident false claim would have been the same defect facing the other way.

- **A whole-file `read` of a large file previewed its head and named no way to narrow** ([#1811](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1811)). The head is the region least likely to be why the file was read, so the preview is often paid for and answers nothing — and the stop was disclosed with no remedy attached. `... (N more lines)` named none at all, and the byte-cap footer named only `read:PATH:OFFSET:LIMIT`, the one spelling this repo has three issues of evidence that callers read as START:END ([#382](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/382), [#1417](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1417), [#1489](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1489)).

  Both footers now close with the two forms that narrow — `read:PATH:START-END` for a region, `read:PATH:::grep=PATTERN` to find one — which is what `between:`'s refusal already does: suggest its own narrowing form at the moment it declines, rather than after the reader has paid.

  **The preview is kept**, against the two alternatives the issue offered. Dropping it for a structure block loses the thing that tells the caller what kind of file this is, which is the input to writing the narrowing call. Previewing an implied region loses because `read:PATH` implies none — that is the shape the issue is about, and guessing a caller's intent is what #382 and #1417 are the record of.

  **The `rtk`-delegated branch is covered too, and it is the one that fires by default where this was reported.** That path returned rtk's render unchanged, so a fix confined to supertool's own footers would not have reached the caller who filed it. rtk owns the preview and its own footer and knows nothing about supertool's call forms — the same argument the line-numbering disclosure on that branch is already there for. The gate is supertool's own caps rather than a parse of rtk's text, which under-fires where rtk compresses a file supertool would have returned intact; a hint printed on a complete read is advice nobody reads, so that is the safe direction.

  It fires only where it is actionable: not on a read that returned the file, not when the caller already typed a window, not under `:full`.

- **`around` says which pattern the colon split settled on** ([#1821](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1821)). `around:PATTERN:PATH[:N]` rejoins a colon-bearing pattern exactly as `grep` does, and where the PATH slot resolves it printed the answer and nothing else — so `around:mode:.*remind|title:DIR` searched for `mode:.*remind|title`, found two files, and named neither half of the split it had just guessed at. It now prints the same `(pattern read as …, path as …)` line `grep` has printed since #1065, with the escape hatch naming `around:@-` rather than `grep:@-`.

    #1821 was filed as an *ordering* defect on `grep` — the wrong answer printed above the note explaining why — and that half does not reproduce: `op_grep` has prepended the line since #1065 and the path since #1166. A test now pins the order rather than leaving it to the next refactor, and `op_around`'s docstring claim that it is "guarded and disclosed exactly as op_grep is" is true for the first time since it was written in #1120.

- **A radar tier that could not reach the forge no longer reports it as a missing credential, and no longer prints a remedy for a cause it did not establish** ([#1823](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1823)). `radar` failed with `RadarUnreachable: gh not authenticated. Run: gh auth login` between two successful authenticated `gh` calls seconds apart. `gh auth status` immediately after reported the same account and the same scopes the surrounding calls had used, and a bare re-run with nothing changed passed. The message named a cause that was false and the remedy it printed would have been a no-op.

  **The predicate was one bare substring.** Both tiers asked "is this an auth failure?" with `if "not logged in" in err.lower() or "401" in err`, and `"401" in err` tests three characters against the whole of a CLI's stderr. GitHub writes those three characters into a user id (`API rate limit exceeded for user ID 44012345`), into a request id (`[request-id: C401:1F2A:9B3D]`), into an epoch and into a byte count; GitLab writes them into a correlation id. Each of those is a failure that says nothing whatever about the credential, and each of them rendered as the one reading with a printable remedy. Reproduced before anything was changed: three such stderrs, driven through `live_open_prs`, all three raising the reported string verbatim.

  **Three states now, and the third is a statement about the probe rather than about the credential.** *Definitely not authenticated* keeps its remedy — `gh`'s own `not logged in` prose, an `HTTP 401` status, `Bad credentials`, or exit 4, which is `gh`'s dedicated auth-configuration code and already had its own class. *Could not tell* is everything else, and it quotes the **exit status and the stderr of the call that did not answer** instead of naming a cause, which is the issue's own fallback. That distinction is not cosmetic: a maintainer loop reading `gh not authenticated` has a documented action — re-authenticate, interactive, outside the loop's authority — where the correct action was to retry. A loop that believes the credential is gone stops; a loop told the tier was unreachable retries and continues.

  **One copy of the predicate, in `_auth_probe.py`** (it landed under `presets/watch/tiers/` and [#1846](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1846) moved it to `presets/` hours later, so that the 23 other call sites carrying the same defect could reach it)**.** The GitHub and GitLab tiers are deliberately parallel modules and stay so, but both carried this defect identically and would have drifted apart while being fixed — the argument that already put `_snapshot.py` in that directory. The markers match a **status** and never a number, and the test that keeps a bare status number out of them is structural rather than by example, because a marker list is exactly where this comes back. `_UNREACHABLE_MARKERS` was tightened with the arms it mirrors: a loose entry there is far cheaper, since it produces "could not reach" rather than a false remedy, but two halves of one story disagreeing about what `401` means is how the next reader picks the wrong one.

  **The stderr this now quotes is the remote's text, and it is flattened.** Quoting what failed is the issue's own remedy, and it is also how GitHub's or GitLab's error body gets a say in a line the reader takes as radar's: radar renders a tier failure at column 0 of its own stderr, so a newline in that body puts whatever follows it at column 0 too, in radar's voice. Both tiers now route it through `_untrusted.flat` at the point the value is bound, which is what the op-level twins (`presets/github/prs.py`, `presets/gitlab/mrs.py`) already did to exactly this value and neither tier did. Found by the audit pass rather than by the fix: the not-authenticated arm used to be a fixed string with no interpolation at all, so adding the evidence to it is what widened the surface — worth saying, because the remedy for one defect created the route for another, and three pre-existing arms in the same function had been quoting it raw the whole time.

  **The positive controls are the test.** An assertion that the remedy is absent passes on a tier that has stopped printing anything at all, so every "must not say it" case is paired with a "must still say it" case driven through the same fake — four of the first fourteen cases were green before the fix and stayed green after, and ten were red first. The three flattening cases were red first too, against the already-fixed tiers.

- **`grep_around` refused a colon-bearing pattern with the interpreter's own sentence about it** ([#1826](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1826)). `grep_around:Class::CONST:PATH` puts `CONST` in the numeric N slot, and `int()` raised through dispatch as `ERROR: argument parsing: invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'CONST'` — no cause, no escape, and the caller's search term quoted back as if it were a number. It is now a refusal that states how the call was read (`pattern=` / `path=`) and gives the payload spelling. The parse is deliberately **not** changed to `grep`'s right-to-left rejoin: three shipped guards read `grep_around`'s slots by position — the containment gate takes the path from slot 2 statically, the `all`-in-N-slot refusal reads slot 3, and #1345's fifth-token refusal counts them — and a rejoin that peels trailing integers would take `all` for the PATH and delete the first two. #1065's `pattern read as` disclosure, extended to `around` in #1821, can never fire for this op at all, because it needs a `:` in slot 1 and slot 1 cannot hold one; the refusal carries the disclosure itself.

- **A payload quoting the literal-block delimiter twice got a bare TOML column number and no hint** ([#1830](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1830)). `_toml_delimiter_hint` fired only on an **odd** count of `'''` runs, on the reasoning that every block opens and closes so a stray one means the content carried its own. The reasoning is sound and the check built from it is not: a run inside a *value* breaks the parse at any count, and even is the ordinary shape for a payload that is about the literal-block syntax — one quoted run in `old`, one in `new`. Hit twice in one agent run while writing #1808/#1814, and again while writing this change. The trigger is now structural and needs no successful parse: each `= '''` opener is walked to the run that closes it, and anything left on that line other than whitespace or a `#` comment means the delimiter closed the value early. The message names the payload line and column of that run. The odd-count trigger is kept behind it, because an unterminated block is odd and has no early close to find.

- **`git commit -a -h` was refused toward `git-commit`, an op that commits** ([#1832](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1832)). It prints usage and commits nothing (measured, git 2.46.2, exit 129), but `_guard_help_state` could not tell a help flag standing behind another flag from that flag's value, so it scored the segment and blocked — naming a next step that does the thing the caller had just declined to do. `_GUARD_VALUELESS_FLAGS`, added on [#1815](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1815)/[#1816](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1816), already carried what settles it: `-a` consumes no separate value, so `-h` behind it is unambiguously a request for help. `git commit -m -h` is unmoved, because `-m` takes the message.

  This is the one edge in the family that turns a **block** into an allow, so it is only as good as the table. Every spelling the four rows generate — 101 of them — was run against git 2.46.2 and every one printed usage; the five value-taking controls (`-m`, `-am`, `-c`, `--author`, `git push origin -o -h main`) do not, and stay ambiguous. The test re-derives that set from the table itself, so a value-taking flag added to a row later fails there rather than shipping as a wrong allow. A cluster is answered whole: `-as` un-blocks, `-am` does not. Known residual, pinned rather than fixed: `git commit -uall -h` stays blocked, because `-uall` is `-u` with an attached value and telling that from a letter cluster needs an arity fact the table does not carry.

- **`gh-pr-edit` said the new body linked no issue on the same receipt that named the issue it links** ([#1834](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1834), [#1788](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1788)). Adding a `Closes` line to a published body that had none printed, in one block:

  ```
  ## Closing references
    the published body linked no issue, and neither does this one
    Issue: #321
  ```

  The first line was false and the second right — GitHub binds the reference. `closing_ref_verdict` decided its message from `old_refs` alone, so once nothing had been *lost* it described the **pre-edit** body and `main` printed `linked_issue_line(new refs)` underneath it. Observed five times across `claude-oss` #268, #273, #277, #331 and #332, the last adding two references at once, so it was never specific to a single one.

  **The gate was never wrong and has not moved.** Nothing was lost, so `ok` and the write were correct, and both writes verified byte-identical on the server. What was wrong was the sentence about the write — this repo's own defect class one line over from where it usually lands.

  **Three gate states, four messages under `ok`**, because *nothing was lost* and *nothing is linked* are different facts: `carried through: #N`, `added: #N — the published body linked none, this one does`, `carried through: #N; added: #M` when it does both, and the original `linked no issue, and neither does this one` when there genuinely is none. The `carried`/`added` split rather than a five-row transition matrix: `some → none` is already the `DROPPED` arm, which refuses and is untouched, and `some → different` refuses on the same arm before any of this is reached — so the surviving branch has exactly two independent axes and composing them beats enumerating them.

  The third row was wrong too and nobody had filed it: a second `Closes` added to a body that already had one read `carried through: #N` and never named `#M`. Pinned by its own test.

- **`help:gh-pr-create` said a malformed `Closes` line was "caught at creation", and it is reported at creation** ([#1835](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1835)). The pull request is opened either way, exit 0. `caught` reads as *prevented*, and that reading is what makes the linked-issues block — the one place the problem is visible — look skippable. It propagated into a consuming repository's maintainer skill as "`gh-pr-create` **refuses** a body with no `Closes #N`", which is false, and four of seven agent-written payloads across two sessions had no working closing reference.

  `help:gh-pr-create` now says the line is **reported** at creation rather than discovered after the merge, and then says what that does not mean: reported, NOT refused — the pull request is opened either way and the exit code is 0, so that block *is* the check and the caller has to read it. `gh-pr-edit` is named as the repair, and as the op in the pair that does gate. `README.md` carried the same word (`gh-pr-create` **catches** a malformed `Closes` line at creation) and is corrected with it.

  **The reader was right in both directions and is untouched**, including refusing a keyword inside a code span, which is the case a substring grep passes.

  **Making `gh-pr-create` actually refuse, with an `unlink`-style escape, was considered and deliberately not built** — handed back for the maintainer to file, not filed here. It is the wider fix — the only one that reaches a hand-written body — but it is not the same shape as `gh-pr-edit`'s refusal. `gh-pr-edit` refuses a **regression**: something was bound, and this write would unbind it, so the escape token is a statement about a change of intent and is rare by construction. Refusing at creation would refuse an **absence**, which has no prior state to regress from and is legitimate on every `Part of #N` pull request. An escape token needed by a legitimate and recurring case is one that lands in the payload template, and a gate every template disables is a gate that no longer fires — the failure mode this issue is already the record of, one layer down.

- **`literal_backslashes` accepts a per-field list, so one payload can write fields that disagree about escapes** ([#1839](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1839)). The flag was payload-wide only: `= true` exempted every field, and the one caller who wanted a doubled run taken literally in `new` while a `content` field in the same batch still meant a doubled backslash had no way to say so short of splitting the payload. #1096's own docstring argued against a per-field key, but the argument was about a key placed INSIDE an `[[ops]]` table, scoped by op *position* — which the doubled-backslash scanner genuinely cannot verify, since op boundaries are a line-counting heuristic over the raw source rather than a fact. `literal_backslashes = ["new"]` is a different shape: a top-level list matched against the bare field NAME the scanner already carries on every finding (`new`, `content`, ...), with no op-boundary heuristic involved at all, so the earlier objection does not apply to it. It still does not solve two OPS that both carry a `new` field and disagree with each other about that field's own intent — that payload is still two payloads, exactly as #1096 said.

  The refusal message now builds its suggested `literal_backslashes = [...]` from the fields it actually flagged, in the order it found them, so the way out is something to paste rather than to adapt -- and, caught in self-review, that suggestion is a UNION with any fields the payload had already exempted, not a replacement: pasting it over an existing `literal_backslashes = ["new"]` no longer silently drops `new` from the list. `docs/input-forms.md` and `docs/operations/edits.md` are updated with the list form and a refreshed refusal transcript.

- **Every `gh` and `glab` error classifier now matches an auth *status* rather than the three characters `401`, so a throttle stops printing `gh auth login`** ([#1846](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1846)). [#1823](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1823) fixed two radar tiers. The identical predicate was still in **23 more call sites** — 16 under `presets/github/`, 7 under `presets/gitlab/`, one file carrying two — and five of them widened it again with a bare `"token" in s`.

  **The reported population was wrong in both directions, and the count is derived rather than quoted.** The filing listed 10 GitHub files and 7 GitLab ones. `presets/github/` actually holds 16 sites in 15 files: the five it missed are `batch_follow.py`, `batch_star.py`, `check.py`, `job.py` and `starred.py`, and the `"token"` half was 5 sites rather than 3 (`check.py` and `job.py` again). The GitLab list was exact.

  **All 23 sites were checked for reachability before being changed, and all 23 were live.** The check that settles it is the arm order, because a broad phrase fenced by an arm above it is not a defect. At every one of these sites the auth arm sits **above** the rate-limit and permission arms, so nothing fences it: `HTTP 403: API rate limit exceeded for user ID 44012345` matched `401` inside the user id and never reached the `rate limit` arm two lines down. The reproduction is the test — the negative assertion was red at 23 of 23 sites before the change and green at 23 after, with the positive control green throughout.

  **The GitLab mechanism is not a request id, it is the request URL.** go-gitlab puts the URL it called into every error string it constructs, so any project, job or pipeline id containing those three digits made a `500` or a `429` render as a missing credential — which needs no exotic input, only an id.

  **`"token" in s` becomes nothing, and that is the fix.** GitHub's own scope error is `Resource not accessible by personal access token`: a 403 about permissions that reached the credential arm and left the permission arm below it unreachable. The precise markers (`bad token`, `token expired`) already cover the credential readings, so the phrase had no work left to do; it now falls through to the arm that says "check repo access".

  **The predicate moved from `presets/watch/tiers/_auth_probe.py` to `presets/_auth_probe.py`.** None of the 23 sites can reach a module nested under `watch/`; they import `presets/_*.py` through the `sys.path` insert every preset script already does. Moving a module merged two hours earlier cost two `_load` call sites and one line of prose; the alternative was a second copy under `presets/`, which is precisely the drift the module was created to prevent, on its first day. The GitLab vocabulary (`unauthenticated`, the `authenticate` stem) is passed in as `extra` rather than folded into the shared tuple, so a GitLab phrase cannot silently widen the GitHub sites or the radar tiers — still one copy of it, where seven files previously had seven.

  **The positive controls are the test, and there is a population pin.** An assertion that a remedy is absent passes on a classifier that returns nothing, so every "must not say it" case is paired at the same site with a "must still say it" case; the pairs ran through the real functions, with `subprocess.run` faked, rather than through a re-implementation of the chain. The structural pin from #1823 now covers `GITLAB_MARKERS` too, and a new sweep test refuses any `"401" in` or `"token" in` in `presets/github/` or `presets/gitlab/` — because a seventeenth file growing its own copy is exactly how this came back the first time.

- **The GitLab radar tier tells its failure kinds apart by class, and the two tiers now share one set of classes** ([#1847](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1847)). `gh-prs` has raised `RadarUnreachable` for "the request never landed" and `RadarUnconfigured` for "no credential is configured" since #1568. `gl-mrs` had neither: a `glab` that was never spawned, one killed by the OOM killer, and a JSON body that arrived and was wrong all raised the same `RadarError` with different prose, so a caller could only tell them apart by matching on the message — and a caller that matches on a message is what #1823 had just finished removing. A loop told the credential is gone stops, where a loop told the tier could not answer retries.

  Both tiers now raise the same three classes out of `presets/watch/tiers/_radar_errors.py`, and `gh_prs.RadarError` **is** `gl_mrs.RadarError` — that identity is the part that was easy to get wrong invisibly. Each tier resolves helpers through its own `_load`, which builds a fresh module object per call, so lifting the classes the obvious way would have produced two unrelated classes with the same name, kept every per-tier test green, and left an `except` that silently never fires across the boundary. The shared module is reached by a plain `import` off `sys.path` instead, and the test pins the identity rather than the names.

  `gl-mrs` classifies on structure only — a spawn that never completed, a negative return code, `_auth_probe`'s answer — and deliberately raises no `RadarUnconfigured`: `glab` publishes no equivalent of `gh`'s exit 4, and the only thing left to split it on is prose. That gap is stated in `docs/presets/watch.md` rather than guessed at, and the class is exported anyway so a caller can write one `except` for the pair.

- **`lint-new` never opened a file a PR only modifies, and the tree-wide ignore hid the same findings locally, so a modified file was unchecked by both at once** ([#1849](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1849)). `F401`, `F841` and `F541` are ignored tree-wide against 263 pre-existing findings in files that have a history ([#797](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/797), [#1481](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1481)); the gate re-enabled them, but only for the paths a PR adds, copies or renames. Between the two scopes sat a hole neither could see. Measured on PR #1843: the leg reported **one** finding, in the only file that PR adds, and the same rule set over the whole diff found **five** — the other four orphaned `import pytest` lines in modified files, which would have shipped. `lint-new : ok` on that diff is not a false negative anybody can spot; it renders identically to a clean one. The gate now checks modified paths too, against their own merge-base revision: a head finding is reported only when its `(code, message)` is not already accounted for at base, counted as a multiset so a second occurrence of a message already there is still new. **Not touched lines**, which is the decision rather than an implementation detail — at `c974d493` all four hunks are pure deletions, the touched-line set is empty, and a touched-lines gate reports 0 of the 4; deleting a fixture orphans whatever only it used, and that is precisely a diff with nothing added. Whole-file over modified paths was rejected: it re-surfaces all 263 and the leg goes permanently red. Re-measured over 200 commits of merged `master` — 443 changed `.py` files, 231 modified — it adds 7s and reports 11 files carrying findings rather than 141. The receipt now states both scopes in full on every run: `1 of 1 file(s) this PR adds, copies or renames` was accurate and was read, by two people in one session, as `1 of 1 file(s) in this PR`.

- **A watch poller whose `poll()` keeps raising now gives up instead of retrying until the machine reboots** ([#1852](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1852)). `_run_poll_loop` broke out on `is_terminal`, but the error branch could not consult it — a failed poll produces no new state — so it wrote `last_error`, slept and `continue`d, forever. An expired token, a deleted MR, a renamed project or a source module that no longer imports polled indefinitely while holding its slot. Measured on one machine: 22 live pollers, the oldest eight days into watching an MR that had stopped being interesting on day one.

  After 120 consecutive failed polls (`MAX_CONSECUTIVE_POLL_FAILURES`, overridable per source with `MAX_CONSECUTIVE_FAILURES`) the poller emits `watcher_gave_up` and leaves through the same `finally` a terminal exit takes, so the pidfile is released and `radar` can re-arm the slot. One successful poll starts the count again, so a forge that answers one poll in ten keeps its watcher. Unlike a terminal exit the state file is **kept**, carrying a new `gave_up` record beside `last_error`: a merged MR has nothing left to explain, but a give-up's reason is the only thing that turns a stopped row on the board into a re-armable one.

  `watcher_gave_up` is the dispatcher's event rather than a source's, so it is in no `events.json` and `only=` does not filter it — a watcher that filtered away its own obituary would stop, release its slot and tell nobody. Nothing here reaps a poller because nothing is bound to the socket, which #511 records as having cost two live watchers, and there is deliberately no absolute lifetime ceiling: ending a poller that is succeeding, on a timer, is the same shape as reaping on `NO LISTENER`.

  The error backoff also became interruptible. It was one `time.sleep(interval)`, and PEP 475 resumes an interrupted sleep for its remaining time, so `unwatch` was honoured within a second by a working poller and ignored for up to a full interval by a failing one.

- **`edit`'s refusal printed `nearest match at lines 114-125 (100%)` directly under `old string not found`** ([#1855](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1855)). Two sentences a caller cannot both believe. The issue reasoned that some normalisation was making the strings equal; measured, nothing was. `SequenceMatcher.ratio()` returns `0.9976209357652657` for a twelve-line block differing by three trailing spaces, and `f"{0.998:.0%}"` is `100%` — the metric was honest and the **render** rounded a near miss up into a claim of identity. So it is a receipt defect, and the fix is one message rather than the matcher.

  A near miss now reports `>99%`, and the receipt names **what kind** of difference it is — `differs only in whitespace` or `differs in 1 of 12 lines` — because the caller's question is never "how close" but "what do I look for". The reported cost was one extra read call spent finding a one-line difference the scan had already measured and thrown away.

  **The genuine 100% is kept and explained rather than capped.** `splitlines()` drops line endings and the hint strips blank lines off both ends of the anchor, so an anchor can be equal line-for-line to a window the byte comparison rejected. Capping that would be a lie in the other direction, so it reads: identical line-for-line, so the difference is outside the compared text — line endings, or blank lines at the ends of the anchor. Leaving it bare would have left the filed contradiction alive in the one case where the number really is 100.

  The comparison itself is untouched, asserted by a control: an anchor that is in the file still matches, writes, and produces no hint at all.

- **A stalled git call no longer reads as "not inside a git repository"** ([#1858](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1858)). Seven ops open by asking `git rev-parse --git-dir` whether they are in a repository, and every one read a non-zero return as *no* — but `_git` returns `TIMEOUT_RC` (124) for a call that never answered, so a contended probe printed `ERROR: not inside a git repository.` about a repo that was mid-merge with live conflict markers. `git-conflicts`, `git-resolve`, `git-diff`, `git-commit`, `git-push` and `git-blame` now say they could not tell and why; `git-status` no longer drops its whole report on a stalled `branch -vv`; and `git-conflicts` stops reporting `no merge/rebase/cherry-pick in progress` for a state probe that did not answer. `git-commit` also stops rendering a stalled index read as an empty index: that read happens *after* `git add`, so a stall printed `Staged: 1 path(s)` and `ERROR: nothing staged — the 1 path(s) you named held no changes to stage` in the same receipt, over paths it had itself just staged. A directory that genuinely is not a repository, and a tree that genuinely has nothing to commit, are both refused exactly as loudly as before — the failure path was the half most at risk from the fix.

- **The doubled-backslash payload refusal fired on two backslashes and not on four, so the more likely reflex wrote silently** ([#1860](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1860)). `_EXACT_DOUBLE_BACKSLASH` — now `_EVEN_BACKSLASH_RUN`, since a constant naming the rule it no longer implements is the next reader's wrong premise — matched a run of *exactly* two, and two tests pinned the exemption on the ground that "three or four were counted, not produced by escape reflex". Four was produced by escape reflex, twice — and the mechanism the original rationale could not have had is that **the refusal manufactures its own blind spot**: four is what a caller writes immediately after reading the two-backslash refusal and doubling again to escape the escape, at the moment they are thinking hardest about backslashes. The guard's own stated premise — the run reaches disk at full length, passes every validator, and is wrong only in string contents — was always as true of four as of two.

  The test is **evenness**, not length: 2, 4 and 6 are refused, and 1, 3 and 5 still write unrefused, because doubling cannot produce an odd run. Without that control the fix would pass by refusing every backslash, which makes the payload route unusable for the regex and Windows-path cases the remedy explicitly sanctions. Both halves are asserted in the same fixture — a silence assertion passes when the harness is broken, so the odd arities are also the proof that the fixture can write a file at all.

  **The receipt names the run it found** rather than quoting a bare pair: the header reads `1 even backslash run`, each occurrence carries `-- a run of 4`, and the caret spans the whole run instead of its first two characters. A caret two wide under a run of four points at half of it, in a receipt whose only job is to say where to look. The remedy line generalised with it — `meant HALF the run` rather than `meant ONE backslash`.

  **Widening a refusal is the move that breaks correct callers, and it is only safe because the escape already existed.** `literal_backslashes = true` records the decision payload-wide and reaches the new arities; a run genuinely meant stays writable at every offset.

  **`old` keeps the note rather than gaining a refusal**, the adjacent gap the issue asked for a recorded decision on. It is an anchor: a doubled one cannot match, the runner reports the skip, and nothing reaches disk. But the note's reach is the scanner's, so it widened too — leaving `old` at two would have put the same blind spot one field over.

- **A CI budget floor sat below the duration it exists to protect** ([#1862](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1862)). `coverage`'s floor in `tests/test_ci_job_timeouts_722.py` was 8 minutes — 480s — against a worst observed CI run of **528s**. The floor's whole job is to make *tightening* a budget fail there rather than in a red leg nobody caused, so a floor under the job's own worst run permitted exactly the tightening it was written to refuse. It read as safe because it was derived from four *local* runs (3m24s-6m04s), and local was faster than CI; the workflow comment beside the budget claimed "~3.3x the worst observed run" where the real CI ratio is 2.3x. Raised to 18.

  Found by doing what the issue asked. #1862 was filed on a stale comment — `lint-new` (#1481) "has never run, so its pair is by analogy" — which had been false on every push since #1481 shipped. Measured 2026-08-20 over the 14 most recent successful `tests` runs, `lint-new` takes 13-33s against a 10-minute budget, so **its number does not change**; only its warrant does, from a guess that happened to land somewhere defensible to a measurement. The finding was one job over.

  Every job class had also got slower without anything noticing: `notifiers` 24-37s to 47-70s, the ubuntu pytest legs 93-125s to 150-301s, over nineteen days. Nothing compared a budget to a duration — only to a hand-written floor.

  **On whether a "no data exists yet" claim should carry something a test can invalidate: yes, and it now does — partially, with the gap stated.** `OBSERVED_WORST_SECONDS` records the worst run per job class with its date, and `test_every_budgeted_job_has_a_measurement` refuses a job that carries a `timeout-minutes` and no measurement, so a new job cannot be sized by analogy in silence the way `lint-new` was. `test_the_floor_clears_the_duration_it_exists_to_protect` is what caught `coverage`. What no offline test can check is whether the date is current — a table untouched for a year reads exactly like one taken this morning — and that limit is written beside the table rather than left to be discovered.

- **Every `gh`/`glab` not-found and permission classifier now matches a status rather than the bare digits `404`/`403`, so a server error whose URL carries a run, job or project id ending in those digits stops classifying as "not found" or "permission denied"** ([#1864](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1864)). #1846 fixed the identical shape for the credential reading (`"401" in err`); this closes the not-found/forbidden half it filed and stopped at the boundary of.
