  **The reported population was derived, not quoted, per the issue's own warning: #1846's filed list said ~17 sites and the tree held 23.** A sweep of `presets/github/`, `presets/gitlab/` and `presets/_declared_workflows.py` found **32 bare `"404" in` / `"403" in` sites across 18 files** — `gh-run`, `gh-pr`, `gh-issue`, `gh-labels`, `gh-branch`, `gh-check`, `gh-job`, `gh-follow`, `gh-star`, `gh-batch-follow`, `gh-batch-star`, all seven `gl-*` classifiers, `gl-runners`' own `radar_report` guard, and `_declared_workflows._api`'s not-found sentinel.

  **`gh` renders a run's own API path into its stderr** (`.../actions/runs/12404999`), and go-gitlab's mechanism is the one #1846 already established for the auth reading — it echoes the request URL into every error string, so any project, job or pipeline id carrying `404` or `403` made a server error classify as missing or forbidden, with no exotic input required.

  **`presets/_status_probe.py` is the new shared predicate, one copy, not folded into `_auth_probe.py`.** `says_not_found` and `says_forbidden` match a status — `could not resolve`, `not found`, `http 404` for the first; `forbidden`, `permission denied`, `http 403` for the second — never a bare digit, with the same structural test `_auth_probe.py`'s markers carry refusing one. Auth is a different question with its own per-platform vocabulary (`extra` for GitLab); not-found and forbidden are not, so a second predicate rather than a second tuple.

  **The positive controls are the test, and there is a population pin.** Every "must not read as X" case is paired at the same site with a "must still read as X" case using a genuine 404 or 403, run through the real functions with `subprocess`/the API call faked. A sweep test refuses any `"404" in` / `"403" in` under the same two directories plus `_declared_workflows.py`, so a nineteenth file growing its own copy is caught the way the seventeenth was for auth.

  **Two follow-on fixes the population sweep forced, both pre-existing tests whose own AST-derivation or taint-model no longer saw what changed underneath them.** `tests/test_repo_target_marker_vocabulary_1807.py`'s call-site derivation resolved only a literal `"x" in s`, so it went blind at every site now routed through `says_not_found`/`says_forbidden` — it now also resolves those two calls into the marker tuple they test, and the call site's own `"404"` marker becomes exactly `_repo_target._ABSENT_TARGET`'s existing `"http 404"` spelling rather than a superstring of it. `tests/test_forged_child_stream_line_1475.py`'s child-stream census flagged all 30 new predicate calls as an untracked escape, the same shape #1846 already fixed for `says_not_authenticated`; `says_not_found` and `says_forbidden` join it in `NOT_TEXT` for the same reason — both return `bool`, so the taint provably stops at the call.

- **`git-commit` with `--all` carries both halves of a staged rename** ([#1865](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1865)). `--all` resolves to the working tree's dirty paths plus everything in the index, and it read the index with `git diff --cached --name-only` — which has rename detection on by default, so a staged `git mv a b` printed `b` alone and the deletion of `a` never appeared. The commit was scoped to the new path, the deletion stayed staged, and half a rename landed: two copies of the moved file in one tree, compiling and passing any test that only touches the new path. The index reads now pass `--no-renames`, so `--all` means what its own contract already said. A call that NAMES its paths still leaves an unrelated staged path alone — "commit everything staged" remains the pathless spelling and a different op (#1228).

- **`gl-mrs` had no transport-marker whitelist and no rate-limit arm, so a `glab` DNS failure told a caller to stop where `gh-prs` tells it to retry** ([#1870](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1870)). `gh_prs` has classified a transport failure -- DNS, a refused connection, a reset socket, Go's `net`/`net/http` vocabulary -- as `RadarUnreachable` since #1568, so a caller catching it knows to retry; `gl_mrs` classified on structure only (a spawn that never completed, a negative returncode, `_auth_probe`'s answer) and let every transport failure fall into the widest class, `RadarError`, which a caller reads as a verdict about the board rather than a reason to try again. `presets/watch/tiers/gl_mrs.py` now carries its own `TRANSPORT_MARKERS` -- a separate tuple from `gh_prs`'s, mirroring #1846's split for the auth markers, since the two Go CLIs' vocabularies are not guaranteed to stay identical -- plus a rate-limit arm on GitLab's own `429` status rather than a port of `gh`'s `403`. Every marker is prose, never a bare status number, for the reason #1864 names. Reasoned, not observed: no authenticated `glab` was available to drive a real transport failure through, so the marker list is ported from `gh_prs`'s own on the argument that both CLIs are Go binaries surfacing the same standard-library net errors verbatim.

- **The two radar tiers no longer assert `killed by signal N` on a returncode nobody has observed on Windows** ([#1871](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1871)). `gh_prs.py` and `gl_mrs.py` both fire on `result.returncode < 0`; on POSIX `subprocess` documents `-N` for a signal, so the old wording was exact there. On Windows the same field is the process exit status, and `_winapi.GetExitCodeProcess` is declared `unsigned long`, so a negative value is unexpected — but the negative spelling of the same DWORD circulates widely enough (shells, Python 2) that the premise is worth distrusting without a runner to check it on. Reasoned, not observed, in either direction.

  Both tiers now state the returncode, which is true on every platform, and hedge the mechanism rather than asserting it: `"...did not finish before it answered (returncode -9, consistent with a killing signal on POSIX — not established on Windows, see #1871): ..."`. The classification — the process did not finish, retry — is unchanged; only the vocabulary moved. One change to both tiers, matching the wording drift PR [#1869](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1869) had already removed once between them.

- **`presets/watch/README.md` no longer says `unwatch` reads the PID file** ([#1872](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1872)). `cmd_unwatch` stops every live poller for the slot, tracked and untracked alike — the #511 multi-kill — and a reader who believed the old bullet would have concluded that an untracked poller survives `unwatch`, the opposite of what happens. `docs/presets/watch.md` already stated it correctly, so the two documents disagreed; the README bullet now matches.

- **`.githooks/pre-push` now runs the suite under `-X utf8`, the flag CI has carried deliberately since #546** ([#1875](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1875)). The hook and `.github/workflows/tests.yml` disagreed about the one flag that decides how a non-ASCII failure message is rendered, and the hook was the exposed half: CI's Windows leg had the flag, a local `git push` did not. pytest writes failure lines on a stream whose codec is the console codepage, so on a codepage that cannot carry the character the local run and the CI run describe the same failure differently.

  **The issue's stated symptom was wrong, and correcting it is what settled the design question.** #1875 said the missing flag makes pytest raise `UnicodeEncodeError` while reporting. It does not — `TerminalWriter.write_raw` catches exactly that and re-emits the line unicode-escaped, so the strict-stream outcome is a diagnostic degraded to a backslash-u escape, not a destroyed one. The genuinely destroyed outcome is the U+FFFD that #546 measured on `windows-latest`, where the stream substitutes instead of raising and pytest's fallback never fires. Observed here on darwin under a latin-1 stdio codec: without the flag a failure message carrying U+0662 comes out escaped, with it the character survives. That the same holds for a Windows console codepage is reasoned, not observed, and whether any Windows user runs this hook is still unmeasured.

  **The alternative the issue offered — `ascii()` at each assertion site — was rejected rather than deferred.** It cannot reach pytest's rendering of compared values, where `assert DIGITS.match(probe)` prints the probe with no message for a source edit to touch; and the ten sites the issue estimated are 430 assert messages across 184 test files once counted, excluding the runtime-valued ones that are the actual shape and cannot be found statically. A flag on the emitter covers all of it in one line. A repo-wide convention against non-ASCII in assertion messages would be a house-style change against prose that uses em dashes on purpose, and belongs in its own issue if it is ever wanted.

  Pinned behaviourally rather than by substring: `tests/test_prepush_utf8_mode_1875.py` runs the hook against the #572 stub interpreters and asserts on the argv it really issued, reads the flag off both the hook and the workflow so dropping it from either goes red, and reproduces the rendering difference with a positive control that fails loudly if the locale stops reproducing anything. Where no non-UTF-8 locale exists the reproduction skips saying what went untested.

- **The four remaining files carrying a stale render size corrected, and every one of them pinned to the render it describes** ([#1877](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1877)). `README.md`, `docs/operations/index.md`, `docs/contributing.md` and `hooks/session-start.sh` stated `ops:full` at 74,838 bytes when it renders ~72.7KB, `ops:roster` at ~1.7KB and ~1.4KB when it renders ~2.0KB, and the SessionStart payload at ~2.7KB when it is ~2.9KB. `tests/test_render_size_claims_1877.py` now grades all fifteen figures against the live render, so the next one to drift reds in the pull request that drifts it rather than in an audit six weeks later. (Thirteen when this fragment was first written; the count was left stale by the two rows the change's own coverage guard demanded afterwards, and an audit caught it — a receipt about the change stating a number the change contradicts, which is the defect the change is about. Re-derived from `pytest --collect-only`, not recounted by eye.)

  **Two figures were older than the issue and describe a tree that has not existed since #1774.** `hooks/session-start.sh` and `docs/operations/index.md` still said `ops` is 47,254 bytes and `ops-compact` 9,067 — figures from before the descriptions moved out of `ops` into `ops:full`. `ops` is now ~3.7KB and fits the 7,168-byte cap on its own; `ops-compact` is ~14.7KB and is now *larger* than `ops`, which is why index.md's row calling it "`ops` with the per-op detail trimmed" was wrong about the direction and not only about the number. `docs/contributing.md` attributed `ops:full`'s size to `ops` for the same reason.

  **The figures were reworded from exact byte counts into the KB form, because an exact count cannot be pinned.** Every one of these renders carries `_preset_disclosure()`, which names the absolute path of the config it read, so its byte count is a function of where the checkout sits on disk — measured at 3,721/3,727 for `ops` and 72,709/72,715 for `ops:full` at a 40- and a 46-character path. `tests/test_ops_roster_1231.py` already stated that as policy for the roster. A tolerance of 0.1KB is 100 bytes, an order above that variance and two orders below the 2,129-byte drift this issue is about.

  **A registry, not a walker, and the reason is measured.** The issue asked for a single test walking every file that states a size for a named render. A deliberately narrow regex — a render name in backticks, a size within 80 characters of it on the same sentence — finds 40 hits in 11 files here, and they are at least five kinds nothing in the text separates: a live claim, a historical record in `CHANGELOG.md` and `changelog.d/`, a past-tense sentence, a SessionStart cap that is not a render size at all, and figures already pinned by `tests/test_meta_doc_figures_1783.py`. A dated measurement is a record and stays; an undated present-tense one is a claim and gets graded. So membership is explicit and a record is simply absent from the list. The half a walker was wanted for is kept: a figure written into a file *already* in the registry and graded by no row is a red test naming it, and `CHANGELOG.md` is never opened.

  **Three states in the grader, because two would have hidden the next rewording.** A row whose pattern finds nothing fails as "this test stopped being able to see the claim" rather than passing as clean — the alternative is a figure going stale again behind a green tick, which is the defect this whole class is. Two disagreeing figures for one render fail rather than being graded at random, which is #1783 item 5. The exemption list carrying the one cap figure the harvester reaches is itself guarded: an entry that matches nothing is reported, because a dead exemption is a blind spot that looks exactly like a working one.

  **One row of the same table was wrong about the direction rather than the number.** `docs/operations/index.md` described bare `ops` as the "full operations reference ... with descriptions and examples", which has not been true since #1774 — it renders signatures and nothing else, at ~3.7KB. Corrected here because this change rewrote the `ops-compact` row two lines below it for the same reason, and a table stating both would be #1783 item 5 again in a new place.

  **Three sites remain, in files this change was scoped out of.** `_supertool.py:2575` (`ops` 47,254, `ops-compact` 9,067) and `_supertool.py:17101` (74,838) were held by another lane, and `tests/test_ops_roster_1231.py:3,181,292` carries the same pre-#1774 pair in an undated docstring. Recorded rather than fixed, and the registry is one line per site when they land.

- **The render-size pin measured how deep your checkout was and reported it as documentation drift** ([#1877](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1877)). Every render it grades carries `_preset_disclosure()`, which names the absolute path of the config it read, so a raw byte count is partly a measurement of the developer's directory layout. The pin absorbed that into its 0.1KB tolerance on a sample of one — PR #1876 had compared two paths six characters apart and got a six-byte difference, and 100 bytes is generous against six. The sample was six; the range is not bounded by anything. Measured 2026-08-21 at `c6dd83ae`, one tree at two paths: `ops` renders 3,724 bytes from a 43-character worktree and 3,811 from a 130-character one. 87 characters of path, 87 bytes of render, 87% of the whole tolerance. `ops` at ~3.7KB is where it bites hardest — 100 bytes is 2.7% there, against 0.14% at `ops:full`.

  **The trigger was a maintainer's false positive, and that is the most useful thing in this entry.** A disposable clone taken under a 129-character scratchpad path failed four rows with `README.md says ops is ~3.7KB; this checkout renders 3.81KB (3,810 bytes)`. That was diagnosed as a composition defect between this pin and [#1881](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1881) — two pull requests each green on its own merge-base, the theory being that a changed op description had moved the `ops` render — and briefed to an agent as a red `master` needing an urgent figure bump. None of it was true. `master` was green (`21 legs, 21 passed`), and all four renders are byte-identical either side of that merge: 3,724 / 72,712 / 14,705 / 1,966, re-measured at one path on both commits. Had the brief been followed, the four sites would have been bumped to ~3.8KB and made wrong at every normal checkout, CI included. The next person to hit this will be holding the same confusing evidence: a red naming a documentation figure, produced entirely by their own working directory.

  **The path is now normalised away before grading rather than tolerated.** `graded_bytes` substitutes one fixed path — CI's own checkout path, pinned as a literal so no environment can move it — for whatever the running checkout is, so the graded figure is the same number everywhere and on every platform. A Linux runner at `/home/runner/work/...` and a Windows runner at `D:\a\...` differ by 12 characters today and by whatever the runner images decide tomorrow. Tolerating the path was worse than it looked in *both* directions: a deep checkout false-fires, and a shallow one hides real drift byte for byte, since a figure measured 90 characters deeper than the reader's checkout eats 90 bytes of the same budget. With the variable gone, 0.1KB means only what [#1884](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/pull/1884) argued it meant — room for prose to round — and stays two orders below the 2,129-byte drift the registry exists for.

  **Substituted rather than deleted, and no documented figure moved.** Stripping the path outright was the first fix written here and it was wrong: it grades a render nobody receives. `ops:roster` comes to 1.907KB stripped, which rounds to ~1.9, so the honest consequence would have been correcting `README.md`, `docs/operations/index.md` and `hooks/session-start.sh` away from the ~2.0KB a reader at any real checkout actually sees — making the prose less true to make the grader more convenient. With a stand-in of realistic length every one of the five stated figures stays exactly as it is, and the tightest of them now sits 68 bytes inside the tolerance rather than 13.

  **`graded_bytes` refuses rather than answering when it cannot normalise.** Caught by the audit of this change, in the guard the change adds: the first version substituted the path only `if path:` and otherwise fell through to the raw byte count. `_preset_disclosure` names `os.getcwd()` when `_CONFIG_PATH` is falsy, so a render in that state is still checkout-dependent while the one string that locates it is gone — the un-normalised number in the shape of a normalised one, failing with the same "this checkout renders N bytes" sentence that started all of this. It now asserts, and the refusal is pinned by a test of its own, because every row reaches the helper through a fixture that always sets a path and a refusal nobody can produce is indistinguishable from one that was never written.

  **The new row asserts the property with a positive control, because on its own it would pass on silence.** If the disclosure ever stopped naming the path, both renders would come back the same length and "the graded size does not move with the path" would pass while checking nothing — the guard reduced to the exact absence it detects. So it first requires the raw sizes at two config paths to differ by *exactly* the path difference, and only then compares. All fifteen rows fail the property before this change and pass after, and the same suite at the 130-character scratchpad path goes from eight red to green.

- **`watches` no longer reports an empty fleet while pollers it can see are running** ([#1881](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1881)). A machine reached load average 409 with 564 orphaned `dispatcher.py poll` processes live across five slots, and the board printed `No active watchers. None recorded as lost either.` The process scan had run, had succeeded, and had seen all 564 — they were another channel's, so `scan_poller_pids` dropped them and the render then denied they existed. That left the operator with no documented route to them at all: `watches` showed nothing and `unwatch:SOURCE:ID` had no slot to name, so the only tool that worked was the `pkill` this preset tells operators not to use.

  The scan keeps its contract — `scan_poller_pids` still answers with this channel's pollers alone, because every caller of it decides an *action* and widening it would restore the cross-channel kill [#1514](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1514) was filed for. What that issue settled was which pollers may be listed as rows and signalled; it did not settle whether their existence may be stated, and the render took the stronger reading. `transport.poller_census` now returns all three of the label's answers, and `watches` discloses the two it may not act on as **counts, never rows** — no SOURCE or ID is printed, because naming one is what invites `unwatch` against a slot this channel does not own.

  The channel token is a digest of the state directory and cannot be reversed, so a bare `chan=43b6d3f23b71` is not something an operator can act on. The sibling directories are hashed forward instead, which names the state directory — and so the `SUPERTOOL_WATCH_NAME` whose own board can stop those pollers. Three states, as everywhere else here: a directory that matches, no directory that matches, and a base directory that could not be listed. When the scan itself did not run, no count is printed at all; `0 pollers on another channel` read off a scan that never happened is the same substitution one layer in.

  The unqualified sentence survives for the genuinely clean case. When pollers were counted above it, the board says `No watchers on this channel` — disclosing 564 processes and denying them in consecutive lines is the defect rendered twice.

- **A `git-status` validator whose git stalled reported the file as clean** ([#1882](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1882)). The adapter wrapped each of its four git calls in a hard-coded `timeout=5` and returned `""` on `TimeoutExpired`; its own parsers read `""` as an answer — `_parse_state("")` is `"clean"`, `_parse_numstat("")` is `(0, 0)` — so a large, cold or network-mounted repository published `ok: true` with a zeroed `metrics` block reading `state: "clean"`, a measurement of a working tree nothing had measured. That is the shape #1202 removed from this adapter's *absent-git* arm; the timeout arm was left behind on the adjacent line, and it fires on every edit rather than only where git is missing. It now declines with `code: "adapter"` — rendered `NOT CHECKED`, never cached, never able to roll an edit back. **`SUPERTOOL_GIT_TIMEOUT` now reaches it** (default **15s**, raised from an unreachable literal `5`), it is one deadline for the whole adapter rather than four in a row, and the registered validator `timeout` moved 5 → 30 so the adapter can state its own decline instead of being killed mid-git by the core — the two were tied at 5, and a tie is a race.
- **A stalled `git-status` validator no longer strands `.git/index.lock`** ([#1882](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1882)). `subprocess.run(timeout=)` calls `Popen.kill()` — SIGKILL on POSIX, no grace — so git never ran its own cleanup and the lock it was holding survived it, failing every later `git add`, `commit` and `checkout` in that repository until somebody deleted the file by hand. The stalled child now gets `SIGTERM` and a 2s grace period first, which is long enough for git to unlink its own lockfile, and is killed anyway if it does not go. **The adapter still never deletes a lock itself**, deliberately: it cannot tell a lock it orphaned from one a concurrent `git commit` legitimately holds, and deleting the second corrupts that commit. Windows gets the same grace period and gains nothing from it — `terminate()` and `kill()` are both `TerminateProcess` there — which is a property of the platform rather than a reason to branch on it.
- **The stop-the-stalled-git handler returned on `OSError` and left the child running** ([#1882](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1882)). Found in review of the fix above, and it is the same bug one layer in: `_stop()` treated an `OSError` out of `communicate()` as "the child is gone" and returned without killing it. But `communicate()` failing is a fact about the **pipes**, and a broken pipe is a different event from a dead process — measured on CPython 3.13.15, closing the stdout fd under a live `sleep 600` raises `OSError(9)` with the child still running and `returncode is None`. So a git that had blown its budget kept running, holding the `.git/index.lock` this change exists to stop stranding, inside the one function whose job is to stop stranding it. The grace check now asks the **process** when the pipes cannot answer — `communicate()`, falling back to `wait()`, which touches no pipe — and `_stop` escalates to `SIGKILL` on either answer. Killing an already-exited child raises nothing (also measured), so the early return had no upside in any state.
- **That budget is interactive latency, and it is now argued rather than assumed** ([#1882](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1882)). Every mutating op blocks on its slowest validator, so raising this adapter's budget from an unreachable 5s to 15s means an edit to a file in a repository whose git does not answer blocks **19s measured** before the decline prints, against roughly 5s before — 5s and a fabricated `state: "clean"`. Roughly 3.4x worse interactive latency on exactly the cold or network-mounted repository the report cites, and it is the direct cost of not lying. `docs/validators.md`, `validators/git-status/README.md` and the `.supertool.example.json` `_doc` now carry the number and the remedy: because a stall is now an honest `NOT CHECKED`, `SUPERTOOL_GIT_TIMEOUT=3` is a legitimate setting for anyone who would rather have a fast decline than a slow measurement — a choice nobody had while the fast answer was a lie.
- **The lock-deletion guard covered four spellings and read as if it covered the class** ([#1882](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1882)). The test pinning "this adapter never deletes a lock" walked for attribute calls named `unlink`/`remove`/`rmtree`/`rmdir`, so `os.system("rm -f " + lock)`, `subprocess.run(["rm", p])` and every `from os import remove` spelling walked straight through — 5 of 7 realistic shapes, measured. A green guard read as *cannot delete a lock* while proving *not via four attribute spellings*: this repository's own defect class, inside the test written to prevent exactly that drift. It now resolves from-import aliases, refuses `os.system`/`os.popen` and `shell=True`, and requires every spawn's `argv[0]` to be git. Ten must-fire and six must-not-fire controls pin the branches — two of which exist because those controls failed on the first draft of the widening — and the docstring states the shapes no AST walk can reach rather than implying completeness.

- **The `git-status` validator's no-argument arm answered `ok: true, state: "clean"` for a working tree nothing had measured** ([#1885](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1885)). A missing or empty file argument is an adapter fault, not a measurement — every sibling adapter that takes a single file argument (`ruff`, `eslint`, `tsc-check`, `phpstan`, `xmllint`, `yaml-check`, and more) already routes it to `code: "adapter"`; this one adapter alone answered a fabricated `clean`. It now matches the convention.
- **The `rev-parse` arm stays as it is, and that is a finding rather than a punt** ([#1885](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1885)). The question this issue asked: can a genuine "not inside a repository" (endorsed as clean by this adapter's own README) be told apart from a real repository whose `rev-parse` faulted — a corrupt `.git`, a permissions problem? Measured rather than assumed: `git rev-parse --is-inside-work-tree` answers both a directory with no repository above it and a repository whose `.git/HEAD` is corrupted with the byte-identical signal — exit 128, empty stdout, "fatal: not a git repository" on stderr. Git itself does not expose the distinction, so the adapter cannot manufacture one without also misrouting the endorsed case, which is the regression [#1883](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/pull/1883) declined to introduce. `test_rev_parse_cannot_tell_outside_a_repo_from_a_faulted_one` pins this so a future git version that starts telling the two apart is a signal to revisit, not a silent gap.

- **`docs/validators.md` and `validators/git-status/README.md` documented `SUPERTOOL_GIT_TIMEOUT` as if it had one default; it has three** ([#1886](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1886)). The same env var is read at `presets/git/status.py` (5s, courtesy calls that write nothing), `presets/git/_git_common.py` (10s, six other presets), and the `git-status` validator (15s, has to survive four sequential calls on a cold repository). Exporting the variable moves all three together, which is intended, but the docs stated one of the three as *the* default. Both files now name all three and why they differ.
- **Unifying the three was considered and deliberately deferred** ([#1886](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1886)). Each default is already justified inline at its own call site by the engineer who chose it, and each budget answers a different question — interactive latency for a courtesy line versus surviving a cold repository for a validator that blocks an edit. The prerequisite for collapsing them into one number is a cost nobody has measured yet: what a `git status` actually costs on a large cold repository, beyond the single >15s data point [#1882](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1882) reported. Correcting the docs to state the three real defaults is this change; picking one number for all three is not.

- **A watch poller's slot could be claimed by more than one process at once** ([#1891](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1891)). `claim_pidfile`'s exclusivity rested on `O_CREAT|O_EXCL`, but the PID was written into the file as a second, separate syscall — so for the interval between "the name now exists" and "the name now holds a PID", the file sat there empty. A second claimant hitting `FileExistsError` in that interval read the empty file the same way it reads a genuinely corrupt one (`content is not a PID`, deliberately reclaimable so a crashed poller cannot wedge a slot shut forever) and reclaimed a slot whose real owner was still mid-claim rather than dead. The first claimant, already holding a descriptor open on what was now an orphaned inode, went on to write its own PID into a file nobody could see any more and returned success regardless. Reproduced with two real, unmodified processes racing the function: more than one reported ownership in roughly half of repeated trials on an otherwise idle machine — not a rare edge, closer to a coin flip.

  This is the half of [#1881](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1881) that [#1890](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/pull/1890) did not reach: that PR's own arithmetic showed all 564 pollers on the original report carried one channel token, so the accumulation was entirely intra-directory, and this is what defeated the singleton inside it. The reporter's six same-minute `write_state` temporaries are not themselves reproduced or explained by this fix — `write_state` has no relationship to slot ownership (`record_death` is reached from plain readers with no lock between them, by design) and a positive-control test now pins that several concurrent non-owning writers on one state file is expected, corruption-free behaviour rather than evidence of a duplicated poller.

  The fix writes the PID into an unpredictable temporary name first and publishes it with `os.link`, which is atomic and — unlike `os.rename` — refuses outright rather than replacing when the destination already exists. There is no longer an interval in which the pidfile's name exists without its content: a second claimant either finds nothing, or finds a fully-written PID it can check for liveness.

- **The test suite no longer leaks `git fsmonitor--daemon` processes through its temp repos** ([#1892](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1892)). Three independent measurements on one machine on 2026-08-21 found 965-979 orphaned daemons at `ppid 1`; with them present, a full suite run hung at 98% for over an hour and a plain `git add` in a fresh temp repo timed out at 30 seconds. `git fsmonitor--daemon run --detach` is by design started once per repository and never torn down by the repository closing — and the suite creates thousands of them, each inheriting whatever `core.fsmonitor` an operator has set globally, an ordinary preference rather than a defect.

  `tests/conftest.py` now sets `GIT_CONFIG_COUNT=1`, `GIT_CONFIG_KEY_0=core.fsmonitor`, `GIT_CONFIG_VALUE_0=false` once, in `pytest_configure`, before any fixture runs. Every `git init` in the suite is a bare `subprocess.run(["git", ...])` with no `env=`, so it inherits the pytest process's environment and the suppression reaches all of them without touching the 27+ files that create one — there is no single shared repo-creation helper to patch instead. A test that deliberately wants the daemon can still force it with `-c core.fsmonitor=true` on the individual invocation, which outranks the environment.

- **`unwatch` reaching zero of this channel's pollers now says when the slot is covered by another channel instead of staying silent** ([#1893](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1893)). `cmd_unwatch` and `reap_duplicate_pollers` are correct to act only on this channel — [#1514](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1514) settled that, and killing another channel's poller is a wrong kill. What it did not settle was whether their existence may be *stated*, and `cmd_unwatch`'s own "nothing to stop" report kept reading the exclusion as covering that too — the same defect [#1890](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1890) fixed in `watches`, one surface over. An operator whose slot was polled entirely by another channel ran `unwatch`, saw `No active watcher`, and the foreign poller kept running with nothing on the board explaining why.

  `cmd_unwatch` now threads the same `poller_census()` `watches` already computes through to `_report_nothing_stopped`, and discloses — as a count, never a PID or a row — any poller on this exact slot that belongs to another channel or to no channel at all. Nothing here widens what either function may act on.

- **`strict_publish` fixture now isolates cwd, not only env** ([#1897](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1897)). `_publish_safety._supertool_config()` walks up from cwd to find `.supertool.json`, but the fixture only cleared the env-var opt-outs (`SUPERTOOL_PUBLISH_BODY_ALLOWLIST`, `SUPERTOOL_NO_PUBLISH_CONFIRM`) and never touched cwd, so two tests in `TestConfirmGate` read the checkout's own `.supertool.json` instead of an isolated one. That fires for any user whose repo config sets `no_publish_confirm` or `publish_body_allowlist`, whether or not this repo does. The fixture now `monkeypatch.chdir(tmp_path)`s as well, so every test using it is isolated by construction rather than by remembering to chdir per test.

- **`git-status.py`'s outer `run()` no longer loses a live `git status` when its FIRST `communicate()` breaks** ([#1912](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1912)). PR #1883 taught `_settled`/`_stop` that a `communicate()` failure is a broken pipe, not a dead child — but only `_stop`'s own call site used them. `run()`'s own `communicate(timeout=remaining)`, the one every one of the four `git` calls this adapter makes goes through, still caught only `subprocess.TimeoutExpired`; an `OSError` there (reproduced against a real child: closing a live child's stdout fd under a running `sleep` raises `OSError(9, "Bad file descriptor")` with the child still alive) propagated past `main()`'s `except _NoAnswer`, so `_stop` was never called and a `git status` holding `.git/index.lock` was left running. `run()` now catches `OSError`/`ValueError` there too, falls back to `_settled` to ask the process directly, and only escalates to `_stop` when the process is still alive — an already-dead child is not sent a stop signal it never needed.

- **`#1475`'s census scored a whole sink node clean when any one value in it carried a mark, discarding every other raw stream on the same line** ([#1918](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1918)). `_unmarked` used to gate on `MARKS & _call_names(node)` — `_call_names` walking the whole subtree — so one `_untrusted.flat(...)` anywhere inside a `print(...)`, including inlined into an f-string, cleared the node entirely. PR #1913 inlined `flat()` into one value of a print that also carried `mr_state` and `pipe_status` raw; both vanished from the census with nothing fixed, the file's count read as a repair, and the ratchet's own failure text told the reader to write the smaller number down.

  **Per-value marking, not per-node.** `_unmarked` now walks the AST directly and stops descending only at a `MARKS` (or `NOT_TEXT`) call's own arguments — the same boundary `_walk_text` already draws for `NOT_TEXT` — so a mark clears the value it wraps and nothing beside it. Two node shapes needed their own rule rather than a blind walk, because a blind walk over them would have turned this fix into the census-inflating one the issue explicitly warned against: `IfExp.test` (a ternary's condition, never its value — five of the sites this fix first surfaced were `_untrusted.flat(tail[-1]) if tail else "…"` guards, where the old walk read `tail` a second time as the boolean test) and a comprehension's `iter`/`ifs` (which decide what is bound and what is kept, never what is produced — `_comprehension_keys` reads a comprehension's value off its `elt`, tainting a loop target only when its own `iter` was tainted, the same rule an ordinary assignment already gets).

  **The real count moved, in both directions, and both are shown rather than adjusted until green.** Measured on this tree: 145 -> 139 sites in 32 files, `UNRESOLVED` 113 -> 109. All of the movement is a correction of pre-existing imprecision in `_streams_in`'s blind subtree walk (ternary-test and comprehension-iter false positives that predate this issue and were not specific to a MARKS site), not a new defect surfacing — no file's count rose. Every changed line is traced and reasoned about in `CENSUS`'s own comments.

  **What per-value marking still cannot see, stated rather than silently assumed**, per two fixture pairs added alongside the fix (`test_a_mark_on_one_value_does_not_clear_its_siblings` / `test_the_same_sink_with_only_the_marked_value_counts_zero`): a mark applied to one name and the same raw value read again under a second, untracked alias — not a new gap, the same blind spot `_streams_in` already had; and a comprehension whose loop target is a tuple (`[a for a, _w in cut]`) — unlike a top-level tuple-unpacking assignment, there is no `ast.Call` node for `_escapes_from` to hang an `UNRESOLVED` disclosure on, so a raw value reaching a sink this way would leave silently. Both live instances of that shape (`status.py`'s `known`, `pipeline.py`'s `summary`) were checked by hand and are genuinely safe; a comprehension shaped this way earns its own disclosure mechanism if one is ever found to matter.

- **`st_hint`'s wrapper probe now answers something on Windows, instead of a check that could never say no there** ([#1919](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1919)). `os.access(wrapper, os.X_OK)` answers true for any existing file on Windows -- there is no execute bit for it to read -- so the probe degraded to "does a file named `supertool` exist", and the helper's third state ("no runnable supertool found") became unreachable on that platform: a stray, unrelated file wearing the name got printed as the runnable wrapper.

  **Both duplicated implementations, not one** -- `presets/git/_git_common.py::st_hint` (since #1061) and `presets/_st_hint.py::st_hint` (added by #1917 that same day) each grow a `_wrapper_is_runnable` helper carrying the identical check, kept as two functions rather than one shared one for the reason #905's own fragment already gives: `test_printed_invocation_worktree_1012.py` pins `conflicts.st_hint.__globals__ is vars(git_common)`, which a re-export from a different module breaks.

  **The replacement reads the first two bytes rather than trusting existence.** On `os.name == "nt"` the probe now asks whether the file opens with a shebang (`#!`), matching what this project's own install instructions (`README.md`) always produce -- a symlink to `supertool.py`, itself `#!/usr/bin/env python3`. Weighed against the other two options the issue named: a `PATHEXT`-suffix check answers nothing for this wrapper's literal, extension-less name, and a spawn attempt is the most truthful of the three but also the most expensive, on a refusal path where the caller is already stuck waiting for the remedy. What the shebang read cannot establish: that the named interpreter exists or is on `PATH`, that a POSIX-aware shell is what receives `./supertool` on the machine at all (native `cmd.exe` and PowerShell ignore shebangs entirely), or that the file is not truncated past those two bytes.

  **Grade: reasoned, not observed** -- there is no Windows host in this project. `tests/test_windows_wrapper_probe_1919.py` reproduces the actual defect on any host by faking `os.access` to the real Windows behaviour (true for any existing file, mode ignored) rather than merely setting `os.name`, since the pre-fix code never branched on `os.name` at all and a POSIX host's real permission bits would otherwise mask the bug. The control pair sits in one fixture: a stray non-executable file must report the third state, and a shebang-carrying file must still print `./supertool` -- both against an explicit `tmp_path` install root, never this checkout's own `./supertool` symlink.

- **`gh-prs`' and `gl-mrs`' unwatched footer disagreed with `radar` and `watches` under a named watch channel** ([#1922](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1922)). Both boards hardcoded their own `STATE_DIR = "/tmp"` as the default poller-pidfile directory for `_watched_numbers`/`_watched_iids`, while `presets/watch/transport.py` resolves the actual directory (`transport.STATE_DIR`) — `/tmp/supertool-watch-<name>` under `SUPERTOOL_WATCH_NAME`, or wherever `SUPERTOOL_WATCH_STATE_DIR` points. `radar` and `watches` already read the resolved directory, so only the board's own footer looked in the wrong place and reported a PR/MR unwatched while a live, emitting poller held its slot — exactly the shape reported live, under `SUPERTOOL_WATCH_NAME=oss-supertool`. Both `main()`s now pass `transport.STATE_DIR` explicitly, the same value `radar`'s tier already passes. `tests/test_gh_prs_footer_state_dir_1922.py` pins the control pair the issue asked for — an armed poller under a non-default state dir reads as covered, a bare one still reads as unwatched — for both boards, plus a direct before/after comparison against the stale default that reproduces the reported mismatch.

- **`git-worktrees`' activity probe read the reflog file's mtime, not its newest entry, so a bare `git fetch --prune` flipped every linked worktree to `occupied` for 15 minutes** ([#1923](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1923)). `git gc` / `git reflog expire` -- auto-triggered by `fetch --prune` -- rewrites `.git/worktrees/<name>/logs/HEAD` for every linked worktree without appending anything: the mtime moves, the content does not. `_newest_write` compared candidate files by `os.stat().st_mtime`, so the rewrite alone read as `reflog written 0s ago`; on the tick that found this, six merged, hours-quiet worktrees all flipped `occupied` seconds after the tick's own fetch, suppressing cleanup on evidence the tick itself manufactured.

  `_newest_write` now reads the reflog's own newest **entry** timestamp for this one candidate rather than the file's mtime, and the control pair is what the fix is graded against: a tree whose reflog was genuinely appended to inside the activity window still reads `occupied`; a tree whose reflog file was only rewritten does not. An entry that cannot be parsed (an empty file, a line in an unrecognised format) deliberately falls back to the file's own mtime rather than dropping the signal -- keeping that failure mode on the side already shown safe here (a spurious `occupied`, never a spurious `idle`, which is the verdict that authorises deleting a worktree). The sweep for the same class found no other stat-based evidence line with this failure mode: `_newest_write`'s tree walk and the lock-file probe both stat real file writes, which git does not rewrite without changing.

  The entry parser only reads the file's last 8KB (a reflog can grow large between `git gc`s), and a fixed-size seek can land inside the newest entry's own commit message, past the tab that marks where its header ends -- silently misreading message digits as a plausible timestamp with no error at all. Caught in review before merge: the read window now grows (bounded at 1 MiB) until a tab is found or it declines rather than guess.

- **The four warm PHP MCP adapters no longer wait out their full timeout on a response they already received** ([#1924](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1924)). `ndjson_call` in `phpunit-mcp`, `phpstan-mcp`, `phpmd-mcp` and `rector-mcp` parsed the daemon's socket buffer one LF-delimited line at a time. When a forked PHP process fatals, the host application can render an HTML error page into the same stream, and the real JSON-RPC response then lands glued to the end of the last HTML line with no separator (`</html>{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":2,...}`) — a line-anchored parser never sees it, so the adapter blocked on `recv()` until the full call timeout (300s for phpunit-mcp) and reported `NOT CHECKED`, indistinguishable from a genuine timeout. Measured: the answer was in the buffer 2 seconds in; the adapter gave up 5 minutes later. `validators/common/ndjson_scan.find_response` now scans the whole accumulated buffer for the response rather than requiring it to open a line, so it is found the moment its bytes arrive. The per-`recv()` socket timeout is also now tied to the call's own deadline rather than reset on every call, so a genuine no-answer still fails at the deadline instead of a further multiple of it, and the error names what was actually in the buffer — no bytes at all, or bytes with no decodable `id`-matching frame — rather than a bare "timeout" that could mean either.

- **The `unwatch` and `watches` channel-token disclosures now flatten the token they print, closing a cursor-control injection through another process's argv** ([#1925](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1925)). Both surfaces read `channel` out of another process's argv via `transport._labelled` and printed it straight into an f-string. `_ps_rows` splits argv on whitespace, which blocks a newline, but a CSI sequence carries no whitespace and passed through intact — `ESC[1G` then `ESC[2K` rewrote the disclosure line from column 0, on the exact surface whose job is to tell an operator that a poller survived. Five sibling fields already routed through `_untrusted.flat()`; the channel token, which comes from a less trustworthy source than any of them, was the one that skipped it.

  `presets/watch/dispatcher.py:220` (`_foreign_slot_lines`, [#1893](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1893)) and `:477` (`_foreign_poller_lines`, [#1890](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1890)) now call `_untrusted.flat(channel)` at the point they render it. No chokepoint already prepares `channel` for either render — each function reads it straight out of `census["other"]`'s own keys inside its own loop — so this is two call sites, not one shared preparation point; flattening the *key* itself at `poller_census()` was ruled out because that same value is also used as a dict lookup against `channel_dirs()`, where equality with the real hash matters. An ordinary hex channel token renders unchanged.

## [0.48.0] - 2026-08-18

### Added

- **`git-worktrees` now answers whether a tree holds uncommitted work, and the exit code says so** ([#1751](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1751)). A detached worktree has no branch, so its merge column is structurally `n/a` — leaving `idle` at exit 0 as the entire verdict standing between `git worktree remove` and work that exists nowhere else. Every row now carries `clean`, `dirty: N` or `dirty unknown`, counted on the `[result]` line, and the scan runs `--no-optional-locks` so an op that promises inspection-only does not write the index of a tree somebody is holding.

  **Exit-code change.** `3` joins the declared values and is not `clean`, so `supertool 'git-worktrees:PATH' && <reap>` declines over a dirty tree. Exit `0` is unchanged in spelling and stricter in meaning — `idle` must now also be clean — and a dirty scan that could not answer lands on `2`, never on `0`. A caller testing `== 1` for `occupied` is untouched.

### Changed

- **`git-worktrees`' description is the contract again, not the case history** ([#1774](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1774)). Documenting the two columns #1750 and #1751 added grew it from 4,832 to 7,021 characters, and #1774's ledger refused the growth. It now reads 2,383: every state of every column is still named, and the incident behind each — the `ps` grep that returned 0 for a live agent, the 24-branch ancestry measurement, the git 2.46.2 reflog result, why the dirty scan runs `--no-optional-locks` — moved to `docs/presets/git.md`, which is where the long form already was.

  The ledger row falls from 4,832 to 2,383 rather than being deleted. Under `MAX_DESCRIPTION` (2,000) it would leave the ledger, and the last 383 characters are reachable only by dropping a column's state list or the exit-code contract — and a reader who does not know that `PR unknown` is not `no open PR`, or that `dirty unknown` is not `clean`, misreads the board in the direction this op exists to prevent. The ratchet asks that the number fall, not that it hit a round one.

  Worth knowing for the next growth refused here: `help:OP` renders the **same** `description` field byte for byte, so there is no long form to move prose *into*. The cheaper home is `docs/presets/git.md`, the issue, or the test's own docstring.

### Fixed

- **A guard refusal no longer closes by naming a harness write tool as the route past it** ([#1706](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1706)). Every `deny` ended "a harness Edit/Write reaches this same path with no op, no validator and no rollback" — a working bypass spelled out in the one sentence a blocked agent is guaranteed to read, and an agent that takes it loses the validator chain and the write rollback the refusal exists to route it into. Inert in this repository, where the `harness-tools-blocked` rule denies those tools; live for every plugin user, which is who the plugin ships to. **Not a revert of [#1671](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1671):** the refusal still says the gate hooks Bash only, that the denial is about the route and not the path, and that any other route to the file gets no op, no validator and no rollback. Only the tool name is gone. The names stay on the surfaces where a reader is deciding rather than being denied — the SessionStart roster, `docs/configuration.md`'s `raw_command_guard` section and the README deny-list recipe — and all three are asserted, so this is a move rather than a deletion.

- **A `NOT COVERED` note no longer claims the op is "the same invocation without" the tokens it declined** ([#1707](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1707)). It was false for exactly the argv the branch exists to catch: drop `v0.43.0` from `git push origin v0.43.0` and you push a **branch**, and the third recorded instance was `git push --force-with-lease origin docs/claude-md-git-c`, where the suggested equivalent also discards the safety on the operation while the note enumerated only the operands. The clause now says what the op performs — "`git-push` performs `git push` and nothing more, which is a different command from this one" — which is true of every argv reaching that branch and asks git nothing. Making it conditional on the dropped tokens being inert was the other option and needs the guard to know what a refspec is, per utility, which is the case work `_GUARD_GLOBAL_OPTIONS` refuses to grow. **The clause also leads the note now instead of closing it**, found in this change's own review: `_guard_notes` truncates a note from the end and the echoed command is caller-supplied, so written last the correction was cut mid-word for the reported force push and vanished entirely for a longer branch name — with `… (+N chars)` disclosing that something was cut and never that it was the correction. The `gh run view --help` instance in the issue's first comment does **not** reproduce and needs no `unless_flag`: `_guard_help_state` has un-claimed every entry for a help flag since #1430, now asserted so a regression is visible.

- **A worktree whose branch has never committed no longer renders `[merged]`** ([#1750](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1750)). "Every commit is already an ancestor of master" is vacuously true of a branch holding nothing, so a brand-new tree and a fully-landed one were the same cell in the column a maintainer reads to decide what is safe to delete — seven of eight live fleet worktrees on `62bc3f0`, each with an agent editing it seconds earlier. The row now reads `no commits yet` and says the work there is uncommitted.

  The issue's own proposed test could not have worked: `git rev-list <base>..<branch>` being empty is the *same predicate* as the ancestry read the op already performs, since a branch is an ancestor of the base iff that range is empty. Measured on git 2.46.2, a branch with three commits merged `--no-ff` and a branch created and never committed to both answer `0`. The branch's reflog is what separates them, it is local, and it costs nothing on the network, so `nopr` still answers. A reflog that cannot be read is the third state and never a silent fall-through to `merged`.

- **The `{arg}` split quoted in prose is now computed, not retyped — and the three copies of it agreed for the first time** ([#1761](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1761)). `tests/test_cmd_placeholder_path_detector_1350.py`'s docstring said the split was `24/8/16`, `docs/contributing.md` said 21/8/13 in words, and `tests/test_arg_placeholder_and_paths_env_1357.py` asserted 20/8/12 green on every run one file away. The docstring had been wrong since [#873](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/873) and survived [#1715](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1715) moving the figure a second time. Re-derived against the shipped manifests before the fix: 20 ops carry `{arg}`, 8 name a path in `syntax`, 12 do not.

  **Correcting the digits was the smaller half.** Three digits last until the next op moves, which is exactly what happened twice already, so every figure in both prose sites is now recomputed from `test_arg_placeholder_and_paths_env_1357.py`'s own helpers and asserted against the text — the prose stays plain readable digits, and the test is what joins it to the measurement. Matching is done against a whitespace-flattened copy, so re-wrapping a paragraph never reddens CI; only a figure changing does. The docstring also refuses a second `N/N/N` triple, which keeps that paragraph one current claim rather than an accumulating history.

  **The third site is why a grep was not enough.** `docs/contributing.md` spelled its figure out as "Twenty-one shipped ops", so a sweep for `24/8/16` and for the component digits could not see it, and it had drifted independently to a value neither of the other two held. The same paragraph block also stated the `syntax` detector's own population as 24 where the live count is 25 — [#1759](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1759) corrected that number in the test file and left the doc behind. Both are corrected and both are pinned, so `docs/contributing.md` is no longer the one unpinned copy of either count.

  The reasoning #1357's un-built `{arg}` lint rests on is unaffected, and was re-checked rather than assumed: it turns on the lint's population being a strict subset of the gate's, which `test_the_arg_lint_would_reach_no_op_the_gate_does_not_already_hold` asserts directly and which does not depend on the magnitude.

- **`@-` in a value field is refused instead of written to the file** ([#1776](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1776)). `paste:victim.txt:@-` did not read stdin. The @payload route is gated on the argument right after the op name, so a `@-` anywhere later fell through to the handler as ordinary content: two characters written over the file, under `rewrote victim.txt (1 lines, 39 → 3 bytes)`. Nothing in that receipt is false and nothing in it says the body written is not the body that was piped in — the byte count was the only tell, and a three-byte intended body would have left none.

  **Five ops that write had it, not two.** The reported case was `paste` and `append`; `edit`, `replace` and `replace_lines` reach the same handler position the same way, each of them measured writing the literal `@-` over a known fixture (`replace_dry` parses it identically and writes nothing). `vim` refused it by accident — its script parser has no verb `@` — which is loud but does not name the route that works. The guard sits once in dispatch, ahead of every handler, scoped to ops that have a payload route: that is what makes it a refusal rather than a dead end, since the message names `OP:@-` and the keys its payload wants.

  **Both colon forms, read ops out, and the reasons for each.** `paste:::PATH:::@-` is refused too — `:::` never routed a payload from a later field either, so it is not where the ambiguity lives, but it is the separator this repository tells agents to reach for first and the two characters land on disk identically. The read ops (`grep`, `around`, `grep_around`, `between`, `read`, `validate`) are deliberately out: a `@-` in one of their value fields is a path, so it already fails by name with nothing written, and the payload hint is built from the mutating registry and would print a remedy with no keys in it.

  **The payload route is untouched, and is the escape hatch.** Fields that arrived through a payload or a batch sub-op are not scanned — there the caller has already said "these bytes, exactly", nothing was tokenized, and that is how to write a literal `@-` to a file. The test asserts the file's bytes rather than the receipt text, and pairs every refusal with a write that must still happen, because a refusal test that also passes when the op stops writing altogether is not a test.

  **The gap the issue names as underlying is not one.** `paste:@-` with a TOML `content` block and `paste:::PATH:::CONTENT` both take a multi-line body today, both measured on 0.47.0, so "no write op takes a multi-line body at all" was wrong when it was written and the refusal leaves no caller stranded. What was missing was discoverability, and `help:paste` / `help:append` — reported as answering `no documented help` on 0.46.0 — have printed the colon form, an example and the payload route since [#1773](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1773).

- **A gh outage no longer renders as "cwd is not a GitHub repo"** ([#1789](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1789)). `gh-pr-merge` reached `no_repo_error()` on *any* failure of its identity read and dropped the reason it was holding, so during a GraphQL outage it told a working clone of a real repository that it was not a GitHub repo — and its third remedy, *run gh directly with --repo*, routes that op onto raw `gh pr merge`, which the raw-command guard refuses and which skips the leg reconciliation and the post-merge read-back. `no_repo_error()` now takes gh's own error and tells *asked, there is no repository here* from *could not ask*, naming the reason and asking for a retry instead of a `cd`. It takes the reason rather than looking the repository up itself: the other twelve call sites match gh's stderr before they call, so a second lookup here could contradict a correct measurement with a fresher one. `cwd_slug()` keeps the two states #1701 gave it, for the reason #1701 gave.

- **The rule that blocks `Read`/`Edit`/`Write`/`Glob`/`Grep` is pinned as not shipping** ([#1791](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1791)). Reported as blocking every file operation in every repository the plugin is installed in, for contributors who never installed supertool. Measured and it does not: there is no `supertool-required.md` in the tree, the rule that matches the description is `harness-tools-blocked.md`, and it has been a recorded absence in `shipped_rules.NOT_SHIPPED` since [#1698](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1698) — `hooks/hooks.json` registers the hook on `Bash|PowerShell`, so no harness file tool reaches it. Fed one directly anyway from a foreign project directory, the hook allows it. Nothing asserted any of that, so `tests/test_harness_tools_do_not_ship_1791.py` now does, each row named with the mutation that reddens it. Shipping that rule would cost more than the report says: its index pattern is `~.`, so it would deny every Bash command in somebody else's repository, not only the file tools.

- **A check run a later run of the same name superseded is a third state, not a red leg** ([#1792](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1792)). `gh-pr:N:status` counted every check run on the head SHA, but GitHub decides a required check on the **latest** run carrying that name — so a pull request the forge reports as `mergeable_state: clean` rendered `NOT ALL GREEN`, and `gh-pr-merge` refused it. Permanently: a concluded check run cannot be withdrawn by any trigger a maintainer has, so the pull request could never satisfy the gate by any action available to them. Reported from outside, against `jbkkz/requivo` PR #18 — six check runs named `fragment` on one SHA, five that failed at 22:23 and one that passed eight hours later.

  **The discriminator is timing, not name.** Latest-per-name is not a safe collapse: GitHub's default code-scanning setup emits two concurrent runs per push, and measured against this repository's own `d1bb0837` those two runs emit check runs whose *names collide* — two `Analyze (javascript-typescript)`, two `Analyze (python)`, two check suites, started in the same second. Collapsing on the name would have reported a leg that never ran as green, which is the defect [#1640](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1640) fixed one op over. A leg is superseded only when another leg of the same name **started strictly after this one completed** — so the code-scanning pair supersedes nothing, and the five stale `fragment` runs all do.

  It is deliberately **narrower** than GitHub's own rule. Two same-named legs overlapping in time with one failed still read red here even where the forge says clean: a loud false alarm costs a reader one look, a quietly-swallowed failure costs a merge.

  **The superseded failure is never invisible.** It takes its own tally term — so `N total` still accounts for every leg on the commit — and its own named disclosure line carrying the state it concluded in and its job id, on `gh-pr:N`, `gh-pr:N:status` and both paths of `gh-pr-merge`:

  ```
  checks: 6 total: 1 passed, 0 failed, 0 pending, 5 superseded
    superseded failed: fragment (job #95528525867), fragment (job #95528526529), …
  ```

  A leg whose completion cannot be read — an absent stamp, `gh`'s `0001-01-01T00:00:00Z` sentinel, or a legacy commit status, which carries no run timing at all — is never superseded. It stays counted and stays red. The reconciliation against what the runs declare still sees every leg, because that is a coverage question and not a verdict.

- **`gh-pr-merge` refused any pull request carrying a failed superseded leg, and printed no reason** ([#1792](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1792)). A regression in that issue's own fix, found by the v0.48.0 release audit. `gate()` returned `(not lines, lines)` and the superseded disclosure was appended to that same list on the **passing** path — so a line whose entire purpose is to say these legs are *not* counted red decided the merge was refused. The maintainer read the note, then `[result] REFUSED`, with **zero `REFUSED:` lines** to act on, and was then offered the raw `gh pr merge` escape hatch: routed onto the path with no leg reconciliation and no post-merge read-back, for no valid reason.

  **Why it was invisible.** `named_disclosure` skips the passed and pending buckets, so a superseded *pass* — the ordinary re-push case — emits no lines and flipped nothing. Only a superseded *failure* emits, and that is precisely the reported case the fix existed for. Four pull requests merged cleanly the afternoon it shipped, every one of them with a superseded pass.

  `lines` now holds two kinds and only one decides. The invariant is one sentence: **`allowed is False` if and only if at least one line says `REFUSED`** — asserted as a property over several rollups rather than as one more example, because the defect was not in any branch, it was in the return contract where every branch meets. A note that spells `REFUSED` anyway is treated as a refusal and said out loud rather than trusted for the list it arrived in; the merge is irreversible, so the classification fails closed. `gh-pr-merge` prints the disclosure on the passing path too, where it was previously discarded along with the rest of the gate's output.

  The misfiled check is **anchored at line start**. Written as an unanchored substring it read over lines that render check-run names verbatim, and a check-run name is written by whoever writes the repo's workflow files — a job called `connection REFUSED` would then have blocked every merge of every pull request carrying it. Same defect class one layer further in, caught by self-review before it shipped.

  The test that let this through asserted that a *phrase* was absent from the findings text — true of a gate refusing for a different reason, and true of a gate refusing while naming nothing. Compounding it, every gate test passed `declared=None`, so the reconciliation declined on all of them and the genuinely-clean passing path was never exercised. Both are fixed: the tests assert the boolean, and pass a reconciled `declared`.

- The jit rule-body budget counts content, not the checkout. `tests/test_jit_rule_body_budget_1433.py` measured each rule body with `stat().st_size`, and git checks these files out with the platform's line endings — so a `windows-latest` leg counted one extra byte per line for byte-identical content and reported a size that exists on no machine the author has. PR #1768's `presets-git.md` is 5,918 bytes / 94 lines with LF and failed all four Windows legs of run #31912614030 at 6,012. The count now collapses CRLF to LF first, and the test states what the number claims and what it deliberately does not: on a CRLF checkout the hook does inject those CRs, which is a property of the checkout to fix at checkout time, not a body the author can shrink. A rule the index names but nobody can read is now reported as unmeasured rather than dropped before the measurement (#1799).

## [0.47.0] - 2026-08-16

### Changed

- **`ops` is every signature; `ops:full` is every description** ([#1774](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1774)). The descriptive listing was 74,838 bytes against a 7,168-byte SessionStart cap — ~19k tokens for the one call whose job is to tell a caller which op answers their question. The default is now the signatures alone, 3,670 bytes in this tree, and the row count is identical: nothing is hidden, the prose moved.

  The cost was never spread evenly. Across the 128 documented ops the median description is 151 characters and the top ten rows are 37,739 — 49% of the corpus in 8% of the ops — because `description` is printed whole by both this listing and `help:OP`, and had become the record of how each op got here. [#1775](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/pull/1775) put a ratchet under that growth; this changes who pays for it.

  The default footer states the exact size of what it withheld and the two tokens that fetch it, measured from the full render rather than described, so a listing that later shrinks reports a smaller saving by construction. `ops:roster` (#1231) and `ops-compact` are unchanged, and a token the op does not have is still refused naming the ones it does.

### Fixed

- **`help:OP` answers for a core op from any directory the plugin is installed in** ([#1773](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1773)). `op_help` read `builtin-ops` out of the config `_load_config()` finds by walking up from cwd, and that block lives in supertool's own `.supertool.json` — not a preset, so it was merged into nobody else's tree. From a plain consumer repo `help:read`, `help:grep`, `help:paste` and `help:edit` all answered `has no documented help` while `help:gh-pr` answered in full: the split was never documented/undocumented, it was preset op / core op, and the core ops are the ones a new caller reaches for first.

  **The plugin install is the route this reaches.** A `pip install` carries no `.supertool.json` — `pyproject.toml` declares two modules and no package data — so on that route the fallback finds nothing and says so, which is a true sentence about a real gap and not the fix working. That gap is [#1783](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1783), found by this release's own audit and filed rather than fixed here, because packaging wants its own CI evidence rather than a re-read of the manifest.

  The project's config still answers first and still wins outright — a project that redefines an op documents its own version. Only a name no section here has heard of reaches the reference that ships beside the binary, and the answer says so rather than letting an entry about the binary read as an entry about this tree. Deliberately a lookup and not a merge: a consumer's `ops` gaining forty builtin descriptions is [#1774](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1774) pointing the other way.

  The refusal that remains — an install whose shipped reference is missing or unreadable — no longer names `docs/operations`, a directory that exists next to this checkout and nowhere else. It names `ops:roster` and the op's own error instead, both true from anywhere.

- **An unreadable shipped reference stops reporting as an absent one, and the `ops` footer names the quantity it measures** ([#1781](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1781)). Both found by the v0.47.0 release audit, in code [#1773](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1773) and [#1774](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1774) had shipped hours earlier.

  `_shipped_config()` caught `OSError` and yielded `{}`, so three different worlds printed one sentence: a reference that was absent, one that could not be read, and one that was read and documents nothing. The audit built all three from this checkout's own binary and `cmp -s` reported the `chmod 000` install byte-for-byte identical to the install with no file at all — while the file beside that binary documented the op the refusal said nothing shipped for. Three states now, not two: the lookup records which world it found and the refusal says so, naming the path, and the unreadable arm answers `UNKNOWN` rather than answering the question at all.

  The `ops` footer said the withheld descriptions were `74838 bytes`; that is `ops:full`'s whole render, headers and signatures included, so the prose withheld was overstated by the size of the default listing. The number stays — it is what asking for the descriptions costs — and the sentence now says which quantity it is.

  `ops:full` also reached no document: `docs/operations/meta.md` still described `ops` as the reference "with descriptions and examples", and a grep for the new token across all 28 files under `docs/` returned nothing. Both are written up now, and the byte counts in `meta.md` and `README.md` — 47,254 and 9,067, stale since well before this release — are re-measured with the command that takes them beside them.

## [0.46.0] - 2026-08-16

### Added

- **`channel:probe` — put one byte through the bridge on demand, and refuse to call the result arrival** ([#1593](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1593)). `channel:health` and `radar`'s delivery line both report on traffic that already happened: a consumer that is bound, verified and counting publishes the same numbers whether it is reading its socket or wedged on it, because those numbers were written by whatever last happened to flow. Nothing could put an event through the path *now*, so the one time it was needed it was done with hand-written Python against `transport.emit_socket` — a private module, and a record shape (`ts`, `source`, `id`, `event`, `payload`, `first_tick`) a caller had to reverse-engineer from the producer to fake correctly. `transport.probe_record()` is now that shape as a function, and `channel:probe` writes one event and reports which of the consumer's own counters moved.

- **The value of the op is the refusal it makes about its own result** ([#1593](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1593)). Arrival inside a Claude session is observable only from inside that session — the bridge sends a JSON-RPC notification, which has no id and no response to wait on — so a probe that renders `forwarded` as receipt would rebuild [#554](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/554) inside the fix for this issue. Instead every verdict prints the exact `<channel watcher_source="channel-probe" id="probe-XXXXXXXX" event="probe">` tag the caller should now look for, with a per-run id so a stale tag on screen cannot answer for a fresh probe; states that the increment is not attributable, because a poller emitting in the same window advances the same counter; and says which half of the bridge is left to suspect when the tag does not appear. `tests/test_watch_channel_probe_1593.py` asserts against the vocabulary, not only the verdict.

- **Three counters, not one, so a slow consumer and a broken one are different answers** ([#1593](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1593)). The issue proposed reading `forwarded`. The consumer also moves `lines_read` when it takes a line off the wire and `dropped` when it refuses one, and reading only the first folds *has not read it yet* into *read it and handed it nowhere*. Six verdicts follow, each with its own exit code: `FORWARDED` (0), `NOT DELIVERING` (1), `CANNOT DETERMINE` (3), `CONTRADICTED` (4), `ACCEPTED, NOT FORWARDED` (6 — a finding about the read loop) and `ACCEPTED, DISCARDED` (7 — the burst budget or an over-long routing key, which the consumer's own stderr names). The wait is bounded at 3s, so a consumer slower than that renders exactly like one that did nothing: every non-advance arm prints the budget it waited, and the arm where nothing was even read is `CANNOT DETERMINE` rather than a finding.

- **A cold baseline is the question, not a reason to decline** ([#1593](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1593)). The first cut of this op aborted with `CANNOT DETERMINE` whenever the consumer's counters were already stale, copying `channel:health`'s verdict — which is `health`'s correct answer, because the file is all it has. Measured 2026-08-15: the consumer over this clone was holding the socket with counters 607s cold, the probe declined, and the event it had just written arrived in a separate session as a rendered `<channel>` tag anyway. The read-and-forward path was working and only the heartbeat was dead, which is exactly the state nothing else can resolve — so the probe was declining in the one case that most needed it. `_health_objection` now takes `allow_stale`, passed on the baseline read and nowhere else: the re-read after the emit waives nothing, a positive still requires the file to come back both fresh and advanced, and a stamp that never comes back is still `CANNOT DETERMINE`. Reports that started from cold counters say so on their own line, because "the path works and the heartbeat is dead" is not "everything is fine".

- **The probe leaves no footprint that could later be read back as evidence** ([#1593](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1593)). Its `source` is the reserved `channel-probe`, so no watcher is impersonated in a session that routes on `watcher_source`, and the reservation is checked against the contents of `presets/watch/sources/` rather than promised in a comment. It goes through `emit_socket` and not `emit_event`, so no watcher state file is written or overwritten — one with a reserved source would show up on `watches` and in `radar`'s delivery survey as a watcher that does not exist, which is the op's own footprint read back as a fact about the fleet.

- **The guard rules `replaces` cannot express now ship to every repo, and the four that do not are named** ([#1698](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1698)). `.claude/jit-context/tools/00-manual/` holds five hand-written rules, each there because no `replaces` entry can reach what it forbids. `claude-jit-context`'s hooks read them out of `$CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR`, so they guarded sessions run inside this checkout and no other repository — measured in `Digital-Process-Tools/claude-oss`, whose whole workflow is ops, `./supertool 'git-push' 2>&1 | tail -6` ran unblocked and the cut removed the `Repo:` and `Upstream:` lines, the two that say which repository was written to. `hooks/shipped_rules.py` is read by the PreToolUse hook `hooks/hooks.json` already registers, so it reaches every plugin user; it reads the same markdown and the same `00-index.tsv` out of `$CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT` rather than copying them, translating the index's awk pattern into Python `re` and declining a POSIX class it does not know instead of approximating it into a different pattern.
