- **One of the five travels, and the other four are a recorded absence with the reason** ([#1698](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1698)). `supertool-no-cut` is a claim about supertool's own output format, so it is true wherever supertool is installed. `merged-is-not-ancestry` encodes a squash-merge workflow and would be a wrong block in a repo that merges with a merge commit; `git-C-has-cwd` names ops that exist only where the `git` preset is loaded; `harness-tools-blocked` fires on `Edit|Write|Read|Grep|Glob`, which no shipped matcher covers and which `plugin.json` already calls the operator's setting; `op-defaults-that-narrow` wants `once,remind`, and once-per-session needs state a PreToolUse hook does not carry. A wrong block in someone else's repository has no escape short of `raw_command_guard: false`, so the bar for travelling is that the rule is about supertool rather than about this repository. `tests/test_shipped_guard_rules_1698.py` partitions every `.md` into the two lists and goes red when a sixth belongs to neither.

- **A repo that does not get a rule is told which and why, rather than left silent** ([#1698](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1698)). `hooks/guard-selftest.py` prints every shipped rule with its state — enforcing, stood down because the project owns its own copy, or skipped with the reason — and then every rule that stays local with its reason. That is the property `.claude/settings.json`'s own registration already keeps when its script is absent (`the command was allowed - this is a statement about the guard, not about the command`): a guard that is quietly not there is worse than one that is loudly missing. Two ordering rules keep the layer honest: a shipped rule is consulted only where the registry returned no block, because a regex cannot express `unless_flag`; and a project carrying its own copy of a rule file owns that rule, per rule, so no supertool worktree refuses one command twice with two different messages ([#1376](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1376)'s option 3). And the layer has three states rather than two: a rule that is indexed, named as shipped and impossible to honour — an untranslatable pattern, a missing body, an index that is not UTF-8 and so raises `UnicodeDecodeError` past a narrower `except OSError` — is a note on every matching call, because returning the same `None` a command nothing claimed gets is a rule that looks shipped and is not. `raw_command_guard: false` turns the layer off with the rest of the guard, so one over-broad regex stays fixable from inside the repository rather than becoming a block with no hatch at all.

- **`gh-pr-edit:NUMBER:@FILE` — correct a published pull request body, from the payload that wrote it** ([#1739](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1739)). `gh-pr-create` writes a body once and nothing updated one, which is the wrong gap for a loop that asks authors to correct their own record. The raw fallback is not one either: `gh pr edit` fetches the pull request through GraphQL before writing and the field set includes `projectCards`, which GitHub has sunset, so on a repository with Projects classic it fails outright — re-derived 2026-08-15, exit 1, nothing written. This goes through REST `PATCH`. It is a separate op rather than `gh-pr-create` taking a number because a number that went missing from the payload would then not fail: it would open a second pull request. Two things the raw `gh api -X PATCH` route cannot do. The **closing-reference gate runs again at update time**, on the difference between the published body and the new one, with the same `_checks.closing_issue_refs` reader `gh-pr` uses — a reference the new body drops, and a published body that could not be read at all, both **refuse and write nothing**, because a check that could not look is not a check that found nothing; `unlink` is the single token that permits a deliberate re-scope. And the **receipt is a byte comparison**: the PATCH response carries the stored body, so `EXACT`, line endings `NORMALISED` by the server, `MISMATCH` naming both lengths and the first differing line, or `UNKNOWN` are answered in the same call, and only the first two exit 0. The raw route printed one timestamp, which says a write happened and not which bytes are on the server. `gh pr edit --body` / `--body-file` / `--title` now name it through `replaces`.

### Fixed

- **`CLAUDE.md` no longer claims the raw-command guard cannot see `git -C <path> <sub>`** ([#1421](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1421)). The line dated from when `argv` matching was a contiguous token prefix; measured on 2026-08-15, `supertool 'guard:git -C /tmp/x commit -m y'` answers `BLOCKED` and names `git-commit`. A stale line about a *missing* capability is the shape this repository's own notes warn about hardest, because it suppresses the one call that would disprove it.

- **`gl-mr:N:status` now sums the pipeline's legs, and the terms add back to the job count** ([#1607](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1607)). `pipeline: failed` was one word where `gh-pr:N:status` sums legs, so [#445](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/445)/[#454](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/454)'s arithmetic was simply absent on the GitLab side of the merge gate. The expensive shape is not the failed pipeline but the green one: GitLab reports `success` for a pipeline whose jobs include `skipped`, `manual` and allow-failure `canceled` legs, so a run where four legs never executed rendered byte-identically to one where every leg passed. The render now carries `legs: 12 total: 8 passed, 0 failed, 0 pending, 2 skipped, 1 manual, 1 canceled ⚠ NOT ALL GREEN` under the pipeline line.

- **The judgement is the one in `presets/_checks.py`, not a second GitLab-only copy** ([#1607](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1607)). [#958](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/958)'s rule is that the render may legitimately differ per platform and the classification may not, and reusing `summarize()` is safe here precisely because that module does not enumerate states: GitLab's one-L `canceled` is in none of its four sets, so it lands in the leftover term and is **named there** rather than mapped onto GitHub's two-L `CANCELLED`. Nothing about the two vocabularies is guessed, and a status GitLab adds after this was written takes its own term for the same reason. `tests/test_gl_mr_status_leg_tally_1607.py` asserts the rendered tally is `summarize()`'s output verbatim, so a second classifier cannot be introduced quietly.

- **An element the jobs array carried and the render could not parse is counted as a leg, not dropped from the total** ([#1607](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1607)). [#1517](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1517) added the `! 2 of 3 pipeline jobs had a shape supertool could not read` note; this adds the arithmetic it belongs to. Unreadable elements normalise to `UNKNOWN` and take their own term, so the note and the count now agree instead of the note saying three while the tally said one. A page that came back exactly `per_page` long still carries the `PAGE FULL` hedge, because the tally off it is a floor.

- **Counting legs costs one `glab api` jobs request per `:status` call, on green pipelines too — stated, not smuggled** ([#1607](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1607)). The fetch was gated on the pipeline already being not-green, which is right for *naming* jobs and wrong for *counting* them: gating on redness cannot see the case the tally exists for. [#815](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/815) forbids buying a per-call round trip **silently** rather than forbidding the purchase, so the cost is in the op's own `description`, the README bullet and `docs/presets/gitlab.md`. The GitHub mirror of a leg tally is not the rollup — that is free and already in the payload — it is `_declared_for_commit`, which fires 1+N requests on every `gh-pr:N:status` including the green ones, on [#804](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/804)'s argument that a request is cheaper than a merge on four green CodeQL legs.

- **A jobs request that could not be completed says so, and never counts to zero** ([#1607](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1607)). `legs: UNKNOWN — <reason>` rather than a zeroed tally, because `0 failed, 0 pending` reads as "everything is accounted for and nothing is outstanding" and over a read nobody completed that is the one reading that is definitely wrong — this repo's most-filed defect class, arriving with arithmetic on top. A pipeline that genuinely carries no jobs answers in GitLab's own vocabulary instead of borrowing `_checks.NO_CHECKS`, whose words are about check runs on a commit.

- **The `:status` parity allowlist lost its stale sentence** ([#1607](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1607)). `_SYNONYMS["ci"]` in `tests/test_gh_gl_status_parity_628.py` said the GitHub side carried a summed leg tally and the GitLab side did not, and that the gap was tracked elsewhere. It is closed, so the reason now records what still differs — where each side prints its tally — rather than a divergence that no longer exists. The three other items #1607 files (approvals on `:status`, `gl-issue`'s `closed_by` endpoint, a `gl-issues` listing op) are untouched and the issue stays open for them.

- **`git-resolve` can now resolve a conflicted file whose name is not ASCII, and the conflicted-path read no longer depends on a git preference** ([#1708](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1708)). `_list_conflicts` read `git diff --name-only --diff-filter=U`, and five `git-resolve` receipt rows were written down as resting on `core.quotePath` octal-quoting every byte above 0x7F out of it. That is a config default rather than a git guarantee, and the issue asked for `-c core.quotePath=true` to make it true by construction.

  Driving the code path first showed the setting has no correct value, measured on git 2.46.2 against a real conflicted merge. At `true` — the default, and what the pin would have frozen — git hands back the octal-escaped *spelling* of an accented name, which is not a filename: `git-resolve` fed it straight back as a pathspec and printed `did not match any file(s) known to git`, so **no conflicted path holding a byte above 0x7F could be resolved at all**. At `false` the name is usable, but one file named with a `U+2028` came back as **two** records, neither of them a file. Pinning either value picks which failure every operator gets.

  The read is `-z` now, which is the answer `git-commit` already reached for the same defect at `diff --cached --name-only -z` ([#1003](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1003)). Paths arrive as their real bytes and the records are NUL-separated — the one byte a pathname cannot hold on any platform — so the split cannot be forged by a filename rather than merely being unlikely to be. What that costs moved to the render: a real path can carry `LF`, `CR` or `U+2028`, so every path printed by `git-resolve`, `git-conflicts` and `git-merge` goes through `_untrusted.flat`, which discloses a separator instead of dropping the tail. The paths handed to `open()` and `git add --` stay unflattened, because the filesystem wants the name.

- **Five tests that asserted a bare digit substring was absent from a whole receipt now assert on the field the receipt attributes to the thing under test, each paired with a must-fire control** ([#1736](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1736)). The census #1691 asked for found sixteen sites; five were fixed in #1731 and six were already defended. These are the six that remained. `"30" not in head` over a grep receipt that prints a results count, a scanned-files count, a `limit`, a `context` and a cap figure became `f"{seen}+ matches total"` and `f"count capped at {seen}"`, both built from the same renderer the assertion is about, so a renamed field reddens rather than making the guard vacuous. `"774" not in out` became `"#774"`, the spelling the listing actually uses for a linked PR. `"33698" not in out` became a row whose SOURCE and ID cells are the slot — the board renders those two as separate fixed-width columns, so the id never appears beside its source and five bare digits matched a PID, a timestamp or a path just as readily.

- **One of the six was not merely loose, it was the one spelling that could not arrive** ([#1736](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1736)). `tests/test_forged_child_stream_line_1475.py` guarded the commit relay's kept tab with `"0009" not in body`. A tab is in C0 and therefore has a Control Picture, so `_untrusted.visible` spells it `[U+0009]` only on a stream that will not name an encoding; under pytest `sys.stdout` names utf-8 and a re-flattened tab spells `␉`. Measured against a deliberately re-flattening `_git_common.relayed_lines`: the receipt read `> PASS␉tests/test_a.py`, and `"0009" not in body` was `True` — green on exactly the regression it was written for. Both spellings are now named, in that file and in `tests/test_git_push_relays_hook_output_1448.py`, whose harness redirects into a `StringIO` and therefore hits the other one.

- **Each rewritten absence is now paired with a must-fire case in the same fixture** ([#1736](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1736)). A must-not-appear is satisfied just as well by a render that printed nothing, and two of these were: with `cmd_list` reduced to printing no rows the pre-change watch-board test passed, and with the linked-PR renderer dropping every node the pre-change `#774` test passed. Both are red now. The eleven-digit `"30993457393" not in out` in `tests/test_gh_pr_names_check_run_id_827.py` is left as written: it already carries its positive control on the line above (`"job #92264786336" in out`), and at eleven digits in a receipt that never prints the details URL there is no path by which it passes for a second reason.

- **The MCP validators now read the auto-spawn flag the core stamps for them, instead of spending their whole spawn budget disobeying it** ([#1743](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1743)). `SUPERTOOL_MCP_AUTOSPAWN=0` has been stamped into every validator adapter's environment since [#475](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/475), and the only reader was the core's own MCP client — a different process, reached only when an adapter shells `supertool diag:`. The four MCP adapters go through `presets/mcp/_spawn.ensure_daemon`, which looked at the socket, the pidfile and the config fingerprint and never at the flag. Measured on a machine with `mcp-rector-warm` installed and no warm daemon: `rector-mcp` with the flag explicitly `0` spent 30194 ms raising a daemon it had been told not to create, then published the spawn timeout as an adapter error about the edited file. `ensure_daemon` now declines before the spawn lock, so the same call returns in milliseconds.

- **A suppressed spawn says so on the receipt** ([#1743](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1743)). A knob that works silently is indistinguishable from one still being ignored, which is how this survived two years. The adapter publishes the third state — `skipped`, verdict keys omitted — whose reason names `SUPERTOOL_MCP_AUTOSPAWN`, its value, and the two ways out: warm the daemon from a caller that can wait, or set `mcp_autospawn` on the validator. It routes through `refusal.absent()`, so a validator named in `$SUPERTOOL_REQUIRE_VALIDATORS` gets the loud arm instead: a gate that did not run is not a gate that passed. Suppression still removes *creation* and never *use* — an already-warm daemon is connected to exactly as before, which is the clause that keeps the fix from degrading into "MCP validators are inert".

- **What the old test asserted, and what joins it** ([#1743](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1743)). `tests/test_mcp_autospawn_provenance_475.py` pinned that the flag is *present* in the child environment — a shape check over the setter, which passes whether the flag is obeyed or ignored, a guard that checks the message was sent and never that it was received. `tests/test_mcp_autospawn_honoured_1743.py` drives the four adapters and the shared spawn path with the flag at `0` and asserts nothing was launched, in under a second of a 30s budget. Every one of those is an assertion that nothing happened, so each is paired with a must-fire control in the same fixture: unset the flag and the same call still launches `daemon.py --detach`. `presets/mcp/_spawn` and the core are pinned to the same falsey vocabulary, because two readers of one variable that disagree about `off` is this bug again at one spelling per release.
- **A suppressed run on a machine with nothing installed still says "install it"** ([#1743](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1743)). `_spawn` declines before its own `preflight`, which is where the analyser binary is resolved, so the first cut of this fix silently replaced [#531](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/531)'s `skipped (mcp-phpstan-warm not found on $PATH — install via: …)` with advice to warm a daemon that cannot boot — on exactly the machine `docs/validators.md` calls the normal case, a `cwd:` into a git worktree where `composer install` never ran. Each adapter now resolves its own binary in the handler, in the same order and for the same reason as the existing no-transport arm: both outcomes are skips, and "install it" is the more actionable of the two. Two costs of the placement are recorded rather than fixed, in `presets/mcp/_spawn.py` and `docs/mcp-warm-process-servers.md`: a suppressed caller no longer blocks on the 60s spawn lock for a daemon another caller is mid-way through starting, and no longer reaps a daemon whose config fingerprint has gone stale — which now squats until its `idle_timeout`, an interactive call or `mcp_stop`. Neither can produce a wrong answer, because `usable()` demands a fingerprint match; whether a caller forbidden to create may still destroy is left open.

- **The tracked `.claude/settings.json` is guarded by an allowlist of top-level keys, so a harness write cannot ride into a commit** ([#1747](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1747)). On 2026-08-15 six lines nobody typed appeared in that file during a session in which `/reload-plugins` was run — an `enabledPlugins` block naming one machine's plugin roster, the same block deleted a day earlier as local state and the same class #1726 closed for four `$HOME`-rooted hook registrations. Both of those fixed the file's *content*; neither stopped it being re-added, because the writer is not a person. `supertool 'grep:enabledPlugins:tests/:8:1'` returned 0 results across 794 files, so a commit carrying the block went green.

  `tests/test_settings_no_machine_state_1747.py` names the keys this repository intends to ship — today `{"hooks"}` — and fails CI on any other. The direction is the decision, not a detail: a denylist of keys the harness is known to write is green the first time it invents one, which is failing open silently, this repository's own defect class. **The cost of the allowlist is that somebody adding a legitimate setting is interrupted by a red leg**, and that is the intended trade: the failure asks whether a human typed the key or the harness wrote it, so widening the set is a line in a pull request rather than a shrug. It reads the top-level surface only — machine state nested inside an allowed key is not caught, and the docstring says so rather than leaving the gap to be inferred.

  `.gitignore` now names `.claude/settings.local.json`, where the per-machine copy belongs. It had been ignored on the maintainer's disk only through `~/.config/git/ignore`, a file no other clone has, so everywhere else it sat untracked and one `git add -A` from committing the same roster under a different filename.

  Untracking `.claude/settings.json` was considered and declined: it is what carries the `pre-bash-guard.sh` registration to every clone, which is exactly what #1698 argues must not wait on a plugin release. Untracking trades a drift `git status` renders for an absence that renders as nothing.

- **The core's own 36 `str.isdigit()` sites, which #1727's sweep never reached — two classes of character, and the quiet one was writing to files** ([#1748](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1748)). [#1727](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1727) replaced the test at 11 sites under `presets/`; `_supertool.py` was outside that lane and held 36 more, every one of them reachable from a plain op string.

  The loud half is the one the issue names. `str.isdigit()` is True for `²` (U+00B2) where `str.isdecimal()` is False, so `int()` raises — `around:PAT:F:²`, `around:PAT:²`, `grep:PAT:F:²`, `between:F:²:3`, `vim:F:²j` and `vim:F:>²j` all came back as `ERROR: argument parsing: invalid literal for int() with base 10: '²'`. That is a refusal, but only by accident of a catch-all two thousand lines away, and it names an interpreter builtin instead of the argument slot.

  The quiet half is worse and was not filed. `٢` (U+0662 ARABIC-INDIC DIGIT TWO) is `isdecimal()` too, so `int()` converted it and every one of those ops ran — `around:PAT:F:٢` rendered a 2-line window, `grep:PAT:F:٢` capped at 2 results, and `vim:F:٢jx` **edited the file** and printed `1. 2j` back in its receipt, a number the caller can neither match to what they typed nor find in their own command. A crash test cannot see that class: the two runs were byte-identical.

  All 36 now go through `_is_ascii_int`, an anchored `^[0-9]+\Z` beside `VERSION` in the core, and a non-ASCII digit is refused exactly like any other non-number — `around:PAT:F:²` and `around:PAT:F:x` produce the same message. The count is what makes this a sweep rather than a gesture, and the 36 partition exhaustively — 36 lines, 37 occurrences, one line carrying two. **10 lines / 8 sites** are the unguarded `isdigit()`-then-`int()` shape the issue names, and 8 is the issue's own figure re-derived: the `between` hint spends two lines on one guard and the vim count parser two more. **18** are index scans that walk a count character by character; they reach no `int()` themselves, but they feed the parsers that do, and one of them is not a parser at all — `<C-a>` scanned the *file's* text, so incrementing a line whose only digit was `٢` overwrote it with `3`. **5** reached `int()` inside a `try`, which closes the raise and not the conversion: they refused `²` with a message about the wrong thing and honoured `٢` in silence. **3** were routing or message-shaping tests that would have disagreed with the parsers once the parsers changed.

  `tests/test_core_ascii_digit_guards_1748.py` guards the file the way `tests/test_ascii_digit_guards_1727.py` guards its eleven — a scan for `.isdigit(`/`.isnumeric(` on code lines, with a positive control for the scanner itself and an assertion that the core actually arrived, because a negative assertion over an empty read passes. The behavioural cases are triples, not pairs: the `²` call must not reach `int()`, the `٢` call must not produce the same output as the `2` call, and the `2` call must work. The first draft compared full stdout and the `--- OP ---` header echoes the op string, so the middle assertion passed against unfixed code — caught by running it red first, which is the only thing that catches it.

  Two things reported rather than done. #1727's own entry above says **"31 code sites remain"** and enumerates eight directories, all of them under `presets/`; it reads as a claim about the whole repository and is what sent a reader past the core. It was folded into this file at v0.45.0, so the published record is left alone — the population it describes is `presets/` only, and this entry is the correction. And `presets/_digits.py` is deliberately not imported here: presets run as standalone subprocesses with only `presets/` on their path, so one shared module would mean either the core importing out of the tree it dispatches into, or every preset paying the core compile cost [#931](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/931) exists to avoid. Two four-line predicates and a recurrence test over each file was the cheaper duplication.

## [0.45.0] - 2026-08-15

### Removed

- **Four `claude-jit-context` hook registrations removed from the tracked `.claude/settings.json`** ([#1726](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1726)). They resolved through `$HOME/Documents/claude-jit-context/scripts/`, a clone on one maintainer's disk, behind `[ -f "$S" ] && bash "$S" || true` — so in every other clone all four ran and did nothing, which is indistinguishable from four rules that matched nothing. The `claude-jit-context` plugin registers the same four itself through `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}`, so on the one machine where both paths existed they fired twice; repointing at `$CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR` was not available, because those scripts are in no checkout of this repository. `.claude/jit-context/` rules are unaffected — the plugin reads them. What stays hand-wired is the raw-command guard, whose script does ship here. `tests/test_settings_hooks_portable_1726.py` refuses a tracked hook command naming `$HOME`, and one that guards on a script's existence without announcing the absent branch.

- **`bin/supertool-workspace` is gone; the `oss` plugin's `bin/oss-workspace` replaces it** ([#1729](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1729)). Every behaviour the local launcher had is in the plugin's — the clone resolved from the script's own location, `SUPERTOOL_WATCH_NAME` derived from the CWD's `.supertool.json` op blocks with a refusal when they disagree, an already-exported name winning and both values named, the consumer registered at local scope with an absolute path, and the development-channel flag passed only when that registration held. Two things it did not have are there: `CDPATH` is cleared before any `cd`, and a `.supertool.json` declaring no radar tiers is reported rather than launching a board that is armed and delivers nothing. Keeping a 197-line subset here meant every fix landed twice or once, and the copy that was not this repo's problem was the one that shipped to everybody. `tests/test_workspace_launcher_1541.py` and `tests/test_workspace_channel_name_1538.py` go with it — they test a launcher this repository no longer owns, and belong against `bin/oss-workspace` in `claude-oss`.

- **The maintainer loop's own definitions are gone from this repo; the `oss` plugin owns them** ([#1729](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1729)). `.claude/skills/opensource-manager/SKILL.md`, `.claude/agents/opensource-developer.md` and `.claude/agents/opensource-triager.md` are deleted in favour of `/oss:manager`, `oss:developer` and `oss:triager`, which ship to every plugin user instead of living in one checkout. A second copy of a brief is a copy that goes stale, and this one had already drifted: the deleted skill was still telling the maintainer to launch with `bin/supertool-workspace`, which the same release deletes. What the plugin's copies do not yet carry is filed upstream rather than kept here — the class table (claude-oss#83), four mechanisms from the manager skill (claude-oss#137), and twelve from the two agent briefs, read line by line (claude-oss#141). `tests/test_developer_brief_commit_form_1303.py` goes with them: it ran every `git-commit` form the local brief prescribed, and there is no local brief to read.

### Fixed

- **`git-push`'s unattributed-stall receipt no longer leaves a dangling sentence, and the test for it stops colliding with the commit sha** ([#1691](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1691)). `test_the_unattributed_recovery_stall_names_no_budget_at_all` asserted `str(push._RECOVER_TIMEOUT) not in out` — the characters `120` absent from a receipt that carries the upstream line — so it reddened whenever the fixture sha contained them, observed on `feature @ 120cb6a`. Roughly a one-in-a-few-hundred red on a suite that runs a 12-leg matrix per PR, and its failure mode reads as a real regression in the budget wording the test names. It could never have meant "no budget figure anywhere" in any case: the receipt's own header prints `Push budget: 600s (:budget — default is 300s)` on every run.

  The assertion now matches the three places `_report_recovery_timeout` actually attributes a stall to a numbered clock, which widens it rather than merely de-flaking it — any number fails it, not just whatever `_RECOVER_TIMEOUT` is this release. Its must-fire pair lives in the neighbouring test, where all three shapes have to be seen, so the empty list means "none quoted" and not "none looked for".

  Writing that pin surfaced a real defect on the arm it covers: with no figure to quote, `allowed is None` dropped the number and nothing else, printing `Retry. If this repo genuinely needs more than to rebase recovery, the budget is ...` to the caller. The unknown clock is a third state, and a third state is a phrase, not an empty string — it now reads `more than the clock it got`.

- **Every validator adapter now publishes a verdict when it crashes, and a crashed checker exits 1 instead of 0** ([#1697](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1697)). An exception escaping an adapter's `main` writes **nothing** to stdout. `validators/common/refusal.guard_main(TOOL, main)` wraps the call in every one of the 36 adapters and publishes `refusal.crashed()` — `ok: false, count: 1`, one `code: "adapter"` row naming the exception class, its message and the last three traceback lines, with a measured `duration_ms`. Measured end to end on a `.json` file holding invalid UTF-8, which makes `jsonlint`'s `open(..., encoding="utf-8")` raise `UnicodeDecodeError` before any handler it owns: `validate:` printed `skipped — jsonlint adapter produced no output` and **exited 0**, so `supertool 'edit:x.json' && git commit` committed on a checker that had died. It now prints `NOT CHECKED — adapter jsonlint adapter crashed and did NOT check this file: UnicodeDecodeError: 'utf-8' codec can't decode byte 0xff in position 7` and **exits 1**.

  **Two things the issue reported are corrected here, and the second changes the count.** It says callers `json.loads()` the empty stdout as a clean run; the core does not, and has not since [#634](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/634) — `_validator_run_one` tests `if not out` before parsing. The cost was never a false clean. It was a **discarded diagnosis** (the traceback goes to a stderr the core captures and never reads) and a **lowered alarm** (a core-produced skip escalates only for a validator named in `$SUPERTOOL_REQUIRE_VALIDATORS`, while an adapter's own `code: "adapter"` row escalates unconditionally). And the population is **35 of 36, not 31**: the four MCP adapters do have an `except Exception`, but it wraps `ensure_daemon` + `ndjson_call` only, leaving their own `print(json.dumps(format_response(...)))` outside every handler they had. A handler that exists is not a handler that covers, which is why the net goes at the call site rather than inside `main`.

  **Not `skipped()`, and the reason is mechanical rather than stylistic.** An adapter cannot set `no_verdict` — a core-only key, stripped on the way in — and `_validator_no_verdict` returns `None` the instant `skipped` is a key, so a crash spelled `skipped` would reach neither `_note_not_checked` nor `_NOT_CHECKED` and would exit **0**: quieter than the bare crash it replaced. `refusal.tool_fault()` already said it in prose — "a fault routed to `skipped` is a validator quietly reporting clean" — and `tests/test_adapter_crash_net_1697.py` now asserts both directions on one fixture rather than leaving it to prose.

  Five spellings became one. `ruby-check`'s hand-rolled module-level net published `str(exc)` alone, so a `KeyError()` or a `RecursionError` — both of which stringify to nothing — rendered a row with a blank reason; its `_STARTED` shim from [#1683](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1683) is gone, because `guard_main` measures its own elapsed. The four MCP copies of the same nine-line handler, differing only in the name each wrote into its payload, are gone too. The guard drives all 36 adapters as `__main__` in a subprocess with a failure injected into their publish path, pairs every must-not-be-silent case with a must-fire one, and requires the shared helper by name so a thirty-seventh adapter cannot arrive without a net.

  Documented in `docs/validators.md` §"Declining instead of guessing", which gains a fourth escalation row; `validators/SCHEMA.md` and `docs/contributing.md` both described a crash as something the *core* observes and are corrected. `docs/contributing.md` also carried the issue's own two wrong claims verbatim ("every caller `json.loads()` that", "surfaces as a `JSONDecodeError`") and now says why neither is true.

- **`no-changelog` can now clear the run that asked for it** ([#1722](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1722)). The changelog check prints `label the PR 'no-changelog' if it genuinely announces nothing`, and taking that branch could not clear the PR. Labelling starts a fresh run which passes, but nothing removes the run that failed before the label existed, and the merge gate is conjunctive over every run on the head sha — correctly so. Re-running did not help either: a re-run replays the event payload the run was created with, so `github.event.pull_request.labels` was the set as it stood *before* the label. The documented remedy therefore ended where it started, and the only route out was an empty commit whose message existed to explain CI mechanics (measured on #1721, twice). The check now reads `repos/{repo}/pulls/{pr}` **live**, so label-then-re-run works, and the workflow declares the `pull-requests: read` scope that needs. The read is budgeted with `timeout 30` where `timeout(1)` exists, because slow and down are different failures and only one of them returns an error to fall back on — this step made no network call at all before, so a degraded api.github.com would otherwise sit until the job's 5-minute ceiling cancelled it, red and receiptless, on every open PR at once. Labels are compared one per line rather than joined: a label name may contain a comma, and `,${LABELS},` against `*,no-changelog,*` could not tell the single label `wontfix,no-changelog` from the two labels `wontfix` and `no-changelog`. Two costs, both stated rather than hidden: the verdict is no longer reproducible from the run's own payload, and a label *removed* after the run started now reddens it — which it must, or the escape hatch outlives the decision to use it. If the live read fails, the job falls back to the run's payload, prints `note (live label read failed …)` instead of answering as though it had read something, and switches its remedy line from "re-run this check" to "push a commit" — that arm behaves exactly as this job did before, so it can turn a finding into a skip and never the reverse, and an outage cannot redden the board.

- `git-status` prints each untracked path's write time, so a file another process dropped in your tree stops rendering identically to one you made and forgot (#1724). A time, never an attribution — nothing on disk records who wrote a file. A write inside the activity window is tagged with the same 15 minutes and the same `SUPERTOOL_WORKTREE_ACTIVE_WINDOW` knob `git-worktrees` uses; an mtime that cannot be read says `mtime UNREADABLE` rather than going silent, since a row with no time under rows that have one reads as "this one is yours". The default view's `... (N more)` marker names the newest write among the rows it hid, so the cap cannot conceal the entry the field was added to surface — and it says `UNKNOWN`, or how many of the hidden mtimes it could not read, rather than letting a tail nobody could time render as a tail with nothing in it.

- **`str.isdigit()` is gone from every preset guard that reads a number, and the strict test lives in one place** ([#1727](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1727)). The issue was filed on `pr_create.py`'s PR-number read-back, where the value is parsed out of `gh`'s own stdout and the blast radius is low. The sweep it asked for is the change: `str.isdigit()` is True for two classes of character, and only the first was known here. Unicode decimals — `٢`, `۲`, `২` — convert through `int()`, so an op proceeded against a number nobody typed. **Superscripts — `²`, `³` — do not**: `str.isdecimal()` is False for them and `int()` raises, so every `isdigit()`-then-`int()` site was an uncaught `ValueError` reachable from a plain op string. `supertool 'gh-issues:per=²'`, `'gh-prs:per=²'`, `'gh-following:²'` and `'gh-starred:²'` all died with `invalid literal for int() with base 10` before anything was fetched. The worst of those is `presets/_filter_tokens.py`, whose `bad_values` is the function that exists to name a filter value the op cannot honour and which crashed on the value it was asked to refuse — shared by `gh-issues`, `gh-prs` and `gl-mrs`.

  The test now lives once, in `presets/_digits.py`, as `is_ascii_int` over an anchored `^[0-9]+\Z` — the `\Z` for [#1188](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1188)'s trailing newline. `presets/_job_argv.py` and `presets/github/run.py` had it right already and each carried a private copy plus its own paragraph of rationale; they now import it, which is the point — the loose spelling next to the strict one is what the next reader copied, nine times. Rewired with it: `gh-check` (both ids, straight off the caller's op string and interpolated into a `gh api` path), `gh-pr-merge`'s number, `gh-pr`'s number-or-branch argument, `gh-pr-create`'s read-back gate, `gh-following`, `gh-starred`, `gh-find-starable`, `gh-find-followable`, and `_filter_tokens`' positive-integer and ISO-date-prefix checks. `tests/test_ascii_digit_guards_1727.py` pairs every "must refuse" case with an ASCII control in the same fixture, and its recurrence scan carries a live positive control so it cannot pass by finding nothing.

  Not covered, and reported rather than fixed, because they are outside this change's lane: **31 code sites remain**, in `presets/devto/` (7), `presets/hashnode/` (5), `presets/git/` (8), `presets/bluesky/` (3), `presets/claude-log/` (3), `presets/gitlab/` (2), `presets/_secrets.py` (2) and `presets/watch/tiers/gl_mrs.py` (1). The count is what makes it a list rather than a gesture — `presets/watch/tiers/` was missing from an earlier draft of this sentence, which is the same "the disclosure is not the population" shape the fix is about. The 32nd hit, `presets/watch/tiers/_snapshot.py`, is `isdecimal()` with its own documented rationale and is deliberately not on the list.

- **#654's sweep boundary was a regex over single lines, so two files sat inside it unswept — and both crashed on the value it exists to catch** ([#1727](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1727)). `tests/test_env_knob_parsing_654.py` declares `BARE_PARSE_ALLOWLIST` empty and says the empty set is "a claim this test keeps honest rather than a formality". It was not: the scan ran `(?:int|float)\(\s*os\.(?:environ\.get|getenv)\(` against one line at a time, and a Python call expression is not a line. `presets/github/find_starable.py` and `presets/github/find_followable.py` each spelled it

  ```
  n = int(parts[1]) if ... else int(
      os.environ.get("SUPERTOOL_DEFAULT_LIMIT", "30"))
  ```

  with the `int(` and the `os.environ.get(` on different lines, so the pattern could never match and the empty allowlist read as "the sweep reached every site" for two files it had never looked at. `SUPERTOOL_DEFAULT_LIMIT=abc python3 presets/github/find_starable.py python` ended in `ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'abc'` — [#654](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/654)'s own reproduction, inside #654's own boundary. Both now read the knob through `_env.env_int`, so the same command prints `note: SUPERTOOL_DEFAULT_LIMIT='abc' is not a whole number - ignoring it and using 30.` and carries on.

  **The scan is parsed now, not grepped** — `bare_parse_lines`, walking the AST, the same move `non_ascii_print_literals` in `tests/test_encoding_seam.py` already made for the same reason. It raises `SyntaxError` on source it cannot read and `_scan_bare_parses` turns that into a named refusal, so a file the scan cannot parse is never counted as a file with nothing in it. `test_the_bare_parse_scan_sees_a_call_wrapped_across_lines` is the positive control the guard should have carried from the start: it pins the wrapped case, the one-line case, and a decoy that must stay unflagged.

  Measured while fixing it, because it cuts both ways: the old regex also matched `int(os.environ.get(` inside a **comment** describing the defect, so prose about the bug would have reddened the build the bug did not. The AST scan reports neither.

  Found only because an unrelated change in this same PR reflowed those two expressions onto one line and the register went red. A guard that cannot see the thing it forbids, in a file whose docstring says it keeps the claim honest, is this repository's standing defect class pointed at one of its own checks.

- An adapter can now state how its `count` relates to its `errors`, and the core refuses to measure a payload that contradicts its own statement (#1728). `_validator_measured_count` is `max(count - absences, len(rows) - absences, 0)`, and the two terms serve two different adapters: the floor stops one whose `count` already excludes its `adapter` stall rows being subtracted from twice, and subtracting from `count` rather than recomputing from `errors` stops a capped list reading fifty findings as five. Neither survives a payload whose `count` is bounded by the same cap that bounds `errors` — `count=4` over four findings and a stall row on both sides of an edit that added a fifth finding measures 4 to 4, so `_validator_regressed` returns false and a `rollback_on_fail` validator does not revert over a genuinely new finding. Nothing ships that shape (`cargo-check` and `phpstan` were both checked and neither caps), and no arithmetic can close it, because a cap is invisible in a single payload unless the adapter says so: every candidate change trades this blind spot for the one `test_a_capped_error_list_is_not_read_as_a_smaller_count` already pins. So the fix is a contract. `count_basis` (`total` or `measured`) and `errors_truncated` are declared together or not at all; an adapter may pre-subtract its stall rows **or** cap its list and not both; `count` may never be truncated by the same cap as `errors`, nor fall below the rows printed under it. A payload breaking any of those is published as an `adapter`-coded fault naming the numbers — `NOT CHECKED`, kept out of the delta, never a rollback, still exiting non-zero — instead of a comparison nobody can read, and never as `skipped`, which would be quieter than the defect it reports. Declaring stays optional at runtime, since a repo's own validator named in `.supertool.json` is part of this population and a mandate would break every third-party adapter on upgrade; it is mandatory for a shipped adapter, held by a set of the 34 that do not yet declare which may only shrink. `cargo-check` (`total`) and `phpstan` (`measured`) declare, because they are the two the core cites as the divergent conventions and so the two the next adapter is copied from — an accident that holds is not a guarantee. Two limits are in the docs rather than implied: declaring changes no number for a conforming payload, so no shipped adapter's counts move, and an adapter that caps while declaring `measured` is indistinguishable from a well-formed `measured` payload within one payload, which is why this is a statement an author makes and not a property the core infers.

- **`claude-log-cost`'s selection tests pin the number the report attributes, not a digit substring of the whole report** ([#1731](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1731)). `test_single_uuid_argument_measures_only_that_session` asserted `"500" not in r.stdout` to mean "session `bbbb`'s 500-byte result was not counted". What it actually said is that three characters appear nowhere in a report that prints byte totals, percentiles, shares and a filesystem path — so it failed under the full suite and passed in isolation on the same commit, order the only difference (`13457 + 1 = 13458`, identical selection). The assertion could not tell its finding from a coincidence, which made a pass no evidence the selection worked and a failure no evidence it did not.

  A `measured()` helper now reads `(sessions, results, bytes)` off the report's own `Measured:` line and raises when that line is absent, so a report that printed nothing reddens instead of satisfying a negative assertion for free. `== (1, 1, 10)` carries both halves at once: the selected session was measured, and the other one's 500 bytes are not in the total. A new sibling test measures the whole project and requires `(2, 2, 510)` from the same fixture — without it the first test would still pass against a `cost.py` that had simply stopped seeing `bbbb`, which is a selection test whose evidence is indistinguishable from a broken reader. Two adjacent assertions of the same shape went with them: `"500" in r.stdout` in the limit test, and `"2000" not in r.stdout` / `"15" in r.stdout` in the non-text disclosure test, where `15` occurs in almost any report.

- **The watch board says which project the channel name belongs to, so a shared fleet stops rendering as a private one** ([#1732](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1732)). `SUPERTOOL_WATCH_NAME` derives one socket and one poller-slot directory, so two projects exporting the same name are one fleet: events from one project's pollers arrive on the other's channel, and each board reports a population that is not its own. `watches`, `radar` and `channel:health` rendered that identically to a correct single-project fleet — the name, the two paths, and no field naming an owner. Reported after four repositories ended up sharing one hand-copied `"SUPERTOOL_WATCH_NAME": "oss-supertool"` in one machine's `.claude/settings.local.json`.

  `naming.declared_names()` reads the `.supertool.json` at or above the cwd and answers in four states, so a look that did not happen can never render as an absence in the world: `found` (an op block declares a `watch_name`), `silent` (a config is there and declares none, so what is in force arrived from an environment this project never asked for), `no-config` (nothing above the cwd claims anything) and `unreadable` — a config that could not be parsed, or a directory in the upward walk this uid cannot traverse, stated as *unknown, not unclaimed*. That last half came out of review: `os.path.isfile` is an `os.stat` inside `except OSError: return False`, so the first version of the walk answered "no config here" for a directory it could not enter and reported an absence in the world off a look that failed. Every render then names the owner: `name X is declared by <path> (ops: …)` for the ordinary case, and the loud form when the name in force is not one this project declares, or when the project's own op blocks disagree. Nothing is printed on the default channel: those paths are shared by construction and have no owner to dispute.

  It also names the watch ops that declare nothing. A `watch_name` in an op block reaches only *that* op's subprocess, and `watch` and `unwatch` are the two that spawn and kill pollers — so declaring the name on `watches` alone reads a private board over a default-channel fleet, which is [#1309](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1309)'s half-configured state arriving through the config door instead of the environment one. This repository declared exactly that shape and now declares all five.

  Precedence is unchanged and deliberately so. An exported `SUPERTOOL_WATCH_NAME` is still authoritative, because it is the value a running poller already captured and a file that outranked it would move the socket and the slot directory underneath a live fleet ([#1477](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1477)). Nothing here changes what is in force; what changes is that a reader can tell whose it is.

### Security

- **`$VAR` in an op ARGUMENT is no longer expanded — a variable's value could be written into a commit because its name appeared in the message** ([#1734](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1734)). `_expand_env` exists so a project's own `cmd` template can carry `$MY_TOOL_HOME` and have it resolved without a shell. It ran over the **assembled** command instead — after `{file}`, `{dir}`, `{arg}`, `{args}` and `{argjoin}` had been interpolated — so it could not tell the template's text from the caller's data and rewrote both. `git-commit:::chore: about $HOME:::f.txt` committed the maintainer's home directory; with the op string single-quoted, so no shell was involved. A secret-shaped variable behaved identically: naming `$FAKE_TOKEN` in a subject put `ghp_…` in the commit object, and a commit gets pushed.

  It survived because it is invisible unless the variable happens to be defined: an undefined name round-trips byte-exact (`_expand_env` leaves unknowns literal, unlike a shell), so the same message is verbatim on one machine and rewritten on another. `help:git-commit` documented no transformation of the message, and the receipt rendered the substituted subject only after the commit existed.

  Placeholder values are now substituted as inert per-call tokens and restored *after* expansion, at all five dispatch sites — preset and custom ops, validators, formatters, and both `resolve` templates. The template keeps its documented `$VAR` feature, including the `KEY=VAL` env-prefix form and `KEY={dir}` prefixes whose value is itself a placeholder; the caller's bytes reach the op untouched. Restoring rather than reordering the two passes is deliberate: expanding the template *before* substitution would have made an environment variable whose value reads `{args}` into a second interpolation site, which is the same defect pointed the other way.

  Two properties of the restore are contract rather than detail, both found by review after the first attempt got them wrong. The token is bracketed by a dot, so it terminates a variable name: with a bare-alphanumeric token, `cmd $PREFIX{file}` read the token as a continuation of `PREFIX`, found no such variable and left `$PREFIX` literal — silently, since leaving an unknown literal is the documented behaviour. And an env value lifted out of a `KEY={dir}` prefix is restored *unquoted*, because `_extract_env_prefix` tokenises through `shlex.split` and always handed the child `MYDIR=my dir`; restoring the `shlex.quote`d form gave it `MYDIR='my dir'`, apostrophes included, for every value that actually needs quoting.

  Four of the five sites take no `{args}` at all — their caller data is the `{file}` path, and a path segment reading `$HOME` or `$USER` was expanded there too. That one was worse than a mis-named file: `{file}` is `shlex.quote`d before expansion, so a value containing a space or a quote shattered the quoting and handed `shlex.split` extra argv tokens, running a validator or formatter against paths nobody named.

  Measured while fixing it, and reported rather than left implicit: **82 shipped ops interpolate caller arguments into their template**, including the publishing ops where a local disclosure becomes a remote one — `bluesky_publish`, `devto_comment`, `hashnode_comment`, `hashnode_reply` all take prose inline, and `devto_publish` / `hashnode_publish` take an argv `TITLE`. `gh-issue-create`, `gh-pr-create` and `gl-issue-create` are **not** in that set for their bodies: argv carries only the payload path and the script reads the body off disk itself — though the path is argv, so a payload filename containing `$NAME` was affected like any other. **No shipped template relies on argument expansion**: a walk of every `cmd` and `resolve` string in the tree found exactly one `$`, and it is a `$(basename …)` in an example, which argv-form never executes and this expander never matched. So the behaviour is removed outright rather than made opt-in per op.

## [0.44.0] - 2026-08-14

### Added

- **`gh-run:ID:attempt=K` reads a prior attempt, and every run render now says which attempt it is** ([#1715](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1715)). `gh-branch` collapses to the highest `run_attempt` by design, and that is what makes the merge gate honest — what matters there is whether the commit is green *now*. The cost is that once a flake is re-run green, the record of why it was red lives in an attempt no op could reach: recovering the evidence that diagnosed [#1709](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1709) meant leaving supertool for `gh api repos/O/R/actions/runs/31815095925/attempts/1/jobs` just to learn the job id `gh-job` was already able to read.

  **The default is unchanged and stays the latest attempt.** Nothing about the collapse moved. What is new is that `gh-run` states it: an `Attempts: K of N` line under the URL, in three states rather than two — `1 of 1` when the run was never re-run, `N of N` naming the earlier attempts as **not** in the table with the call that reads one, and `UNKNOWN` when the payload carried no readable `run_attempt`, because a field nobody read must not settle whether a whole attempt's legs are missing. That absence was the defect: the table has only ever been one attempt's legs, and nothing said so.

  A superseded attempt is labelled `HISTORICAL` in its own header and body — a stale red that does not announce itself as stale is read as the state of the run now — and it skips the `filter=all` leg reconciliation, whose count is the union across every attempt and would manufacture a shortfall against a single one. The second `gh` call is bought only when the attempt asked for is not the latest; naming the current one costs the same single round trip it always did.

  Both values that reach the `gh` argv are gated before anything is fetched. The attempt must match a digits-only pattern and is re-rendered from `int()`, so the caller's string never reaches the subprocess; an attempt past the last one is refused by name off the count the first read already returned, rather than bought as a 404 that `gh` renders as `failed to get run` — a different, wrong answer. The run id is now digit-gated too, the guard `gh-job` has carried since [#1145](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1145), which was a courtesy about the header there and is a precondition of the fetch here.

### Changed

- Three hand-rolled copies of `gh repo view --json nameWithOwner` now share
  `_repo_target.effective_slug()`, and the two that were counted as copies turn
  out not to be
  ([#1701](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1701)).
  The issue named five sites and `cwd_slug()` (#1700) as the shared answer none
  of them used. Re-derived, both halves were different. `cwd_slug()` answers
  `""` under a `repo:` target on purpose — its caller substitutes the target
  itself — while all five callers are target-*first*, so adopting it would have
  printed the cwd's repository in a header for a call made about another one.
  And `github/branch.py` and `github/pr_merge.py` read
  `nameWithOwner,defaultBranchRef` in one call and return a third element
  carrying the error their `main()` aborts on: they already tell *could not
  ask* from *asked, got nothing*, and folding them in would have traded a
  three-state answer for a two-state one. They keep their own reader.

  `effective_slug()` is `target()` first, then the cwd's clone, then `""`. Two
  states rather than three because no caller of it consumes a reason: each
  keeps its own sentinel at its own boundary, so `gh-labels` still renders `""`
  (`— repository UNKNOWN (gh could not name it)`), the `gh_prs` radar tier
  still renders `"?"`, and `claims` still returns `None`. Nothing any of the
  three prints on failure changed.

  One site was actually wrong. `presets/claims/check.py` read
  `os.environ["SUPERTOOL_REPO"]` directly instead of through `target()`, so it
  skipped the rule that a blank export is absence rather than an empty target:
  a whitespace-only value became the slug, reached `gh issue view --repo "   "`,
  and every issue citation in the document rendered "couldn't check" against
  gh's complaint — while the cwd, which could have answered, was never asked.

  A sweep for the subcommand found seven calls across four distinct questions,
  two of which the issue never counted (`--json owner,name` in `issues.py`,
  `--json defaultBranchRef` in `pr_create.py`). The regression pin is keyed on
  the exact single-field argv rather than on `gh repo view`, because a guard
  that refused all four would be worked around rather than obeyed.

### Fixed

- A cursor-control sequence in `gh`'s stdout reached six lines of the receipt
  `gh-pr-create` writes, including its own `[result]` verdict
  ([#1660](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1660)).
  `str.splitlines()` consumes every line *separator*, so the URL line selected
  out of `gh pr create` cannot be forged — that half holds. It does not consume
  ESC. The selected line was printed raw at column 0 as `URL:`, and `number` is
  derived from it, so it also reached `PR:`, all three `## Next` commands and
  the `[result]` line, two lines under a `title` that was already flattened.
  The value is now `_untrusted.flat()`ed at the seam where it is extracted
  rather than at each print, so the escape is disclosed as `␛` instead of
  moving the cursor, and a clean URL is untouched. This is the ESC half of
  [#851](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/851)
  arriving at a site that sweep did not cover.

  The register entry in `tests/test_preset_twin_splitlines_register_1119.py`
  read "the extracted value is printed, not parsed", which answers
  forgery-by-separator and is silent on control characters — an entry that
  answers one question reads as though it answered the other. Corrected to say
  which question it answers and which it does not.

- **`git-worktrees` answered `occupied` and supertool exited `0`** ([#1705](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1705)). Declaring an op's exit code a value (#1672) spent the fail-safe as well as the verdict: `supertool 'git-worktrees:PATH' && rm -rf PATH` had held because any non-zero child collapsed to a non-zero supertool exit, and afterwards `occupied` and `cannot tell` both passed the guard. [#1282](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1282) records a consumer of exactly that shape.
- **`exitStatus` now takes a `clean` list** — `{ "values": [0, 1, 2], "clean": [0] }` — naming which of an op's answers a caller may proceed on. A declared value outside it makes supertool's own exit non-zero. `0` is always clean and listing it is documentation only; a missing or malformed `clean` collapses to `[0]`, the loud direction, because the quiet one is a caller proceeding on `occupied`.
- **It is still not a refusal, which is #1672 and it stands.** The receipt says `PASS`, the refusal count does not include it, and the batch footer does not call it one. The answer reaches the exit code through its own per-call channel, beside the skipped write and the rolled-back edit that already got there without being refusals — and the batch footer names it rather than reciting the counters, so `Exit 1 is a skipped write, a rolled-back edit or a validator that could not run` is no longer printed for a cause the call knows precisely. A single-op call prints no footer at all, so the `PASS` line carries the same disclosure.
- **The sweep this asked for:** `git-worktrees` is the only op in `presets/*.json` declaring `exitStatus`, and a test now fails if a future one declares `values` without `clean`, so the implicit `0` cannot be inherited again.

- A stalled `node --check` on **one** of a page's `<script>` blocks was read as a
  verdict about the whole file ([#1709](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1709)).
  `html-check` spawns the tool once per block, so a two-block page can spend its
  30s budget on the first block and get a real syntax finding on the second — and
  the suite's stall gate required *every* reported error to be a wall before it
  would decline. The mixture was classified as a complete verdict, and
  `count == 1` — a claim about how many blocks got an answer, not about the file
  — read `assert 2 == 1` on `pytest (windows-latest, 3.10)`.
  `tests/_adapter_verdict.stalled_at_its_own_wall` now declines a **partial**
  wall: at least one `adapter` error naming a timeout, and no `adapter` error
  that is not one. A missing `node`, a crashed adapter and a wall reported faster
  than the adapter's own budget all still redden the board, standing beside a
  wall or not, and the decline is counted under the existing `adapter-wall`
  register rather than being silent. The adapter itself is unchanged: its
  per-block finding was correct.

- **A `jit-index` run that stalled partway no longer reads as a complete one** ([#1714](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1714)). When awk could not be run — a timeout, or a spawn that failed — and the adapter already held a finding, the list of patterns it never compiled was discarded. A run that compiled 2 of 20 rows and stopped rendered as `2 err`, byte-identical to a complete run that found two things. The findings are now published beside an `adapter` row naming the rows nobody looked at. A stall with *no* finding still emits `skipped`, so a machine that hiccups cannot roll back a correct edit; the loud arm is reachable only once `ok: false` is already owed to a real finding.

- **The `changelog.d/` note now teaches the fragment rule an author cannot infer** ([#1716](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1716)). The jit-context note injected before any write to that directory never mentioned that an entry must name its own issue (#1251), and the one worked example in it named none — copied verbatim it produced a fragment the write-time validator refuses. It now opens with a complete, correct fragment, and every markdown example in it is checked against the project's own fragment rules, so an example that would be refused is a red test rather than a lesson somebody pays for.

- A validator that reported real findings *and* could not finish one of its rows reverted a correct edit. The `adapter` code is the schema's channel for "no verdict was obtained", and `validators/SCHEMA.md` promises per result that the core never subtracts it from a baseline in either direction — but the guard delivering that promise tested `all(code == "adapter")`, which is a per-payload test. A mixed payload failed it and fell through to arithmetic that counted the stall as a new finding, so on a `rollback_on_fail` validator the edit was written back to its pre-edit bytes. `cargo-check` ships exactly that shape: a crate diagnostic naming another file keeps its text and takes `code: "adapter"` beside the real findings. The guard stays as it is — an adapter that reported findings *has* measured the file, and rendering it `NOT CHECKED` would be the same defect pointing the other way — and the subtraction now drops the `adapter` rows on both sides instead (#1717).

## [0.43.0] - 2026-08-14

### Changed

- **`gh-prs`'s `syntax` was 243 characters against a p90 of 66, because a sentence had been appended to a parameter list** ([#1590](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1590)). Every consumer prints the field whole — the `ops` roster, `registry`, `help:gh-prs`, and the synonym suggestion [#1524](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1524) added — so the invocation a caller needed began around character 255 of the rendered line. Measured across every shipped preset: 86 ops declare a `syntax`, and exactly 1 carried a double-dash clause or an issue number. The #1524 reviewer refused to teach the render to split on that separator, on the grounds that a convention inferred from one field is not a convention, and was right; the defect was the field.

  **The guarantee did not have to move, because it was never on the prose.** #1405 pinned the substring `merged-since=TAG,state=merged` into `syntax` so a deleted op's replacement could not go missing — and that substring is an *invocation*, not a sentence. It stays, as the second of two ` | `-separated forms, which is the shape `gh-check`, `bluesky_list`, `devto_list` and `hashnode_list` already use for an alternate call. What left is the narration around it, which `description` already carried word for word and where #1405's own test also pins it. Both existing pinning tests pass unchanged.

  The convention is now written down in `docs/contributing.md` and enforced across the whole corpus rather than on the one field: no `syntax` carries an issue reference, none carries a double-dash clause, none exceeds 200 characters (the longest pure grammar in the tree is `gl-mrs` at 165), and every ` | `-separated form begins with its own op's name.

- **`paste` over an existing file now keeps the bytes it displaces** ([#1650](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1650)). An agent writing a working note pasted 1990 bytes over a path it believed did not exist. It did: an earlier agent had left 8922 bytes there. The receipt was honest and complete — `rewrote ... 8922 -> 1990 bytes` — and it printed one step after the only moment it could have helped. The path was gitignored, so there was no git copy, and the disposable clone used for the suite did not carry it. Unrecoverable. The outgoing bytes are now copied to `~/.cache/supertool/paste-backup/` **before** the write, and the receipt names the copy: `previous contents kept at PATH`.

  **Nothing is refused, and that is the design.** A guard that blocked the overwrite would have to offer a `force` token, `paste` over an existing file is documented and ordinary, and a `force` typed by reflex is the guard deleting itself. A copy has no case it was not written for — the write the caller asked for happens either way, and a false positive costs one cache file that `gc` reaps in seven days.

  **`paste` is guarded alone because of an asymmetry, not because it is the biggest hammer.** `edit` and `replace` match a string first; `replace_lines` refuses an `END` past the file length; `vim` errors on a path that does not exist and echoes the removed text back as a diff. `vim` can still empty a file completely with `ggdG`, so this is not a claim that nothing else destroys bytes — it is that nothing else can do it to a file the caller believes is not there, which is the mechanism that produced the incident. A test pins `vim` refusing a missing path, so a future create-if-missing arm cannot open that hole silently.

  **There is no shrink ratio and no byte-loss floor.** The issue proposed both. Both are blind to 8922 bytes replaced by 9000 different ones, which loses exactly as much and is exactly as unrecoverable, so the trigger is the op's own semantics — `paste` replaces the entire file — and there is no number to tune. The one number present is a resource bound, not a trigger: a file over 8 MB is not copied, and the receipt says so rather than staying silent, because an unbacked overwrite that reads like a backed one would land on the largest files, where the loss is worst.

  **A write a validator rolls back still leaves a copy.** The snapshot is taken before the write and validation happens after it, so a rolled-back `paste` prints `previous contents kept at PATH` above `[rolled back] … the file was NOT edited`. Both sentences are true — the file on disk is the original and PATH holds those same bytes — so the copy is redundant rather than wrong, and `gc` reaps it with the rest.

  Three states, never silence: `previous contents kept at PATH`, no line at all when nothing was displaced, and `no backup of the previous contents — WHY` when the copy failed. The store is registered in the cache reaper at seven days; a writer without a retention entry is how `~/.cache/supertool` reached 1.0 GB in the first place.

### Fixed

- **`map`'s three tiers are a per-file chain again — tier 2 was unreachable on any machine where tree-sitter merely imported** ([#913](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/913)). `use_ctags = not use_ts and _has_ctags()` decided ctags once for the whole run, so the per-file `if not symbols_found and use_ctags` fallback below it was dead code whenever the language pack was installed. The documented cascade 1 → 2 → 3 was really tree-sitter XOR ctags, then regex. `map:notes.rst` — a file no tier-1 grammar claims, which is exactly what ctags exists to cover — went straight to regex and reported `tier: none`, and someone who installed universal-ctags on that advice got nothing back and was told nothing.

  **The fallback is gated on tier 1 being blind to the file, not on it coming back empty.** A file whose extension has no tree-sitter grammar, or whose grammar failed to load, drops to ctags. A file tree-sitter read and found no definitions in does not: the answer is already known. That distinction is the whole cost of the fix and it was measured rather than argued. On this repository at 100 mapped files, 14 produce no tree-sitter symbols and every one of the 14 is the second kind — changelog fragments, an empty `__init__.py`. A ctags call costs ~41ms per file on macOS, ~33ms of it bare process spawn, so falling back on emptiness would have added ~0.6s to `map:.` to reach the same empty lists, and put a per-file subprocess on the shape that has reddened Windows legs four times ([#1296](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1296), [#1360](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1360), [#1461](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1461), [#1501](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1501)). Under the gate the added spawn count on both those runs is zero.

  **`; ctags found nothing` now means ctags ran.** The note in the `no symbol parser for .ext` line was appended from ctags being *available*, so it could report an empty result from a tier that was never asked — the absence-produced-by-the-tool shape, inside the render that exists to keep that shape visible ([#887](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/887)). It is now driven by whether the call was made on that file.

  Behaviour with no tree-sitter installed is unchanged: every file still goes 2 → 3, and that is pinned.

- **`.supertool.example.json` told readers to export an environment variable nothing reads** ([#1021](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1021)). `ops.dashboard._doc` ended "Passes through as `SUPERTOOL_DASHBOARD_LANE_PREFIX`". The preset reads `SUPERTOOL_LANE_PREFIX`, and the runner exports `SUPERTOOL_<KEY.upper()>` for each key of the entry — the key alone, never namespaced by op name. Someone who prefers an env override to a config edit exported the documented name, got no error, and watched the lanes section correctly print `!! unread — no lane vocabulary configured`: the op was right and the reader had been told the op was broken. Misreports, on the shipped artifact rather than on the code.

  **The prose was the defect, not the runner.** The op-namespaced form is not a design nobody implemented: three other entries in the same file document the flat form and are correct, every preset reads the flat name, and `test_the_config_key_reaches_the_preset_under_the_name_it_reads` pins it. Changing the runner to match one sentence would have broken all of them.

  **The mistake is copy-paste-shaped, so the pin is the rule rather than the sentence.** The sibling `ops.radar._doc` directly below is right — but only because its key is `radar_tiers`, not because the op name is prepended, so copying it onto a key called `lane_prefix` silently changes what it claims. A new test sweeps both `.supertool.json` and `.supertool.example.json`, and refuses any `SUPERTOOL_*` name in an entry's prose that is not `SUPERTOOL_<KEY.upper()>` for a non-reserved key of that same entry, naming the entry and listing the keys that would have been right. A bare `SUPERTOOL_*` is a mention of the mechanism, not a claim about a key, and does not match. The sweep found exactly the one instance filed.

- **A config found and skipped was reported as a config that was never there** ([#1162](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1162)). Git writes conflict markers into `.supertool.json` during a rebase; the file stops parsing, the loader skips it and keeps walking, and with nothing usable above, no preset ops load at all. The refusal then read `No .supertool.json was found from X or any parent` — one line under a stderr warning naming the file it had just skipped. Two lines of one render disagreeing about whether the config exists, and a reader who sees only the ERROR goes looking for a missing file that is present.

  The refusal and `ops`' preset-disclosure line now both name the file, say why it was unusable, and — when it holds conflict markers — say so and give the marker line numbers, which is the one fact `git-conflicts` would have supplied from the code that can still supply it. `|||||||` counts as a marker, for the line list rather than for detection: every merge style emits `<<<<<<<` and `>>>>>>>`, so a diff3 conflict is detected either way — what the base marker buys is that the line list is complete. A reader told to go resolve markers, handed a list with one of them missing, goes back to the file for it.

  A `.supertool.json` that is a *directory* — or a dangling symlink — is now reported the same way. `_load_config` gates on `os.path.isfile`, which is false for both, so it walked past and every render called the config absent with one sitting in the cwd: this issue's own defect one `stat` over. The loader's behaviour is deliberately unchanged; only the sentence about it is.

  Neither dead remedy is offered for the conflicted case. `cwd:<other-project>` retargets the working directory, so a git op would report *that* repo's conflicts — [#678](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/678)'s shape arriving through the remedy line — and there is no other root to move to, because the broken file is in the tree the caller is standing in.

  The issue's second option — loading the git preset from defaults when the config is unparseable — was **declined**. Running ops out of a config the user cannot see is a guess, and `docs/validators.md`'s "Declining instead of guessing" is the rule it would break. The circularity is real and stays: the message says what is true instead of inventing a way around it.

- **Three registry claims the dispatcher contradicted, and a guard so the next one reddens a test** ([#1245](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1245)). `.supertool.json`'s `builtin-ops` is what a machine reads to learn what this binary accepts, and it carried `read-grep` and `grep-count` — documentation for *forms* of `read` and `grep` (`read:PATH:::grep=PATTERN`, `grep:P:PATH:L:C:count`), neither of which dispatches. `.supertool.example.json`, the template users copy, carried a third the issue had not counted: `grep-no-exclude`. Enumerating from the two files rather than from the issue body is what found it.

  All three are kept, because each carries `"hint": true` and its example is what survives `ops-compact` into the SessionStart listing — the one place a non-obvious payload shape gets discovered. They now **declare** what they are: `"form": "grep"` names the op the entry is a spelling of. `_configured_op_names` skips a form entry, and `_build_at_file_registry` no longer derives a `@payload` route from one — `read-grep` had been sitting in `_AT_FILE_DROPPED_ROUTES`, the #770 diagnostic that says "a route was intended here and discarded", reporting about a name that is not an op. `tests/test_registry_matches_dispatcher_1245.py` holds both directions across both shipped configs: a `builtin-ops` key either dispatches or declares a `form` whose parent dispatches and whose `syntax` starts with it.

  **`status` was documented as informational and is not.** `docs/contributing.md`'s op-config schema called it `"experimental"` / `"stable"`, informational only. The code reads it as **truthy**, and a falsy value suppresses the op from `ops`, `ops-compact` and `ops:roster` while it still dispatches — an op that ships, dispatches, and cannot be found. Both documented spellings are non-empty strings, which is why a wrong claim survived. `docs/configuration.md` had it right all along, so the two pages disagreed. The row now describes the gate, and the behaviour is pinned in both directions.

  **The "~40 ops across five categories" claim was already fixed and is already guarded** — no change was needed. `docs/operations/index.md` opens with the real count, and `tests/test_ops_index_complete_1371.py` holds it there along with a phantom-name check on that page.

- **A file `paste` creates now lands at the process umask, and the receipt says which mode that is** ([#1275](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1275)). An agent wrote a new shell script into a directory where every sibling was `0755`. It arrived `0600`, and nothing in the receipt mentioned a mode, so the only thing that would have surfaced it was running the script — which is what the next person does after the merge rather than before it. A created file is now `0666 & ~umask` (`0644` under the common `umask 022`), the same as `>`, `tee`, `cp` and every editor produce, and the receipt carries `↳ mode 0644, from the process umask`. `append` creates too, through the same chokepoint, and discloses the same way.

  **`0600` was never a chosen default.** `_atomic_write` renames a `tempfile.mkstemp` temp file over the target, and mkstemp creates at `0600`; #259 re-applies an *existing* file's mode before the rename, so the tight bit only ever applied to files that were not there before.
