A property that holds for creates, not for rewrites, is undocumented and unmentioned in the receipt is not a security guarantee — it is a temp file's mode leaking through a rename. A caller who wants owner-only files sets `umask 077`, which is what the mask is for, and gets it for every op rather than for half of them.

  **Said plainly, because it is a widening:** on a default `umask 022` a created file is group- and world-*readable* where it used to be owner-only, and a payload can hold a secret. Three things bound that. The mask is the caller's own declared policy and is now honoured rather than overridden; the mode is stated in the receipt on every create, so the widening is never silent; and an overwrite is untouched, so a file that is already `0600` stays `0600` through any number of pastes.

  **`paste` does not infer the executable bit, and that is deliberate.** Not from the shebang, not from the modes of the file's neighbours, not from a flag. Each is a guess, and the neighbours-match rule is most likely to be right and most surprising when it is wrong. What it does instead is state a fact it can be certain of: content beginning `#!` that is not executable gets a second line naming `chmod +x PATH`. The mode on disk is identical either way, so a wrong reading of the content costs one line of prose rather than a permission nobody asked for.

  **Nothing is printed on Windows**, where the executable bit does not exist and `os.chmod` honours only the read-only flag — `st_mode` reads back `0o666` whatever was asked for, so a mode line would be a statement about access that is not true there. The tests gate on a probe that creates a file with an explicit `0666` and reads it back, not on a platform name, so a filesystem mounted without permission bits skips for the reason it actually has.

  **What the issue claimed and the code did not do:** git does not record a wrong mode. It stores only the executable bit, so a `0600` create and a `0644` shell redirect are byte-identical in the index — `100644` for both, which is a correct record of a file that is not executable. Verified with `git ls-files -s` over one of each. The defect was on disk and in the receipt's silence; the index was never wrong.

- **A loaded CI runner's timeout is no longer published as a verdict about your file** ([#1604](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1604)). Fifth instance of one defect after [#1296](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1296), [#1360](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1360), [#1461](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1461) and [#1501](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1501), each fixed one adapter at a time: `cargo check` blew its 120s wall on a `windows-latest` leg and the assertion read `timeout (cargo check exceeded 120s)` as a statement about `sibling.rs`, on two pull requests whose diffs went nowhere near cargo. Both cleared on a plain re-run, so the price was never the re-run — it was that every Windows red on this repo had to be read before it could be dismissed.

  **The product half is `ruby-check`, and it is why the class kept needing a new issue.** It was the only adapter that gave its tool a `timeout=` and had no `except subprocess.TimeoutExpired` arm, so the wall escaped into the module-level `except Exception`, whose payload hardcodes `duration_ms: 0`. `after 0ms` beside "timed out after 30 seconds" reads as a rendering nit; it was load-bearing. The suite tells a real wall from an adapter whose error routing is broken by whether the elapsed time reaches the budget, so a 30-second stall reporting zero was unclassifiable and got published as a finding about a Ruby file with nothing wrong with it. It now reports the time it actually spent, names the budget it blew, and `TIMEOUT_S` is hoisted so the test budget derived from it tracks automatically.

  **The decline is counted, which is the half that decides between the two repairs.** Normalising a wall away erases it; declining without counting hides it one layer up, because `N skipped` on a Windows leg could not be resolved to `N tests did not get an adapter verdict`. The [#794](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/794) decline had carried no token through all four earlier instances, so each was filed as a fresh mystery. It carries one now, and the terminal summary prints the count, its denominator and its population every run — including at zero, because a line that appears only on trouble is indistinguishable from one that was never evaluated. The population sentence states plainly that most of this suite's adapter-spawning files are still ungated, so the zero is a claim about the gated sites and not about the suite.

  **The class is now checked rather than remembered.** [#1464](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1464)'s sweep reads every adapter's timeout arm and refuses any error code but `adapter` — so an adapter with no arm at all had nothing to inspect and passed it vacuously, which is this repo's own defect class sitting inside the guard written against it. A second sweep now asks the complementary question: every adapter that grants itself a wall must have somewhere for that wall to land.

- **The cohort burn-down asked for the open column one search at a time, and by 16 cohorts that returned nothing at all** ([#1628](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1628)). `gh-labels:tally=PREFIX` cost `2N + 2` search calls per family against an API allowing 30 a minute. On 2026-08-13 it refused at 15 labels; on 2026-08-14, past `GH_LABELS_TALLY_MAX=16`, it answered **34 of 34 cells `?`** — where the day before the same escape hatch had dropped 2 of 32. The family grows by one label per release, so there was no future state of this repository in which the query plan started working again.

  **The open column never needed a search.** `fetch_open_issue_rows` was already reading the whole open set on every tally call, for the multi-label check — the run that returned 34 `?` still printed `Multi-label: none of all 74 open issues …` from the listing it was holding and then discarded. The per-label open counts are a client-side group-by over exactly that data, so `open` is now tallied from it and only `closed`, where enumerating would render a floor as a burn-down denominator, still costs a search per label. A family is `N + 1` calls, and `GH_LABELS_TALLY_MAX` rises from 14 to 24 on that arithmetic.

  Not to 29, which `N + 1 <= 30` alone would give. The old bound sat exactly on the limit — 14 labels, 30 calls — and did not hold: a whole board lost to a two-call overrun only happens if the minute's budget was already partly spent, which on a maintainer tick it always is. Five calls of headroom is the measurement, and the env var stays for a caller who knows their minute is quiet.

  **The two columns now fail independently and say so separately.** A rate-limited search costs the `closed` column and leaves `open` intact — which is the number the tick actually turns on — so the header carries an `Open:` sentence and a `Closed:` sentence instead of one covering both. The refusal is unchanged in kind: past the bound it still declines rather than rendering a half-read board, and it quotes the cost it now actually pays. The three states carry to the new source too: an unreadable listing leaves every open cell `?` and never `0`, and a listing that hit `GH_LABELS_ISSUE_CAP` makes each open cell a floor (`>=N`) that carries into `frozen` — an enumeration has a cap where a search did not, and that is the cost of the move, stated rather than absorbed.

- **`lint-new` reported the number of files it checked as the number carrying findings; it now reports both, as `N of M`** ([#1629](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1629)). The finding arm formatted `len(files)` — the set handed to ruff — into the sentence `N file(s) this PR adds, copies or renames carry lint findings`. Measured on a 40-commit range with one dirty path, it printed `46 file(s) … carry lint findings` above a single listed line. The two counts coincide whenever every checked file is dirty, which is the single-file diff that ships most often, so the wrong one read correctly nearly every time.

  **Files scanned, files with findings, and findings total are three different questions**, and a bare count answers whichever one the reader arrived with. On PR [#1622](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/pull/1622) a `1 file(s) … carry lint findings` line was read as "one of several shown" and became a brief sending an agent to look for findings that did not exist. The headline is now `1 of 2 file(s) this PR adds, copies or renames carry lint findings`, which cannot be read as either of the other two.

  **A finding line the parser cannot attribute to a path leaves the count unstated** rather than lowering it. ruff's `concise` output has always carried `path:line:col:`, so the arm should never fire — which is why it is pinned: a gate that silently under-counts its own findings is the same defect with a smaller number on it.

- **`gh-branch`'s conjunction now covers every run on the commit, not the newest run of each workflow name** ([#1640](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1640)). GitHub's default code-scanning setup emits **two distinct Actions runs per push**, sharing one `workflow_id`, one `path` and the one name `gh` renders. `latest_per_workflow` kept the higher run id, so on `d1bb0837` — the v0.42.0 release candidate — the release gate reported `GREEN … 18 legs across 2 workflows` over a population of 21 legs across 3 runs, and the run it dropped carried `Analyze (actions)`, a scan no other run on that commit performed. Everything was green, so the verdict was true by luck; a failure in the dropped run would have rendered identically.

  **The justification in the code named the wrong mechanism.** It kept one run per workflow because "a re-run supersedes the run it replaces" — but `gh run rerun` reuses the run id and bumps `run_attempt`, which the table's own note has said since [#1409](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1409). Attempts and runs are two axes; the code collapsed the second while naming the first. Attempts still collapse, now keyed on the run id that actually performs the supersession, highest `run_attempt` winning.

  **The discriminator cannot be the display name, the `workflow_id` or the `path`**, because the two runs share all three. Selection is keyed per run (`runs_on_sha`), and a workflow with two runs on one commit shows **both** rows, labelled `NAME (run ID)`, because a reader who cannot see the second row cannot check the verdict; a name with one run keeps its bare name and every ordinary render is unchanged (with the one exception [#1687](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1687) added: a name that itself contains the `(run <id>)` shape is neutralised, so it cannot arrive as supertool's own annotation). The green counts what it covered — `21 legs across 3 runs` rather than `across 2 workflows`. Workflow-scoped questions (the declared-set comparison, the previous-head comparison) read the names off the run objects through `workflow_names()` / `missing_workflows()`, so they still ask about workflows while the verdict asks about runs — `presets/dashboard/dashboard.py` and `presets/watch/tiers/gh_prs.py` go through the same seams and are fixed with it.

  **Ties break towards strictness.** A run whose `databaseId` cannot be read becomes its own entry rather than merging into another: two runs that cannot be told apart are counted twice and the conjunction gets stricter. A gate that over-reports pending is recoverable; this issue is what the other direction costs.

- **`gh-branch` now says when it could not rank the previous head by time** ([#1644](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1644)). [#1618](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1618) replaced list position with `createdAt` as the previous-head ordering, and `_created` reads exactly one spelling — `%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ`. `2026-08-13T21:52:04+00:00` is the same instant in legal RFC3339 and parses to nothing, so an undated run was dropped from the ranking silently, and a listing where *no* candidate parsed fell back to list position — precisely the behaviour #1618 was written to remove. The previous-head line read identically in all three cases.

  **Disclosure, not a wider parser.** Accepting more spellings would make the assumption invisible again rather than declared; the third state is "I could not date these N runs". `previous_head_basis()` reports `time` / `position` / `none` with the counts, and `previous_head_lines()` renders one sentence naming how many candidates went unranked and whether the answer therefore came from position. Nothing prints when every candidate parsed, which is every call against GitHub today — `gh run list --json createdAt` emits the `Z` form on this repo, verified rather than assumed.

  **It prints above the `Workflows with a run on the previous head …` block and independently of it.** An empty missing-list derived from the wrong previous head is a false negative, and it is the one that would otherwise print nothing at all. The position fallback itself is kept: refusing to name a previous head would delete the only evidence there is for "ran last time and not this time", which is a worse trade than qualifying it.

- **Four GitLab error classifiers matched `glpat_`; GitLab mints `glpat-`** ([#1645](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1645)). `gl-issue`, `gl-mr`, `gl-pipeline` and `gl-job` each tested `glab`'s stderr for `glpat_` before taking the "not authenticated. Run: glab auth login" arm. Underscore, where every one of GitLab's thirteen documented token prefixes is hyphenated. So an error naming a real token missed that arm and took the generic relay — the wrong advice, and the branch that echoes the remote's text back to stdout and, since [#1602](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1602), to a desktop notification.

  **The test was written to the typo.** `tests/test_security_glab.py`'s `FAKE_TOKEN` used `glpat_` too, so the one check over these classifiers agreed with the thing it was checking and would have passed against a build that matched nothing at all. Correcting both literals reproduces that structure exactly, so the prefix list now lives once — `presets/_secrets.GITLAB_TOKEN_PREFIXES`, read by the redaction rule and by the four classifiers through `mentions_gitlab_token()`, which shares the redactor's compiled pattern rather than testing for a bare prefix — `gldt-`, `glft-`, `glwt-` and `glrt-` are five characters, and a substring test over them reads `gldt-staging.example.internal` as a credential and routes a connection failure to `glab auth login` with the remote's own message discarded — and `tests/test_glab_token_prefix_1645.py` holds GitLab's own documented list, cited to `https://docs.gitlab.com/security/tokens/` and dated, asserting the shared tuple against it. A literal is unavoidable (nothing in CI can reach that page, and no test can mint a token); it is now singular, cited, and load-bearing for two subsystems rather than five copies agreeing with each other.

  **Seven prefixes the redactor did not know.** The same list widened `_secrets`' `gitlab-token` rule from six prefixes to the documented thirteen — `glrtr-`, `gloas-`, `glft-`, `glimt-`, `glagent-`, `glwt-` and `glffct-` were minted by GitLab and unrecognised, so a transcript carrying one was relayed whole by `claude-log` and `git-resolve`.

- **`git-push`'s option-shaped-remote guard now really does run before anything spends the value** ([#1647](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1647)). The #1617 chokepoint comment stated that `reject_fetch_option` is called "before the argv is built rather than inside each arm, so a future arm cannot reintroduce the hole by forgetting". It was not: `_remote_sha(upstream)` ran `git rev-parse --short <upstream>` 33 lines above the guard, spending the same `@{upstream}`-derived value the guard exists to refuse.

  Not exploitable on today's code — `rev-parse` spawns no helper, so a leading-dash upstream dies as an unknown option — and that is the whole severity. What was wrong is the invariant, not the argv. The sentence is the thing the next contributor relies on when adding an arm without re-reading the function, and any git call placed above the old guard silently inherited a pre-guard slot the comment said could not exist.

  Fixed by moving the guard above its first consumer rather than by editing the sentence down to something weaker but true. Editing it would have been honest and would have preserved a gap for no reason. The pre-push remote SHA is now read after the refusal, and a test asserts that no git call at all spends an option-shaped upstream before the guard — the existing #1617 spy watched `push`, `fetch` and `rebase` only, which is why a `rev-parse` above the guard went unseen by the tests written to pin it.

- **`git-push` no longer launches its recovery on an allowance nothing completes in, then reports the result as a timeout** ([#1649](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1649)). Since [#1615](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1615) the recovery fetch, rebase and re-push draw from the push deadline instead of spending 240s beside it — correct, and it left the decline firing at exactly zero. A push that spent 295s of its 300s budget and was *then* rejected non-fast-forward launched the fetch on **5s**, timed out, and produced `fetch TIMED OUT (5s)`: true about the fetch, and misleading about the cause, since nothing was ever going to finish. The caller then raises a number that never cut.

  **The floor is 30s, and it is derived rather than picked.** It is what this op already gives `git ls-remote` — one network round-trip to the same remote, ref advertisement and nothing else — and a recovery fetch is that round-trip plus negotiation plus a packfile, so it cannot be worth less. Measured against github.com from a fast link on 2026-08-14: an already-current `git fetch origin master` took 1.77–2.02s, and one that actually transferred (`--depth 200` onto a `--depth 1` clone) 4.33s. 5s sits inside the noise of the good case.

  **Declining, not clamping.** Below the floor the step is not attempted and the receipt says how many seconds were left, what the minimum is, and that a retry gets a fresh budget — the third state this file argues for everywhere else (`docs/validators.md`, "Declining instead of guessing"). "The budget was spent" and "5s of 300 were left" are now two different sentences, because they send the caller to two different numbers.

  Reported as reasoned from the code rather than observed — the reproduction needs a diverged remote and a slow push. The arm is reachable: it is pinned by a test that stubs the remaining budget and drives a real non-fast-forward through a bare-remote sandbox.

- **The test suite no longer writes outside its own tree** ([#1656](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1656)). Three sites, measured: 52 files and 288 KB per full run landing in the developer's real `~/.cache/supertool/paste-backup/` (the store [#1650](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1650) added), a file named `@-` created and unlinked in the live checkout root — which is typically symlinked as the operator's `supertool` binary, and which two concurrent runs race on — and two `os.environ["XDG_CACHE_HOME"]` assignments popped rather than restored in their teardown.

  **`XDG_CACHE_HOME` is redirected for the whole session instead of a switch per store.** `_cache_root()` is the one place `~/.cache/supertool` is spelled, so one line covers the paste-backup store, the read-elide cache, the GC and the vim cursor/undo store — including whichever store is added next, which under the old convention would have needed a fourth switch nobody would remember to write. No product surface moves: the alternative was a `SUPERTOOL_PASTE_NO_BACKUP` knob that silently disables a data-loss net, which would then need a fourth `paste` receipt state to stay honest, and which fixes one instance of the three.

  **The pop had to go first, and that ordering is the whole reason instance 3 belongs here.** A `pop` is not a restore: with a session-wide redirect in place, the first test to pop it leaves every test after it in that worker writing to the operator's real cache — silently, and in the direction that reads as a pass.

- **`git-push`'s `:budget=SECONDS` is now checked against the op timeout your project set, not only against the module constant** ([#1659](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1659)). #1631 made `ops.git-push.timeout` a value a repository chooses and taught the config path to validate `ops.git-push.budget` against the merged entry; the flag path was left checking `_PUSH_TIMEOUT_MAX = 1800` alone. A project writing `{"ops": {"git-push": {"timeout": 60}}}` could still ask for `:budget=1700` and be accepted — 28x its own op cap — and supertool then killed the child at 60s, which is exactly the outcome the flag's own refusal text cited: a bare `FAIL (timeout)` for a push that may have landed ([#399](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/399)), and on the recovery path the loss of the receipt that would have said the worktree is paused mid-rebase ([#1615](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1615)).

  **Both ceilings apply, and the smaller one binds.** They are not two spellings of one rule, which is why neither is now dead: `ops.git-push.timeout` is where supertool kills the process, and 1800 is the longest this op will make a caller wait — a repository raising its own timeout has said something about the first and nothing about the second. The rule lives in one function, `_budget_ceiling_refusal`, used by the flag path and the config path alike; two copies of it is what produced the asymmetry.

  **Two false sentences went with it.** The flag's refusal said the ceiling "has to stay strictly under `ops.git-push.timeout` **in presets/git.json**" — a claim about a value #1631 had just made a repository's to override, sending whoever read it to edit the shipped preset instead of their own config. And the `v0.42.0` entry for #1631 said the config path was "matching what `_parse_budget` already does for the flag". It was not, at the time it was written; it is now. That entry stands as the record of what v0.42.0 shipped rather than being edited after the fact.

- **The `$1`-shim gate's dispatcher exemption now requires a `shift` that runs, not the letters `shift` somewhere in the loop** ([#1661](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1661)). The exemption shipped as `if "shift" in m.group(0)` over the loop body text, so any loop mentioning the word — in an `echo`, a comment, a variable name — was read as a dispatcher walking argv, and every `$1` subcommand decision inside it was exempted. A shim could opt itself out of the class by printing a message. The gate's live population was zero at the time, in the file whose entire subject is a detector whose zero meant "I did not look".

  **What counts now is command position, read off the literal with its quoted spans and comments blanked in place.** `shift` has to sit where the shell can start a command — at the beginning, after `;`, `&`, `|`, a brace, a paren or a newline, or after `do`, `then`, `else`, `elif` — with `shift=1` excluded as an assignment and `shiftcount` excluded by the word boundary. Blanking rather than deleting is the point: it preserves offsets, so the loop span and the `shift` inside it are found in the one reading that knows the `;` in `echo "trap: ; shift"` is part of an argument. The first cut of this fix checked for a `shift` per *literal* and then took its spans from the quote-stripped text, which rebuilt the same defect one level in — any real `shift` anywhere licensed a loop whose only `shift` was a quoted word. Review caught it; it is pinned.

  **The `$1` tests are counted in a second reading, and the two have to agree.** Blanking a quoted span would take `"$1"` with it, so the tests are located in a copy where only the quote characters became spaces. `[ x"$1" = x"status" ]` is one test to the quote-*deleting* reading and none to that one, because deletion joins `x` to `$1`. When the two counts differ the exemption is refused rather than aligned against a set of tests the code cannot count.

  **Every arm fails closed.** No `shift` that runs, no loop carrying one, no readable `$1` test — each returns "not exempt" rather than a guess, because an exemption that cannot be established is not an exemption. Measured over `tests/` after the change: 5 string literals test `$1`, exactly 1 is exempted by this rule and it is the real `while`/`shift` dispatcher in `tests/_gitshim.py`, the other 4 are exempted by the option rule from [#1412](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1412), and the gate still reports 0 hits — a zero the run now earns.

- **`git-push` names the wrong line, and the wrong word, on a push that never reached the remote** ([#1669](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1669)). Three fields of the receipt asserted things the `[result]` line under them denied. All three now come from one state.

  `First error:` promoted a footnote out of the pre-push hook's own **success** disclosure — a `^ counts skips carrying that token only …` continuation from a skip counter — while the real cause, `Connection to github.com closed by remote host.`, sat last and unselected. The selector was measured rather than guessed, because the issue asked which of three candidates it was: not proximity (the line sat ~200 lines earlier in a passing summary), not the head/tail elision, but a bare `"error" in line.lower()` matching inside the identifier `OSError`. That keyword scan is now word-anchored, and the pick itself is partitioned on the `To <url>` boundary `_split_hook_stdout` already draws — git's stderr and its own output first, the hook's transcript second. A hook-blocked push still surfaces its failing assertion, because git writes only `error: failed to push some refs to '<url>'` on that arm and a line naming nobody is never the answer while another line exists.

  The same push's verdict read `NOT PUSHED - REJECTED`, one line above a `Hint:` that correctly said the push was stopped before it reached the remote and that a rebase would not help. `_ref_status` already knew — git reported no per-ref line at all — so the headline and the verdict read it too now: `PUSH STOPPED BEFORE THE REMOTE` where git never spoke to the remote, `REJECTED` only where it did.

  There is exactly one `Status:` line per receipt now, which is the load-bearing half: the rebase-recovery route printed its own `Status: pushed ✓ (rebased onto remote)` and then let the shared receipt print a second one below it, so the two disagreed on a rebase that turned out to move nothing. A caller with something to say about *how* the push got here adds a clause to the one line. `tests/test_git_push.py::test_main_non_ff_rebase_clean_pushes` had been asserting `pushed ✓` on a fixture whose own `[result]` read `NOT PUSHED - already up to date` — this issue's contradiction, sitting green in the suite.

  On a no-op push, `Status: pushed ✓` sat three lines above `[result] NOT PUSHED - already up to date`, with the sentence that reconciles them between them and outside the two-field window a reader greps for precisely because the receipt is long. The `Status:` line is now rendered by `_success_receipt` from the same `moved` state as the verdict, and reads `nothing to push ✓ — the remote ref already matched`. git exiting 0 was never the same claim as the ref having moved.

- **`gh-pr-merge`'s cleanup section opened by denying a capability it offers 70 lines later, and printed a delete command carrying `{owner}/{repo}`** ([#1670](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1670)). Two halves of one receipt, both in the arm rendered when `cleanup` was not asked for.

  **The header.** It read `## Cleanup — not run by this op`. The op does clean up — `|cleanup` has run it since [#1256](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1256), and the line offering it sat 69 lines below. A property of the invocation was stated as a property of the op, and a reader who stops at a header concludes the capability is missing: the shape where a stale absence claim suppresses the call that would disprove it. It now reads `## Cleanup — not run by this invocation (add `|cleanup`)`, and the three refusal arms each say that `|cleanup` refuses on the same ground, so the offer is never left standing where it would not be taken. The test pins the property rather than the wording — whatever token the header offers in backticks has to be one `parse_argv` turns into `cleanup=True`, so deleting the route reddens it and rewording the header does not.

  **The printed path.** `_repo_target.api_path` leaves gh's `{owner}`/`{repo}` in place when no `repo:` target is set, because `gh api` expands them from the cwd's remote and a target has to *replace* rather than accompany them ([#1281](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1281)). That is right for a path this process executes and wrong for one pasted by a reader: the command silently changes meaning with the directory it lands in, while the same render prints the concrete slug twice, in its own header and its `URL:` line. Printed paths go through a new `api_path_for_display(suffix, slug)` instead, which fills in the slug the op read back off `gh repo view` and declines to a placeholder path when it did not get a well-formed one — a partial answer is not a path to build. Every executed path still goes through `api_path` unchanged, and under a `repo:` target the two functions return the same string, so the split cannot become a route by which a target is accompanied instead of replacing.

- **The raw-command guard is one route wide, and now says so.** `hooks/hooks.json` registers it with `"matcher": "Bash|PowerShell"`, so Claude Code's own `Write`/`Edit` never reach it — on `Digital-Process-Tools/claude-5h-window-spread` a `python3 - <<EOF` heredoc rewriting `.oss.json` was denied and an `Edit` making the same one-key change to the same file succeeded, minutes apart. Same file, same edit, opposite verdicts, and nothing in the successful call said it had bypassed the gate that had just refused. Four surfaces now state the scope rather than implying a wider one: the SessionStart roster gains one line (+170 bytes of a ~7,168-byte budget, measured — the listing is the only account of file routes a session is given, and it read as complete), the refusal trailer gains one clause where it already names the op and the off switch, `docs/configuration.md`'s canonical `raw_command_guard` section — which reasoned carefully about *which commands* are covered and never once about *which tools* — gains that second axis, and `README.md`'s hard-block recipe — the thing an operator reaches for to close the other door — now denies `Edit`, `Write`, `MultiEdit` and `NotebookEdit`, which it had omitted while claiming to block the competing tools. `Write`/`Edit` are deliberately **not** blocked by the plugin: it has no hook that can see them. What is fixed is a boundary reported wider than it is — a refusal naming a path reads as *this file is protected* when what is true is *this route is protected*, which is this repository's own three-states defect arriving in the thing that enforces boundaries. `docs/configuration.md` also qualifies its own dogfooding claim: this checkout blocks `Edit`/`Write` with `.claude/jit-context/tools/00-manual/harness-tools-blocked.md`, a hand-written rule that does not ship, so the maintainers never experienced the gap every plugin user has. ([#1671](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1671))
- **The plugin manifest advertised an enforcement mode that does not exist.** `.claude-plugin/plugin.json` claimed "an opt-in enforcement mode that blocks competing tools". No shipped hook matcher names `Edit` or `Write`, and no config key turns one on; the nearest real thing is a `README.md` recipe configuring Claude Code's own `permissions.deny`, which is the operator's setting and not the plugin's — and which did not list the write tools either. The description now says what the plugin ships, and a test derives the check from `hooks/hooks.json`'s matchers rather than from the sentence, so the claim cannot be reintroduced without the hook that would make it true. ([#1671](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1671))

- **An op whose exit code is its answer is no longer counted as a refusal — three correct `git-worktrees` answers rendered `FAIL` under a footer saying `all 3 refused`** ([#1672](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1672)). `git-worktrees` deliberately compresses its occupancy verdict into the process exit status — `0 = idle, 1 = occupied, 2 = cannot tell` — and documents it in the line immediately above the footer. The dispatcher reads any non-zero child exit as a refusal, so the composition asserted, in words, in the one line a reader keeps, that a scan which had answered three times had not run. This is not [#1291](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1291): [#1297](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1297)'s structural dispatch is correct that the exit was non-zero, and could not know that for this op non-zero is not failure — which is a property of the op, so it is now declared where the op's other properties are.

  **A registry entry may declare which exit codes are values.** `"exitStatus": {"values": [0, 1, 2]}`, beside `paths` and `safety`. Every listed integer is read as an answer; a code outside the list is still a refusal, so a crash exiting 127 is still a crash. The verdict line discloses it rather than leaving `PASS` to be reconciled against the op's own exit note two lines down: `PASS (7.79s) [exit 1 is this op's answer, not a verdict — its registry entry declares the exit code a value]`.

  **Declaring it spends a channel, so the failure has to arrive on another one.** For a listed non-zero code the verdict is taken from a line at column 0 beginning `ERROR: ` anywhere in the op's output, or anything on stderr. Both matter for this op specifically: `git-worktrees` returns 2 for `cannot tell` **and** for `git worktree list` failing outright, and a traceback exits 1, which is a listed value. Exit 0 is unchanged — it has always been a pass whatever the op printed.

  **The third direction in the issue — stop overloading the exit code — was priced before being declined, and the price is that it buys nothing.** `main` collapses every failing op to exit 1 and always has, so `supertool 'git-worktrees:PATH'` returned 1 to the shell for both `occupied` and `cannot tell` and never 2: measured on a `cannot tell` path, the preset exited 2 and the shell saw 1. Nothing can be branching on the integer through supertool, so removing it would break nothing and fix nothing; what crossed the boundary was only the false `refused`. The op's registry description said the caller saw those integers and no longer does.

  `docs/configuration.md`'s copy of the reserved-key list was three keys behind before this change (`restartMcp`, `replaces`, `paths`) and is now current — a config key wrongly believed reserved is one the author expects in the subprocess environment and does not get.

- **`gh-check` and `gh-job` printed four `gh api` commands that named no repository, and no test could exercise a `repo:`-targeted `gh-pr-merge`** ([#1679](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1679)). Two ways `repo:` targeting was honoured by the argv path and invisible everywhere else in `presets/github`.

  **The printed commands.** `check.py`'s two 404 messages and `job.py`'s missing-log and empty-log blocks each hand a reader a `gh api repos/{owner}/{repo}/…` line to paste. `gh api` resolves those two placeholders from the cwd's remote, which is right for a path this process executes and wrong for one a reader pastes: the same command names a different repository in every checkout and says nothing about having changed meaning — the distinction [#1670](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1670) drew in `pr_merge`. The four now go through `_repo_target.api_path_printable`, which fills in the cwd's own slug and declines to the placeholders when `gh repo view` does not answer. `api_path_for_display` from #1670 took a slug the caller "had already read", and outside `pr_merge` no caller had one; `cwd_slug()` is that missing half, put next to it rather than becoming a sixth hand-rolled copy of `gh repo view --json nameWithOwner` — there are five today, returning three different absence sentinels between them.

  **The issue's own claim that these named the wrong repository under a `repo:` target was wrong**, and the fix is not built around it: all four already went through `_repo_target.api_path`, which substitutes a target whenever one is set. The defect was only ever the untargeted case, and a test now pins the targeted one so the claim cannot be re-derived from the code.

  **The blind harness.** `tests/test_gh_pr_merge_main_950.py` routed the PR read on `"statusCheckRollup" in args[-1]`, but `gh_args()` appends `--repo OWNER/NAME` *after* the field list — so under a target the last argument is the slug, the branch never matched, and the read fell through to the post-merge read-back. `main()` then saw `MERGED` and refused a PR it had never read. No test in that file exercised a targeted run, so the refusal read as a legitimate gate outcome: a harness rendering its own blindness as a product verdict. It now matches over every argument, and two tests run a targeted `main()` end to end.

- **`map` says `could not read` instead of describing a file it never opened** ([#1680](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1680)). `chmod 000 secret.py && supertool 'map:secret.py'` printed three claims nothing had earned: `tier: regex`, naming a tier that read no bytes; `(0 lines)`, which is `_count_lines` swallowing the `OSError` and returning its documented `on_error` sentinel; and `(no symbols)`, the tool's own failure stated as a property of the file. That is this repository's canonical defect — an absence produced by the tool, read as an absence in the world — sitting inside the [#887](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/887) render built to make exactly that shape visible.

  `map` had three states and now has four: parsed, no parser, no symbols, and **could not read**. An unreadable file renders `(unreadable)` with the reason the operating system gave, no line count and no tier, and it never contributes a tier name to the header — a file that was the only one asked about reports `tier: none`.

  **The state is established once, ahead of the three functions that each swallowed the error.** `_count_lines`, `_ts_extract` and `_regex_extract` all catch `OSError` independently, and composing a verdict from them is not available: `_count_lines`'s `on_error` sentinel is contracted to differ per caller ([#388](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/388)), so a `0` arriving at the render cannot be told from a genuinely empty file. The distinction is destroyed one layer down, not merely unreported. One `open` and one byte per file, before anything reports on it.

  A permission-denied file is the easy reproduction; the same arm covers a file removed between the directory walk and the read, a dangling symlink, and an ACL — all of which arrive as `OSError`, which is why the reason is reported rather than classified. `read:PATH` in abstract mode falls back to raw source on the new marker, as it already did on `(no symbols)` — and says which of the two it hit, in its own arm: reporting `no symbols found in X (python)` about a file nothing opened is this defect one layer up in the caller, and the tree-sitter footnote under that line would have explained which tier ran for a file no tier received a byte of.

- **An adapter's `duration_ms` on a failure path is measured rather than written down** ([#1683](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1683)). Thirteen adapters emitted their own timeout budget as a literal in the `TimeoutExpired` arm — `30000`, `120000`, `TIMEOUT_S * 1000` — and `ruby-check`'s module-level crash handler emitted `0` whenever it fired, because `main`'s `start` was not in its scope. All fourteen now read a clock.

  The number is not decoration. `tests/_adapter_verdict.stalled_at_its_own_wall` declines to assert on a payload whose `duration_ms` reaches the adapter's internal budget, on the stated grounds that an adapter reporting a timeout in 12ms did not time out and its error routing is broken. A literal equal to the budget satisfies that floor whatever actually happened, so the clause could not fail for the thirteen adapters that wrote one: the routing defect it exists to expose would have been declined as a stall instead. #1604 is the same clause working from the other side, where a hardcoded `0` made a real 30-second wall unclassifiable.

  `tests/test_adapter_duration_is_measured_1683.py` keeps it that way. It reads every `duration_ms` inside an `except` handler across every `validators/*/*.py` and requires the value to resolve — through names, and through functions defined in the same file — to a clock read. Argv arms reporting `0` before any clock starts are deliberately out of scope: there is no elapsed there to report, and demanding one would be demanding a fabricated number.

- **The directory-removal register can see `.cleanup()`** ([#1683](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1683)). `tests/test_directory_removal_ownership_1635.py` counted `TemporaryDirectory` as an ownership source while its removal side had no matching verb, so `.cleanup()` on any receiver was a directory removal the register did not see — a guard reporting clean because it could not look. The #1656 cache-home teardown added in #1682 was exactly that site, and its own comment had to say so.

  The receiver is now the target, the same shape `rmdir` already resolved, so the ownership question asked of it is the one asked of every other site. Only the no-argument spelling counts: a `cleanup` taking arguments is another object's method. `tests/conftest.py` holds the object in a module list rather than on `config`, because a `getattr` off an attribute is a chain nothing in the file can follow — the site is proved by the register now instead of being invisible to it.

- **A refusal no longer prescribes an op that does something the blocked command declined to do** ([#1684](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1684)). `git push origin v0.2.0` was BLOCKED and told to run `git-push`, which pushes the **current branch**: obeying the refusal published a ref the caller never named, reported success, and left the tag uncreated. The matcher keyed on the verb and not on the invocation.

  **`replaces` entries gain `unless_args: N`** — the entry does not claim an invocation carrying more than N positional arguments past its declared `argv`. Every `git push` entry declares `1`, so a remote is still claimed and a refspec is not. The discrimination the schema docs called impossible ("telling `git push origin master` from `git push origin v0.34.0` means asking the repository whether a ref is a tag") is not the one needed: **both** name an explicit refspec, `git-push` names none, and arity decides it from the argv alone without asking git anything.

  **A fourth verdict state, `uncovered`, rather than silence.** The command runs and the guard says *no op covers this form — raw `git` is correct here*, naming the op as the same invocation without those arguments rather than as a substitute for it. Not folded into `undecided`: that state says the guard could not answer, and rendering a decided "no op covers this" as "the guard did not run" is the same misdirection one layer down.

  **What it costs, stated rather than hidden.** `git push origin master` is no longer refused — a missed block on a command `git-push` does answer when you happen to be on `master`. That is the direction this guard is allowed to be wrong in: a wrong block has no per-command escape short of `raw_command_guard: false`, which disarms every mapping in the repository. The retirement gate for the `git-push-has-an-op.md` JIT rule ([#1376](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1376)) is weakened with it, from a block that also named the op to a disclosure that names the op on every such call.

  **And the refusal quotes the command that was typed.** `git push origin v0.2.0 2>&1` was echoed as `git push origin v0.2.0 2` — `shlex` splits `2>&1` into `2`, `>&`, `1`, and the file descriptor stayed on the end of the argv. Descriptors are now dropped by POSIX's own rule (a run of digits that begins a word and is immediately followed by `<` or `>`), so `git push origin 2 >&1` keeps its `2`, which really is an argument. The word **after** a redirection is dropped too: `git status > gh` left `gh` standing where a command word is read, a wrong block waiting for the first single-token `argv` anyone declares.

  The second instance reported — `git checkout REF -- PATH` refused with `git-checkout:REF`, which switches branches — **does not reproduce against the shipped registry**: no `replaces` entry for `git checkout` exists in this tree or anywhere in its history. The mechanism is pinned against an injected entry that reproduces the reported refusal exactly.

### Security

- **An interpreter that exited 0 wrote the Bash guard's permission verdict, because the wrapper forwarded its whole envelope verbatim** ([#1625](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1625)). `hooks/pre-bash-guard.sh` matched a prefix of the rung's stdout and printed the rest unchanged, so a `$VIRTUAL_ENV/bin/python3` that wrote a well-formed `hookSpecificOutput` document carrying `"permissionDecision":"allow"` had authored the harness's own decision. Well-formed JSON, so nothing for [#1613](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1613) — that fix closed the route where a *path* writes the field by concatenation, this is the route where the rung's own stdout does. Same `usurps` class, different door — and the guard had no way to tell its own answer from a forgery, because the two were the same bytes.
- **The fix is a shape change, not a filter.** `hooks/pre_bash_guard.py` no longer writes JSON at all: it writes `supertool-guard-v1 ` and one of three words — `silent`, `note`, `deny` — then a newline, then the text. The wrapper authors every structural byte of the envelope, `permissionDecision` is a literal next to the only value it can hold, and the rung's text reaches JSON only through the escaper [#1613](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1613) added. Authenticating the channel was the other candidate and it cannot work here: any token proving *my rung wrote this* has to be handed to the rung, and the interpreter is what executes the script, so no secret separates "ran it" from "read it and lied".
- **A verb the wrapper does not know is declined and disclosed, never dropped and never relayed.** Two installs disagreeing about the vocabulary would otherwise be a gate that silently said nothing on every call. The stated cost of a closed vocabulary: a field the `PreToolUse` protocol gains has to be added to both files before it can be emitted — an open channel into someone else's schema, exchanged for a closed one this repository owns both ends of.
- **The bound, unchanged and still the reason this is not a release blocker.** Reaching the sink needs `$VIRTUAL_ENV` pointed at a directory whose `bin/python3` the attacker controls, and running that binary is already an execution primitive. A rung that is lying can still fabricate a `deny` reason, or suppress one by staying silent — which it could always do by not answering. What it can no longer write is `allow`, the one value that removes the user's own permission prompt, or any other field of the hook protocol.
- **Two Windows-only regressions the change introduced were closed with it, both graded reasoned rather than observed.** A text-mode `sys.stdout` turns the new line feed into CR LF there, which would have left the wrapper reading a verb with a carriage return stuck to it — an unknown dialect, so every `deny` on Windows would have become a disclosed allow. A text-mode write also encodes with the console code page, so a non-ASCII path inside a refusal could raise instead of writing. `json.dumps` escaped both into ASCII for free, and that is the property not writing JSON gives up, so the hook writes UTF-8 bytes through `sys.stdout.buffer` and the wrapper strips a trailing carriage return from the verb. `_json_string` also escapes line feed, carriage return and tab now rather than replacing them with `?`: `guard_refusal` is a multi-line document and it reaches JSON through bash now, not through `json.dumps`.

- ([#1638](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1638))
  `git-resolve` relayed three failed child streams into its receipt unmarked —
  `git checkout --ours/--theirs`'s stderr, the staging `git add`'s stderr, and
  the same `git add` on the block-selector path. Each reaches a
  `✗ PATH: REASON` row, and `_untrusted.split_lines` cuts on LF/CR/CRLF alone by
  design, so a U+2028 in that text puts chosen content at the start of a line
  where a `[result]` a consumer greps for sorts first. All three now go through
  `_untrusted.flat`, the treatment fifteen `presets/github/` sites got in #1622.
  The blast radius is narrower than that one's and worth stating: these are
  `git`'s own local streams on a merge the caller initiated, so reaching them
  means controlling a path name, a ref name, or a merge driver's output.
- The `cannot read: {e}` / `cannot write: {e}` reasons beside them are
  deliberately **not** flattened, and there is now a test saying why:
  `str(OSError)` reprs the filename, so a U+2028 in a conflicted path arrives
  already spelled as its escape — ASCII that cannot open a line. They were
  flattened in a first cut of this change and then un-flattened.

- ([#1654](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1654))
  Four error relays let the writer of a subprocess's stderr choose which segment
  became the whole message, and the other half was dropped rather than
  disclosed. `gl-issue`'s related-MR decline, `gl-mr`'s `_glab_fail_detail` and
  `gl-mr`'s `merge-tree` decline each took one line of `glab` or `git` stderr
  with `str.splitlines()`, which cuts on U+2028; `git-merge` took the *last*
  line of a failed fetch's stderr, a stream a remote writes `remote:` lines
  onto, and rendered it unflattened into the `WARN: fetch … failed` the caller
  acts on. All four now decide the boundary with `_untrusted.split_lines` and
  flatten the segment, so the whole line survives on one line with the
  separator spelled `[U+2028]`.
- `gl-issue-create` put whatever `glab` last printed into its `OK iid=… url=…`
  receipt, unmarked and selected with `str.splitlines()[-1]`. A stdout of
  `gateway said no, the issue was NOT created` + U+2028 + `[result] PASS 0
  problems (verified)` rendered as
  `gl-issue-create OK iid=[result] PASS 0 problems (verified) url=…`: the
  failure dropped, the writer's own `[result]` line inside a success receipt.
  This is the direct twin of the `url=` fallback #1648 narrowed on the GitHub
  side, and it was the weaker of the two, because its matched arm is a
  substring test rather than a regex that rejects U+2028.
- `git-worktrees` read one published remote ref back as two records, so a
  hostile remote could spell your branch name in the tail of another and an
  unpushed branch read as pushed. `git check-ref-format` exits 0 on a refname
  whose middle component ends in U+2028 followed by a second
  `refs/remotes/origin/…`, verified. The register listed this as an open risk
  and nobody had closed it.
- The `presets/git/` `str.splitlines()` register published one deciding rule —
  `core.quotePath` is on, so git quotes the separator away — and it answered
  for 3 of its 27 entries. Measured on git 2.46.2: quoting covers **pathnames**,
  while `log --format=%s`, `for-each-ref`, `branch -vv`, `show` content and
  `blame --line-porcelain` all hand back a U+2028 raw, and stderr is never a
  pathname at all. Every entry now opens with the ground it actually rests on
  and the register refuses one that names none.

- ([#1681](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1681))
  Eleven renders under `presets/git/` split a log stream with `str.splitlines()`
  and printed **every** line, counted — so a U+2028 in a commit subject, an
  author name, a refname or a stash message added a row nobody committed and
  chose the number beside it. `core.quotePath` quotes pathnames; measured again
  on git 2.46.2, `log --format=%s` hands the separator back raw. The sites are
  `git-checkout`'s last-3-commits list, `git-diverge`'s commit list,
  `git-push`'s force-discard and incoming-commit lists, `git-status`'s other-branches,
  last-5-commits and stash sections, and all three of `git-trail`'s.
- **`_untrusted.split_lines` alone would have been the wrong fix, and that is
  the whole finding.** Everywhere else in this tree the site *selects* one line,
  where consuming the separator is right. These render all of them, so narrowing
  the split alone keeps the count honest and hands the separator to the terminal
  live, inside a row the tool presents as its own output — an inflated count
  traded for a cursor command. Every one of the eleven gets `split_lines` **and**
  `visible()` per rendered line, with `keep` set to the TAB only where the line
  is parsed on a TAB field (`for-each-ref`) or is indented source (`git show`
  hunks).
- **One of them was never a forged row at all.** `git-trail`'s pickaxe render
  feeds each line's first token back to `git show` as argv, and `git show
  --output=<file>` writes that file — verified on git 2.46.2. So a commit
  subject ending `<U+2028>--output=/path` became a *line* whose first token was
  that option, and a commit message chose a path on the reader's disk. That is
  `splices`, not `forges`, and `split_lines` is what closes it.
- `git-status` lost a real branch rather than gaining a fake one, which is why
  the register had ruled it survivable. `check-ref-format` accepts U+2028 in a
  refname, so `feat<U+2028>ure` split into a head fragment with no TAB — dropped
  by the `"ahead" in track` test — and a surviving row rendered under the name
  `ure`, which no branch in the repository has. The reader was told about
  unpushed work on a branch they cannot check out, and the real one was named
  nowhere.
- The `presets/git/` `str.splitlines()` register is down to 27 call sites in 24
  functions across 9 files, from 38 / 27 / 11. Three entries are gone entirely
  and three are now `QUOTED PATH`, each down to its one `--porcelain` /
  `--name-status` read. `git-status`'s dead `branch -vv` split — assigning a
  `current_branch` nothing ever read — is deleted rather than re-registered.

- **A `paste` over a `0600` file wrote its bytes to a world-readable backup** ([#1685](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1685)). The snapshot #1650 shipped one release earlier was written with a bare `open(dest, "wb")`, so the copy landed at `0666 & ~umask` — `0644` on a stock box — whatever the source's mode was. A `paste` over a `0600` `.env`, `id_rsa`, `.netrc` or `.pypirc` therefore left the credentials group- and world-readable under `~/.cache/supertool/paste-backup/` for the whole seven-day retention window, unredacted and unmentioned. Reproduced end to end: `0o600` on the source, `0o644` on the copy, the `glpat-` token in it verbatim. The copy now inherits the source's own mode, and a mode that cannot be read falls back to `0600` rather than to the umask default — never wider than whatever the source turns out to have been.

  **Not fixed by refusing to snapshot a mode-restricted file.** That would close the disclosure by deleting the data-loss net #1650 exists to be, which is choosing a different failure rather than removing one. The snapshot is also still unredacted, deliberately: a redacted backup is not a backup. What has to hold instead is that reading the copy is never easier than reading the original.

  **The receipt now says which mode it used**, on the line that already names the copy: `previous contents kept at PATH (mode 0600, the file's own)`. #1275 shipped `_created_mode_note` in the same release precisely because a widening nobody is told about is the defect being removed, and it went on the **create** path while the path carrying the **displaced** bytes said nothing. The mode is read back off disk rather than quoted from the request, because the umask subtracts from what `os.open` is given; nothing is printed on Windows, where `st_mode` reads back `0o666` whatever was asked for.

  **A `paste-backup` that is a symlink is declined rather than followed.** `mkdir(exist_ok=True)` succeeds on a symlink pointing at a directory and the write went wherever it pointed, so one symlink planted under a shared cache root redirected every later snapshot — the `time_ns()` leaf is unpredictable, the directory is a fixed name. It is now refused out loud as a `no backup of the previous contents — WHY`. That check alone is check-then-act, so it is the message rather than the guarantee: where the platform has them the store is *opened* with `O_DIRECTORY | O_NOFOLLOW` and the leaf created relative to that descriptor with `O_EXCL | O_NOFOLLOW`, which refuses a symlink swapped in after the check instead of resolving through it. The mode is applied with `os.fchmod` on the open descriptor before the bytes, not with a `chmod` by path after the handle closes — that would re-resolve the name and hand back the window `O_NOFOLLOW` had just shut.

  **What this does not touch, and a reader should not assume it did:** `_cache_root()` still reads `XDG_CACHE_HOME` with no shape check, so an environment read chooses where full file contents land, and a symlink at `~/.cache/supertool` itself is the same class one level up. That is the store's location rather than this writer's mode, it changes where five other cache kinds live, and it is left to its own diff.

- **A workflow name could arrive as `gh-branch`'s own `(run ID)` annotation, byte for byte** ([#1687](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1687)). `runs_on_sha` labels a row `NAME (run ID)` when one workflow name has two runs on the commit ([#1640](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1640)), and `NAME` is `workflowName` — remote text, chosen by whoever controls the repo's `.github/workflows`. A workflow literally named `Analyze (run 12345)` therefore rendered identically to supertool's annotation of a workflow named `Analyze`, in the first column of the table the merge gate and the release gate are both read off.

  `_untrusted.flat` does not reach it: every character is printable, and what was missing is a *boundary*, not a control-character strip. The tool's own shape is now neutralised where it appears in a name — `(run-tag in name, neutralised)`, ASCII so it survives every console this repo supports — which is what `_untrusted.scrub` already does for the fence markers. After it, the only `(run <digits>)` in a label is the one supertool wrote, and `run_id_note()` says so instead of teaching the reader to trust the ambiguous form.

  Declined rather than censored: the rest of the name survives, and a name with one run is neutralised too, since a bare row that looks annotated is the same forgery with a shorter reach. Only the *label* changes — `workflow_names()` reads the name off the run object, so the declared-set check and the previous-head comparison still see the real name, and #1640's two rows are still both listed and both still have to pass.

  Bound: this needs write access to the repository's workflow files, which is an actor who can already affect the verdict by editing what runs. The class is what makes it worth recording rather than the reach.

- **A line in a file you `git-investigate` could forge the blame row that names who wrote it** ([#1693](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1693)). `git blame --line-porcelain` interleaves porcelain headers with the blamed file's **own lines**, and the parse split that stream with `str.splitlines()` — which folds on U+2028, U+0085 and the vertical tab, none of which git writes there. A source line spelling `<U+2028>author X<U+2028><TAB>text` therefore added a row to the blame hotspots carrying an author, a date and a line number no commit ever had, in the one section a reader consults to answer *who changed this and when*. The bar is a line in a file you blame, which is far below a commit subject.

  `_untrusted.split_lines` is not the repair and would not have closed it, because the parse was not the only line reader in the path. `_git_common._git` runs `subprocess.run(text=True)`, and text mode rewrites a lone CR **and** a CRLF into LF before any preset sees the stream — measured against real git 2.46.2, a file holding `x = 1<CR>author Mallory<CR><TAB>I did this` reached the parser as three lines, two of them reading as git's. That is the same forgery over plain ASCII, and no choice of splitter undoes it once the bytes are gone. So the blame call goes through a new `_git_verbatim` — the same budget and the same `TIMEOUT_RC` contract, with the translation off — and the parse then splits on git's own LF, which a file line cannot contain by definition. The crafted text is still shown, in the row it belongs to and with its separators disclosed; the old reader silently discarded everything past the first one.

  The log render and the two diff renders in the same function are [#1681](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1681)'s shape one function further on — every line rendered and counted, with the count as the product — and take `split_lines` plus `visible()`. `presets/git` is out of `NOT QUOTED, open` entries; the ground is kept with a count of 0 so the next one has a spelling, and the register is down to 23 sites / 23 functions / 8 files.

- **The ground under `git-resolve`'s five raw path renders, written down** ([#1693](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1693)). The `✓` / `⊘` / `✗` rows interpolate `path` with no `_untrusted.flat`, and nothing said why that was sound — not the register, not the file, not the docs — so the next auditor either repairs five provable no-ops or leaves them and cannot say why. Re-derived, the ground is stronger than the report: a caller's comma-separated `PATH` list is not a second source beside `git diff --name-only --diff-filter=U`, it is a **filter** over it, refused unless every element is already conflicted. So `core.quotePath` reaches all five. Recorded at the code, in the register and in the docs, and pinned by a test — if that refusal is ever relaxed, the ground is gone and the five need flattening the same day.

## [0.42.0] - 2026-08-14

### Added

- **A comment event now says whether your own account wrote it** ([#1612](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1612)). A session that comments on a PR as part of its normal loop got its own comment back thirty seconds later, as an event indistinguishable from somebody answering it. `comment_added` (`github-pr`) and `issue_comment_added` (`github-issue-feed`) carry `author_is_viewer`, four-valued: `true` when every comment new since the last poll was written by the account the poller authenticates as, `false` when none was, `mixed` when the batch has a stranger in it, and `unknown` when the poller cannot tell. `github-pr` reads GitHub's own `viewerDidAuthor` off the `comments` array it already fetches, so this costs no extra API call and needs no identity lookup; `github-issue-feed` says `unknown` always, because one `/issues` page carries a comment count and no authorship at all, and saying so out loud is the point. Nothing is suppressed — a dropped real comment is invisible, and a consumer can filter on a field it can see. The field is `author_is_viewer` rather than `by_you` because the token a session posts under is also what a human maintainer comments under by hand, and no poller can tell those two apart.

- **`ops.git-push.budget` — a repository can now state its own push budget, instead of every push to `master` timing out to learn the same fact** ([#1631](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1631)). `_PUSH_TIMEOUT = 300` was a module constant reachable from nothing but the per-call `:budget=SECONDS` flag, and its own comment made the case against itself: what decides the right number "is not visible from here". It is visible from the project's config, because *this repo's pre-push hook runs a suite* is a property of the repo. Measured while filing: two pushes of one markdown commit failed at 302.70s and 302.90s with nothing sent, and the third at `:budget=1500` printed `12868 passed, 51 skipped in 309.86s` and landed. Ten seconds over the default — so the failure is total rather than occasional, and a merely bigger constant would have produced the worse regime where the same command sometimes works. A repo with no pre-push hook wants a *shorter* budget for the opposite reason. Per-repo in both directions is what makes it configuration.

  Precedence is **`:budget=SECONDS` > `ops.git-push.budget` > 300**, and 300 is still the answer when neither is set. The key merges over the preset entry key-by-key like every other per-op key, so `{"git-push": {"budget": 1500}}` keeps the op's `cmd` and `timeout`; the receipt names the source of the number actually in force, and a budget the flag overrode is not consulted at all.

  **Refused, never clamped.** The configured budget is validated against `ops.git-push.timeout` **from the same merged entry** and refused when it is not strictly under it, naming both numbers — matching what `_parse_budget` already does for the flag. Past the op-level cap supertool kills the process, and a killed push can verify nothing, so the caller acts on a bare `FAIL (timeout)` for a push that landed ([#399](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/399)); on the recovery path `_report_recovery_timeout` is the only thing that would have said the worktree is paused mid-rebase ([#1615](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1615)). A clamp would convert *the caller asked for a number and got a different one* into a discovery made at the moment a push cannot be verified.

  This value is not an op argument — it arrives from a config file and ends up as `timeout=` on a `subprocess` call, so nothing in `_safe_path` or the op's `paths` declaration stands in front of it. Every shape is checked before anything is pushed: a JSON number, whole (`bool` is an `int` in Python and is refused), positive, at most 1800, and strictly under the op timeout. A `timeout` that itself does not read as a positive whole number is a third state — the budget is refused rather than assumed safe, because a check that could not run must not return the shape of a clean result. Both keys come from one read of the merged entry rather than one from the environment and one from disk: core exports `budget` to the subprocess as `SUPERTOOL_BUDGET` for free, but `timeout` is reserved and deliberately does not, and validating two answers to the same question against each other is not a check.

### Fixed

- **The global-lifetime guard checked "is this a mutable container"; the property it is named for is "does this carry state between calls"** ([#1107](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1107)). A `str`, `bool` or `None`-sentinel memo carries state across calls exactly as a cache dict does, and no `isinstance` over `dict`/`list`/`set` can see one. The core has 27 module-level names a call rebinds, and 19 of them held no declared lifetime anywhere: 10 were probe flags the test fixture restored by hand with no declaration, and 9 were classified by nobody.

  **The new check is decidable from the source and needs no type judgement**: `tests/test_core_global_lifetimes_1107.py` fails the build on any module-level name declared `global` inside a function — the only way Python can rebind one from a call — unless it is in `conftest.RESET_GLOBALS`, `conftest.RESET_EXEMPT_GLOBALS`, or the newly-named `conftest.FIXTURE_RESTORED_GLOBALS`, which is the autouse fixture's own save/restore block and is verified against that block's source rather than believed. Deliberately not "classify every module-level name", which [#686](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/686) rules out for the reason that matters: a guard that is 90% noise gets exempted without reading.

  The sibling was renamed rather than widened — `test_every_mutable_container_global_in_supertool_py_is_accounted_for` — because neither check subsumes the other. `_WRITE_WARNINGS.append(...)` mutates in place and needs no `global`; `_VALIDATOR_MEANING_VERSION = h(...)` rebinds and is no container.

  **Nine names were unclassified, and three of them were armed.** `_VALIDATOR_MEANING_VERSION` (the case the issue was filed from) and `_UNTRUSTED_FLAT`/`_UNTRUSTED_FLAT_TRIED` are built at first use from `_INSTALL_DIR`, which tests patch — [#1322](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1322)'s mechanism, in types that guard cannot reach. A memo built under a patched install dir keys the validator cache to a directory that no longer exists, and a failed `_untrusted` probe silently downgrades every later secret in that worker to `repr()`. `_GREP_EXTENSIONS_EFFECTIVE` memoises `builtin-ops.grep.extensions` out of a config the fixture blanks per test. All nine now declare a lifetime, and `_reset_module_state` rebinds anything that is not a live container, since `current[:] = pristine` raises `TypeError` on a bool and reaches nothing on a str.

- `git-worktrees` takes the publication count against the remote the branch
  actually tracks, and the row names that ref (#1525). The ref used to be
  chosen by preferring `origin` unconditionally whenever two remotes carried
  the same branch name, and the sentence reporting the count named no remote at
  all — so on a fork layout (upstream `fork/X`, an `origin/X` at a different
  commit) the row answered a question nobody asked and the reader could not
  check it. Measured on a two-remote sandbox before the fix: a branch one
  commit ahead of its `fork` upstream read *in sync with its remote ref … the
  work is published but unproposed*.
- A branch with **no upstream** is a third state, not a zero. The same-named
  ref is still measured — the commits really are on it — but the row says it
  was `picked by name: this branch has no upstream configured` (#1525).
- A branch whose upstream is **not in this clone** — deleted on the remote, or
  never fetched — is not measured at all, rather than counted against whichever
  other remote carries the name. The row reads `sync not measured, no open PR`
  and names the ref it was looking for. That token is new and is the point:
  *not measured* used to render as `no open PR`, identical to *measured,
  nothing missing* (#1525).

- The #1475 census no longer publishes an unchecked total (#1570). Its docstring claimed 174 sites in 36 files, its own sweep measured 154, and `docs/presets/git.md` carried a third copy of the wrong number; `test_the_published_total_is_the_measured_one` now asserts every live document's figure against the sweep, so the prose cannot drift from the measurement again. `CHANGELOG.md` is deliberately excluded — it records what a release shipped, wrong numbers included.
- The census also publishes `UNRESOLVED`, the number of child-stream values that flow into a call the scan does not model at all. It is not a defect count; it is the size of the population a zero from the census says nothing about, and it is asserted exact in both directions so that narrowing the scan lowers it and fails visibly rather than reading as progress.

- [#1584](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1584) The suite-wide network block stated its blind spot as one thing — "it binds `socket` in the pytest process only" — and six in-process egress routes stayed open behind that sentence. Measured from inside an armed context, `connect_ex`, `sendto`, `gethostbyname`, `gethostbyname_ex`, `gethostbyaddr` and `getnameinfo` all walked out, and `gethostbyname` returned a live-resolved address. All six are refused now, along with `sendmsg`. Nothing in the suite took them, so no green was ever wrong — the boundary was.
- The fix is not a longer list, because a longer list is read exactly as trustingly as a short one. `tests/_netblock.py` now carries a register classifying **every callable the `socket` module and the `socket.socket` type expose** as patched, reached-via-a-patched-route, local, inert, or open-with-a-reason, and `tests/test_netblock_egress_register_1584.py` goes red when a name arrives that nobody has classified. The four routes no in-process patch can reach — a child process, a C extension calling libc directly, a descriptor connected before the guard was armed, and `os.read`/`os.write` on such a descriptor — are named rather than counted as blocked.
- A register derived from the running interpreter can only see the platform it runs on, and #1584's could not see `socket.socket.ioctl` — Windows-only, classified nowhere, red on all four Windows legs of the next PR while macOS and Linux stayed green. It is `OPEN` now with its reason: it addresses no peer, but `SIO_RCVALL` puts the interface into promiscuous receive, and the traffic that then arrives at `recv` has no destination for a destination-refusing guard to check. `_netblock.PLATFORM_ONLY` states the Windows-only names so the register stops learning one of them per release, and a test asserts each is absent on POSIX and present on Windows — the presence half is observed by the Windows legs, not by whoever wrote the list.

- [#1598](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1598) The suite's `$1`-shim gate scanned `tests/test_*.py`, so a shim in a helper module returned the same clean zero. It now reads every Python module under `tests/`, recursively — `_gitshim.py`, `_git_decline.py`, `conftest.py` and everything in `tests/fixtures/` were never opened, and a *shared* shim is exactly what a helper module holds. The widened population produces one hit, `tests/_gitshim.py`'s `while`/`shift` dispatcher, which is the correct implementation of the pattern; it is exempted by its **shape** rather than by its filename, because `$1` inside a loop that consumes arguments is the argument under the cursor and has no position to slide to. Naming the file would have re-created the allowlist [#1412](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1412) deleted, and would bless every shim that file ever acquires.

- **Three validator adapters read an empty run as a clean verdict about a file the linter may never have opened** ([#1601](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1601)). `prettier-check`, `markdownlint` and `stylelint` each published `ok: true, count: 0` on a zero exit with no output, which is what an *ignored* file produces too. They do not share a probe, so they do not share a fix — the precedent is `ruff` after [#1587](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1587): ask on the zero-finding arm only, and let the question have three answers.

  **`prettier-check` asks `prettier --file-info`**, which resolves the same ignore files and answers `{"ignored": true|false}`. It is handed the same `--config`/`--ignore-path` flags as the check, because a probe reading a different ignore set answers about a different run; a probe that cannot answer — non-zero, unparseable, no `ignored` key, gone, hung — is `skipped` with its own reason and never falls back to `ok`. It is bounded by what is left of the adapter's own budget rather than given a second full one, with no floor under that remainder — a floor is an overrun wearing a guarantee — so the worst case still fits inside the `timeout` the validator is registered with; past that the core kills the adapter and the caller gets `NOT CHECKED` naming no question at all. A budget already spent when the check returns is the third state too, naming the budget.

  **`markdownlint` needs no second spawn, because the first one already says so.** markdownlint-cli honours `.markdownlintignore` while resolving its arguments to a file list, and when nothing survives — an ignore match, or a path that is not there — it prints its usage banner on stdout and exits 0 (measured, markdownlint-cli 0.49.1). A file it genuinely linted clean prints nothing there, so output on **stdout** at a zero exit is the tell, and the skip quotes the first line of it. A missing `.md` was `ok: true` until now. stderr is deliberately not part of that question: markdownlint is a Node program and Node chatters on stderr over runs that worked, so reading both streams would let one `[DEP0040] DeprecationWarning` turn every clean markdown file into a decline naming a cause that is not the real one.

  **`stylelint` was worse than the issue said, and reading one stream was why.** It writes its `--formatter json` report to **stderr** — `process.stderr.write(report)` in its own `cli.mjs`, stdout being reserved for `--fix` output — and older releases wrote it to stdout. The adapter read stdout and called emptiness clean, so against stylelint 16+ every CSS file came back clean including one holding a `CssSyntaxError`: not the ignore case at all, but every run. Both streams are now offered to the JSON reader, since the stream is not the question and the report is. No report on either is a `NOT CHECKED` fault, except the one case stylelint names itself (`AllFilesIgnoredError`), which is a scope decline and is `skipped`; no probe was invented for it, because it has none and needs none.

  Two adjacent arms in the same class, fixed with it: `stylelint` absent was an `adapter` error, so a repo registering it on a machine without it failed every CSS edit — it is `refusal.absent()` now, quiet unless named in `$SUPERTOOL_REQUIRE_VALIDATORS`, like every other adapter since [#1202](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1202). And `pyright` with nothing on either stream reported `ok: true`; it declines instead.
