A third, found by running the fixed `markdownlint` against the real CLI: its row parser predates the severity word markdownlint-cli now prints between the position and the rule (`b.md:1:1 error MD018/...`), so every located finding missed the pattern and fell through to the whole-output catch-all — four findings arriving as one `lint` error with `line: null`, no source context and a count of 1.

- `watch:gitlab-mr-feed` now announces an outage instead of going quiet ([#1602](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1602)). An unreachable GitLab, an expired token or a scope carrying an unknown filter token made the poller return an empty tick — alive, green in `watches`, and silent forever, which is exactly what a feed with nothing to report looks like. It now emits one `mrs_unreachable` per outage, carrying the reason and the last population size it could see, and keeps `known` so recovery does not re-announce every open MR as new. `radar` gains its own warning line and a `feed sight:` row under `radar:--state`, distinct from a poller that crashed, and a board whose feed cannot see no longer counts as healthy. `mrs_unreachable` ships in `DEFAULT_FEED_ONLY`.

- **The GitHub error relays let the server choose which line its text landed on** ([#1606](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1606)). `gh` echoes the GitHub API's own error body on stderr, and five renders in `presets/github/` printed it into a line at column 0 with no `_untrusted.flat` — `gh-issue`, `gh-job`, `gh-run`, `gh-prs` and `gh-issue-create`. `_untrusted.split_lines` cuts on LF/CR/CRLF alone by design, so a U+2028 survives inside what the render treats as one line and puts everything after it back at column 0 for any consumer that splits the way `str.splitlines()` does. Every one of the five renders **above** the trailer the core appends, so a forged `[result]` sorts first at all of them — the answer does not differ per site. `presets/github/pr.py` was already correct ([#1475](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1475)) and is the shape the five adopted; this is the GitHub half of what [#1485](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1485) did for GitLab, predicted by the [#628](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/628) parity survey.

  `gh-issue-create` did not import `_untrusted` at all, and relays `stderr or stdout` — both arms, so the fallback is a second relay and a fix that only covered stderr would have left it raw.

  **Ten more sites in the same directory went with them, found by sweeping for the shape rather than by reading the filed table**: `gh-labels` and `gh-branch`'s `_format_error` terminal arms, both `gh-issues` relays (its repo lookup and its list failure), `gh-check` (flattened once in `GhCall`'s constructor, which covers all three prints that render `.error` plus the not-found probe's), `gh-pr-create`, and `gh-following`, `gh-starred`, `gh-find-followable` and `gh-find-starable` — the last four the sharpest, since [#981](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/981) flattened every login, repository name and description those files render and walked past the error relay a few lines above them. In the two `find-*` ops the relay is sliced to 200 characters, and the flatten goes first: a cut made first leaves whatever the separator started ([#970](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/970)), which is the ordering both files already spell out for a description twenty lines below. Fifteen sites, not five.

  `gh-pr-create` is the one where the harm is not hypothetical about a consumer's trailer: it prints the remote's body on the line directly **above** its own `[result] no PR created (...)`, so the forged verdict sorts above a real one this op wrote itself.

  **Named here rather than left silent, and fixed in [#1648](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1648)**: seven sites dumped an unparseable remote body verbatim — four spelled `ERROR: invalid JSON from gh` (`gh-run`, `gh-pr` twice, `gh-issue`) and three `ERROR: bad JSON` (`gh-following`, `gh-starred`, `gh-find-starable`) — which is a multi-line relay by design and wanted a fence rather than a flatten, and `gh-pr-merge`'s `_gh_json` took `str.splitlines()[-1]` of the remote's text — which selects the *forged* line rather than forging one, and landed in a merge gate. `presets/github/check.py`'s three `.error` prints, `gh-following`, `gh-starred`, `gh-find-followable` and `gh-find-starable` were all invisible to [#1475](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1475)'s per-file census, which counts `.stdout`/`.stderr` attribute reads reaching a sink and so sees neither a helper's `.error` field nor a `sys.stderr.write`.

  Disclosed, not stripped: the operator still reads the remote's sentence, with the separator spelled `[U+2028]` and a cursor command spelled `␛`. `tests/test_gh_error_relay_untrusted_1606.py` asserts on what a `[result]` consumer counts rather than on `_untrusted.flat` having been called, and asserts the separator reached the render — a site that dropped the text would otherwise pass for the wrong reason.

- **`edit`'s tie disclosure was unreachable for any anchor over 20 lines, so the confidently-wrong line number came back for the case it was written about** ([#1614](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1614)). `_nearest_block_candidates` char-scores at most `_EDIT_NEAR_WINDOWS` (20) of the windows that tied on the line pass, and returns a `tie_floor` meaning *more places tied than were scored*. `_edit_nearest_hint` consulted that floor only inside `if rivals:`, where `rivals` first discards every candidate within the anchor's own height of the leader as one neighbourhood. For an anchor taller than 20 lines all 20 sampled starts sit inside one such neighbourhood by arithmetic, so `rivals` was always empty and the floor was dead code. A 30-line anchor over a file with 34 tied windows got `nearest match at lines 1-30 (98%)` — one sample of 20, named as a fact, roughly 470 lines from the block the caller wrote.

  **The floor is its own trigger now**, not a modifier on `rivals`: more tied than scored means the unscored ones were never located, so the hint declines with `at least 34 places score the same` rather than naming one. The "and N more" count is also taken against the lines actually listed rather than a hardcoded three — with `rivals` empty only the leader is named, and the old arithmetic under-reported the withheld places by two.

- **`git-push:budget=N` was spent twice on the rebase-recovery path, so above ~840s the ceiling that guarantees a verdict did not hold** ([#1615](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1615)). `_push_budget()` was handed to `git push` at both push sites — the initial attempt and the re-push after a clean rebase — with `_RECOVER_TIMEOUT` for the fetch and again for the rebase in between, and nothing accounting for the time already spent. Worst case `2N + 240` against `ops.git-push.timeout = 1920`, so any `N > 840` could reach supertool's outer cap; `:budget=1800` asked for 3840s. Past that cap the process is killed, on the recovery path, where `_report_recovery_timeout` is the only thing that would have told the caller their worktree is paused mid-rebase — the outcome `_parse_budget`'s own ceiling text says the ceiling exists to prevent ([#399](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/399)). The default (300, so 840 total) was safe; this arrived with the caller-supplied budget in [#1530](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1530).

  **`:budget=N` is now a deadline on this op's pushing, not a per-call timeout.** The clock opens at the first `git push` and the recovery fetch, the rebase and the re-push each take the smaller of their own budget and what is left of it. The single-push case is unchanged to the second — the preamble that picks a remote and the receipt that reads the result stay outside the clock, the receipt deliberately, because an expiring clock past the point of no return must never cost the caller the verdict ([#675](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/675)).

  **What it costs, since a deadline and a per-call timeout are different contracts and this is the trade:** a first push that spends most of `N` and is *then* rejected non-fast-forward now leaves little or nothing for the recovery. That recovery is **declined rather than run short** — a third state, `NOT PUSHED - BUDGET SPENT`, naming whether the rebase had already replayed the branch, because a `git push` launched on an expired clock is killed before it can verify anything and the verdict is the whole product. Previously it ran for another `N + 240` and could be killed with no receipt at all.

  **The receipt for a stall nobody can attribute now names no number at all.** `_report_recovery_timeout`'s third caller is a backstop wrapping the whole recovery in `except subprocess.TimeoutExpired`, for calls that do not report their own stage — it knows a call stalled, not which one. It used to default to `_RECOVER_TIMEOUT`, which was safe while that constant *was* the clock on every call it covers; it no longer is, so a number there would be a budget nothing was measured against. Three states for the receipt's own field, on the same terms as everything else here. Found reviewing this change, not by the issue.

  The timeout receipt reads the clock the push was actually launched with rather than the budget it was cut from, and says which is which when they differ — a receipt quoting a clock that did not cut sends the caller to raise a number they never reached, which is #1530's own defect one indirection further in. `_report_recovery_timeout` does the same for `_RECOVER_TIMEOUT`.

- **`read` announced the byte cap had cut a window short when it had returned every byte, contradicting the byte-exact remedy `grep` prints to send callers there** ([#1616](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1616)). `grep` names `read:PATH:N-N` as the way back to a line it truncated ([#1489](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1489)). The read delivered all 25,006 bytes and then said `stopping at line 2: cut short by the 20000-byte cap and the limit was reached coincide here — which one ended the window cannot be told apart`, with a footer offering `truncated at 20000 bytes ... (2 more lines)` for lines nobody had asked for. The cap is tested *after* a whole line is emitted, so it never truncates a line — it drops the ones that would have followed, and when the loop stopped at the window's own end there were none to drop.

  **Reaching the cap and being cut by it are two facts now.** Only a read that stopped short of its own limit and of EOF is reported as cut; a window that ended anyway says so, and the cap is disclosed as a fact instead — `the 20000-byte cap was reached on that line and dropped nothing; it stops whole lines and never truncates one, so these bytes are complete`. Silence would have been the other half of the same defect: the output *is* at the cap, and a wider window will lose lines. A cap that genuinely did drop lines still says `cut short`, pinned by its own test.

  **The `grep=` branch made the same misattribution one render over**, and is fixed with it. A filtered read whose scan stopped at the cap correctly says the remaining lines were never searched — but when the LIMIT ended the scan on a line that happened to carry the total over the cap, the unsearched lines are the limit's and the note credited them to the cap, telling the caller to widen the wrong bound. Found reviewing this change, not by the issue.

- **`gh-branch` reported `did NOT run on this commit` for a workflow whose run the same listing returned three minutes later** ([#1618](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1618)). Hit at the v0.41.0 release gate, which is the caller this op exists for. GitHub created two runs on master's head `339d04d` at 16:19:44Z; at 16:31Z `gh run list --branch master --limit 60` returned neither, and at 16:34Z, unchanged head, it returned both. The `NO RUN` verdict itself held — it is its own state, it named the ~15min creation window and it said a run was still expected, which is why this cost nothing — but the block under it flattened the same absence into a fact: `tests — did NOT run on this commit`, with the hedge attached to the *reason* rather than to the fact. At a release gate the two readings take opposite actions: a genuine absence means the commit is uncovered, a listing that has not caught up means wait and re-ask.

  **The sentence now says what was observed.** `no run for it was RETURNED on this commit`, which is a different sentence from `ran and passed` and a different one again from `did not run`. When the listing returned no run at all on the head *and* the head is still inside the creation window, one more line says so outright and names the incident, so a reader can tell a query that has not caught up from a commit nothing covers. Past the window the extra line stops: a commit with no runs is then an ordinary, legitimate state, and a hedge printed forever is a disclosure that gets tuned out.

  **The previous head was named from list position, and that was a second defect on the same line.** `previous_head` took the first entry with a different SHA — the newest one only if GitHub hands the list back in descending order. It does not always: the incident named `d7e67ee` as master's previous head, a commit 527 commits and 17 days behind, carrying one run, which a newest-60 window on that branch cannot contain. So the flat sentence was wrong about *which* commit it was comparing against as well as about the absence. Selection is now by `createdAt`, tie-broken by run id, falling back to list position only when no entry carries a readable timestamp. `dashboard` and `watch`'s `gh-prs` tier call the same helper and get the same fix.

  **The gap is stated, because 23 seconds and 17 days are not the same news.** When the disclosure fires it also prints how far the newest run anywhere in the listing predates the head commit. A listing seconds behind has plainly not caught up yet; one 17 days behind answered about a different slice of history, and a reader shown only `zero workflow runs` cannot tell those apart.

- **A wall-clock assertion in `edit`'s minified-file test measured the runner, not the product, and blocked the v0.41.0 release push** ([#1623](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1623)). `test_a_minified_file_does_not_hang_the_diagnostic` asserted `elapsed < 15`. The bound it guards is real — `_EDIT_NEAR_BUDGET` caps `_edit_nearest_hint`'s scan in cells — but the assertion measured how loaded the machine was: it went red three times in one hour on 2026-08-13, on a laptop running five suites, while the same commit was green on all 18 CI legs. One of those reds was the pre-push hook on the release commit, where the correct reading of a red ("do not ship") is the reading it made wrong. A test harness rendering an environment limit as a product verdict is this repo's own defect class ([#1143](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1143)) relocated into the thing meant to detect it.

  **It now counts the cells handed to `difflib` instead**, against `_EDIT_NEAR_BUDGET` and the `_EDIT_NEAR_MAX_CHARS` per-comparison clip, and requires the decline to be the *budget* one by its wording. Both halves were load-bearing: with the budget lifted, this same input still declines — for a tie, at 100% across 60 places — so the old `cannot suggest` assertion passed against an unbounded scan and only the clock was holding the line. Nothing about the product changed.

- **Two `presets/watch` modules only imported when somebody else had prepared `sys.path`** ([#1624](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1624)). `transport.py` and `channel.py` put `presets/` on the path for `_proc` and then did a bare `import naming` out of their own directory, which nothing put there — so loading either by path worked only when some other module had already inserted it. Under `-n auto` that made a test's green a fact about which worker it landed in; [#1621](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1621) fixed the one test that tripped over it, which closed the instance and left the class. Both modules now state their own neighbourhood, and a new test loads every module under `presets/watch/` in a fresh interpreter nobody prepared, so the next one to grow this shape fails on the PR.

- The #1475 census now searches five sink shapes, not two (#1626). `print(...)` and `return <expr>` were the whole set, so a child stream reaching `sys.stderr.write(...)`, `list.append(...)` or `list.extend(...)` scored zero. Measured on the fifteen `presets/github/` relays #1606 fixed: four of them (`find_followable`, `find_starable`, `following`, `starred`) counted 0 both before and after the fix, and a fifth (`check.py`) did not move because a false positive one line up took the fixed site's place. The widened sweep discloses 17 relays the old one could not see, in `git/checkout.py`, `git/commit.py`, `git/push.py`, `git/resolve.py`, `git/status.py`, `gitlab/issue.py` and the three `bad JSON` dumps in `presets/github/`.
- The shapes are written down as `SINK_SHAPES` and each is probed by a test, so a shape the scan stops matching fails rather than reading as a shape with no instances.

### Security

- **A directory name wrote the Bash guard's own permission verdict** ([#1613](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1613)). `hooks/pre-bash-guard.sh`'s `decline()` built its `hookSpecificOutput` envelope by string concatenation, and three of its four call sites pass a value the hook did not author: `$LAST_TRIED` and `$PARTIAL_TRIED` are the argv of the rung that failed, whose first rung is `"$VIRTUAL_ENV/bin/python3"`. A `"` in that path closed `additionalContext`, and everything after it was parsed as sibling keys of the same object — so `VIRTUAL_ENV` set to a directory named `x","permissionDecision":"allow","z":"` made Claude Code read `allow` as the guard's decision on the outer command. That is the `usurps` class: a value the tool did not author landing in a structured field the caller treats as the tool's own. Pre-existing (it reproduces at `3185244`); [#1608](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1608) added the second sink, and the issue named that one — the `$LAST_TRIED` sink is reached by an interpreter that merely runs and fails, which is the lower prerequisite of the two.
- **The same concatenation made a malformed envelope reachable with no payload at all, which is the silent fail-open [#1608](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1608) exists to refuse.** A bare `"` forges nothing; it makes the document unparseable, so Claude Code gets no decision *and* no note — a gate that did not run, reading as a command that complied. A backslash (`Invalid \escape`) and a raw control character (`Invalid control character`) are two more spellings of it, and a POSIX path may contain either. `decline()` now escapes at the seam rather than at its call sites, so a fifth sink cannot reintroduce this: backslash and quote are escaped, everything non-printable is replaced with `?`. Escaped in bash — three parameter expansions, no fork, 0.049ms per call over 10,000 iterations under bash 3.2 — rather than serialised by an interpreter, because `decline()` is reached precisely when the ladder has just finished proving no interpreter answers. Backslashes are escaped rather than replaced so a Windows disclosure still names the path it means ([#1378](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1378)).

- **An option-shaped remote name reached the argv `git-push` builds, and git executed it** ([#1617](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1617)). `reject_fetch_option` is the chokepoint written for exactly this ([#818](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/818)) and ran at the recovery fetch and in `presets/git/merge.py`, but not before `push_args += ["-u", remote_name, "HEAD"]`. Neither value there is an op argument: `_resolve_push_remote` takes `branch.<b>.pushRemote` and `remote.pushDefault` **verbatim** by design, because git accepts a URL in those keys, and `_split_upstream` reads `@{upstream}` — a remote-tracking ref name whoever controls the remote can choose. `_safe_path` and the `paths` declarations are not involved; the value never crosses that chokepoint.

  **The issue graded its own evidence as resolution-only. It is not.** On git 2.46.2 / macOS 15 the exact argv this file builds runs the payload: `git push --porcelain -u --receive-pack=<cmd> HEAD` spawns `<cmd>`, because git eats the option, `HEAD` slides into the repository slot, and git starts the receive-pack program for that local path *before* failing to find a repository there. The `fatal:` that follows is not a mitigation, it just happens afterwards. One remote is enough — no second remote and no steering config, contrary to the issue's caveat. The reproduction is kept as a test rather than written down, so a claim about git's argument parser cannot go stale between releases without something saying so.

  The refusal is placed before the argv is built rather than inside each arm, so a future arm cannot reintroduce the hole by forgetting, and because `remote_name` also reaches `ls-remote` and the post-push advisories on the arm that does not put it in the push argv at all. The `:to-upstream` arm did **not** execute on the same git — `HEAD:<ref>` parses as an scp-style ssh URL, so receive-pack runs on the far side of a hostname that does not resolve — and is guarded anyway: the refusal belongs at the sink, not at whichever argv shape happens to be reachable this release.

- **The eight GitHub relays [#1606](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1606) named and left, closed** ([#1648](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1648)). `gh-pr-merge`'s `_gh_json` relayed a failing `gh` call's body as `str.splitlines()[-1]`, and `str.splitlines()` cuts on U+2028 while `_untrusted.split_lines` deliberately does not — so a server that controls the error body chose which segment became the *whole* error, unflattened, at column 0, inside the receipt the merge gate prints (`ERROR: PR #N could not be read ...: {err}`). Seven more sites dumped an unparseable remote body verbatim: four spelled `ERROR: invalid JSON from gh` (`gh-run`, `gh-pr` twice, `gh-issue`) and three `ERROR: bad JSON` (`gh-following`, `gh-starred`, `gh-find-starable`). Pre-existing — every one of them ships in v0.41.0 — and disclosed rather than left silent, which is why they were findable at all.

  **`flat` and `split_lines` are not one decision, and the eight sites split three ways.** A *selection* picks which segment **is** the error, so the split has to be right even after a flatten: `_gh_json` now takes `_untrusted.split_lines(...)[-1]` and flattens the segment it selected. A *verbatim body* is a block by design and keeps its lines, so the four `invalid JSON` dumps are fenced, not flattened — `scrub()` inside `_untrusted.fence` discloses every separator and neutralises the marker shape, so the fence cannot be closed from inside it, and the slice comes first because the markers are the outermost thing. A *one-line inline diagnostic* has nowhere to put a fence, so the three `bad JSON` writes flatten and then slice, the order those same three files already spell out for the descriptions below them ([#970](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/970)). Each of the four fenced sites prints `_untrusted.banner()` above the fence, because markers with nothing explaining them are a convention the reader has not been let in on.

  **Two more, neither on the disclosed list, both found by sweeping for the shape rather than reading the table.** `gh-pr-create` has its own copy of `_gh_json` with the same `str.splitlines()[-1]` and the same defect, one file over — its `read_err` renders above the op's own `[result] no PR created`. And `gh-issue-create`'s `url=` fallback selects the last line `gh` printed the same way; the harm there is the selection rather than a column-0 forgery, since the server's chosen segment silently replaces the URL on an `OK` receipt.

  **And the reasoning that kept four of them, which was half an argument.** `tests/test_preset_twin_splitlines_register_1119.py` registered `pr.py::_fetch_review_threads_detailed`, `issue.py::_print_linked_prs` and both `_gh_json` twins as *deliberate* `str.splitlines()` sites, on the ground that narrowing them would be worse — `str.splitlines()` **consumes** an exotic separator, where `_untrusted.split_lines` would leave a forged U+2028 inside the extracted string, and [#1346](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1346) pinned that claim with a test. It is true, and it is not the whole argument: consuming the separator means discarding everything before it, so the server still chose which segment became the message and the real error was dropped rather than disclosed — an absence produced by the tool, wearing a green test. All five entries are retired, the remaining two sites (`pr.py`'s threads decline, `gh-issue`'s linked-PR decline) are fixed the same way, and the #1346 assertion now says which half of the question it answers.

  `tests/test_gh_remote_body_relay_1648.py` feeds a U+2028-bearing body through each real relay and asserts on what a `[result]` consumer counts, never on `_untrusted.flat` having been called — a site can call it and print the raw value anyway. It also asserts the separator reached the render, so a site that dropped the text cannot pass for the wrong reason, and that a body which types the fence's own closing marker cannot close it. The [#1475](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1475) census ratchet caught every sink going away and is re-baselined at 158 sites in 34 files, with `UNRESOLVED` at 106 after locating the added site rather than before.

## [0.41.0] - 2026-08-13

### Added

- **`watch:github-issue-feed:<scope>` — GitHub issues, watched as a population rather than one at a time** ([#525](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/525)). Labels land, assignees change, someone answers a question you asked days ago, and until now nothing in `watch` noticed. Six bundled sources covered pipelines and merge requests; none covered the thing that *starts* the work. The scope is a filter string — `@open`, or `state=open,label=lane-watch` for exactly the label-triggered handoff the issue was filed about — and every poll is one `GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/issues` call whatever the population size. Eleven events: `issue_opened`, `issue_reopened`, `issue_entered_feed`, `issue_labeled`, `issue_unlabeled`, `issue_assigned`, `issue_unassigned`, `issue_comment_added`, `issue_closed`, `issue_left_feed`, `issues_unreachable`.

  **It is a feed and there is deliberately no per-id companion, which is the opposite of what #525's body asked for.** The body specified `watch:github-issue:<n>`; the issue's own comment then argued that shape cannot serve the case that motivated it, and the comment is right — a label-triggered workflow fires on issues no poller was spawned for, and *was an issue created* is unanswerable by construction from a watcher over a number that already exists. The reason no per-id tier is needed on top is specific rather than a preference: `gitlab-mr-feed` has to spawn per-MR pollers because pipelines, conflicts and approvals are absent from its list payload, whereas every fact #525 named — `labels`, `assignees`, `comments`, `state_reason`, `created_at` — is carried by the population rows themselves. So this source has one tier, no fan-out, and none of the cross-tier duplicate suppression ([#434](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/434)) that a second tier would require.

  **An arrival gets three answers, not one.** `issue_opened` is claimed only when the row was created after the previous poll's own recorded instant; a number this feed watched close and then saw return is `issue_reopened`, observed rather than inferred; everything else is `issue_entered_feed`, which reports the arrival and carries `created_at` and `state_reason` without asserting a cause the population query cannot establish. GitHub leaves `state_reason: reopened` on an issue permanently, so reading it as an edge would announce a reopen that happened months ago as one that happened now.

  **A population that could not be established is never a short one.** A gh failure, junk JSON, a scope carrying a filter token this source cannot apply, or more rows than the five-page cap all return no population at all and emit one `issues_unreachable` per outage — not once per poll. Returning the prefix that fit would fire a departure event for every issue past it, which is this repository's house defect wearing a page cursor. `known`, `observed_at` and `closed_recent` survive the outage untouched, so recovery re-announces nothing.

  **Pull requests are dropped, and that is load-bearing.** `GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/issues` serves issues and pull requests from one array and distinguishes them only by a `pull_request` key — 2 of the 79 rows on this repository at the time of writing. Without the drop, every PR anyone opens arrives as `issue_opened`.

- **Two claims in [#525](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/525)'s design notes were already false when it was filed, and both were re-derived rather than carried forward.** It states that the `gitlab-mr` source excludes `comment_added` from `DEFAULT_ONLY` because `user_notes_count` counts system notes. `presets/watch/defaults.py` has carried `comment_added` in `DEFAULT_ONLY` since [#519](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/519), and the belief it was held out for was itself disproved there against a live instance over twelve merge requests. The GitHub analogue is sound for the same reason: REST `comments` is a count of issue comments, so a label edit does not move it and `issue_comment_added` cannot fire with nothing to read.

- **`gh-pr:N:status` and `gl-mr:N:status` are pinned to the same fact set, and two divergences the pin caught are fixed** ([#628](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/628)). The two ops are visibly forked from a common ancestor with nothing holding them together, so improving one side reached the other only if somebody remembered. [#620](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/620) is what that costs: an identical `_load_payload` defect in both `issue_create.py` files, fixed on one side by hand. `tests/test_gh_gl_status_parity_628.py` renders both ops against merged and open fixtures and refuses any fact one side carries and the other does not.

  The bar is `docs/validators.md`'s three-state contract applied to output shape rather than to checks: **every fact one side reports, the other reports or explicitly declines.** "Not applicable on this platform" is an answer; silence is not. So the code stays forked — sharing a renderer fights real API differences — and the *test* is the thing that fails the day one side improves alone. Divergences are legal only with an entry carrying a reason: `mergeable:`/`merge_status:` and `checks:`/`pipeline:` are recorded as one fact under each platform's own vocabulary (`MERGEABLE`/`CONFLICTING`/`UNKNOWN` and `can_be_merged`/`cannot_be_merged`/`unchecked` do not share a domain; a flat list of check runs and a pipeline whose jobs nest in stages do not share a shape), and `review:` is the single exemption, because GitHub's `reviewDecision` rides in a call already being made while GitLab approvals cost a separate request on the poll-loop render. Three further tests stop that list decaying into a record of every divergence nobody could be bothered to fix: a paired spelling that stops being emitted fails, an exemption for a fact the exempted side now reports fails, and an entry with no stated reason fails.

  **`gh-pr:N:status` now prints `merged_at:`.** `gh pr merge` can print nothing on success, so a merge has to be read back off the remote — and this op answered only half of that, which cost four hand-rolled `gh pr view --json state,mergedAt,mergeCommit` calls in a single evening while the GitLab twin handed all three over free. `mergedAt` rides in the dashboard fetch already being made, so the line costs no extra call, and it prints unconditionally with `-` for absent the way `gl-mr` does: a key that appears only on merged PRs cannot be grepped for on an open one.

  **`gl-mr:N:status`'s `merge_status:` reads the same field `:full` does.** `:full` has always been `merge_status or detailed_merge_status or "?"`; `:status` was `.get("merge_status", "?")` — same file, same payload, strictly less, on the render read most often. A key present and empty never reaches a `.get` default, so the line rendered **blank**, which reads as a rendering bug rather than as an unanswered question; and GitLab deprecated `merge_status` in favour of `detailed_merge_status`, so an instance that has stopped populating the old key got a literal `?` printed over a value already in the fetched payload. `?` still means unknown, and now only means unknown.

  **What was deliberately not changed:** `gl-issue`'s `Related MRs:` heading, against the wording drift reported on #628. It is not drift. `gh-issue` asks GraphQL `closedByPullRequestsReferences` — "will this close it", the distinction [#780](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/780) exists to protect — while `gl-issue` asks `related_merge_requests`, which is the broader set including MRs that merely reference the issue. Renaming it to `Linked` would make the word claim a stronger fact GitLab was never asked for. The reason is now recorded next to both the endpoint and the heading, so the next reader does not re-derive it as a bug.

- **`hooks/guard-selftest.py` — a bash-free check for whether the raw-command guard is enforcing on this host** ([#1378](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1378)). `hooks.json` invokes the guard through `bash`. Under native `cmd.exe` or PowerShell with no Git Bash and no WSL it never executes, every raw command an op supersedes runs unguarded, and the session is byte-identical to one where the guard ran and had nothing to say — the house defect at the platform layer, with no disclosure channel at all.

  **The disclosure cannot be a hook.** Every hook this plugin ships is a bash script, `session-start.sh` included, so a line added to one is a line that cannot run on the host it would describe; and [#1382](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1382) has already ruled that a non-zero SessionStart hook is a broken session on every platform to report a missing interpreter on one. So it is a check the user runs — `py -3 hooks/guard-selftest.py` on Windows, `python3 hooks/guard-selftest.py` anywhere else — written in Python because Python is what such a host has.

  Three states, the guard's own: `enforcing` (the wrapper ran here and denied a command the registry replaces, end to end through the shell it will really use), `could not run` (naming what was tried), and `nothing to test` (the registry replaces nothing, so `enforcing` would be an empty claim). It says plainly that it **cannot tell** whether Claude Code invokes the hook — that is not observable from there, and claiming otherwise would be the same absence-read-as-presence one layer up. A `bash` is chosen by what it does, not by what it is called: on Windows `bash.exe` on PATH is commonly the WSL launcher, which is not a shell and cost PR [#1399](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/pull/1399) four `windows-latest` legs.

  **The README said the opposite, which is what made the gap invisible.** Its platform section stated that a native `cmd.exe`/PowerShell host has no `Bash` tool "so there is nothing for the raw-command guard to gate". That is contradicted by this repo's own [#1413](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1413): where the PowerShell tool is enabled Claude treats PowerShell as the primary shell and routes shell commands through it, which is why `hooks.json` matches `Bash|PowerShell`. There are commands to gate and no bash to gate them with. The sentence is gone and the check is documented in its place.

  Windows evidence grade, the [#627](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/627) convention: everything here about native `cmd.exe` and PowerShell is **reasoned, not observed** — nobody on this project has that host. What is observed is that the wrapper is bash, that `hooks.json` names bash, and that denying a POSIX host a usable bash produces exactly the state described.

- **CI now lints the files a pull request adds, copies or renames — and nothing else** ([#1481](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1481)). An error that arrives already dead was invisible to both existing gates at once. The pytest matrix runs no `ruff check .` step, deliberately: a tree-wide gate reds an unrelated contributor's PR the day the linter ships a new rule, and that cost is paid by whoever pushes next. The post-edit `ruff` validator covers the other side, but only for what an edit newly *introduces* — and a file split, a rename or a new module arrives whole, introducing nothing relative to a baseline it does not have. PR #1473 merged 22/22 green with three unreachable imports in a file it created, every edit to which truthfully reported `ruff : ok (no new errors)`.

  The new `lint-new` job scopes to the diff rather than the tree, so "pre-existing" is not a category the checked paths can be in and a new ruff rule only reds a PR already touching the file. Neither existing gate is reversed.

  **Two things the issue's own body had wrong, re-derived before building.** It states that `F401` is enforced repo-wide; `pyproject.toml` in fact carries a global `ignore = ["F401", "F841", "F541"]` from [#797](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/797), so a plain `ruff check` of the offending file at `ffe47ed` returns `All checks passed!` — the gate as described would have reproduced the green it was filed against. That ignore was bought against 263 pre-existing findings in files that have a history, so the three rules are re-enabled for paths that do not, and the debt stops growing without anybody paying it down. And the offending file is `R065` in `git diff --name-status -M`, not `A`: a gate scoped to additions alone would have missed the instance it exists for, which is why copies and renames are in the filter. Measured cost of that, rather than assumed: 141 of 902 tracked `.py` files carry one of the three today, so renaming one reds until its author deletes the dead line — on the person moving the file, which is the test `tests.yml` sets.

  **Three states on every run, and the third is the point.** `ok`, a `finding`, and `declined` — an unresolvable base ref, no ruff, a checker that could not start or timed out. An unresolvable base yields an empty file list, an empty file list is one branch from "nothing to check", and "nothing to check" prints exactly like "I checked and it was clean". That equivalence is the whole of #1481 and must not be reproduced by the fix for it, so those arms exit 2 rather than 0. A push, which has no PR scope at all, is named `skipped` rather than left silent.

- **`git-push:budget=SECONDS`** ([#1530](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1530)). The push had a fixed 300s budget and no way to ask for more, which on any repository whose pre-push hook runs a test suite makes a push to the default branch impossible rather than slow. Measured live: `FAIL (302.86s)` on a one-line docs commit, against a full suite that took 530.71s and 288.17s in two worktrees the same night. The three routes that existed were each wrong differently — `:no-verify` skips the gate the hook exists to be and is the flag a caller reaches for because it is the only one that helps; raw `git push` is refused by the shipped guard, which names this op as the remedy; a retry costs another 300s and fails again. It bites hardest during a release, where the version-bump commit goes to `master` by definition.

    **Refused, never clamped.** An unreadable value, a non-positive one, two `budget=` tokens that disagree, or anything above the 1800s ceiling stops the op before it pushes, naming the token and why — the same contract an unknown flag has had since [#647](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/647). A budget quietly rounded down to 300 is that defect wearing this one's clothes: the caller believes they asked for twenty minutes and the clock cuts in five. The ceiling exists because the budget has to stay strictly under `ops.git-push.timeout` (raised to 1920s to hold it), or a push killed by supertool's outer cap cannot ask the remote what landed ([#399](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/399)).

    **Not self-sizing, deliberately.** The op can see that a hook would run and knows the destination ref, so it could size itself from "protected branch plus a hook exists" — but it cannot see what any hook *does*, and "master means the full suite" is this repository's convention, not a property of git. A guess that is low is the original defect with extra machinery; one that is high makes a genuinely hung push wait out somebody else's suite length. What decides the number is the load on the caller's machine at the moment they push.

    The timeout receipt is unchanged in substance — it still reads the remote back, refuses to infer success from a clock, names the pre-push hook as the likely consumer of the time, and forbids a force-push on a timeout alone. It gains the remedy it lacked and now reports the budget that actually cut rather than interpolating the default.

### Changed

- **The PreToolUse guard imported 25,000 lines of `_supertool` and spawned two interpreters before deciding it had nothing to say about `ls`** ([#1377](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1377)). That is a tax on every Bash call of every plugin user, and it is now paid only by commands that could actually be replaced.

  **What the cost actually was, measured rather than assumed.** macOS, median of 15 runs of `hooks/pre-bash-guard.sh` on `ls -la /tmp`: whole wrapper 301ms, of which a bare `python3.13 -c pass` is 52ms and importing `_supertool` is 194ms. In-process after the import: `_load_config` 2.2ms, `_guard_replacements` 0.1ms, `guard_command` 0.1ms. The issue listed three costs and ranked them wrong — **the registry walk is not a cost**, three orders of magnitude below the term it was named beside, and the interpreter probe is 52ms of 301 rather than the largest. The import is the cost.

  **One interpreter spawn per call, not two.** A candidate used to be proved a Python 3 by a throwaway `-c` run and then spawned again for the real answer. The envelope the real run writes proves the same thing and more, so the wrapper now reads the first bytes of the answer instead. [#1402](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1402)'s protection against a launcher that prints a preamble survives as a prefix test rather than an equality test, and [#1390](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1390)'s "ran and said nothing" stays reachable — no envelope, no verdict, next rung. A rung that fails now advances instead of declining outright, so a host with a broken `python3.14` and a working `python3.12` keeps its guard.

  **`_supertool` is not imported at all when the command names nothing the registry replaces.** The word list is read straight off `presets/*.json` with a flat scan that returns "unknown" on anything unexpected. `_find_preset_file` resolves three tiers and all three are accounted for: the shipped and the user-level `~/.config/supertool/presets` are scanned for words, and a project `.supertool.json` — or a project `presets/` that is not the plugin's own — declaring any `replaces` turns the fast path off wholesale rather than being parsed. The user tier was missed in the first draft and found in review: a project enabling a user-level preset has no literal `"replaces"` anywhere in its own tree, so nothing bailed and the word was not in the list either, and the command ran unguarded. `tests/test_guard_hook_cost_1377.py::test_a_user_level_preset_is_not_invisible_to_the_screen` pins it. Reproducing which words a project override contributes is `_op_registry`'s job ([#1356](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1356) says so), so nothing is cached and nothing is re-implemented: the check is cheap and the answer stays the real guard's. `tests/test_guard_hook_cost_1377.py` pins the containment against `guard_command_words` preset by preset, which is what keeps two readers of one registry from drifting apart silently.

  Interleaved A/B against `origin/master` on one host, 4x25 runs per arm, min of the two medians: `ls -la /tmp` 307.5ms to 114.4ms, `pytest tests -q` 307.9ms to 112.6ms, `git push` 305.8ms to 262.1ms, `echo $HOME` 301.5ms to 262.9ms. Output byte-identical on all four. A macOS number, and macOS is the platform whose spawn cost this project can see — where a spawn is 150-800ms the two removed interpreter startups are worth more than they are here.

  **What it costs, stated.** A command that names nothing replaced no longer gets the `undecided` note about a part of it that could not be read — `. ./script.sh` no longer says its argument went unread. That is the narrowing [#1413](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1413) already applied to the PowerShell disclosure, for the reason it gives there: a line under every command anyone writes is one nobody reads. A command containing `$` or a backtick is never fast-pathed, because expansion can produce a replaced word the text does not contain, so the DENY direction loses nothing.

### Fixed

- **A dying interpreter had the fragment of its verdict forwarded as the verdict** ([#1377](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1377)). #1377 removed the guard wrapper's separate probe spawn, so an envelope on stdout became both the proof that a candidate is a Python 3 and the answer itself, matched as a prefix. The exit code stopped being consulted. An interpreter killed part-way through `sys.stdout.write` — OOM, a signal, a launcher wrapping the child — leaves a *prefix* of that envelope, which is exactly what the prefix test accepts: `hooks/pre-bash-guard.sh` printed the fragment verbatim and exited 0. Claude Code cannot parse it, so there was no decision and no `additionalContext` at all — the silent fail-open the wrapper's own header exists to refuse, in the shape [#1347](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1347) opens with.
- An envelope is now forwarded only from a rung that also exited 0, which every path through `hooks/pre_bash_guard.py` does by construction. This is not the pre-#1377 shape returning: a rung that fails is still only recorded and the walk still continues to the next name, so a host with a broken `python3.14` and a working `python3.12` keeps its guard. What it costs is a whole envelope followed by a non-zero exit for an unrelated reason, whose answer is dropped — bash cannot tell that from a fragment, and dropping it buys a disclosed decline where forwarding it buys silence (#1377).
- The decline now distinguishes the two failures, because they send a reader to different places: a rung that "began writing a verdict and then exited N" is a dying interpreter, where "exited N without writing a verdict" is one that never answered. **The first of those is sticky**, reported in preference to the last rung's generic failure — the walk continues past a dying rung, so a message built from whichever rung was tried last named one that was never going to answer and buried the one that crashed mid-write (#1377).

- **On a Windows host with no bash, one dead hook was disclosed and the other was not** ([#1401](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1401)). `hooks.json` runs both shipped hooks through `bash`, so the same missing shell kills both — and the two failures are not alike. The guard's is *silent* — it is asked (the matcher has been `Bash|PowerShell` since [#1413](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1413)), it cannot run, and a session where the gate never ran reads exactly like one where it ran and found nothing. `SessionStart` is gated by nothing at all, fires under any tool configuration, and its failure opens the session with no `./supertool` wrapper and no op roster. `hooks/guard-selftest.py` — the one channel that needs no shell — reported only the guard, and the README's platform section pointed a reader at that note as if it were the whole cost. The more visible loss was the unwritten one.
- The self-check's `could not run` state now names `hooks/session-start.sh` alongside the guard, says what the session loses, and gives the way back, which needs no shell either: call the tool by path — `py -3 supertool.py 'ops:roster'` on Windows — and read `./supertool` in the docs as that path (#1401).
- **The gap itself is accepted and disclosed, not fixed, and the reasoning is now written down rather than re-derived.** Adding `args` switches the hooks to exec form, where `command` *is* resolved on `PATH` — the `CreateProcess` search that finds System32's WSL launcher under the name `bash` — so the obvious repair introduces the defect; `tests/test_hook_interpreter_windows_1401_1402.py` refuses it. Rewriting the hooks in Python does not escape it, because exec form would still have to name an interpreter and none is portable: `python`/`python3` are the App Execution Alias stubs [#572](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/572) banned for blocking rather than erroring, `python3.9`–`python3.14` are absent on a standard Windows install ([#1402](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1402)), and `py -3` is absent everywhere else. Resolving that is what `hooks/python-ladder.sh` is for, and it is itself a shell script (#1401).
- Every claim here about native `cmd.exe`/PowerShell is graded **reasoned, not observed** (the [#627](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/627) convention): nobody on this project has that host, and CI's twelve legs cannot reach it either. What is observed is that both `hooks.json` entries name `bash`, that `SessionStart` carries no matcher, and that denying a macOS host a usable bash produces exactly the state described (#1401).

- **The #1206 shim gate read the quoting instead of the defect** ([#1419](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1419)). `tests/test_git_shim_subcommand_1206.py` scans the suite for shell shims that decide a git subcommand from `$1` — the defect being that git's global flags precede the subcommand, so `git -C <path> status` puts `status` in `$2` and the shim silently stops standing in. The scan was anchored on `"[$]1"`, which matches `$1` only inside double quotes, so `[ $1 = status ]` and `[ '$1' = 'status' ]` were the same defect and invisible to it. A meta-test whose zero means "nobody in this suite has this bug" was reading one spelling of three — the house defect, relocated into the detector — and self-corroborating, because every shim it has ever caught was written in the style it reads.
- The gate is now quoting-blind: quotes are stripped before the grammar is applied, so double-quoted, single-quoted, bare and `${1}` spellings are one rule rather than one rule each, and a style nobody has invented yet arrives already handled. It also reads `[[ ... ]]`, `test ... = ...`, `case $1 in`, the `[ x$1 = xstatus ]` idiom that guards an unset `$1`, and a comparison written backwards as `[ status = $1 ]` (#1419).
- Widening the match alone would have been wrong. The question the gate asks is whether `$1` is *tested*, not whether it appears, so it now keys on the shell constructs that decide on a word. Six literals in the suite hold a bare `$1` that decides nothing — three `awk '{print $1}'` field references and three shellcheck fixtures spelled `rm $1` — and a match widened to any occurrence turns all six red; a gate that cries wolf gets its allowlist grown until it means nothing (#1419).
- What the widened scan actually found across the 696 modules it reads (698 `test_*.py`, less itself and the one filename exemption): five literals test `$1`, four of them exempt because the operand is an option (`-3`, `-c`) and git's grammar leaves an option no position to slide to, one the pre-existing `test_watch_mine_defaults.py` exemption where `$1` really is a supertool op. **Zero new defects.** The judgement half [#1412](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/pull/1412) derived from git's grammar holds under the wider match, and the three original #1206 shims are still caught verbatim (#1419).

- **`edit`'s nearest-match hint scored the first non-blank line of the anchor and nothing else, so a multi-line anchor was pointed at whichever copy of its boilerplate came first.** The run that filed [#1489](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1489) was sent to a line ~800 away from the correct one, at an identical 68%, twice: `SequenceMatcher.ratio()` of a `def` line is a fact about that `def` line, and every copy of it in the file scores the same. Raising the floor was the wrong repair — the number is not too low, it is measuring something else — so the metric moved instead. A multi-line anchor is now located by a sliding multiset of whitespace-normalised lines over every window of the anchor's height (O(file)), then char-scored on the top-ranked windows only, and the receipt names the window: `nearest match at lines 804-806 (91%): read:app.py:804-806`.

- **The hint has a third state.** Where two or more positions score within 2 points of the leader, `cannot suggest a nearest match: N places score the same (91%) — lines 1, 44` replaces the coin flip, because a confidently wrong line number costs more than no line number: the caller reads the wrong 30 lines and re-anchors against them (#1489).

- **The same scan could not be finished on a minified file, and said nothing about it.** `_EDIT_DIAG_MAX_LINES` bounds the diagnostic by line COUNT — the one dimension a minified bundle is small in — while `SequenceMatcher.ratio()` is O(len(a) × len(b)). Measured on 60 lines of 40 KB with a 39 KB anchor: 220s for a single comparison and over 30 minutes for the file, on a courtesy that runs on a failure path. Each comparison is now clipped to 1000 characters, the total is capped in cells, and a percentage computed over a clipped line says `scored on the first 1000 characters` rather than presenting a prefix score as a line score. An exhausted budget is a decline, not a best-so-far reported as a best (#1489).

- **`grep`'s `… (+N chars)` named no way to recover the line it cut.** That is what a caller wants precisely when the cut line is the `edit` anchor they came for, and the run that filed #1489 dropped to `python3` to read the raw bytes. A `note:` above the results now gives the call — `read:PATH:LINE-LINE` returns the whole line byte-exactly — with the first cut line's own coordinates as the example. The read render was suspected of being lossy and is not: measured byte-identical to raw on files from 500 to 20000 chars with tabs, trailing spaces and unicode, so the remedy existed and was simply not written where the truncation happens (#1489).

- **`read:PATH:OFFSET:LIMIT` disclosed the OFFSET:LIMIT grammar twice, the second time under the output it would have saved.** [#1432](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1432) moved this disclosure above the body; a trailing `note:` from #382 stayed behind and repeated it, after the reader had already paid for the 60-line window it was warning them about. #382's gate is unchanged and still decides which of the two guesses is offered — it now writes its clause into the `window:` line instead of a second paragraph of its own (#1489).

- **`restartMcp` server names reached a supertool-authored status line unflattened.** A name is an arbitrary JSON string and `', '.join` would put a line of its choosing at column 0 — a second `mcp: restarted 9 daemon(s)` the tool never said. Lower severity than #1583's five payload-key sites, since these come from `.supertool.json`, which #146's trust note places at the same level as the validators and custom ops declared beside them; routed through the same `_flat_keys` anyway, because the alternative is one call cheaper and leaves every future reader to re-derive why (#1489).

- **`watches` on a named channel listed the default channel's pollers as its own orphans, and `radar`'s reap stopped them ([#1514](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1514)).** `transport.poller_argv` writes the label every reader matches on, and it carried `(source, id)` with no channel dimension. So a scan under `SUPERTOOL_WATCH_NAME=oss-supertool` enumerated every labelled poller on the machine, found no pid file for the other channel's ones under *its* state directory, and rendered four of them with `no pidfile` — the one marker an operator acts on, and `unwatch:SOURCE:ID` on any of them would have stopped a watcher belonging to a different channel. Two renders in one call disagreed: the board listed four watchers, `channel:health` said that channel had never spawned anything.

  **The reap was the sharper half and the issue had left it open.** `dispatcher.reap_duplicate_pollers` reads the same scan. One poller per channel on the same `(source, id)` grouped as one slot with two pollers; the survivor is the PID *this* channel's pid file names, so the other channel's was signalled. A cross-channel kill, reached through a listing bug.

  **The label now carries the state directory, digested, as a trailing `chan=` token.** The slot is a pid file held `O_CREAT|O_EXCL` by one process per state directory (#476), so two pollers are on one slot only when they contend for one pid file — which makes `STATE_DIR` the right dimension, not the channel name: a name and an explicit `SUPERTOOL_WATCH_STATE_DIR` can name one directory, and two names can be pointed at one. A digest and not the path, because `ps` output is split on whitespace and an operator-supplied directory may contain some, because `ps` is world-readable, and because a fixed 12 characters keeps the command line readable. Appended rather than inserted, so `dispatcher._parse_args` — which already ignores unrecognised trailing tokens — parses a re-exec'd poller back unchanged.

  **Three states, and only one is acted on.** `transport._labelled` now answers `(channel, source, id)` where the channel is this one, another one, or `None`. `scan_poller_pids` returns only the first, because every caller of it decides an action: `unwatch`'s multi-kill, the reap's signal, the board's `no pidfile` marker. A PID is acted on only when its own argv proves it is ours.

  **What that costs, stated rather than hidden.** A poller started before the `chan=` token carries no channel and becomes invisible to the scan. It is not reported as this channel's and not as another's, because nothing in its argv can tell them apart. That is the same by-design blindness `docs/presets/watch.md` already describes for pollers predating the #511 labelling, one generation later, and it clears the same way — `pkill -f 'presets/watch/'` once, or a `radar` tick that respawns the fleet. A poller whose pid file this channel holds is unaffected: `watcher_pids` unions the pid file's own PID, and the pid file is per state directory by construction.

  **Windows.** No platform-specific code and no path literal. The key is `hashlib.sha256` over `os.path.normpath(STATE_DIR)`, so a trailing separator cannot split one directory into two channels, and the parent and its exec'd child agree by construction because `poller_env` pins the resolved value into the child's environment rather than letting it re-derive. Pinned by `tests/test_watch_channel_scoped_labels_1514.py`, which spawns, signals and reaps nothing: the process table is a list, liveness is a set, and `_stop_pid` only records.

- **Three renders put somebody else's text at column 0 — a watch note, a job step name and a verbose validator message** ([#1522](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1522)). A value from outside supertool was interpolated into a render without `_untrusted.flat`, so an embedded separator wrote a whole line where the tool's own structural lines live. `presets/_untrusted.split_lines` was not the seam for any of them: it splits on LF/CR/CRLF *by design*, because it is the parser-side helper (#1081), and U+2028/U+2029/U+0085/VT/FF are exactly what walked through in #1470. It is unchanged. The fix is flattening at each render.

  The reproduction: a newline in `SUPERTOOL_WATCH_SOCK` forged a second `watches: ...` row claiming everything was fine. The sweep found the class was wider than the three instances filed — the same two environment variables reach nineteen interpolations across `naming`, `channel`, `transport`, `dispatcher` and the `gh-prs` tier — so `naming.flat_path` is one seam all of them now use. It takes `disclose_newline=True` (#1557): a path can contain a newline and rendering it as a space names a directory that is not on disk. The values used to `connect()` and to `listdir()` are untouched — flattening a path before *using* it would be a different defect.

  `presets/github/run.py` flattened a failed job's name cell and not the step names printed under it, which are whatever the branch's own CI config called them. `op_format(verbose=True)` rendered an adapter's `msg` with `.strip().replace(newline, " ")` — one separator out of the ten `str.splitlines()` breaks on, and a lone carriage return returns the cursor to column 0 without making a line at all — where every sibling render already used `_flat_cell`.

  Found while testing that last one and fixed with it: `_formatter_render_row` interpolated the adapter's `name`, `raw` and `msg` into its own row with no flattening whatsoever, and cut `msg` at 120 characters with no marker, so a message that ended there and one that was truncated read alike. The validator twin has routed all three through `_flat_cell` since #895. `raw` keeps its lines — it is a block, and the reader asked for the tool's output verbatim — but every line after the first is now indented under the row. `op_format`'s silent-no-op arm builds its own row instead of calling that function, and flattens its name the same way; that one is the seam rather than a live hole, since `_formatter_run_one` overwrites the name on every arm with the configured key.

- Typing `gh-since-tag`, the release-gate op [#1405](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1405) deleted into `gh-prs`, answered `Did you mean: gh-prs (preset 'github')` and stopped there — and bare `gh-prs` is every open PR on the repo, a different board from `gh-prs:merged-since=TAG,state=merged`, which is what the caller typed. `_OP_SYNONYMS`'s own header states the rule it was bending (*a synonym carries a NAME, not an invocation*) and then cited the mechanism that closed the gap: the target's description, "which the unknown-op message already prints for a preset op". It did not, and never had — `_near_miss_ops` pairs a candidate with a provenance label (`builtin`, `preset 'github'`, `project op`) and nothing else. The suggestion line now carries the target's registry `syntax`, which names the release-gate invocation — at its end, after 243 characters of filter grammar, because that field is carrying prose that belongs in `description`. Printed whole rather than split on the `  --  ` between the two halves: 86 shipped ops declare a `syntax` and exactly 1 contains that separator, so splitting would be a convention inferred from a single field (#1524).
- Only the synonym route, never an edit-distance guess. The synonym table is ops "whose intended target is a documented fact rather than a guess", and that is what pays for the extra line; `gh-prr` yields two candidates from edit distance, and a syntax line each would put ~500 characters of filter grammar above a roster [#1222](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1222) already fought to keep readable. A target with no registry `syntax` — every built-in, so `write -> paste` and `vi -> vim` — prints nothing extra (#1524).
- The synonym suggestion fired only when the target op was **loaded**, which made a documented mapping silently conditional on the caller's cwd: run from a directory with no `.supertool.json` above it, `gh-since-tag` produced no suggestion at all, the bare unknown-op hole #1405 went to some lengths not to leave. A shipped-but-not-loaded target is now named and labelled as such (#1524).

- **A live `gh` API call ran on the per-push critical path, so a network hiccup — or a runner with no credentials — reddened legs that said nothing about the change under test** ([#1568](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1568)). `tests/test_watch_radar_gh_prs_859.py::test_live_board_over_this_repo` shells out to real GitHub. It exists because the fixtures in that module cannot produce the shapes real GitHub does.

  **It is now `slow`, which in this repo means it runs on a schedule rather than nowhere.** `.github/workflows/slow-tests.yml` selects that marker daily on one ubuntu leg and its header exists to make exactly this distinction; the job now carries `GH_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }}` and `pull-requests: read`, so the test genuinely reaches the API there. Measured: it ran nowhere in CI before this. The `gh auth status` probe that used to guard it exits non-zero on a runner with no credentials, so it skipped on all twelve legs of every run since it was written — the marker moves it from nowhere to somewhere, and takes it off the path where a rate limit can red an unrelated diff.

  The token is deliberately **not** set on the twelve pytest legs. That would put a live call back on the per-push path, hand a credential to the environment of ~12,400 tests and the ~900 subprocesses they spawn, and buy nothing — the response is a JSON payload, identical on all three platforms, so twelve legs answer one question twelve times. It also sits against [#1341](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1341), whose autouse fixture refuses non-loopback sockets for every test and which `conftest` documents a subprocess as *escaping* rather than as being permitted.

  **Wherever it runs, the tier now tells "the API did not answer" apart from "the board says X".** `presets/watch/tiers/gh_prs.py` raises `RadarUnreachable` — a `RadarError` subclass, so radar is untouched — from every arm where the request never landed: spawn failure, timeout, a signal kill, a rejected token, throttling, or the socket. `RadarUnconfigured` narrows that to the standing case, keyed on `gh`'s own exit code 4 rather than on its prose: measured on gh 2.50.0, both spellings of "no credentials" exit 4 and nothing else does, while a *rejected* token exits 1 with `HTTP 401` and every product failure exits 1. That distinction is exact — a rejected token means the request landed. Everything unrecognised stays a plain `RadarError` and stays red, because the alternative swallows a product bug wearing a flake's clothes.

  **The skip is countable, and the two states are counted apart.** `tests/_live_gh.py::reachable` skips on those classes and re-raises everything else; `conftest` prints `live-gh(#1568): N of M skipped tests did NOT reach the live GitHub API` every run including at zero, breaking out how many of the N were the unconfigured kind. One number would make the second unreadable: after a token is set its expected value is 0, so a non-zero one is a finding about the workflow — but only if it is not summed with a transient blip whose expected value is not 0 ([#1274](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1274)'s argument, one level over). The three counters `conftest` now prints share one reader instead of three copies of the same `longrepr` walk.

- **A colon argument the dispatcher peeled and never read was dropped, not refused, on every fixed-slot read op.** `read:CLAUDE.md:::lines=66-76` returned all 102 lines — 13549 bytes where about 1500 were asked for — because `lines` is not one of read's fields and nothing said so. This is the worst shape the class has: an ignored *narrowing* returns MORE than was asked for, and more always reads as a superset of correct, so nothing in the render distinguishes it from a call that did what was typed. Measured on `2c8eaf9`, twelve read ops were probed with one junk token appended and twelve answered and dropped it. Every non-empty token past the last slot an op reads is now refused, naming the token and quoting the op's own `syntax` line; `lines=A-B` additionally gets the range form spelled out for the call it was typed on, because that is the spelling a reader reaches for after seeing `START-END`. The one documented colon key, `read:PATH:::grep=PATTERN`, is unchanged (#1582).
- **`grep:PAT:PATH:5:3:2` ran limit 5 and context 3 and dropped the `2`** — exit 0, no note, a well-formed answer to a question nobody typed. The parser peels every trailing digit and reads two; it never compared the two counts. The identical argument had already been written down beside the `all` case #1328 closed, and only `all` was fixed there. Refused now, naming the slot order. `all` outside the LIMIT slot keeps #1328's more specific message (#1345).
- **`read:PATH:START-END:full` from a human shell returned lines START..EOF, and the window note called it `range START-EOF (START-END form)`** — the END the caller typed discarded, then laundered by the line written to disclose the window. Found while auditing read's tail for the above. `full` and the byte cap were one flag: `full` lifts the *default* line cap, and a range is not a default. The two lifts are now separate, so the byte cap stays off (`read:BIG:1-5000:full` still comes back whole) and the window the caller typed is honoured (#1582).
- **A ranged read that ends on the last line declined to say which of the file end and the limit closed the window, one line under a header printing the file total.** `end == total` decides it, and the two callers it separates want different next actions — one has everything from line N, the other hit a cap and needs a wider window. The file end now settles it and the limit is still named beside it. The genuine tie, the byte cap and the limit landing together with file remaining, still declines (#1342).

- **Five refusals rendered a caller-written payload key name unflattened, so a newline in it put a whole line of somebody else's choosing inside a system-authored denial.** A TOML or JSON key is an arbitrary string; `', '.join(unknown)` therefore let a key spelled `x`, newline, `  the edit was applied to probe.txt (1 replacement)` render its second half at column 0 of a refusal, on a path where nothing was performed. The two arms #1551 added (`_at_file_to_parts`, and the batch-wrapper unknown-key arm) plus three pre-existing siblings — the batch sub-op unknown-field and no-declared-field-order arms, and `_read_op_from_payload`'s unknown-field arm. The issue named four; the sweep found five, and the fifth is reachable with any batch sub-op that has no declared payload field order. All five now go through one `_flat_keys` helper built on `_flat_field`, the repo's single implementation of "this value occupies exactly one line" across the ten separators `str.splitlines()` folds on. `_flat_field` rather than #1554's `_guard_quote`: the two differ only by a cap that is `guard_refusal`'s own byte budget, and a truncated key leaves the caller unable to find the field in their own payload — the refusal still has to name it. An ordinary key is printable and renders byte-identically, non-ASCII included. `lower_payload` lowercased the key on four of the five, which bounded the forge to lowercase prose and did not close it — every op's own body text is lowercase prose, and the batch-wrapper arm sorted the raw keys, so an uppercase `SYSTEM:` line was reachable there (#1583).
- **A sixth site, found by sweeping the file rather than the four the issue named, and it is a different mechanism.** `_toml_literal_double_backslashes` excerpts the caller's own payload VALUE for the doubled-backslash note and refusal, and calls the excerpt a "line" — but it cut on `chr(10)` alone. This repo's own definition of one line is `str.splitlines()`, ten separators (#886), so a U+2028 (and eight others) survived inside the excerpt: a `content` literal block holding `U+2028` then `the file was written (0 changes)` then a doubled backslash put that sentence at column 0 of a refusal, and the same shape under `old` put it at column 0 of the note. The excerpt now goes through `_flat_field` at the point it is built, so the tuple's third element means what its name says at both render sites rather than at neither (#1583).

- **A file `[tool.ruff] exclude` covers was reported `ok`, count 0, by a run in which ruff never opened it** ([#1587](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1587)). The adapter passes `--force-exclude`, which applies the project's `exclude` patterns to the single explicit path it names. A match makes ruff exit 0 with an empty JSON array — byte for byte a clean file — so the receipt carried a verdict nothing had earned. Inert on this repo, which sets no `exclude`; live for anyone who does.

  **The zero-finding arm now asks a second question.** `ruff check --no-cache --force-exclude --show-files <file>` resolves the same configuration and prints the paths that survive exclusion; an empty list means the file was never opened, and the result is `skipped` naming the exclusion instead of `ok`. It runs only where the answer is ambiguous — a run that reported findings has demonstrably read the file — and costs one extra spawn, ~50ms measured against ruff 0.16.1 on macOS and not measured on Windows, where process creation is dearer. It shares the lint's own 30s budget rather than carrying a tighter one, so a loaded machine cannot decline a file the lint itself had time to read. A probe that cannot answer returns `skipped` too, because a zero it could not attribute is not a pass, and the reason names no single config key — the flag enforces `exclude`, `extend-exclude` and ruff's built-in defaults at once, and `--show-files` reports the outcome rather than the cause.

  **The decision behind that shape: an `exclude` entry governs the file you just edited, so the honest answer is a decline rather than a lint.** The other coherent repair was dropping the flag, which is what the [#1481](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1481) release gate does — correctly, because its question is whether anything unlinted reached the tree and its file list is built by hand from a diff. A post-edit validator asks a different question, and `eslint` had already answered it the same way one adapter over: a file matching an ignore pattern is `skipped`, not `ok`. Two adapters in one directory answering it two ways is worse than either answer alone.

  Asking ruff rather than reading `pyproject.toml` is deliberate — exclusion resolution walks up for `pyproject.toml`/`ruff.toml`, honours `extend-exclude`, and carries a default list (`.venv`, `build`, `node_modules`, …) a hand-written check would drift from on every release. `respect-gitignore` is not part of it: measured on 0.16.1, a gitignored path handed over explicitly is still linted.

### Security

- **A path the tool picked up reached ruff's option parser, and the gate reported it clean** ([#1609](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1609)). `.github/scripts/lint_new_files.py` built ruff's argv with no separator token, and its file list comes from `git diff --name-status` — values the tool picked up, never arguments anyone passed. The `.py` suffix filter was the only barrier, and a filename suffix is not a security property: a file named `--stdin-filename=x.py` passes it, is consumed as an option, leaves ruff with no positional path, and ruff exits 0 with an empty stdout — so the gate printed `all clean` about a file nothing opened. That is [#1481](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1481)'s own failure mode inside the gate written to close it. `validators/ruff/ruff.py` takes the same token in both invocations — the `--show-files` scope probe from #1600 and the main `check` it inherited the omission from — where the direction is safe but the sentence is not: the adapter emitted `skipped` blaming an exclude that is not there. Measured with ruff 0.16.1.

## [0.40.0] - 2026-08-13

### Changed

- **The `SessionStart` hook's behaviour on a native Windows host with no Git for Windows is stated rather than fixed** ([#1401](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1401)). That host has no `Bash` tool, so the `PreToolUse` guard never fires there — but `SessionStart` is not tool-gated, and it loses the `./supertool` symlink and the op roster every session. Nothing inside a `.sh` file repairs a host that cannot run a `.sh` file: `args` would switch the entry to exec form and introduce the `PATH` search the issue was originally about, a second PowerShell entry would break every POSIX session to serve one Windows one, and a string valid under both `sh -c` and PowerShell is a polyglot shipped to every plugin user on the strength of a Mac.

  `docs/configuration.md` now carries the gap with its evidence grades — which claims are *observed* and which are *reasoned from Claude Code's documentation* — because nobody on this project has a Windows box and CI's twelve legs cannot settle it either.

### Fixed

- **A test-only cache exempted from the per-test reset could preserve an *empty* answer for a whole xdist worker** ([#1322](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1322)). `conftest.RESET_EXEMPT_GLOBALS` listed `_REPO_TARGET_MODES` and `_SHIPPED_PRESET_OPS` as process-lifetime state, on the reasoning that they describe the install rather than the run. True of their inputs, false of the values: both are `None` at import and built at first use from `_INSTALL_DIR`, which tests patch. A cache built under that patch is empty, and being exempt it survived the teardown that would have rebuilt it — after which `_repo_target_ops()` reported that no op accepts a repo target and every `repo:` call refused every op it was handed.
