  Both names moved to `RESET_GLOBALS`, and `_reset_module_state` learned to rebind a `None` sentinel rather than clear a dict in place: clearing leaves a *built and empty* map, which is indistinguishable from "this install declares no repo-targetable ops" and is the defect itself.

  **The reported flake no longer reproduces on this base, and that is not the same as fixed.** A full run under `-n 8` with a teardown probe on the cache saw 12246 pass and zero poisoned teardowns, so nothing in the suite currently populates it under a patch. The mechanism was still live: adding one test that patches `_INSTALL_DIR` and calls the builder took `test_repo_target_673.py` from `32 passed` to `6 failed, 26 passed`, and back to `32 passed` with this change. `tests/test_lazy_cache_lifetimes_1322.py` now fails the build when any new `None`-sentinel name is added to the exempt tuple, so the classification cannot go stale again in silence.

- **The preset transport seam is now enforced by the socket rather than by a convention** ([#1341](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1341)). `presets/_http.py` binds `_OPEN` at import and every preset calls through it, so a test that stubs `MODULE.urllib.request.urlopen` replaces a name nothing consults: the request goes out to the real host and the test passes on whatever comes back. Two tests in `tests/test_security_error_echo_691.py` were in that state for months, one of them a credential-redaction regression test whose injected payload had never once been delivered ([#1312](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1312) repointed them).

  Repointing the stubs was not the fix. `monkeypatch.setattr` and `mock.patch` already raise on a name that does not exist, so *renaming* `_OPEN` would redden its stubs; the defect was the opposite shape and no rename check reaches it, because the stubbed name existed and was live — it just was not the one the product calls. `tests/_netblock.py::block_outbound` is now armed by an autouse fixture in `tests/conftest.py` for every test in the suite, instead of being a per-file fixture each author had to remember.

  The fixture builds its own `pytest.MonkeyPatch.context()` rather than requesting the shared `monkeypatch` fixture, and that is load-bearing. It is autouse and defined early in `conftest.py`, so it is set up first and torn down last; asking it for `monkeypatch` instantiates that fixture there and moves `undo()` past `_guard_repo_git_state`'s teardown. `test_git_resolve.py` and `test_git_resolve_validate_scope_876.py` patch `os.path.isfile` to `lambda p: True`, CPython 3.13+ routes `Path.is_file()` through `os.path.isfile`, and the git guard's after-snapshot then read every *directory* under `refs/heads/` as an unreadable ref — 18 teardown errors across those two files, blaming tests that had changed nothing, plus a nineteenth in a concurrent worker via the shared-repo fan-out #433 documents.

  **Named blind spot, because a green here must not be read as "nothing reached the network":** it binds `socket` in the pytest process only, so a test that shells out to `supertool.py` or a preset gets an unpatched child. The static `tests/`-side grep the issue proposed is deliberately not shipped alongside it — #1312 measured a grep for transport tokens at 2 of 3 live leaks against the socket recorder's 3 of 3, and a second guard whose green means strictly less than the first one's is how a green stops meaning anything.

- **The SessionStart hook no longer spawns the bare name `python3`, and both shipped hooks now resolve one shared ladder** ([#1382](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1382)). `hooks/session-start.sh` ran `python3` directly while `hooks/pre-bash-guard.sh`, a few lines away in the same directory, went to some length not to — #572 banned that name from every spawn position because on Windows it can resolve to the App Execution Alias stub and on a stock macOS to the Xcode Command Line Tools stub, and both *block* rather than error. At session start that is not an error anyone can act on; it is Claude Code taking a hook timeout to come up and then saying nothing about supertool.

  The ladder moved to `hooks/python-ladder.sh` and both hooks source it, so the next hook written here inherits the decision instead of making a third one. What each caller does when no rung answers stays its own: the guard declines in words and allows the command, and the session hook now prints one line naming the rungs it tried and exits 0 — keeping the `./supertool` symlink, which never needed an interpreter at all. Not a bare `python3` as a last rung, which would preserve the hang for exactly the hosts with no alternative, and not a loud failure, which is a broken session on every platform in order to report a missing interpreter on one.

- **27 preset scripts died mid-render on a Windows console, not 2** ([#1388](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1388)). `gh-starred` printed `→` and `gh-find-starable` printed `★` straight to stdout. Run straight from a shell — no supertool in front to pin `PYTHONIOENCODING=utf-8` — a console codec with no mapping for the character raises `UnicodeEncodeError` partway through the output, so the work lands and the receipt says it crashed. Every preset entry point that prints a non-ASCII literal of its own now calls `use_utf8_stdout()` as the first statement of `main()`, from the new `presets/_console.py`.

  The issue named two instances; the census says 27, and which ones die depends on the codepage rather than on the file. cp1252 encodes `—`, `…`, `•` and `·`, so only `→` (`starred.py`), `★` (`find_starable.py`) and `↳` (`mcp/status.py`) raise there. cp437 and cp850 — the actual default of a US Windows console — encode none of the em dashes, so all 27 raise. Observed on macOS against a real cp1252 stream, not reasoned: `PYTHONIOENCODING=cp1252 python3 presets/github/starred.py 5` printed two lines and then died on U+2192, while the same call through `supertool gh-starred:5` under the same environment completed.

  **No exemption route, deliberately.** The issue asked for a per-literal rule — a glyph goes through a degrading writer or declares an exemption — and worried that a loose exemption makes the scan's zero meaningless. The per-literal framing is what does not survive: there are 325 non-ASCII print literals in shipped code, `_untrusted` exposes no writer for a glyph the *tool* wrote, and the property that decides whether a `print` survives is `sys.stdout.encoding` — settled once per process, not per literal. At that granularity nothing an entry point could state would make a raising `print()` acceptable, and the precondition costs one line.

  `tests/test_encoding_seam.py` enumerates it in three states rather than two: pinned, unpinned, and **unreadable** — an entry point printing a glyph whose `main()` the rule cannot find. The `presets/git/` scan it generalises has two states and silently `continue`s past that third, so such a file has always read as compliant; ten preset entry points are in that shape today and pass only because none of them prints a glyph. Both floors are asserted too, so a zero means the scan looked rather than that it stopped looking.

  **Knowingly left stale, because the file is held by another branch:**
  `presets/_untrusted.py`'s docstring argues that reconfiguring stdout to UTF-8
  "is the wrong one here", written when no module that imports it did so. 23 of
  the 27 entry points changed here import `_untrusted`, so on a genuinely cp437
  console `_stream()` now always reads `utf-8` and prints guillemet markers
  where [#863](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/863)
  intended the ASCII fallback. The behaviour is unchanged on the supertool path,
  where `PYTHONIOENCODING=utf-8` already produced it; the paragraph is what needs
  correcting, and the correction belongs with whoever next holds that file.

- **`docs/contributing.md` said the subprocess-encoding scan skipped `tests/`** ([#1388](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1388)). It has held `tests/` to the same rule as shipped code since #862, and the paragraph still described the pre-#862 exclusion and cited 125 violations that are not there.

- Eleven `paths/` jit rules declared a `mode:` that no reader consumes, and the two spellings sitting side by side are what made #1442 ask which rules should fire less often. A paths row is `pattern<TAB>file`; `build_path_tsv` reads only `match:`; and `pre-path-hook.sh` dedups every paths rule per session *before* the pattern is tried. So all of them are already once-per-session, none can be `block`, and adding `once` to the two lacking it would have changed nothing. The measurement: on 2026-08-12 `jit-context.md` (no `once`) and `docs-index.md` (`once`) fired at the same three timestamps — the repeats are one per session across parallel agents, and `once` was never the variable. The inert lines are removed and a test refuses new ones (#1442).
- The per-match body budget selected its `paths/` half by that same dead field, so it happened to guard a 3,023-byte rule while exempting a 5,847-byte one — an arbitrary line, not a lenient one. Tools rules keep the 3,200-byte per-match ceiling; paths rules now get a per-session ceiling of their own, set the same way the first one was, as a ratchet just above today's largest (#1442, #1433).

- A failing `git add` under `git-commit` used to answer every caller with `Paths are separated by ':::' — not by commas, not by spaces`, whatever route they were on and whatever the pathspec held. On the `@payload` route that is the *other* route's convention quoted at someone who followed this one, and two agents in one afternoon re-read the syntax they had got right; the payload refusal now names the shape this route wants — `paths` is a TOML array, one entry per path — and offers the split of a `:::`- or `,`-joined entry as a question. Where no separator is in play at all, a single path spelled wrong, the note is now withheld rather than reworded: git already named the fault and there is no one-line remedy to add, and a fresh wrong remedy reads as a freshly checked one (#1489).

- **A re-exec'd poller never re-verified its state directory, because the path it inherited looked operator-supplied ([#1534](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1534)).** `transport.poller_env` pins the resolved state directory into the child's environment (#1477), so the child's `naming.resolve` saw an explicit `SUPERTOOL_WATCH_STATE_DIR` and set `state_dir_is_derived` to `False` — the flag every establishment guard is behind. `naming.ensure_state_dir` returned `""` without asking anything, so `claim_pidfile` and, since #1540, every `write_state` in a poller skipped the check entirely. The parent verified once before the spawn and nothing re-established it after: a race window on the public, committed leaf `/tmp/supertool-watch-<name>`, not an open door.

  **The flag conflated two facts and is now only one of them.** *The operator supplied this path* is theirs, and manufacturing it would trade a loud refusal for a poller spawned into a directory nobody asked for (#693). *This is the path the name derives* is ours. `state_dir_is_derived` is now equality with `state_dir_for(name)` — a question about the **value**, not about which variable delivered it. That needs no marker to survive the exec and adds nothing new to forge: an environment naming a *different* directory is the operator-supplied case it always was, and one naming the derivation is asking for the directory this code already owns.

  `state_dir_env_set` carries the other half, and only `state_dir_provenance` reads it. That function feeds the operator-facing refusal in `dispatcher.py`, which under the old flag sent a re-exec'd poller's operator to `SUPERTOOL_WATCH_STATE_DIR`, and under the new flag alone would have told them the variable is unset inside a process whose own environment sets it.

  **Two more things the same equality removes.** Both precedence notes read `... is set and overrides the name: poller slots are in /tmp/supertool-watch-oss, not /tmp/supertool-watch-oss` — and the same for the socket — in every re-exec'd poller, because `poller_env` pins both halves. An override notice for an override that did not happen, on the one surface this module exists to keep trustworthy. Each note is now gated on the value actually differing. And the establishment is re-asked per write in the child exactly as #1540 specified for the parent, rather than memoized by accident of the exec.

  **Windows.** No platform-specific code and no path literal: the comparison is against `state_dir_for(name)`, the same f-string that produced the value. `_image_root.ensure` is unchanged and keeps its own documented Windows split — `lstat` in place of `O_NOFOLLOW`, ownership and mode declined rather than faked. Pinned everywhere by `tests/test_watch_poller_state_dir_reverify_1534.py`, whose one subprocess spawns `sys.executable` and does not shell out.

- `lsp-diag` read cclsp's `Found N diagnostic(s) for X:` header as framing, dropped it, and never compared `N` against the records its parser actually built — the one place the adapter could notice its own parse had lost something. It now reconciles the two and discloses a disagreement as a `code: "adapter"`, `severity: "warning"` record naming both numbers and the direction: fewer records than `N` means findings may be missing and the receipt's count is a floor, more means records were built that the server never framed. Agreement is silent, and so is output carrying no header at all — no number is a different fact from two numbers that match, and a disclosure firing on every run is one nobody reads. `N` is read from the first physical line only — not the first line that carries something, because echoed source reaches the start of a physical line through an unescaped LF or one of the five inline breaks, so a leading newline would let the file choose the number. In the bulletless variant, where the server sends no header at all, a first line matching the header shape end to end is indistinguishable from one; that is contained rather than solved, by the record being `severity: "warning"` — a forged `N` buys one misleading advisory line and cannot make `ok` false, reach `NOT CHECKED`, or revert an edit (#1537).
- The same header is now the interlock on a clean verdict the file wrote for itself. `lsp-diag` matches `No diagnostics found` and `no errors, warnings, or hints` as substrings of the whole tool output, so a diagnostic *message* quoting either phrase returned an empty finding list for the entire file — a `.py` or `.php` comment erasing every real diagnostic on it, the #482 shape reached from the inside. Genuinely clean output carries no `Found N` header, so a header claiming entries alongside that phrase is now reported as a disagreement instead of rendering the file clean (#1537).

- `phpstan` exiting 0 with nothing on stdout is now `skipped`, not a clean pass. The adapter synthesised `{"totals": {"file_errors": 0}}` for that case, which is `ok: true` about a file nothing opened. Measured against phpstan 2.1.55, a clean run under `--error-format=json` always writes its object — `{"totals":{"errors":0,"file_errors":0},"files":{},"errors":[]}` — so silence there is a run that produced no report, not a file with no findings (#1547).
- `phpmd-mcp` no longer throws away a report it was handed. The `structuredContent["error"]` branch returned before `structuredContent["output"]` was read, so a run that set both published a message about the analysis in place of the analysis. The report is parsed first now and never dropped — both its bodies, the violations under `files[]` and the processing failures under `errors`: a genuine runtime error is one additional error beside them, and a scope refusal is dropped rather than counted, because a declination and a report are two mutually exclusive claims and only one of them carries evidence — the same rule #1527 applied to the cold phpstan adapter. Whether the `mcp-phpmd-warm` server can set both keys is not answerable from this repository, so the adapter no longer depends on the answer (#1547).

- The stock refusal patterns in `validators/common/refusal.py` now carry their provenance. `"--paths allowlist"` and what `refusal.outside_roots()` emits (`path outside <VAR> allowlist`) were read as a drifted pair; they are two mechanisms that never meet — the patterns classify the *analyser's* own message, and `outside_roots()` is a local short-circuit whose string goes straight to `skipped()` — and neither side was wrong. `"--paths allowlist"` is live: it is a substring of the daemon's measured emission `analyse: path is outside the configured --paths allowlist.`. Each pattern is now paired in the suite with the emission it was written for, or named explicitly as a spelling variant nobody has seen fire, so a pattern that matches nothing stops being indistinguishable from a refusal that never happened (#1548).

- The mutating `@payload` route was the one input surface that dropped an unrecognised key without a word. `edit:@-` handed a `count = N` ran with no count and answered `found 3 times - ambiguous` — correct about the match, silent about the constraint the caller believed they had applied. An unknown key is now refused by name against the op's own `syntax` fields, alongside `replace_all` on `edit` and the route keys `op` and `literal_backslashes`, which is the line every other surface already held (#1551).
- The same drop one level out: the top of a `batch` payload read `ops` and `continue_on_error` and ignored everything else, so a misspelt `continue_on_error` ran the rest of the batch past a failed op while the payload said to stop. Refused now, naming the key and the accepted set (#1551).

- The raw-command guard blocked `git commit` and named the `git-commit` op, in a directory where no preset op is loaded because no `.supertool.json` sits above it — a remedy that cannot run where the command was refused. The block now says where the named op is loaded from and that it does not exist outside such a project, so the round-trip is not spent learning it (#1554).
- Worse, and found while fixing that: the op's own unavailable-here refusal offered `cwd:<project-path>` without saying that `cwd:` moves the directory the op **acts on** as well as the one its config is read from. Obeyed from a throwaway repository under a scratchpad path, that commits a different repository. Both spellings of the refusal now state the scope and say plainly that for a repository no project covers this op has no route to it (#1554).

- `_dropped_tokens_refusal` told the caller to widen a `{file}` template to `{args}` — the exact manoeuvre the module declines to make internally, and for the stated reason that it puts a second path downstream of the containment check. Measured on a fixture op declaring `"paths": {"args": [1], "root": "cwd"}`: position 1 was refused and, after obeying the advice, position 2 printed a file outside the boundary. For an op that declares a containment boundary the refusal no longer offers that remedy at all. It names the positions the declaration actually gates, says that extending the `args` list alongside a widened template is necessary and not sufficient — a fixed index list holds an unbounded `{args}` tail only up to the highest index it names — and states that there is no one-line `cmd` change that keeps such an op contained. An op declaring `"args": []`, or none at all, keeps the plain remedy (#1560).

- The `supertool-no-cut` jit rule spanned a command separator, so a *different* command's pipe refused the op before it: the wildcard between the op string and the bar excluded only a newline, and walked straight through `;` and `&&`. A compound call whose `tail -2` belonged to the `pytest` after the `&&` was blocked, with a refusal naming a cut that was not happening — three wrong blocks on 2026-08-13, on top of the four in one evening #1433 records. The span now stops at `;` and at `&&` (#1565).
- `|` and a bare `&` deliberately stay inside that span, against the issue's own proposal to exclude all three separators. A genuine cut of an op's output routinely has both: the cut need not be the first stage (`gh-job:N:raw` into `grep` into `awk` is real, and was already pinned), and `2>&1` before the bar is the commonest spelling of one in this repo's transcripts. Only `&` followed by another `&` or by whitespace is a separator, so the span reads `([^;&\n]|&[^&[:space:]])*` rather than a flat negated class. Both directions are pinned through awk itself, and the fix was driven end-to-end through the real hook: eleven of eleven, four false blocks gone with no real cut lost (#1565).

- **The committed jit-context indexes are now derived state, so regenerating them is a no-op** ([#1579](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1579)). `.claude/jit-context/*/00-manual/00-index.tsv` had been part hand-typed, and `rebuild-tsv.sh` — which lives in the sibling `claude-jit-context` repository, not here — cannot know that. Measured against the tree as committed: two `require:` columns dropped, the `pyproject.toml → version-sites.md` paths row deleted, `once, remind` respaced, and both files reordered. Every regenerated row is well-formed, so `jit-index` reports `ok` on the weaker file.
- The three that were data now live in the frontmatter the generator already reads: `require:` on `merged-is-not-ancestry.md` and `git-C-has-cwd.md` (`build_tool_tsv` has read that field all along — the issue's "no frontmatter field expresses those columns" was wrong for the tools family), and `pyproject.toml` folded into `version-sites.md`'s own `match:` as an alternation, since the paths column is handed to awk `match()` and one entry file yields exactly one row. Verified through the real hook: both paths still reach the rule, both blocks still fire, and `git status` and `git -c user.name=x commit` still do not (#1579).
- **No rule is broader than it was.** The paths row loss was the only change in coverage — a `require` on a `mode: block` rule cannot alter the verdict, because the block is unconditional either way; it decides the refusal text, and on a `remind` rule it would be the verdict. Both columns are pinned by name so a future "just regenerate it" cannot satisfy the round-trip by deleting them (#1579).
- `tests/test_jit_index_round_trips_1579.py` re-derives both indexes from the frontmatter in Python and diffs them. Deliberately a reimplementation rather than a call to the script: the script is in another repository, and a test that skips when a neighbour is not cloned is a test that never runs in CI — which is how this drifted unseen. `CLAUDE.md` and the `jit-context` note also had the tools row as `tool⇥match⇥file⇥mode⇥keyword`; there is no `keyword` column, and calling `require` and `forbid` something else is part of why nobody put them in the frontmatter (#1579).

## [0.39.0] - 2026-08-13

### Fixed

- **A custom op's `{file}`/`{arg}` got only the first `:`-token and the rest was discarded in silence** ([#873](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/873)). `{file}`, `{dir}` and `{arg}` substitute `parts[1]` — the first argument and nothing after it — so an op registered as `"cmd": "tool.py {arg}"` and called as `op:all:dry` ran with `argv == ["all"]`. No warning, no error, no mention in the receipt. In the filed case that token was a safety flag: the op ran in live mode and force-pushed two branches while its caller read the receipt as a dry run, and two "fixes" to the script's own flag parsing passed their unit tests because they were written against an argv shape the tool never produces.

  Refused now, above the subprocess, naming the text it will not pass and pointing at the placeholder that would have carried it. Not passed through: widening a single-token placeholder to the whole remainder would interpolate `parts[2:]` into `{file}`, whose `"paths"` declaration gates index 1 only — a second path-shaped token arriving downstream of the containment check, which is the failure [#1135](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1135) was filed about — and it would change what all 24 `{arg}` ops shipping at the time receive, several of which index their `|`-separated fields positionally. The refusal sits after `_preset_path_containment`, so it adds no path slot, moves none, and a call that both escapes the boundary and drops a token still reports the escape.

  **Preset ops take the same route** — one `_resolve_custom_op`, one substitution pass. The difference was never the kind of op, only which placeholder its author picked: zero shipped presets write `{file}`, 58 wrote `{args}`/`{argjoin}` and got every token, 24 wrote `{arg}` and got one — 61 and 21 after the three repairs below. So the trap was undocumented and invisible, and it had already fired inside the shipped set: `hashnode_list`, `devto_list` and `hashnode_search` each documented a second `[:N]` token and each split its one argument on `:` for a field discarded upstream — the documented limit was never honoured and the default was used in silence. All three now take `{args}` and rejoin. A test walks every manifest, so an op documenting a token its `cmd` cannot reach is red at write time.

  The issue proposed exit 2 for this, citing #647. There is no exit-2 route in this core — a refusal is an `ERROR:` line and the run exits 1 — so it follows the house shape instead.

- **A filename could forge a `[rolled back]` or a `[result]` line** ([#1019](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1019)). `--- {arg} ---`, the op header printed above every answer, and `edited {path} (line N)`, the edit receipt's own success claim, interpolated their path raw — and so did every line of `_path_not_found`, the shared "not found" refusal. A path is not always typed by the operator: `validate:` walks a tree, a batch payload carries one, and a repository that accepts contributed fixtures is named by strangers. `str.splitlines()` breaks on ten separators, so a file called `a<U+2028>[rolled back] forged.txt` wrote two forged marker lines at column 0 *above* any genuine one, and a reader — or the anchored grep the receipt is written to be read with — saw a rollback that did not happen against a file that had in fact been edited.

  Every path these renders print now goes through `_flat_field`, the one implementation of "this value occupies exactly one line" (#886). `_flat_field` and not `_flat_cell`: the row variant strips and bounds its value, and a header that silently drops a trailing space or truncates a long path is answering about a different file. Disclosed, never stripped — the name still reads, as `[U+2028]`.

  Every path these helpers *use* is still the raw one. The stat, the `abspath` and the join run on the name the filesystem holds, so the refusal keeps naming the path that was actually opened (#1300).

- A post-edit lint that blew its wall-clock budget no longer reddens the suite as though the product had failed ([#1360](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1360)). `test_xml_lint` broke `pytest (windows-latest, 3.10)` on PR #1355 with one failure in 9711: the product declined correctly — `POST-EDIT LINT TIMED OUT — xmllint (30s)`, naming the knob — and the test converted that decline into a red leg. That is this repo's own defect class relocated into the thing meant to detect it. [#553](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/553) is the same failure at a 5s budget, so raising the number a third time buys an interval of quiet against an unbounded tail, not a fix.
- Three states, not two: `tests/_lint_budget.py` sits in front of a verdict assertion and returns when the checker reached a verdict, **skips** carrying `lint-budget(#1360)` when it timed out, and **fails** otherwise. `conftest` prints the count, its denominator and its population every run including at zero, so `N skipped` on a Windows leg resolves to `N did not reach a lint verdict here` rather than reading as coverage.
- The skip is deliberately narrow, because the alternative trades the loud bug for the quiet one. A `POST-EDIT LINT DECLINED — could not start the checker (FileNotFoundError)` is [#997](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/997)'s Windows-only spawn failure and stays red; so does a *timeout* naming a budget that is not the one `SUPERTOOL_LINT_TIMEOUT` resolves to, which is the knob not reaching the subprocess — a product bug wearing the flake's clothes, told apart without guessing because the receipt states the budget it used.
- Applied to the class, not the instance: seven sites across `.php`, `.xml` and `.py` assert a verdict from a subprocess-backed checker, and `py_compile` spawns a fresh interpreter — the more expensive of the two. `tests/test_lint_budget_gating_1360.py` derives that population from the AST rather than listing it, asserts every member is gated, and asserts the population has not collapsed to nothing, which is how a hand-listed register passes vacuously ([#1232](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1232), [#1274](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1274)). "Gated" means a real **call** to the gate **above** the first verdict assertion — #1232's `_called_before` lesson, and both halves are load-bearing: a gate written below the assertion it guards is #1360 verbatim, since the assertion runs first.
- The gate reads `_supertool._LINT_TIMEOUT_PREFIX`, now named in the product and used by the branch that emits it, instead of matching a copied message. A predicate that sniffs prose to tell an environment limit from a finding is one reword away from swallowing the finding.
- `pytest_terminal_summary` no longer returns early when one gating helper is absent from the tree, which would have printed the symlink verdict and silently omitted the lint one — the same absence, one layer up.

- **A child process's stdout reached a receipt at column 0 in seven more places, and nothing detected the eighth** ([#1475](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1475)). The class behind #1470, which closed it for `git-push` alone. `gh` echoes the GitHub API's own error body on its stderr and a commit hook writes whatever it likes, and both reached a line the tool owns with no `_untrusted` call in between. `_untrusted.split_lines` cuts on LF / CR / CRLF only, by design (#1081), so a U+2028 survives *inside* a relayed line and puts everything after it back at column 0 for any consumer that splits the way `str.splitlines()` does.

  **The fix is at the seam, not at the sites**, which is the whole argument: seven named sites is what a per-site fix earns, one re-filing per call site. `_git_common._first_error_line` now flattens what it returns, so `git-commit`, `git-push` and whatever is written next are covered at once — `_untrusted.flat` is idempotent, so the callers that already flattened pay a no-op rather than a second substitution. It also parses with `_untrusted.split_lines` instead of `str.splitlines()`: a writer who put a U+2028 in a line was choosing which line the error scan returned, and the tail it hid was dropped from the receipt rather than disclosed. `pr._format_error` is the single sink both `gh-pr` error prints share and flattens there; `gh-pr`'s diff header and diff-failure reason go the same way. `git-commit`'s whole refused-commit render moved into `_failure_receipt`, which relays the hook's transcript with `split_lines`, then `visible(keep=tab)` per line, so tabs survive and separators are shown rather than dropped. *(Corrected in [#1569](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1569): this said "exactly as `git-push` relays its own", and it was not — the `> ` prefix was dropped, so the hook's lines still sat at column 0. The relay is now one shared `_git_common.relayed_block` and the claim is true.)*

  **The detector is the part worth more than the seven, and it is a ratchet rather than a gate — deliberately.** An AST scan for "a child stream reaches `print` or a `return` without a marker" reports **174 candidates in 36 files** across `presets/git`, `presets/github` and `presets/gitlab`. Not every one is a defect (`push._local_head` returns `r.stdout.strip()`, and that is a SHA), and closing them is four lanes of work. So `tests/test_forged_child_stream_line_1475.py` records a **count per file that may only fall**: a new relay anywhere in those trees raises a number and fails, a fixed one lowers it and fails with the message telling you to write the smaller number down. It is not an allowlist — there is nothing to add a site to, and both directions are one visible line in a diff. What it does not catch is stated in the test: a relay added to `push.py` in the same commit that fixes another one nets out. That is the price of a ratchet, and the gate costs 174 fixes first.

- **Three `gh-run` / `gh-pr` test fixtures stubbed `subprocess.run` for every call, so a run's JSON payload was fed to commands nobody modelled** ([#1488](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1488)). `monkeypatch.setattr(run.subprocess, "run", ...)` sets the attribute on the shared `subprocess` module, so it replaces every spawn in the process rather than the preset's own. With a fall-through, an unmodelled command was answered with the payload — a fixture that answers every spawn cannot tell "the product rendered this" from "my stub echoed this", and the bar this repo applies, *would this still pass if the code did nothing?*, cannot be evaluated at all while it is that wide. Each fixture now models the commands it stubs and raises `unstubbed command` on anything else.

  Narrowing found a live instance rather than only a latent one. `presets/_declared_legs.py` reads `gh api .../jobs?filter=all` as the **second** leg source, and the fall-through handed it the run payload — which carries its own `jobs` list, so it parsed. The second source was silently the first source: [#804](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/804)'s own defect ("a second source read through the first one is not a second source") reproduced inside #804's fixtures.

  One of the two suites the issue names as unfixed, `tests/test_gh_run_matrix_reconcile_804.py`, had already been narrowed under [#850](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/850); `tests/test_gh_pr_run_coverage_804.py` had not, and its fall-through also recorded the unmodelled command as the `gh pr view` argv it reported having fetched.

- **`gh-issue` wrote attachments into a fixed world-writable `/tmp` path, and joined an API-supplied number onto it with no check at all** ([#1506](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1506)). Two defects in one file, and they are [#1493](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1493) and [#1484](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1484) one forge over, both already fixed for `gl-issue`. `IMAGE_DIR` was the literal `/tmp/supertool-images/gh` — a fixed name any local user can take first, as a directory of their own or as a symlink pointing anywhere, and a POSIX literal that anchors to the current drive on Windows. And `os.path.join(IMAGE_DIR, issue_number)` took `number` straight out of the `gh issue view --json` reply: no numeric check, and no containment check anywhere in the module. `_local_path` sanitizes the basename, so the *directory* component was whatever the remote said. An absolute number makes `os.path.join` discard the root outright; `../x` resolved outside it. Precondition class is #1484's: a hostile or compromised host on the other end of the API call, since `number` is server-assigned.

  Three checks now, and their order is most of the fix. A non-numeric number is refused **before the root is created** — a directory created is already a write and no later guard un-creates it, so the traversing and absolute cases leave nothing on disk at all, not even the root. Then the root is established by `_image_root.ensure(default_root("-gh"))`: `gettempdir()` plus a per-uid suffix, created non-recursively at `0700`, held open `O_RDONLY | O_DIRECTORY | O_NOFOLLOW` with the `fchmod`, the ownership check and the mode check asked of that one descriptor. Then every leaf is checked against **that root**, never against the derived per-issue directory — anchoring a check to the value it is meant to constrain was #1484.

  **The root is a sibling of `gl-issue`'s, not a child.** `supertool-images-<uid>-gh` beside `supertool-images-<uid>`, so each is established in its own right and neither depends on the other having been created first.

  `_is_inside` moved to `_image_root.is_inside` rather than being copied. Two forge presets asking the same containment question against a root the same module hands out is two chances for one copy to drift; `presets/gitlab/issue.py._is_inside` keeps its name and delegates.

  **The eight `#817` cases that asserted a refused image leaves no directory now assert it leaves no *per-issue* directory, and that is a re-aiming rather than a relaxation.** The property somebody paid for is that a refused issue leaves no record it was ever read, and `_http.download` still makes the destination's parent only after the body has passed the destination policy and the byte cap — so `<root>/<number>/` is still absent. The root is not a record of anything: it is per-user, says nothing about which issue was fetched, and after any one successful call it exists for the life of the temp directory, so "the root is absent after a refusal" only ever held on the first call a machine ever made. It is also the boundary those destinations are checked *against*, and a boundary that does not exist yet cannot be proven to be ours — which is the whole of #1493.

  **`gl-issue` establishes the per-issue directory a second time and `gh-issue` does not, deliberately.** That second call is what would create `<root>/<number>` up front — the record a refused issue must not leave, which `gl-issue` has no equivalent of because it writes through `glab` rather than through `_http.download`. What it buys there is covered here by the leaf check: a link planted at `<root>/<number>` resolves outside the root and every URL is refused before `download` is reached. What is not replaced is the `0700` on the per-issue directory, which `os.makedirs` leaves at the umask default — not load-bearing inside a root only its owner can traverse, which is why the root's mode is checked and this one's is not.

  **The two seams the issue named were both declined.** Hoisting the destination decision out of `download` duplicates a security check. Adding a `prepare` callback to `download` puts a new refusal grade and a caller-supplied predicate into a module four other presets import, for its one caller, to buy a property that decomposes instead.

  **A destination refusal is a refusal, and it still produces one `ImageResult` per URL.** A root that cannot be established, or a leaf that does not resolve inside it, is graded `refused` with the reason — not dropped, and not shortened out of the list, because a URL that vanishes reads as an issue that did not have that image. The `## Images` footer now says whether the URL or the destination on this machine was refused, instead of advising every refusal be answered by widening the allowlist.

  A number carrying a bare CR is flattened through `_untrusted.flat` before it is printed, so the value cannot overwrite the line printed about it — the same rule the refused URLs on the lines below already followed.

  **Windows.** The old value was a POSIX literal anchored to the current drive; `gettempdir()` resolves inside the user profile there, which is not the shared directory the finding rests on. The `O_NOFOLLOW` branch is absent, so `_image_root` uses `os.lstat` and refuses a symlink or a reparse point, and the ownership and mode arms are *skipped* rather than faked. Those claims are inherited from #1493 and are **reasoned from CPython's documented behaviour, not observed on a Windows host**. The new tests carry no POSIX path literals: the traversal is built from `os.pardir`, paths are compared as `Path` objects, and the mode assertion is gated on `hasattr(os, "geteuid")` rather than passing vacuously.

- **`node --check`'s line number was published under a different definition of "line"** ([#1507](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1507)). V8 treats U+2028 and U+2029 as ECMAScript LineTerminators; `split_lines`, `source_context` and a reader's editor do not ([#1486](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1486)). So one U+2028 inside a string literal — legal since ES2019, ordinary in a minified bundle — shifted every line number after it, and the shift was in the gift of the file under validation. Measured on node v22.22.1: a two-line file whose first line held one had its line-2 syntax error published as **line 3**, with `source_context` rendering lines 1-2 and the arrow on neither. `node-check` and `html-check` now map the reported number back through `linebreaks.lf_line_of_v8_line`, and a number no counting of the file can reach is published as `line: null` with the number disclosed in the message rather than as a location the file does not have.

  `html-check` reached it through its own arithmetic: a block is padded with LF so node's numbers already are the page's, which holds exactly until the body carries one of the two. The page's line 4 was published as line 5. It maps against the exact text node read, so nothing depends on the temp file outliving the check.

- **The forge #1507 was filed about turned out to be unreachable, and that is now pinned rather than asserted** ([#1507](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1507)). The shared `LOCATION` pattern really does mis-capture across an inline break — `"real.js:12<U+2028>forged.js:99"` yields `("real.js:12<U+2028>forged.js", "99")`, [#1500](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1500)'s shape in two more adapters. What neutralises it is not the pattern but `diagnostic_line`, which compares the captured path's `normcase(realpath(...))` against the target's: a capture carrying a break and a second path cannot resolve to the file, so the forged number is discarded with it and `finditer` walks on to node's own header, which is the first physical line of the report and cannot have anything printed before it. Nothing is lost either — the genuine location is still matched, so this is not the "rejected, and the finding lands unattributed" outcome the issue's third branch describes. Tests pin the mitigation for both adapters and all five separators, so a later rewrite to a basename or suffix match cannot quietly re-open it, and pin the residual in the safe direction: where a fragment does reach a capture, the number is **lost**, never forged.

- **`gh-prs` counted unresolved review threads over one capped page, so a busy PR could lose its thread flag entirely** ([#1508](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1508)). #1491's defect one op over, and it lands on a flag rather than on a number: the board never printed the count, it printed `threads` when the count was non-zero. At `reviewThreads(first: 100)` that count is a floor, and a floor of **zero** carries no information — so a pull request with more than 100 threads whose first page happens to be all-resolved rendered with no thread marker at all, indistinguishable from one that has none. GraphQL returns threads in creation order, which puts the newest and least-resolved ones on the page nobody fetched.

  That is [#1445](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1445)'s mechanism reached by a second route. Not an omitted number: the removal of the one marker that would have made somebody look, on the read that decides which PR to open next. A row at the page cap with nothing unresolved on it now flags `threads?` — the same "could not be established" state a declined GraphQL call already used — and a line above the board says how many rows hit the cap, so that `threads?` is not confused with a call that failed.

  A floor **above** zero is untouched and still flags a plain `threads`. Once the render is a boolean, `at least 1 unresolved` and `1 unresolved` make the same claim, and hedging a number the reply does establish would be the same defect pointed the other way. The cap constant is imported from `gh-pr`, which is where the query that fetched under it is built, rather than copied.

- **`gl-mr` tallied one unpaginated page and printed the number as a total** ([#1517](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1517)). `Unresolved threads: 0 / 12` on a merge blocker, off a single `per_page=100` fetch — and GitLab pages oldest-first, so the threads that were never fetched are the newest and least resolved.

  `_fetch_array` does not paginate and is shared with callers that do not tally, so the fact is returned alongside the array instead of being fixed inside it: `_fetch_tally` reads the `per_page` back off the endpoint string it was handed, which is how the GitHub side's cap-constant guarantee is bought on a platform where the cap is a literal in an f-string URL.

  Four sites, not the three the issue names. The fourth is `## Comments (N)` off `per_page=50`, in the same render, with its own neighbouring comment already arguing the case: a wrong number is indistinguishable from a right one, where a missing line is at least visibly missing. A tally over a page that was **not** capped still prints exact.

- **Two counters in `gh-prs` rendered a measurement that never happened as one that found nothing** ([#1521](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1521)). The repo's house defect, on both halves of the same op.

  `merged-since=DATE` threw away `filter_merged`'s third return value. A row whose `mergedAt` will not parse has not been shown to be outside the window — it has not been placed at all — and the tag branch has always disclosed those as `UNPLACED: N`. On the date branch they vanished from the listing with nothing said and an exit of 0. Both branches now share one `unplaced_note`, so the same absence cannot be worded two ways again.

  `split_tagged_commit` returns `(rest, tagged, compared)` rather than two values. It returns early when the boundary carries no commit sha, and `tagged is None` there is identical to what a comparison that ran and matched nothing returns — so `assess` printed `boundary PR: none — no returned row's merge commit is the tagged commit` on a path where nothing had been compared to anything. That path now says `NOT COMPARED` and says what it rests on instead.

- **A pytest session in which every core-timeout-gated call declined now exits non-zero instead of reading as a pass** ([#1523](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1523)). [#1501](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1501) gave 42 unit-test call sites the right to decline when the core's own spawn wall fires, and nothing put a floor under that right: a uniformly loaded runner mutes the whole population at once, pytest prints `0 failed`, and the suite has said nothing at all about the validator core. `tests/_core_timeout_census.py` counts the gated calls themselves — not skipped reports, whose denominator moves with the platform — and prints `D of C gated calls declined` in the terminal summary whether the count is zero or not.

  Three states, not two: `NOT CHECKED` when no gated call ran in the selection (which is not a pass), the ratio when some declined, and a finding when *all* of them did. The bar is categorical rather than a percentage because the measured baseline is zero — `0 of 61` on a full macOS run — so any percentage would be a number nobody measured, and a false red on a slow Windows leg is the exact publication #1501 exists to prevent.

- **A `SUPERTOOL_WATCH_NAME` exported in a maintainer's shell can no longer decide what the test suite measures** ([#1523](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1523)). `tests/conftest.py` has cleared the three watch variables since the [#1502](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1502) fix, and nothing asserted that it does. CI exports none of them, so deleting those three lines was invisible to every leg while costing a maintainer five reds about their shell rather than their diff — a guard that was itself unguarded. Now pinned by a probe that resolves the socket path against `naming.resolve({})` rather than a `/tmp` literal, so the assertion means the same thing on Windows.

- **A repository that tags releases by date could not name its own tag, and two interpreters disagreed about which values are date-shaped** ([#1526](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1526)).

  `gh-prs:merged-since=` routes on whether the value parses as a date, and that question was answered by `datetime.fromisoformat`, whose grammar widened in 3.11. Measured on CPython 3.9.6 against 3.11.11: `20260809` and `2026-W32-1` raise on the first and parse on the second. So the same call was a date boundary at midnight UTC on one interpreter and a tag name hunted in the local clone on another, with nothing disclosed either way. The accepted spelling is now written out in `presets/_filter_tokens.py` — extended ISO-8601, the floor's grammar, on every interpreter.

  `merged-since=refs/tags/2026-08-09` is the spelling a date-tagging repository was missing. A bare date-shaped value is still read as the date, deliberately: `2026-13-45` is a typo in a date, and "no tag by that name" is the wrong sentence to hand whoever typed one. The refusal named a remedy this input had neither of; the full ref path is git's own escape, contains no `:`, and can never parse as a date.

- `phpstan` no longer reports a whole file `skipped` because a refusal phrase appeared somewhere in its output. The check ran `refusal.is_refusal` — a lowercased substring test — over `stdout` and `stderr` concatenated, and fired ahead of the two error arms below it, so a stock phrase in PHP bootstrap noise or any `PHPSTAN_SKIP_PATTERNS` entry the repo added turned a run that had *reported* into a non-verdict. Under `--error-format=json` the report is one JSON object on stdout and a declination is on stderr with stdout empty, so a skip now requires stdout to hold nothing beyond the refusal statement itself; anything else there means phpstan reported and the adapter could not read it, which is an `adapter` error and exits non-zero. That exit code is what the defect cost — neither verdict rolls back an edit, so the issue's `rollback_on_fail` framing does not hold (#1527).
- `phpstan`'s `phpstan output not json` error now carries the bytes that would not parse, capped at 200 characters, instead of naming the fault and none of its evidence (#1527).

- A worktree's `.git` is a gitfile naming the real git directory, so a `cp -a` copy of one shares it: every git command in the copy reads and writes the *original* worktree's index, HEAD and refs, and nothing said so. `git-status` and `git-worktrees` now lead with `⚠ COPIED WORKTREE` naming the tree the writes reach, and the `Repo:` line on `git-commit` and `git-push` — which exists to say where a write landed — carries it too, instead of naming the copy, which is the one directory the write does not reach (#1536).
- `git-status` used to render a staged revert written by a process in another directory as ordinary staged work. It cannot tell who staged something, so it now names what it could not determine: a staged path whose file on disk still matches HEAD is disclosed as `⚠ STAGED CONTENT NOT IN THIS TREE` — content no file here has, the shape a stray `git checkout <sha> -- <path>` leaves and equally that of a stage undone by hand — and the list is disclosed, never suppressed. A `git diff --name-only -z HEAD` that does not answer prints `⚠ Staged provenance UNKNOWN` rather than the silence that reads as clean — except in a repository with no commits, where there is no HEAD for the index to revert and the question is meaningless rather than unanswered (#1536).

- `channel:health` reported `FORWARDING` with no session subscribed to the channel, which is the one state it exists to catch: a consumer held the socket, verified as its own socket-holder and published fresh counters, while the session that spawned it had refused the channel tag at startup and every event was read and then discarded. A fifth state, `BOUND, NOT SUBSCRIBED` (exit 5), now carries that finding, and `radar`'s `DELIVERY` banner — the same producer-only view one surface up — says it too (#1543).
- Subscription is only partly observable from outside the target session, and `channel:health` now claims exactly the part that is: which process spawned the socket-holder, and whether the channel tag in its argv names an MCP server the harness has configured (`claude mcp get`, the same question `bin/supertool-workspace` asks before registering the consumer). No tag, an unconfigured tag, or a session that has since exited are definite negatives; anything that could not be asked — no `ps`, no `claude` on PATH, an argv that does not parse — is `CANNOT DETERMINE` with the reason, never `FORWARDING` (#1543).

- `bin/supertool-workspace` now registers the channel consumer itself, at local scope with an absolute path, instead of tagging `claude-channel` from the plugin's `.mcp.json` — whose `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}` is empty outside a plugin load, so that server never spawned and the workspace armed itself against nothing while the board rendered normally (#1544).

- **A directory name could write lines into `git-status`'s own report** ([#1557](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1557)). The copied-worktree banner added in [#1536](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1536) interpolated two paths raw, and both come off disk: `.git/worktrees/<name>/gitdir` holds whatever wrote it, and git itself writes the path handed to `git worktree add` into that file. So a worktree whose directory name contains a line separator put text at column 0 of the render — a fabricated `### Staged (0)` / `nothing staged, tree is clean` pair, indistinguishable from the sections the op writes itself, and equally so to a consumer grepping the output. No hostile file and no attacker were required; a newline in a directory name was enough.

  Both values are now flattened by `foreign_worktree()` itself rather than at any render, because there were four renders and not the one the finding named: the banner, the prose line under it in `git-status`, the same line in `git-worktrees`, and `repo_label()` — the `Repo:` line of `git-commit` and `git-push`, i.e. the ops that write. `repo_label()`'s own `git rev-parse --show-toplevel` is flattened too, which needed no copied worktree at all.

  The separator is **disclosed**, not elided: it renders as `␊` (or `[U+000A]` on a stream that cannot carry the control pictures), so the banner still names a directory the reader can identify on disk. `_untrusted.flat()` takes a `disclose_newline` keyword for this — a title cannot contain a newline and reads better with a space in its place, a path can and does not.

- `channel:health`'s subscription probe could not fit inside its own op timeout, so the one case where `CANNOT DETERMINE` is the right answer was the one case it could never give: the probe spends `PS_TIMEOUT * 2` plus a `claude mcp get` per channel tag, the op was declared at 15s, and because the report is one string printed at the end there was nothing to emit — the reader got a bare `TIMEOUT` with an empty body. The lookups now share a declared 12s budget, a tag the budget did not reach is named as unasked rather than as unconfigured, and a test pins the arithmetic (the declared op timeout must exceed the probe's worst case) rather than either number (#1558).
- `channel` is no longer declared `read-only`. `claude mcp get` health-checks by spawning the named server, and the name is parsed out of another process's argv, so a blind probe of this op starts whatever the harness has configured under that name — `acts`, by consequence rather than by mechanism (#1558).
- The same audit asked for the connect status under exit 0 to be read as a dead server, and that half was refused with the measurement: the lookup spawns a *second* instance, and this repo's consumer refuses to start one beside a live incumbent (#550), so `Status: Failed to connect` is what a healthy singleton prints. Measured 2026-08-13 against `supertool-channel` while it held the socket and forwarded 8 of 8 events; reading that line would have turned a correct `FORWARDING` into a false negative (#1558).

- A channel tag read out of another process's argv reached `subprocess.run` with no shape check, and `channel:health` returned a definite `FORWARDING` off a flag rather than a server: `_channel_tags` filters *tokens* beginning with `-`, which says nothing about the remainder after `server:`, so `server:--help` arrived as the server name `--help` and `claude mcp get --help` exits 0. The tag is now shape-checked and passed after `--`, at the construction site — the containment declarations gate arguments a *caller* supplies into a filename slot, and this value enters inside the op from `ps` output, so nothing else on the path had anything to say about it (#1559).
- The shape excludes only what no configured server name can be — empty, a leading `-`, a control character — because `claude.ai Gmail` and `plugin:supertool:claude-channel` are both real names and a narrower charset would refuse a working setup. A tag this reader will not ask about is reported as declined, never as a server the harness has never heard of (#1559).

- `git-status` no longer relays a failed `git diff`'s stderr into its own
  `Staged provenance UNKNOWN` line unmarked — a separator in that text could
  start a line at column 0 in a receipt the tool owns. Routed through
  `_untrusted.flat`, and the no-HEAD probe's stderr is now weighed as a
  predicate rather than read as text, so the #1475 census holds again (#1562).

- **Five more renders put a value off disk at column 0, and a sixth said in its own docstring that it did not** ([#1569](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1569)). Round 2 of the class [#1557](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1557) opened. `git-diff`'s `Repo:` line — the op you run before every commit — printed `git rev-parse --show-toplevel` raw, so a repository checked out under a name containing a newline wrote a second `Repo:` and a `Scope:` of its own choosing. `git-status` printed the whole of a failed `git branch -vv`'s stderr, which a crafted `core.abbrev` in `.git/config` is enough to fill with `Working tree: clean` and `Stashes: 0`. `git-commit`'s refused-commit transcript relayed a pre-commit hook's lines at column 0 under `--- git output ---`, so a hook could write `Status: COMMITTED` and `[result] 1 op run, 1 write` into a receipt that says the opposite. And `read`'s `↳ to modify:` footer interpolated the filename raw, two lines below a header [#1019](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1019) had already flattened, inside what reads as a command to run.

  **Why there were five and not one, which is the finding.** #1557 and [#1475](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1475) were closed by flattening the sites they named. Each shape here already had a seam and the site simply did not use it: `_git_common.repo_label()` for a repository path (`git-diff` never called it, although `repo_label`'s own docstring names `git-diff` as the op that has printed a `Repo:` line for years), and `status._reason()` for why a git call did not answer (five of its six callers went through it; the `branch -vv` sink did not). The third shape had no reachable seam at all: the relay lived in `push.py`, which a sibling preset cannot import, so `commit._failure_receipt` restated its body — and the half it dropped was the `> ` prefix, while its docstring claimed it relayed "exactly as `push._relayed_lines` does it".

  So the relay moved into `_git_common` as `relayed_block()`, which emits the `--- git output ---` header and the `> ` prefix **together**. A header is an opening delimiter with no close; on its own it never separated anyone's lines from ours. `git-push`'s three dumps were on the same footing and moved with it, so all four now carry the prefix. Two visible consequences: every line under that header gains two leading characters, and `git-commit`'s dump is now **bounded** at the same head/tail 5/30 as `git-push`'s — it was the one dump in the pair that still relayed a hook transcript in full, and a pre-commit hook that runs a suite is precisely the hook that produces one. `tests/test_column_zero_renders_1569.py` closes the loop with an AST census: no file in `presets/git/` other than the seam may render that header at all, which is what makes the next copy fail at the moment it is written rather than one audit round later.

  **One correction, because a wrong mechanism in a comment is folklore.** `presets/git/commit.py:498` justified three of #1475's edits with "`str.split()` folds ASCII whitespace and nothing else, so a U+2028 walked through this one-line normaliser untouched". Python does not do that — `str.split(None)` uses the *Unicode* whitespace predicate, so U+2028, U+0085 and the vertical tab all fold, and the forged-line mechanism that sentence names was never reachable through those sites. The edits stay: they close **ANSI/C0** disclosure, which `split()` does not touch. `_reason()` has the identical construct and was still exposed to `ESC [2K ESC [1A`, an erase-line/cursor-up pair that deletes the receipt line above it ([#851](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/851)) — and the false premise is exactly what made it look already covered.

## [0.38.0] - 2026-08-13

### Added

- **`SUPERTOOL_WATCH_NAME` names a whole watch channel, deriving both paths that used to have to agree by hand** ([#1477](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1477)). A private channel took `SUPERTOOL_WATCH_SOCK` *and* `SUPERTOOL_WATCH_STATE_DIR`, and setting only the socket is worse than setting neither (#1309): the poller slot is held `O_CREAT|O_EXCL` per state directory (#476), so a second session sharing `/tmp` spawns no pollers at all and both boards render healthy. The two variables are never independently useful — the only arrangement they can express that one name cannot is exactly the broken one.

  The name is an ordinary environment variable, so a non-reserved key in an op's `.supertool.json` block reaches it with no new plumbing. It derives `/tmp/supertool-watch-<name>.sock` and `/tmp/supertool-watch-<name>`, the second created `0700` — and only when it was *derived*: a state directory the operator supplied stays unanswerable when it is missing, which `watch` reports rather than manufacturing (#693).

  **The consumer is the asymmetry, and the check for it is the deliverable.** `claude-channel` is spawned by the harness from `.mcp.json`, never by supertool, so a name in `.supertool.json` configures three of four surfaces and leaves the consumer on the default path — the half-configured state through a new door. `channel.ts` now reads the same variable with the same precedence and derives the same path, and `channel:health` reads `.mcp.json` at the plugin root and at the current directory and compares what each declares against the socket this process uses: they agree, they disagree with both paths named, or nothing was established, which is said rather than rendered as agreement.

  **Precedence is printed, never silent.** An explicit `SUPERTOOL_WATCH_SOCK` or `SUPERTOOL_WATCH_STATE_DIR` overrides the name — it is the value a running poller already captured and cannot migrate away from — and the report names both the path in force and the path the name would have produced. A name that is not usable as a path component is ignored and said so, leaving the channel on the defaults rather than on half a private one.

- `bin/supertool-workspace` opens a Claude session over this clone's radar with the watch channel armed. Both halves are easy to get wrong on their own: `radar` reads its tiers from the CWD's project root, so the directory is the board selection, and `<channel>` events only reach a session started with the development-channel flag — without it the pollers still spawn and nothing reads them. The clone is resolved from the script's own location rather than from `$HOME`, so a symlink into `~/.local/bin` works for any checkout, the same route `supertool` already takes (#1538).

### Changed

- **`gh-since-tag` is deleted into `gh-prs:merged-since=TAG,state=merged`, and the release boundary became a commit rather than an instant** ([#1405](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1405)). Two changes in one, because the second is what made the first cheap.

  **The defect.** The gate excluded the PR whose merge *is* the tagged commit by comparing instants — keep rows strictly after the boundary. That only holds if GitHub's `merged_at` equals the merge commit's committer date, and it does not: GitHub stamps `merged_at` after writing the commit. Measured across this repository's own releases, tagged commit vs the release PR's `merged_at` — v0.30.0 `06:29:26Z`/`06:29:26Z`, v0.31.0 `15:13:43Z`/`15:13:43Z`, **v0.32.0 `22:35:33Z`/`22:35:34Z`**, v0.33.0 `00:39:57Z`/`00:39:57Z`, **v0.34.0 `13:34:34Z`/`13:34:35Z`**. Two in five, not "every release" as the issue title said. On the two that lost the coin flip the release PR was counted as merged-since *and* reported absent from `TAG..master` — which excludes the tagged commit by construction — so the gate rendered `UNVERIFIED` with the count off by one, at the exact moment it is read. `merge_commit_sha` equalled the tagged sha in all five, so the exclusion is identity on `mergeCommit.oid` now, disclosed in the footer rather than dropped silently. A row carrying no `mergeCommit` is not guessed at, and a tagged commit **amended** after its merge no longer matches, so that row keeps its refusal — history was rewritten under the tag and the two sources genuinely do disagree.

  **The fold, and why a tag name.** supertool splits an op argument on `:`, so `merged-since=2026-08-11T18:57:19Z` is three segments and the value is gone before any filter is parsed; the op's own refusal says there is no escape. That left a bare date, which is midnight UTC, and against v0.35.0's real boundary `merged:>2026-08-11T00:00:00+00:00` returns **75 PRs** where `merged:>2026-08-11T18:57:19+00:00` returns **20**. A tag name contains no `:`, which is what makes the boundary expressible on a listing at all. `AMBIGUOUS` now **refuses** rather than printing a count with a warning: that was right for an op owning its whole render, and wrong for a filter, because the board underneath the warning would be a real board answering a question nobody asked. A filter value may be refused; it may not be picked between.

  **What it costs, stated rather than absorbed.** The `changelog.d/` read and the `repo:` refusal did not become unnecessary — they relocated onto this repository's most-called op. `gh-prs` was one `gh` call and on the boundary slice it now also reads tags, walks `git log` and scans a directory; the guard is one predicate with one input, and on every other call nothing local runs. The `repo:` refusal is narrower than it was: only `merged-since=<tag>` is refused, since a date boundary reads nothing local and follows a target whole. And **one thing is genuinely lost** — there is no default boundary any more. `gh-since-tag` with no argument chose the newest version-shaped tag reachable from the default branch; a filter value cannot, because that choice has three outcomes and a listing has nowhere to carry "two boundaries are defensible here". The tag must be named.

  **Every conditional read states whether it ran.** The boundary-row exclusion, the local-history cross-check and the `changelog.d` count each report their own state on every boundary call — `RAN and AGREED`, `RAN and DISAGREED`, or `DID NOT RUN` with the reason (a role filter narrows the API side only; a `repo:` target means two populations; `git log` did not answer). A cross-check that did not run counts as unreconciled, so the count renders `UNVERIFIED` rather than `EXACT`: `EXACT` means two sources agreed, and "I did not look" is not agreement. `failed` beside `merged-since=` is refused rather than answered from `statusCheckRollup`, which the boundary slice deliberately does not fetch.

  Two assertions in `tests/test_gh_prs_merged_since_1411.py` are **deliberately reversed** and say so where they sit: `gh-prs` was pinned against acquiring the changelog read and the `repo:` refusal, and against accepting a tag name as a filter value. Both were right for the shape #1411 left behind. **The op is deleted outright** — no registry entry, no `presets/github/since_tag.py`. What a user who types `gh-since-tag` now sees is the difference between a deletion and a hole, so it is worth stating exactly: `ERROR: unknown operation: gh-since-tag` followed by `Did you mean: gh-prs (preset 'github')`, above the roster. That pointer is `_supertool._OP_SYNONYMS`, the table that already answers `write:` with `paste` — its first entry whose target is a **preset** op rather than a builtin. No new mechanism was needed at runtime: `_near_miss_ops` has always searched builtins plus the loaded config's ops. What forbade it was the table's own pinning test in `tests/test_refusals_name_the_next_op_1334.py`, which measured targets against `_valid_op_names()` — builtins only — and went red with `refusals name ops that do not exist: ['gh-prs']`. It now admits `_shipped_preset_ops()` too, which keeps the guarantee whole: the target still has to exist in something this binary ships, and renaming or dropping `gh-prs` still fails it. Deliberately *not* widened to the loaded config's ops, which are the checkout's rather than the binary's and would pass here while failing for a user whose project does not load the preset.

  A synonym carries a **name**, not an invocation, and `gh-prs` alone is only two-thirds of the answer. Rather than widen the table into a second mechanism for the same job, the rest of the sentence sits where the pointer sends the reader: `gh-prs`'s `syntax` line ends `-- the release gate is gh-prs:merged-since=TAG,state=merged (was gh-since-tag, deleted #1405)` and its description opens on the same fact instead of burying it 2,000 characters in.

  `tests/test_github_since_tag_1209.py` is **renamed, not deleted** — `tests/test_release_gate_boundary_1209.py`, by `git mv` so the history follows. Every test in it was retargeted and none removed, which was the whole judgement: the file never invoked the op. It pins pure functions — instant parsing, boundary selection, the count's states, the fragment count, the reconcile, the render, the repo-target refusal — and all of them moved intact into `_release_gate.py`. Nothing in it had lost its subject.

- **`radar` and `watches` name the channel they are a board of, and any export overriding it** ([#1495](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1495)). Both printed the socket and the state directory as bare paths, and the override disclosure — *`SUPERTOOL_WATCH_SOCK` is set and overrides the name: the socket is X, not Y* — was computed on every run and printed by `channel:health` alone. So an operator running a named channel with a stale socket exported read two healthy boards, neither of which said the name was not in force: #1477's half-set knob relocated one surface over.

  One formatter in `naming`, reached through one `transport` accessor, so the three surfaces cannot disagree about the same resolution. Silent on the default paths with no override — a header printed on every board is one nobody reads — and the name is flattened before it reaches a fixed-width table, because it arrives from an op's config block rather than from this repo.

  The disclosure stays in the renders and out of `transport`, which the #1476 review argued for and this keeps: `transport` is imported by a detached poller whose stdout has no reader, so a print there writes into nothing.

- **`channel:health` says when it declined to ask who holds the socket** ([#1495](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1495)). The arm for a socket that could not be probed is right to make no claim about a holder — `peer_pid()` connects, and the connect is the one that just failed — but it omitted the line the other arms print, and an omitted line reads exactly like a *no holder* line to anyone scanning for one. It now states the skip and its reason, and still names no holder.

### Fixed

- **A crashing `stop.py` reported its traceback as terminal escape sequences, and the 500-character budget was spent on them** ([#1333](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1333)). `_mcp_stop_server` captures the child's stderr into `_StopOutcome.detail`, which is printed for a human under `SUPERTOOL_DEBUG`. CPython colourises its own tracebacks from 3.13 on, and `_colorize` consults `FORCE_COLOR` **before** it asks whether the stream is a tty — so a parent with that variable set gets an escape-laden traceback out of a child whose stderr is a pipe. `detail` is now stripped of CSI, OSC and two-character escapes, before the cap rather than after: the cap keeps the *last* 500 characters, and every escape byte was budget spent on something that renders as nothing, so a long enough coloured traceback evicted the exception line — the only part worth keeping.

  The second of this issue's two permanent local reds, and it is a product defect rather than the environment limit the acceptance assumed. The standing hypothesis was the local interpreter (CPython 3.14.6, outside CI's 3.9-3.12). Half right: the trigger is two conditions, ≥3.13 **and** `FORCE_COLOR` in the environment, and this repo's own agent harness exports `FORCE_COLOR=3`. So skipping with a stated reason would have buried a real defect that CI's Python range happens to hide — every 3.13+ user in a coloured terminal reads escape sequences out of that debug line today.

  With this and [#1499](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1499) fixed, a local full-suite run carries no known permanent reds. What the count still cannot tell you is whether the tree has accumulated a new one from a stale artefact git does not see, and nothing here makes that class legible rather than remembered.

- **`channel:health` names the process holding the socket in the two arms that used to decline without asking** ([#1476](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1476)). *nothing is consuming this socket* and *another session is consuming it* call for opposite actions — launch a consumer, or accept that delivery works and this session is simply not the listener — and both printed the same two lines under `CANNOT DETERMINE`.

  `peer_pid()` shipped with #1192 and had exactly one caller: the point past `read_health()` where a record already exists. The arms that return before it — no readable health file, and a health file the op objects to — never asked a question the platform can answer. The first is the arm that fires when the consumer is a Claude session launched with the channel flag, because it publishes no health file at all.

  Three states, and the third is the one that used to be everything: `socket-holder: pid N — not this process (this process is pid M)`; `socket-holder: pid N — this process`; or `socket-holder NOT resolved — <the refusal the probe returned>`, which is where Windows and FreeBSD land, by name. The verdict does not move — naming the holder is not evidence of delivery, so both arms stay `CANNOT DETERMINE` and the ceiling is still printed. What changes is that a reader can tell *no listener* from *not my listener*.

- `gh-run` renders each job's id beside its name, not only for the legs that failed ([#1482](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1482)). The `## Failed jobs` section was the one place an id appeared, so reading the log of a leg that **passed** meant leaving supertool for a raw `gh api` call — the same seam #1409 closed in `gh-branch`. A `Job id` column plus a `gh-job:<id>` pointer under the table closes it here.
- Every id `gh-run` prints is labelled `job #`, and that is established by the endpoint rather than inferred per row: `gh run view --json jobs` reads a run's Actions jobs, and a check run is in no run's job list. `gh-job` answers for both of GitHub's overlapping id namespaces, so an id offered without its namespace is one that can resolve in the wrong one.
- An unreadable job id renders `id unread` rather than `job #None`. `.get("databaseId", "?")` returned `None` for a key present with a null value, and the failed-jobs section printed it in the shape of an id.

- **A file under validation could mint itself an extra finding, and `count` is baseline arithmetic** ([#1486](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1486)). Every validator adapter parsed its tool's stdout with `str.splitlines()`, which breaks on U+2028, U+2029, U+0085, VT and FF as well as on LF/CR/CRLF. No analyser frames its output that way, and most echo the source text they are complaining about verbatim into the diagnostic — so one of those five characters inside a string literal ended the adapter's idea of a line mid-diagnostic, the fragment re-matched the adapter's own regex, and it was published as a second record. Reproduced on `go-vet`: one diagnostic from `go vet`, `count: 2` on the receipt.

  Not cosmetic. `count` is the number `_validator_regressed` subtracts, so the file being checked partly chose its own baseline, and on a `rollback_on_fail` validator that baseline reverts edits.

  `validators/common/linebreaks.py` is the local `split_lines()` — `presets/_untrusted.split_lines` ([#1081](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1081)) restated because `validators/` cannot import from `presets/`, pinned equal to the core's own definition by a test.

  All 31 call sites were partitioned rather than swept. **Nineteen fixed**, in `go-vet`, `tsc-check`, `markdownlint`, `hadolint`, `cargo-check`, `xmllint`, `ruby-check`, `bash-check`, `gofmt-check`, `phpmd`, `phpstan`, `phplint`, `lsp-diag`, `terraform-check`, `jit-index` and `common/source_context.py`. **Twelve refused with a reason**: four JSON-RPC frame readers over `bytes`, where a mis-split fragment fails `json.loads` and can withhold a response but never mint one; four `traceback.format_exc()` reads of our own text; two message flatteners (`terraform-check.plain()`, `pyright`) where splitting on *more* separators is what neutralises them; and two quotes of `awk`'s own output. A test walks the tree and refuses any new call site that is neither fixed nor on that list with its reason.
