  Two of the nineteen are not extra records but the same seam elsewhere. `lsp-diag` looked for a line starting `diag:` to detect an infrastructure failure, so a diagnostic's own text could turn a real verdict into a `skipped`. `common/source_context.py` numbered the *source file* by `str.splitlines()` while every tool numbers by LF, so a separator anywhere above a finding printed the wrong source line under a correct line number, for all thirty adapters at once.

- **`git-push`'s rebase-recovery route now carries the pre-push hook disclosure and the same output bound as the straight route** ([#1490](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1490)). A non-fast-forward hands the push to `_recover_by_rebase`, which runs its own `git push` and prints its own receipts — and neither the hook relay ([#1448](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1448)) nor the head/tail bound on a relayed git dump ([#1454](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1454)) had ever followed it there. `Status: pushed ✓ (rebased onto remote)` was therefore the one landed-push receipt in the op that said nothing about the local gate at all.

  That is #1448's premise turned back on it. A push that lands *after* a rebase is precisely a push whose hook has just run, so it was the receipt most in need of the line. The success arm now prints the three-state `Pre-push hook:` line plus the relay above its status, and the rejected-after-rebase arm prints the state line only, exactly as the straight route's rejected arm does — the dump beneath it already carries the child's own words.

  Both of that route's `--- git output ---` dumps are bounded to head 5 / tail 30 with the elision counted. The rejected-after-rebase arm is where the transcript is largest for the same reason the arm exists: the hook has just run the suite, and #1454 measured an unbounded dump at ~11,000 lines inside a receipt. The `rebase could not start` arm prints no hook line, deliberately — no push of that route's own has run yet, so there is nothing about a hook it could state that would be about the failure it is reporting.

- **`gh-pr` printed a GraphQL page cap as if it were the pull request's total** ([#1491](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1491)). `reviewThreads(first: 100)` requests no `pageInfo`, so the reply cannot say whether it saw everything — and both renders divided by what it got: `Unresolved threads: N / 100` in the default dashboard and `Threads: N unresolved of 100` in `gh-pr:N:threads`. A fetch limit stated as a fact about the PR, one line under `Unresolved threads: 0 / 0 — read, not assumed.`

  A reply holding exactly the cap and a PR holding exactly the cap are the same bytes, so at the cap every number taken off the fetched set is printed as a floor — the unresolved tally too, since it is counted over the same truncated list. `… N more not indexed here` was computed off that set and under-reported by the same amount; it is a floor there as well. Below the cap the total *is* established and prints bare, unchanged: qualifying a number that is known would be the same defect pointed the other way.

  The comment list inside one thread was capped at 50 and said nothing at all, so a thread cut mid-way read as a thread that ended. `gh-pr:N:threads` now closes such a thread by naming the cut. Both caps are named constants used to build the query itself — the render infers truncation from the length it got against the cap, which is sound only while the two agree, and the number used to be a literal in the query string plus a hand-copy of it in a comment.

- **`gl-issue` downloaded attachments into a fixed `/tmp` path any local user could own, and the containment check could not tell** ([#1493](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1493)). `IMAGE_DIR` was the literal `/tmp/supertool-images` — a fixed name in a world-writable directory, so a co-tenant could take it first, as a directory of their own or as a symlink pointing anywhere. `_is_inside` calls `os.path.realpath` on **both** of its arguments, so a symlink planted at the root was resolved through on both sides and containment answered `True` about the attacker's directory. The check was never wrong; nothing established what it was checking against. `#1484`'s fix constrained the value the *remote* chooses and is untouched by this — this is the root that value is joined onto.

  The root is now `presets/_image_root.default_root()`: `tempfile.gettempdir()` plus a per-uid suffix, created non-recursively at `0700`, then held open as `O_RDONLY | O_DIRECTORY | O_NOFOLLOW` so the tightening (`fchmod`), the ownership check and the mode check are three questions about one descriptor rather than three independent path resolutions. A root that is a symlink, a reparse point, not a directory, owned by another uid, or reachable by group or other after the chmod is a **refusal naming which of those it was** — three states, not two, per `docs/validators.md` §"Declining instead of guessing". `os.makedirs` no longer raises out of the op when something non-directory sits on the name.

  **`tempfile.mkdtemp()` per invocation was rejected on purpose.** It is the airtight answer and `gl-issue` prints the attachment paths under `## Images` for the reader to open, so a root that moves every call makes the receipt a path that existed only during the call that printed it. Stability is kept and its safety comes from proof rather than from luck.

  **What is not closed, stated rather than implied.** Another local uid can still squat `<temp>/supertool-images-<your uid>` before you, and the op then refuses rather than writing into it — attachments stop working until it is removed. A loud refusal is the correct side of that trade, and the per-uid suffix keeps two ordinary users on one machine from colliding by accident.

  **Windows.** The old value was a POSIX literal: a leading-slash path is anchored to the current drive there, so it landed in a `tmp/supertool-images` at the drive root rather than under the platform temp directory. `gettempdir()` on Windows resolves inside the user profile, which is not the shared world-writable directory the finding rests on, so moving off the literal is most of the repair. There is no `O_NOFOLLOW` or `O_DIRECTORY`; that branch uses `os.lstat`, which does not follow the final component, and refuses a symlink or a reparse point — a junction is a directory that `stat.S_ISLNK` denies, so `st_reparse_tag` is the only way to see one. The ownership and mode arms are **skipped** there rather than faked: `st_uid` is a constant on Windows and the permission bits are synthesized, so a verdict from either would be a sentence with no measurement behind it. Those Windows claims are **reasoned from CPython's documented behaviour, not observed on a Windows host** — the grade #627 recorded for itself.

  `_is_inside`'s docstring said what it compares and left a reader to infer a property it never had. It now states that it is a containment test and not an ownership test, and that realpathing both sides — which is correct for the leaf, and is what makes a remote-chosen `..` resolve to where the write would land — establishes nothing about the root.

  The ownership and mode arms are pinned through `_image_root.refusal`, a pure function of a stat result, precisely because the filesystem cannot reach them on Windows: a `skipif` there would have reported a coverage the suite does not have on the one platform whose reds are load-bearing in this repo.

- **`git-worktrees` no longer calls a branch with unpushed commits `published`, and every exit code now names itself in the body** ([#1496](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1496)).

  The row read `the branch is pushed and no open PR tracks it - the work is published but unproposed` off the *existence* of a remote-tracking ref alone. Hit live on the default branch: the clone was one commit ahead of `origin/master` and the row said `published`. Existence of `refs/remotes/origin/<branch>` and being in sync with it are different questions, and read in the direction that matters - somebody deciding whether a tree can be discarded - `published` reads as `safe to remove`.

  So the count is taken, with three answers and no fourth silent one: in sync (published, unproposed), `N commit(s) here are NOT on it` (not published, and the row line itself carries `N unpushed, no open PR` so a scan that never reaches the evidence still sees it), or the count could not be taken - which renders `UNKNOWN` with the reason and never as `0`. It is measured against the ref the row is about rather than `@{upstream}`, because `git worktree add -b X ... master` writes an upstream of `origin/master` for a branch that has never left the machine. One local `rev-list` per pushed branch; no extra network call.

  The second half: the same call exited `1` with no line in the body naming a failure, because nothing had failed - the `1` was the occupancy verdict. A caller gating on the status and a caller reading the render disagreed about the same call. Every return now prints an `[exit N]` line saying which verdict or which refusal produced it, and whether the op itself failed. It sits **above** `[result]`, not below: that line is what `gh-pr-merge` and every `| tail -1` reader take the tally off.

- **Every type error `tsc` found arrived as one unlocatable finding carrying a terminal dump** ([#1499](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1499)). TypeScript 5.x emits *pretty* output by default whether or not stdout is a tty — ANSI-coloured, four lines per diagnostic, a caret rule under the column, a trailing `Found N errors` tally. `tsc-check`'s parse reads the plain one-line form, so it matched nothing and the adapter published a single error with `code: "syntax"`, `line: null` and the whole coloured dump as `msg`. N type errors rendered as one problem with no location, and a reader acting on it looked in the wrong place.

  Fixed by asking for the plain form — `--pretty false` on the argv. The alternative on the table was stripping ANSI before the regex, and measured against a real `tsc 5.x` dump that fixes nothing: stripped, the pretty form reads `bad.ts:1:7 - error TS2322: …`, which is not the `bad.ts(1,7): error TS2322: …` the pattern requires, and zero lines match. Colour was never the whole problem; the layout was. The strip is applied as well, before the parse and to the excerpt, because it is `--pretty false` that removes the colour today and nothing `tsc` documents keeps the two coupled.

  A parse that still comes back empty is now `code: "adapter"` — the code the core reads on every error as "no verdict was obtained about this file" (`_validator_not_checked`), so it renders as the third state, is never cached and never rolls back. Not `skipped`, which omits `errors` entirely and would drop `tsc`'s own objection with it (`validators/SCHEMA.md` §"A located diagnostic still has to be about *this* file (#754)"). The same arm now also covers a non-zero exit with **no** output, which used to emit `ok: false, count: 0, errors: []` — a verdict of "not clean" carrying nothing to act on, and an absence the core could not recognise either, because it looks for the reason on an error that was not there.

  This was one of the two permanent local reds in [#1333](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1333). It inverts how that red should have been read: the machines where `tests/test_tsc_check.py::test_source_context_present_on_error` passed were the ones whose `tsc` happened to emit the plain form, so the green was the accident.

- **A fragment of the file under validation could take the location off a real `lsp-diag` finding** ([#1500](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1500)). `parse_cclsp_diagnostics` reads a diagnostic's `at line N, col M` with an end-of-line anchor, so the tail it picks is whichever one is **last** on the line. That anchor is what defends against a tail sitting mid-message, and it works. What it does not survive is [#1486](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1486): U+2028, U+2029, U+0085, VT and FF are deliberately no longer line ends for an adapter parsing a line-oriented protocol, so a fragment after one of them now sits on the *same* line as the real diagnostic and its tail is the last one. One record, well formed, pointing at a line the language server never mentioned.

  Only the segment before the first inline break is parsed now. The remainder is not dropped — a message may legitimately contain one of the five — but it is carried into the message labelled as the rest of one line rather than as a second diagnostic and not as a location. A line that *opens* with a fragment publishes no location at all, and its text is attached to a neighbouring record rather than becoming one: `count` is what `_validator_regressed` subtracts, so a fragment must not mint a record, and it must not vanish either. The first cut of this fix dropped exactly those remainders silently — an absence produced by the tool, inside the fix for an absence produced by the tool — and review caught it.

  Found while fixing it, same mechanism, fixed here: all five characters are `str.isspace()`, so `str.strip()` deletes a **leading** one. The infrastructure probe read `ln.strip().startswith("diag:")`, so a fragment at the start of a physical line still imitated supertool's own message prefix — and that does not move one field of one record, it replaces the whole receipt with `skipped` and discards every real finding on the file ([#482](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/482)'s shape, with the file under validation choosing it).

- **The suite asserted a validator verdict where the core's own spawn wall could fire** ([#1501](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1501)). `master` went red on `pytest (windows-latest, 3.12)` with `assert 1 == 2` in `tests/test_validator_warm_unsafe_345.py`, on a commit touching nothing near validators, on a leg that took 8m41s. The `1` was not the adapter's: `_validator_run_one`'s `TimeoutExpired` arm fabricates `count: 1` with `timeout: True` when a cold CPython spawn misses the spec's 10s, and `assert out["count"] == 2` cannot tell that from two real findings. A machine limit was being published as a verdict about the file — this repo's own defect class inside the thing built to detect it.

  The arm is unchanged: it is an absence, it says so, and [#969](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/969) pins that it never rolls an edit back. The assertion sites moved instead. `tests/_adapter_verdict.py` gains `core_timed_out` / `skip_if_core_timed_out` — the sibling of [#794](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/794)'s `skip_if_stalled`, which classifies a stall at the *adapter's* own wall and cannot see this one — and `run_one_or_skip`, the adopted call form at all 42 sites across seven files that hand the core a `cmd` it really spawns.

  **`timeout is True` is the only clause, and that is the design.** It is written in exactly one place in `_supertool.py` and `_validator_strip_core_keys` drops it from anything an adapter or a cache entry says ([#1036](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1036), [#1044](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1044)), so nothing else can claim it. Declining on `count == 1` — the number in the log — would mute every genuine one-error verdict in the suite, and matching the message would swallow a real finding about somebody's `timeout` setting. Both directions are pinned.

  **The sweep is enforced, not asserted in a PR body.** An `ast` walk fails on any raw `_validator_run_one` call left in `tests/` whose spec can spawn. Two exclusions, both mechanical rather than a line-number list: a `{"builtin": ...}` spec returns in-process before any subprocess ([#477](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/477)), and a `# core-timeout: asserted on` comment marks a test that provokes the wall deliberately. That marker exists because the blanket conversion silently muted `test_adapter_timeout_stays_loud`, which is the one test whose subject *is* the arm — caught by running it, not by reading the diff.

- **`watches` no longer dies on a state directory no spawn has created** ([#1502](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1502)). Adding `watch_name` to an op block and running the first read raised `FileNotFoundError: '/tmp/supertool-watch-oss'` out of `os.listdir` and refused every other op in the same call — `[batch] 2 ops ran — all 2 refused`. The default state directory is `/tmp` itself, so that enumeration was unreachable-by-luck on the default and guaranteed to fire on the first read after naming a channel, which is the headline feature of the release before it.

  Three states, not two. An absent directory is a *knowable* fact — zero watchers, nothing has ever spawned on this channel — and now renders as one line saying so, naming the directory and the variable that chose it. A directory that exists and could not be listed is *unknown*: it prints a warning and never the words `No active watchers`, which would be a claim about the fleet built on a listing that never ran. An empty directory that exists still reads exactly as it did.

  Nothing on a read path creates the directory, deliberately. Only a spawn creates a *derived* one, and a `SUPERTOOL_WATCH_STATE_DIR` the operator supplied is never manufactured at all ([#693](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/693)) — a read with side effects is a worse trade than a read that says which of the two states it is in.

  Swept rather than patched at the reported line: every enumeration of the state directory under `presets/watch/` now goes through one classifier in `naming`, and a test refuses a bare `os.listdir` anywhere else in the preset. `radar:--state` survived this by never enumerating, which was luck and not a guard.

  The sweep found a second reading of the same gap, one file over. `channel.stranded_watchers` never *raised* — it has caught `OSError` since #1191 — but it returned an empty list for a directory that was absent and for one it could not list, and `channel:health` then printed `watchers : none recorded an emit into this socket`. That is a claim about the fleet built on a listing that never happened, on the arm a freshly named channel lands on, so the strongest false claim on the report was also the likeliest. #1191 gave every unreadable *file* its own line and left the directory itself with two states; it has three now, from the same classifier.

- **A symlink planted on a named watch channel's state directory was adopted, and every poller write landed in it ([#1518](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1518)).** `SUPERTOOL_WATCH_NAME=x` derives `/tmp/supertool-watch-x`, and `naming.ensure_state_dir` created it with `os.makedirs(..., mode=0o700, exist_ok=True)`. `exist_ok=True` accepts whatever already holds the name and reaches it through `os.path.isdir`, which follows symlinks, so a link planted at the leaf was taken over in silence; `mode=0o700` applies only to directories that call creates, so it was not a defence in the pre-taken case. `transport.claim_pidfile` calls this before its `O_CREAT|O_EXCL` pidfile open — which a *new* file inside the planter's directory satisfies perfectly — and `write_state` opens `<path>.tmp` by path, so pid files and state files both landed there. `/tmp` is world-writable and the name is public rather than per-uid: this repo commits `"watch_name": "oss-supertool"` to its own `.supertool.json`. The leaf is now established by `presets/_image_root.ensure`, the boundary written for `gl-issue`'s attachment root in this same release rather than a third hand-rolled one: created non-recursively, held open `O_RDONLY | O_DIRECTORY | O_NOFOLLOW`, `fchmod`ed and then asked about ownership and mode through that one descriptor. A symlink, a reparse point, a file, another uid's directory or a mode group or other can reach is a refusal naming which, and no slot is claimed there. **Not closed:** another local uid can squat the name ahead of you, and that channel then refuses rather than writing into their directory until it is removed — the same residual `docs/presets/gitlab.md` discloses for the attachment root. On Windows there is no `O_NOFOLLOW`, so the check is `os.lstat`, and the ownership and mode arms are skipped rather than faked because `st_uid` is a constant and the permission bits are synthesized there.

- **`tsc-check` trusted the target on the way out and `tsc`'s path on the way back** ([#1519](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1519)). Two instances of one defect, both from the v0.38.0 release audits.

  The target went into argv with nothing separating it from `tsc`'s own option grammar. `tsc` reads a leading `@` as a **response file** — its command line comes from that file instead — so `--noEmit` did not survive it. Measured on tsc 6.0.3 with `@r.ts` on disk beside an `r.ts` holding `--noEmit false --outDir out`: the receipt read `ok: true, count: 0` for a file whose one line is a type error, and `out/a.js` and `out/b.js` were written, against this page's own "`--noEmit` — no output files written". A leading `-` is the same class one character over. Escaping is not the fix — this is `tsc`'s grammar, not the shell's — and neither is `--`, which `tsc` rejects outright (`error TS5023`). A relative target now carries a `./` prefix, spelled with the platform's separator; `tsc` normalises it back, so the diagnostic it prints is unchanged.

  And `tsc --noEmit FILE` type-checks the whole import graph, so a diagnostic about an **imported** file is the common case rather than an edge one. The parse threw the reported path away, so an imported file's error was published as a located finding in the target, with `context_fields` printing *this* file's source at *that* file's line as the evidence. The recommended `.ts` registration is `rollback_on_fail: true`, which made that arithmetic capable of reverting a correct edit over a defect in a file the edit never touched. The path is now compared through `validators/common/pkg_paths.attribute` against the directory the adapter ran `tsc` in, and a foreign or unplaceable diagnostic keeps `ok: false` with `line`/`col` null, `code: "adapter"` and no `source_context` — `validators/SCHEMA.md` §"A located diagnostic still has to be about *this* file (#754)". It is kept, not filtered: the program genuinely does not type-check.

- **`lsp-diag` parsed a shape the server chooses, and each arm disclosed the opposite of what it did** ([#1520](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1520)). Three instances of one class, from the v0.38.0 release audits.

  [#1500](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1500) bounded the parse to the first segment of a physical line, where a segment ends at one of the five *inline* breaks. LF is not one of them by construction — it is the framing character — so a server message carrying an LF was still split into physical lines and every line after the first was read as a fresh diagnostic at a location the message chose. Where the server marks its list, an unmarked line is now a continuation of the entry above it rather than an entry of its own. The framing is decided from the *first* framed line and never from any line: a bulletless document can contain an echoed `*` in its source, and letting that flip the answer would turn every real finding into a continuation.

  A non-empty line matching neither pattern used to fall off the end of the loop body, taking its already-computed remainder with it — and the whole-text fallback runs only when *nothing* matched, so with any other line holding a record both halves left no trace anywhere in the receipt. `remainder_note`'s own docstring said "Not dropped". It is kept and labelled now, like every other fragment.

  `_REMAINDER_MAX` capped each fragment and its comment stated the invariant "a record must not grow without bound", but nothing capped how many fragments one `msg` collected. A file whose echoed source carries an inline break on hundreds of physical lines grew a single record past 100kB. The aggregate is bounded, the ceiling on any one `msg` is applied last so it is a property of the receipt, and what is over it is reported as a number rather than being silently absent.

- This repository named its own watch channel `oss-supertool` in `.supertool.json` and never told `.mcp.json`, so its producers bound `/tmp/supertool-watch-oss-supertool.sock` while the consumer bound the default — every event emitted here was lost at the source. `channel:health` reported it correctly; nothing pinned the two files against each other, which is what let a two-file change ship as a one-file change (#1538).

- **A symlink planted on a watch state file's temporary name was written through by every reader, and only the poller path had ever checked ([#1540](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1540)).** #1518 established the derived state directory through `presets/_image_root.ensure` and wired it into `transport.claim_pidfile` -- the one path that spawns a poller, and the one path that was never the problem. `transport.write_state` opened `f"{state_path}.tmp"` with a plain `open(..., "w")`, and it is reached from `record_death` (`watches`, `unwatch`, the `radar` heal) and `clear_deaths` (`watch`, `unwatch`) in processes that never claim a slot. The channel name is public -- this repo commits `"watch_name": "oss-supertool"` to its own `.supertool.json` -- so a co-tenant creating `/tmp/supertool-watch-<name>/` first, with a stale pid file and a symlink at `supertool-watch-<src>__<id>.state.json.tmp`, got any file the victim can write truncated and refilled with state JSON whose `last_event.payload` is remote text. The temporary is now created by `tempfile.mkstemp` -- a name carrying ~40 random bits that nobody can pre-take, opened `O_CREAT|O_EXCL` so it comes into existence with our create and there is no window to plant anything at it, with `O_NOFOLLOW` and `O_BINARY` added where the platform has them. The first cut of this fix instead opened the fixed `<path>.tmp` with `O_WRONLY|O_CREAT|O_TRUNC|O_NOFOLLOW`, the write mirror of the `O_RDONLY|O_NOFOLLOW` that `read_state_checked` and `read_pid_checked` have carried since #1197/#1200 -- and `O_NOFOLLOW` does not exist on Windows, where `getattr(os, "O_NOFOLLOW", 0)` is `0`, so the open followed the planted link in silence and three `windows-latest` legs overwrote the victim while ubuntu and macOS were green. A guard that cannot run on a platform rendering as a guard that passed, arriving inside the fix for exactly that. A *derived* directory is also established through `ensure` on every write -- not memoized, because `O_NOFOLLOW` guards the final component only and a cached "established" would report an old measurement of the parent as a current fact -- so a reader refuses a squatted directory the same way a poller already did. `write_state` returns the refusal instead of swallowing it, and `record_death` and `clear_deaths` return `False` when nothing reached disk -- they used to report a death as recorded and a ledger as cleared after an `OSError` they discarded. **Not closed:** a co-tenant who takes `/tmp/supertool-watch-<name>` before you still owns it, and every write to that channel -- reader and poller alike -- now refuses until it is removed; and the unnamed default keeps its state files loose in world-writable `/tmp`, where there is no directory to establish and the temporary's unpredictable name is the whole of the write-side boundary. `tiers/_snapshot.write` -- `radar`'s delta snapshot, in the same directory under a name of the same shape -- opened `f"{target}.tmp"` with a plain `open(..., "w")` and had no guard at all, so #1540's mechanism applied to it unchanged and on every platform; both writers now go through one `transport.write_json_contained`. The residual of the unpredictable name is litter rather than exposure: a hard kill between the create and the rename leaves one `<name>.state.json.<random>.tmp` that nothing collects, where a fixed name was reused by the next write. On Windows `_image_root` still declines the `st_uid` and mode arms on the *directory* rather than faking them; that `os.replace` replaces a link planted at the final state name rather than following it is observed on POSIX and only reasoned on Windows, and there is now a test whose Windows leg answers it.

- **The watch channel name no longer ships in `.mcp.json`.** That file is the *plugin's* — its `args` use `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}` and `channel:health` reads it at the plugin root — so a name true of exactly one checkout reconfigured every install: their consumer bound `/tmp/supertool-watch-oss-supertool.sock` while their own pollers bound the default, the half-configured state `presets/watch/README.md` calls worse than setting neither. The name is workspace state and now has one home, this clone's `.supertool.json`, which `bin/supertool-workspace` reads and exports before launching. Measured against claude 2.1.219: a stdio MCP server the harness spawns inherits the launching process's environment, which is what carries it to the consumer (#1541).
- **`channel:health` no longer reports a consumer that declares nothing as a consumer on another channel.** With the name arriving by inheritance, an `.mcp.json` naming no channel variable says nothing about where the consumer bound — and this process cannot read the environment the session was launched with. It is now the third state, naming what it could not establish, instead of a flat "nothing a poller emits here reaches it" printed under a `FORWARDING` verdict that contradicts it (#1541).
- **`bin/supertool-workspace` says when it does not append its own prompt.** `claude` reads only its first positional as the prompt and silently ignores later ones, and a variadic option such as `--add-dir` swallows whatever follows it — so `... "$@" "/opensource-manager"` delivered the prompt only when there were no arguments, and dropped it in silence otherwise. It is appended when there is nothing else to pass, and otherwise the argv is left exactly as given and the omission is stated on stderr (#1541).
- **The launcher's shipped mode is checked in git's index, not in the checkout.** `st_mode & S_IXUSR` is a fact about the runner's filesystem, and NTFS has no execute bit, so it reddened all four `windows-latest` legs at `mode 0o100666` while the committed `100755` was correct. `git ls-files -s` answers the question that was meant on every platform, so the check is not skipped anywhere (#1541).
- **`assert_change_is_findable` no longer accepts a number found inside a longer number.** `1541` occurs inside `154177` in `CHANGELOG.md`, so the guard passed for a module whose change was documented nowhere. Exactly one call site depended on the loose match — that one (#1541).

## [0.37.0] - 2026-08-12

### Added

- `go-vet` validator adapter — `go vet` over the edited file's package (#669). Go's only bundled validator was `gofmt-check`, which answers a formatting question, so a `fmt.Printf` verb that does not match its argument shipped clean. `go vet` ships with the Go toolchain, so it costs no install a Go repo has not already paid.
- A `go vet` diagnostic belonging to a sibling file in the same package is published with `line`/`col` null and `code: "adapter"` rather than under the edited file's name (#754, #669), and a file in no module is `skipped` — never `ok`. `rollback_on_fail` is false: a vet finding is a suspicious construct, not a broken file.

- **The GitLab read ops answer about another project** ([#676](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/676)). A leading `repo:GROUP[/SUBGROUP]/PROJECT` now points `gl-issue`, `gl-mr`, `gl-pipeline` and `gl-job` at a project other than the cwd's, closing the asymmetry [#673](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/673) left on this side: `gl-issue-create` had taken a project in its payload since it shipped, and no read op could name one at all.

  It is not [#673](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/673)'s mechanism under a new name. `glab api` has no repo flag — the project *is* a path segment — so the target replaces glab's `projects/:id` placeholder as a url-encoded full path rather than being appended beside it, and leaving the placeholder in place would have meant the call still resolved from the directory it was made in. Only `glab issue view` and `glab mr view` take a flag (`-R`).

  The accepted shape now follows the call's own ops rather than one fixed rule. GitLab allows subgroups and GitHub does not, so core reads which preset each repo-targetable op is declared in and applies that forge's shape: a three-segment path in a `gh-*` call is refused instead of reaching `gh`, and a call naming both families is refused outright because one target cannot be a repository on both forges. Every segment must also be letters, digits, `.`, `_` or `-`, because the value is substituted into an API path and handed to a CLI that attaches the live `Private-Token`.

  `gl-mrs`, `gl-runners` and `gl-api` are **not** opted in, and a `repo:` call naming one refuses rather than half-applying. The first two feed `radar`, which respawns watchers off a `(source, id)` watch-state key with no project dimension — under a target that key would attribute one project's `!12` to another, and a supervisor acting on that is not a display bug. `gl-api` names its own path, so a project is already sayable there.

  `gl-issue-create` now gets the accurate refusal rather than the generic one. It routes its target through its own payload exactly as `gh-issue-create` does, but reads `project` where the GitHub op reads `repo`, so a manifest may now declare `"repo_target": "payload:KEY"` and the message quotes the field the payload validator actually looks at instead of naming one it does not.

### Removed

- **`oss_train` is gone** ([#1472](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1472)). It batch-rebased and force-pushed every branch under `~/Documents/st-wt` in one call, and it automated a problem that [#906](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/906) removed: per-issue `changelog.d/` fragments mean two open PRs share no file. Measured 2026-08-12 — eight PRs merged in one afternoon, zero rebases, not one call to it. What it did, `git-push` now does per branch on demand, at the moment the branch needs it. Against that it carried three containment-class repairs in four days — [#1246](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1246) (it force-pushed any repository the caller named), [#1247](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1247), [#1298](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1298) (a pre-rebase guard reading a `git status` configured not to look; it went on to force-push a worktree an agent was working in) — on a tool with no caller.

  Nothing else batch-rebases N branches. That is deliberate, and bringing it back is a decision to make deliberately rather than by improvising a force-push loop: `docs/contributing.md` records the contract those three issues cost.

- **The path-declaration detector's `cmd` arm keeps a live instance.** `_entry_names_a_path` reads two signals OR'd — a `PATH`/`FILE` component in `syntax`, or `{file}`/`{dir}` in the `cmd` template. `oss_train` was the **only** shipped op the second arm found, so deleting it would have left that half with zero instances: the guard still compiles, every test around the first arm still passes, and nothing reports that half stopped being exercised. A check with no instance is indistinguishable from a check that passes, which is this repo's signature defect landing inside the guard built to prevent it. The arm now has a fixture — a real `.supertool.json` written to disk, read by `_load_config()` and driven through `dispatch()`, so it reaches the detector by the route a shipped project op takes rather than by being handed the entry as a literal. Its reach is asserted rather than assumed: the same fixture, declared, runs its command end to end, which is the control saying the refusal came from the detector and not from something earlier declining the op. Verified red by disabling the arm — the undeclared fixture then returned `PASS` on `cmd_arm_probe:/etc/passwd`.

- **A swept directory that no longer exists is declared, not counted as zero.** `tests/test_git_status_display_config_gates_1295.py` sweeps `presets/git`, `presets/github` and `scripts` for `git status` call sites. `scripts/` held only `oss_train.py`, so it is now empty — and an absent directory contributes zero sites, which renders identically to a directory with nothing to find. It stays in the swept set so a script written there next month is swept on the day it lands, and its absence is recorded in `ABSENT_TREES` with the reason; the register reds both if an undeclared tree goes missing and if a declared one comes back.

### Fixed

- `.githooks/pre-push` no longer runs the full test suite for a push that
  updates nothing (#1242). Git invokes the hook even when everything is already
  up to date, and legitimately hands it zero ref lines; the hook read that as
  "I could not read the refs" and fell through to the ~296s suite — against
  `git-push`'s own 300s budget, which is what made a legitimate push look like
  a coin flip. The two cases are told apart by argv, which git always fills
  with the remote name and URL, so a hook run by something that is not git
  still runs the suite. The skip is disclosed, like the feature-branch one.

- `git-push`'s timeout receipt now says whether a local pre-push hook was in
  play (#1242), in three states — it names the hook path, says no hook ran, or
  declines when git did not answer where the hook lives. A timeout whose budget
  went to a local suite and one that went to a hanging network were previously
  indistinguishable, and the receipt's advice ("the push may still be in
  flight") reads as the second. The verdict, the remote read-back, both shas
  and the do-not-force-push advice are unchanged.

- **Four refusals held the answer to the round-trip they cost** ([#1334](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1334), [#1372](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1372)). A receipt owes `what happened / proof / what is next`, and these dropped the third column while already holding it. `edit`, `replace_lines`, `vim` and `replace` on a path that is not there now name the two ops that create one; `grep`'s LIMIT-0 refusal names a spelling for each of the two readings it declines to guess between; the `edit:@-` payload route says the file is missing rather than naming a field no value of which could have worked.

  **`edit` never reached the shared not-found helper at all.** #1372 designed its suggestion around the `tried:` line #1300 added, on the premise that it was already printing. It was not: `op_edit`, `op_replace_lines` and `_op_vim_impl` each returned a bare `f"ERROR: file not found: {path}"`, so three of this repo's mutating ops had neither the absolute path that separates a typo from a drifted cwd nor the `exists at <root> — prefix with cwd:` branch. They route through `_path_not_found` now, which is what makes naming a creating op safe rather than a guess.

  **The clause fires on one arm and is suppressed on the rest.** `file not found` from a write op has two causes and only one wants `paste`: a caller who meant to create, and a caller who typo'd a path to a file that does exist — for whom taking the suggestion writes a second file and leaves the real one unedited, which is [#1424](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1424)'s `misdirects` class and strictly worse than the refusal. So it renders only on the generic `wrong CWD?` fallback, never where the helper has positively identified a different mistake (cwd drift, `around`'s digit-path heuristic, a comma or whitespace path list, an unexpandable `~user`), and both readings are stated rather than one chosen. Read ops never pass it: nothing was to be written, so there is no next step to name.

  **`grep:PATTERN:PATH:0` said it would not guess between "unlimited" and "the default" — and gave a spelling for neither, while the op accepts both.** `all` has been the unlimited token since [#1328](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1328) and went unnamed by the one message whose reader is asking for it. The default is now printed as a number, resolved at call time from `grep.max_results` rather than frozen at import, so a project that overrode the cap is told its own cap instead of the shipped constant.

  **Adjacent, found while writing the clause: a directory was reported as a missing file.** `edit:::a:::b:::docs` answered `ERROR: file not found: docs` about a directory sitting right there, and every line after it — the cwd-drift hint, and the new create clause, which would have offered to `paste` a whole file over it — was advice about a path that is not the problem. `_path_not_found` had two states where it needed three; exists-but-wrong-kind is neither `ok` nor gone. It now says so and points at `ls:` / `tree:`. Every op that shares the helper gains it, `read` included, whose own test had been pinning the wrong sentence.

  **The payload clause stats behind the containment gate, which the first commit did not.** `_missing_field_create_clause` is reached from `_at_file_to_parts`, which runs *before* dispatch applies `_op_path_gate` — so "there is no file at X" would have differed by whether an out-of-boundary file exists, for exactly the paths every other route refuses to answer about. Raised by an independent review of the committed diff and fixed through `_containment_error` rather than a second copy of the rule ([#882](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/882) is the filing about what a second copy costs). The test drops the suite-wide `SUPERTOOL_ALLOW_OUTSIDE_CWD=1` and asserts the two receipts are byte-identical.

  **There is no registry-derived route to these names, and the honest answer was a hand-written table with a test.** `replaces` — the registry key the raw-command guard quotes so its advice cannot go stale ([#1376](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1376)) — maps a raw *shell command* onto an op, and only preset and project ops carry one. Every substitute named here is a built-in, and a built-in has no registry entry: `registry:paste` says so in as many words, and `help:paste` reads `.supertool.json` and returns nothing outside a project. So `_CREATING_OPS` is written by hand beside `_OP_SYNONYMS`, and one test enumerates both against `_valid_op_names()` and fails the day a named target is renamed or dropped.

- **Containment was verified in a checkout that opts out of it** ([#1353](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1353)). This repository's own `.supertool.json` has set `allow_outside_cwd: true` since before v0.33.0, so #1287's boundary is read, resolved, and then declined here. Anyone reproducing a containment fix by running it in this clone gets a pass that is a fact about the config rather than about the guard — this repo's own defect class, arriving through the config instead of through code.

  **The setting stays and the suite stops depending on it.** Removing it would break the cross-worktree reads agents here legitimately make, and a runtime disclosure of which mode a check passed in would print under every call, which is the shape nobody reads. `tests/test_containment_config_independence_1353.py` spawns `supertool.py` from a project directory whose config does *not* opt out, and pins both the core boundary (`read`) and a declared preset boundary (`claims`, `root: repo`).

  **The exposure was narrower than the issue stated, and the scoping is the useful half.** In-process tests were never affected: `tests/conftest.py`'s autouse fixture hands every test `_CONFIG = {}` with `_CONFIG_CHECKED = True`, so `_safe_path`'s config lookup cannot see this checkout's file at all, and deleting the env var is sufficient. It is a *spawned* supertool with a cwd inside this repo that walks up to the real `.supertool.json`. Both halves are now asserted rather than assumed, so if conftest ever stops neutralising the config, one named test says so instead of every in-process containment test quietly becoming a statement about `.supertool.json`.

- **A containment declaration travelled into the environment of the process it constrains** ([#1357](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1357)). `paths` was not in `_RESERVED_KEYS`, so every declaring op exported it to its own subprocess as `SUPERTOOL_PATHS`. Nothing reads it — a tree-wide grep returns zero — and the core has already enforced the declaration by the time the subprocess is spawned. Reserved, on the same terms as `replaces` in #1347, rather than left exported with a note: "our own config, so harmless" is a judgement that would otherwise have to be re-made by every future reader.

  **The `{arg}` lint the same issue proposed is measured and not built.** The proposal was to flag `{arg}` appearing beside a `PATH`-shaped `syntax`. Walked over every shipped manifest: 24 ops carry `{arg}`, 8 of those name a path in `syntax`, and all 8 are already either refused at dispatch by `_entry_names_a_path` unless they declare, or named in `_UNDECLARED_PATH_OPS`. The lint's population is a strict subset of a gate's, and a refusal is strictly stronger than a warning, so it reaches nothing.

  **It is also pointed at the wrong half of the residue.** The op #1357 is about is one that *means* a path and writes `{arg}` behind a `syntax` that does not say `PATH` — and that op is invisible to a lint keyed on the `syntax` saying `PATH`. Closing it would mean promoting `{arg}` to a path signal, which refuses the 16 shipped ops that pass a handle, a ref, a tag, an ID or a repo slug through it and take no path. The residue stays open by decision, pinned by a test that asserts the gate returns `None` for exactly that shape, so the proposal is not re-derived from the issue text alone.

- **A quoted pattern searched the quote characters, and the zero said `scanned 1 files`** ([#1435](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1435)). `grep:'beta':q.txt` returned `(0 results in 0 files, scanned 1 files)` while `grep:beta:q.txt` returned the line — the `'` were matched as literal text. Every clause was true, and `scanned N files` is precisely the disclosure that tells a reader the op *looked*, so the strongest available statement of an absence was made about the pattern and read as one about the file. Quoting a phrase is not a mistake anyone gets warned out of; it is what a shell user does with a pattern containing a space.

  **Nothing is stripped and nothing is refused.** A caller hunting a genuinely quoted phrase — quoted JSON, a quoted word in prose — typed exactly what they meant, and their result is unchanged: no note is printed when the search matched. What changes is only the silence after a zero, and it changes in three states rather than two. The unwrapped spelling is probed over the same population the zero was about, so the render says either `Without them, 'beta' DOES match here — this zero is about the quotes` or `Without them, 'nowhere' matches nothing here either — the quotes are not why this is zero`. The second state is what stops the note becoming noise: a deliberate quoted search looking at a real absence is told so, instead of being sent to re-run a query that comes back just as empty.

  **Only a matched pair counts.** `'zzz'|'yyy'` begins and ends with `'` and is not one — unwrapping it yields a pattern nobody typed — so a further occurrence of the quote character disqualifies it, as does an empty body.

  Swept across the surfaces that share the concept rather than fixed at the entry point that was filed: `grep`, `grep` with context (`grep_around`), `grep`'s count-only mode, `around`, and `read:PATH:::grep=`. Two known divergences are left standing and filed rather than folded in: `between:re:START:END:PATH` reaches none of the shared pattern machinery at all — not this note, not the BRE rewrite, not the saturation refusal — and `gh-job:N:grep:PATTERN` runs in a preset process with its own reader.

- **`gh-pr:NUMBER` indexes the review threads it had only ever counted** ([#1445](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1445)). The header printed `Unresolved threads: 2 / 2` and then nothing, with `## Comments (0)` — a true statement about a different population — as the next thing a reader saw, so the only route to two real bot findings was `gh api repos/OWNER/REPO/pulls/N/comments`. The count is now followed by one row per thread: state, `path:line`, author, and the comment's first line, capped at 20 with the remainder stated. Resolved threads are shown too, lowercased and sorted last, because "resolved" is one person's decision about another person's finding and a reader who cannot see it cannot disagree with it; the count line states the split. The bodies stay behind `gh-pr:NUMBER:threads`, which each row names — a bot review runs to kilobytes per thread and the dashboard is not where that belongs.

- **A thread fetch that failed used to render as no line at all** ([#1445](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1445)). The dashboard ran a second, lossy fetcher that returned `[]` for a rate limit, a 404, a timeout and a genuinely empty list alike, and the caller printed the count only when that list was non-empty. So the two most different answers — "this PR has threads and I could not read them" and "this PR has none" — produced the same silence. There is now one three-state fetcher behind `gh-pr`, `gh-pr:NUMBER:threads` and `gh-prs`, and the header prints in all three: a count, `0 / 0 — read, not assumed`, or `UNKNOWN — they could not be read (<reason>)`. `gl-mr` has answered this way since #812; GitHub was the side that had drifted.

- **`gh-prs` counted an unreadable thread call as zero and dropped the flag** ([#1445](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1445)). Same fetcher, worse position: the board is the read that decides which PR to open, so a PR whose per-PR GraphQL call declined rendered without the `threads` marker and looked clean. It now flags `threads?`, which is a third state — distinct from `threads`, from no flag, and from a PR past the enrichment cap that was never asked at all.

- **A malformed GraphQL reply aborted the whole PR dashboard** ([#1445](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1445)). The thread reply was walked with an `or {}` chain, so a `data` that arrived as a list — GraphQL's error envelope is one shape that does this — raised `AttributeError` out of the fetcher and killed a render the caller wanted for its checks and its diff stat. Each hop is now type-checked and a reply of the wrong shape declines by name. The deleted lossy fetcher happened to catch that exception and return `[]`, which is how one line of code was both a crash and a silence.

- **An unreadable file rendered exactly like a file with no context to show** ([#1446](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1446)). `validators/common/source_context.py` swallowed `OSError` and returned `[]` — the same value a located finding gets when its window falls outside the file. Every receipt printed the two identically, and thirty adapters inherited it.

  The finding survives, because it does not depend on us: the tool said something is wrong at that line whether or not we can reprint the line. So only the illustration is qualified. The helper now returns *fields* rather than a list — `**context_fields(target, line)` — and a read that failed carries a `context_unavailable` reason beside the empty `source_context`, rendered in verbose mode as `[no source context: FileNotFoundError reading ...]`. Three states where there were two: lines, no lines, and could-not-look.

  Not theoretical, and not Windows-only the way the `pkg_paths` instance in #1443 was. Measured against `Path.read_text` on macOS: a directory raises `IsADirectoryError`, a `chmod 000` file `PermissionError`, a deleted target `FileNotFoundError`, a symlink loop `OSError` errno 62. `phpunit-mcp` renders context from a path taken out of the tool's own output, and a `slow`-tier validator runs at the end of the call, by which time the target may be gone.

  `source_context()` is removed rather than deprecated: left in place, the next adapter copies the call that was already in twenty-eight files. `phpstan-mcp` and `phpunit-mcp` carried private copies of the same swallow and now use the shared helper; a test refuses any new copy of either.

- `git-push` now relays the local pre-push hook's own output, so a gate that
  announces it is not gating is heard (#1448). Since #894 and #1242 the hook is
  selective — it runs the full suite for `master`/`main` and deliberately skips
  it for a feature branch — and it says which arm it took every time. None of
  that reached the operator: two pushes 30x apart in wall clock (7.45s and
  226.99s, the second running ~9,600 tests) produced receipts of the same shape,
  so a skipped suite and a passed one were indistinguishable and "it pushed
  fine" carried a local-green claim it had not earned.

- The relay is verbatim, never a summary: the op asserting what the hook did is
  the inference it refuses everywhere else. The hook's lines are told apart from
  git's own by process ordering, not by pattern — git prints its `To <url>`
  porcelain header only after the hook has exited, so everything above it on
  stdout was written by the hook and nothing below it was. With no header there
  is nothing to delimit against, and the receipt says the boundary is unknown
  instead of claiming the stream. A long transcript keeps its first three and
  last twelve lines (a hook announces its arm first and its outcome last), and
  the elision is named rather than silent.

- The hook's stderr is relayed as well, since many hooks write their advice
  there — but under `>` and marked `provenance UNKNOWN`, not under the hook's
  name. Stdout has the `To` header to attribute against; stderr has no
  equivalent, and git and the remote's own hooks write to it too.

- Above the relay sits a state line in three states: the hook path when one ran,
  `none ran` with the reason (including `--no-verify`, now disclosed rather than
  left as a bare flag name), and `UNKNOWN` when git did not answer where the
  hook lives. It is what makes an empty relay readable, since a hook that
  printed nothing and no hook at all are different facts that render alike.

- The `--- git output ---` dump on a refused push is bounded the same way, at
  five lines and thirty (#1448). It used to print the child's whole output, and
  when the thing that refused the push is a hook running the suite that is an
  11,449-item pytest transcript inside a receipt. Both ends survive, which is
  where the arm the hook announced and the tests it refused on both live.

- The timeout receipt keeps everything #1242 and #1447 put in it and gains one
  sentence: a timed-out push is killed and its captured output goes with it, so
  a missing relay there is not a hook that stayed silent.

- **An `unless_flag` token sitting in another option's value slot un-claimed the entry, so `gh pr create -t --dry-run -b y` was `clean` and really opens a pull request titled `--dry-run`** ([#1450](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1450)). The guard read the `--dry-run` in `-t`'s value slot as an exclusion — the same defect [#1430](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1430) had for help flags, one function over. `clean` is a positive claim that nothing in the command is replaced, made about a command that opens a PR.

  **It is disclosed, not blocked, and that is the opposite call to the help fix.** A help flag is terminal and rarely combined, so blocking its ambiguous slot costs a legible wrong block. The flags entries exclude are the ones people put together: seven shipped invocations flip clean → blocked if this slot is scored, five of them previews of a destructive push — `git push --force-with-lease --dry-run`, `git push --no-verify --dry-run`, `git push -u --dry-run origin main`, `git push --set-upstream --dry-run origin main`, `git push --force-with-lease -n` — and a refusal that names `git-push` under a blocked `--dry-run` performs exactly what the blocked command declined to do.

  So `_guard_excluded()` becomes `_guard_exclusion_state()` with three answers — `none`, `excluded`, and `value` for a token the guard cannot tell from the preceding option's value. `value` un-claims the entry exactly as before, nothing new is blocked, and the segment is `undecided` with a note instead of `clean`. One unambiguous exclusion anywhere in the argv decides the whole argv, so `git commit --amend --dry-run`, `git push --dry-run` and `git status -s -z` stay silently clean; a long option carrying its value attached (`--title=x --dry-run`) leaves no slot open either.

- **`_checks.shortfall()` now flattens the leg names its callers hand it, instead of trusting that they already did** ([#1451](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1451)). It renders caller-supplied text and did not flatten it, so the [#851](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/851) boundary held or did not depending on which caller you arrived through. The issue left open whether any caller outside `presets/github/branch.py` actually passes unreviewed text; three do. `gh-run` passes names read straight off the jobs API, `gh-pr` and `gh-pr-merge` pass names parsed out of a workflow file, and on one route the declined-count `reason` is built from a child process's stderr. Only `gh-branch` was flattening, and it was flattening at its own call site.

  The `reason` string is flattened too. `_untrusted.flat()` is idempotent, so the caller that already flattened pays a no-op rather than a second substitution — which is what makes the seam the right place for it rather than a rendering change.

  The comma is deliberately left alone here, unlike in `label()`: a matrix leg is routinely named `build (ubuntu-latest, 3.11)`, and substituting that separator would mangle real data to defend against nothing.

  `named_disclosure()` gets the same treatment in the same commit. It is `shortfall()`'s sibling — one answers "how many legs are missing", the other "which legs failed" — and it interpolated a caller-supplied leg name, its kind word and its id straight into its own `  <label>: <text>` line. Neither issue named it; an independent review of the diff found it by reading the file around the change rather than the change.

- **The example quoted three times as the reason the ambiguous help slot blocks does not block** ([#1452](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1452)). `git push --force -h` is `clean`: `--force` is an `unless_flag` of every `git push` entry, so all five are un-claimed before the help classifier is reached. The sentence shipped in `_guard_help_state`'s docstring, in `docs/contributing.md` and in the v0.36.0 changelog entry. The argument survives untouched and only the illustration was wrong — `git push origin -o -h main`, the other example in the same paragraph, does block and is the case the trade-off is actually about.

  `tests/test_guard_help_example_and_project_entries_1452.py` now extracts every command those three files call a wrong block and runs it against the guard, so the next example that stops matching the code fails a test rather than teaching a wrong fact.

- **`docs/contributing.md` now says that a `replaces` entry must not name a command whose `-h` is a real option.** The guard treats `-h` and `--help` as terminal for every entry in every registry, which is measured-correct for the shipped mappings — every one of them a `git` or a `gh` invocation, pinned by a test rather than by the entry count the paragraph used to carry — and wrong for `ls -h`, `du -h`, `sort -h` and `grep -h` — a `clean` verdict on a command that runs, reintroduced by configuration rather than by code. Not reachable in this tree, so this is a schema rule rather than a code change; the behaviour it warns about is pinned by a test, so the warning cannot come to describe a guard that does something else.

- **A state token from a remote check could add a line to the tally that reports it** ([#1453](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1453)). `_checks.normalize()` stripped only leading and trailing whitespace, so an internal newline in a job's `conclusion`, `status` or `state` survived into `summarize()`'s leftover term — and from there into `gh-branch`'s two-space-indented table and its `Legs:` line, the two lines [#1449](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/pull/1449) had just flattened four other fields on. The flatten now happens in `normalize()` itself rather than at either render, which also closes the five other places that print its return value unchanged: `gh-pr-merge`'s `mergeable` and `mergeStateStatus` lines, the dashboard's equivalents, and `gh-branch`'s run conclusion. Fixing the two lines the issue named would have left five open, which is the per-call-site failure #1449 rejected one file over.

  It cannot change a verdict: no member of `PASSED_STATES`, `FAILED_STATES`, `PENDING_STATES` or `BENIGN_STATES` contains whitespace, so a token that gains a space can neither enter a set nor leave one.

  `label()` additionally substitutes the comma, because that is a second forgery on the same line and flattening does not reach it. `summarize()` promises its output "can be audited by arithmetic instead of by trusting the labels" and its terms are comma-separated, so a state reading `x, 5 passed` rendered as `1 x, 5 passed` and forged a term inside the audited list. Only there — a comma is never legitimate in a state token, and routinely is in the matrix job names `shortfall()` renders.

- **The undecided disclosure had no text budget, so 200 chained segments rendered 27,634 characters into the operator's context** ([#1454](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1454)). [#1449](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1449) capped `guard_refusal()` after a 61,942-character refusal and left the other joins of `verdict.notes` uncapped. Nothing is blocked on this path and nothing runs that should not; the cost is a wall of text from a hook whose whole job is a one-line disclosure, sized by accident- or attacker-controlled input and re-paid on every occurrence.

  Every renderer now goes through one bounded formatter rather than gaining its own cap, because a cap per channel is what left this one. **There were three channels, not the two the issue names**: `hooks/pre_bash_guard.py` had its own copy of `"; ".join(verdict.notes)` and never called `guard_undecided_note()` at all — 27,632 characters measured through the shipped hook. It calls `guard_notes_text()` now, which also flattens each note, so a note carrying registry text can no longer forge a line in the hook's `additionalContext` either.

- **`go vet` ran out of wall on a cold Windows runner and the suite read that as a dirty package** ([#1461](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1461)). `test_a_clean_package_is_clean` reddened `pytest (windows-latest, 3.10)` on a PR touching `presets/_checks.py` and nothing else. The adapter was right — a timeout is `ok: false, count: 1` with `code: "adapter"`, which is the channel `validators/SCHEMA.md` gives an absence and which the core renders `NOT CHECKED`, keeps out of the delta, never caches and never rolls an edit back over. What was wrong was a test asserting a lint verdict about a package no tool had finished analysing.

  `_adapter_verdict.skip_if_stalled` has existed for this since #794 and was extended for it in #1296. `tests/test_validators_go_vet_669.py` is the fourth adapter suite to hit the failure and the first not to have adopted it; it does now, at the one spawn site, so a stall declines once instead of at nine call sites. A real printf finding, a clean package reported dirty, an absent toolchain, a `skipped` third state and a timeout claimed in 12ms all still reach the assertion written for them.

  **The guard could not see the payload that produced the report.** `stalled_at_its_own_wall` matched the substring `timeout`, and this adapter says "timed out"; every other clause of the predicate matched, so the one shape it was built to classify was the one it read as a verdict. It now matches either spelling. `validators/pyright/pyright.py` is invisible to it for the same reason and for a second one — it codes that error `timeout` rather than `adapter`, so the core does not render it `NOT CHECKED` either. Filed separately, not fixed here.

  **The budget is unchanged at 60s, deliberately.** Measured on macOS/go1.22.3 with `GOCACHE` pointed at an empty directory: a cold `go vet` costs **3.54s** against **0.24s** warm, because it compiles the standard library before analysing anything. That is once per build cache and it is a property of the machine, so raising a product timeout to cover a first run on a CI image would slow the real failure mode — a `go vet` that hangs on somebody's edit — for every user, to fix a test. The suite pays the cold cost once instead, vetting a throwaway module before any adapter spawn: `GOCACHE` is content-keyed rather than module-scoped, so a second, never-seen module vets in 0.22s after it. The warm-up is a convenience and never a gate; when it does not fit its own budget it reports the reason through the warnings summary rather than skipping the module or failing it.

  **The macOS runners have no Go, and nothing in CI installs one.** There is no `setup-go` step in `.github/`, so each leg gets whatever its image ships; the ubuntu and windows images ship Go and the macOS images do not. `needs_go` therefore skips 10 of `tests/test_validators_go_vet_669.py`'s 27 tests on every macOS leg — every test of what `go vet` actually says about a package: the clean verdict, the printf finding, sibling attribution, the receipt cap and its truncation notice, the package that does not type-check. That is why only Windows ever hit the timeout: the other four legs were not exercising the path at all. It also caught this change's own first attempt, which provoked the timeout arm without stubbing the binary lookup `main()` runs before it spawns anything — four red macOS legs asserting on a payload that cannot exist where there is no toolchain, which is #1205's shape landing inside the fix for #1205's shape. The four assertions that are about the adapter's *error routing* rather than about Go now stub that lookup and run on every runner; the one test that genuinely executes `go` is gated on the suite's existing `needs_go`, whose reason ("go not on PATH") is not confusable with the one `skip_if_stalled` writes ("adapter spent its whole 60s internal budget without reaching a verdict"). Absent toolchain and slow toolchain are different facts and the skip list keeps them apart.

  Whether a first `go vet` on a GitHub Windows runner is reliably over 60s remains unmeasured, and this change no longer depends on the answer: over it, the suite declines with a named reason instead of publishing a machine limit as a product defect.

- **A pyright that hung was a finding about your file, and could roll your edit back** ([#1464](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1464)). The adapter's `TimeoutExpired` arm emitted `code: "timeout"`. `adapter` is the one word the core routes to the third state — it is the only member of `_NONDETERMINISTIC_ERROR_CODES` an adapter may use, and the only code `_validator_not_checked` accepts — so a stall was read as one error on the file: cached until the file's hash changed, subtracted from a baseline as if it were real, and counted as a new finding by `rollback_on_fail`, which reverts the edit with nothing to restore it from. `validators/SCHEMA.md` already reserved `adapter` for "a binary that is absent, a timeout, output that would not parse", so this was a violated contract rather than a design gap.

  The failure is silent by construction — the payload is well-formed, nothing warns, and the only symptom is a fault presenting as a finding — so the class is pinned rather than the instance: a sweep now parses every adapter's `except subprocess.TimeoutExpired` arm and refuses any literal error code other than `adapter`. 26 such arms across the 36 adapters, 18 of which name a code literally rather than through a helper; exactly one of the 18 was wrong.

- **`paste` on a new file reported a ruff baseline it never measured, and printed a `-1` improvement against a file that did not exist** ([#1466](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1466)). The baseline pass ran the whole validator fan-out *before* the write, against a path that was not there. Most of the 36 adapters answer that with `code: "adapter"`, which the core already routes to `? → N (baseline not measured)` — which is why `py-syntax` was right. Three answer instead, because a missing file is a finding in their own vocabulary rather than an adapter fault: ruff calls it `E902`, `tsc-check` `TS6053`, `prettier-check` `formatting`. Those fabricated counts were accepted as measurements, so one call printed `ruff : 1 → 0 (-1) ✓` and `py-syntax : ? → 0` in the same block, disagreeing about whether the file had a past.

  Fixed above the adapter layer rather than in the three: `_pre_existed` is already sampled before the op for the rollback arms, and a file that did not exist has no pre-op state for *any* adapter to measure, so the baseline pass is skipped and every row takes the `?` road. Patching the adapters would have been one adapter's memory at a time — the shape #1202 had to undo across sixteen of them — and it also spares a full validator fan-out on every file `paste` creates.

  The `1` was arithmetic and not only prose. `_validator_regressed` subtracts the baseline, so an invented `1` against a real post-write finding of `1` is equal counts and equal `ok`: a finding the create had just introduced was excused as `(pre-existing — not from this edit)`. The sign only ever ran that way — a fabricated baseline is higher than the true zero, so it suppresses regressions and cannot manufacture one — so the defect misreported rather than reverting an edit.

  Removing it restores that arm, which is a behaviour change and not only a display one: for those three adapters a finding on a created file now regresses, so the `[left on disk]` disclosure fires where it could not before — ruff is the case `_left_on_disk_line` names by name, and it was inert for ruff until now — and a `rollback_on_fail` registration would unlink the create. No shipped registration reaches the second, because every `rollback_on_fail` validator in both config files answers a missing file with `code: "adapter"` or `skipped` and so already had no baseline. The tests pin the arm and audit that intersection rather than asserting it.

- **A remote could choose what `git-push`'s receipt said it did** ([#1470](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1470)). Since #1448 the op relays the push's stderr under `> ` on the success path, where nothing rendered it before — and `remote:` lines are written by whatever server you push to. Neither relay went through `_untrusted.flat`. `_untrusted.split_lines` cuts on LF / CR / CRLF alone, by design, so a U+2028 survived *inside* a relayed line and put everything after it back at column 0. A `pre-receive` hook printing `ok<U+2028>[result] PUSHED  master -> origin/master @ cafed00d  (verified)` produced a receipt with two `[result]` lines, the forged one first, for any consumer splitting the way `str.splitlines()` does — and #623 made `[result]` the line a caller reads as the verdict. An `ESC [2K ESC [1A` relayed verbatim deleted the receipt line above it instead of adding one.

  Every line of a child's output now passes through `_untrusted` on its way to the receipt: both relays, all three `--- git output ---` dumps on the refused arms, the `First error:` line, and the same string where it is interpolated into `[result]` itself. Disclosed, never stripped — the forged text still reads, as `[U+2028]` and `[U+001B]`. The local pre-push hook's half goes through it too: it is code already running on your machine and no escalation on its own, but the seam is the same one, it costs nothing, and a half-flattened seam is the one that gets re-filed.

  Tabs survive, which is why the relay uses `visible(keep=tab)` rather than `flat()`. `flat()` drops them and is right to — it renders a one-line *field* on a line the tool owns, where a tab can imitate a board's column structure. A relayed transcript is neither: it is the child's own lines under a prefix or a header, nobody parses it by column, and a tab can neither make a line nor move a cursor anywhere it has not already been. Dropping them would have rendered every tab-aligned hook transcript and git porcelain block as `[U+0009]` soup, breaking what #1448 shipped four hours earlier, and prevented no forgery. The one-line fields — `First error:`, the `[result]` tail — keep `flat()`, where a tab could imitate structure.

  The dumps at column 0 carry no `| ` or `> ` prefix at all, so they were the same defect with even that much removed. The `First error:` string cannot carry a U+2028 — `_first_error_line` splits with `str.splitlines()`, which consumes it — but nothing made it ESC-free.

  `tests/test_git_push_relays_hook_output_1448.py` had 13 tests and no forgery case. It now drives a real `pre-receive` hook on the bare remote, which is the third-party writer, and asserts on what a `[result]` consumer counts rather than on `flat` having been called — a site can call it and print the raw value anyway.

  The harness had the house defect aimed at the thing meant to detect it. The generated hooks wrote their lines through `sys.stdout` / `sys.stderr`, which encode through the *child interpreter's* console codec — cp1252 on every Windows runner, and cp1252 cannot hold U+2028. The two streams then disagreed, and only one of them said so: `sys.stdout` is strict, so it raised `UnicodeEncodeError`, the hook exited non-zero, the push was rejected and the local-hook forgery test went red on `pytest (windows-latest, 3.9)`. `sys.stderr` defaults to `errors="backslashreplace"`, so it substituted a six-character escape spelling, no forgery was attempted at all, and both `pre-receive` U+2028 tests passed on Windows for the wrong reason — on the one platform where relaying a third party's bytes is hardest to reason about. The hooks now encode and write to the raw stream, which needs no environment to be true and is what a real remote does; `PYTHONIOENCODING` and `reconfigure()` were rejected because both are claims about an environment the test would then have to assert survived `sh` to `exec` to git's own hook spawn, and their failure mode is exactly the vacuous green — silent, and shaped like a pass.

  The product never had that ceiling and does not inherit the fix: a remote's bytes cross the wire byte-transparently through git's sideband and `_git` decodes them with an explicit `encoding="utf-8"`, so a real U+2028 reaches the relay on Windows exactly as it does elsewhere. What was capped was a Python child writing text on the same machine.

  `assert SEP not in out` is satisfied just as well by a separator that never arrived as by one the relay flattened, which is this repo's own absence-read-as-presence in the assertions written to catch it — and it is why the Windows leg went green on the two `pre-receive` U+2028 tests while testing nothing. Each U+2028 case now also asserts the `[U+2028]` disclosure, which only a separator that reached the render can produce, and the ESC cases assert theirs. A cp1252 pin and its control run on all twelve legs, so the reproduction cannot quietly stop reproducing (#546).

  Asserting the disclosure then found the same class a third time, pointing the other way: the ESC cases went red on `pytest (macos-latest, 3.10)`, homebrew git 2.55.0, while passing on every older git in the matrix. git 2.55 added `strbuf_add_sanitized()` to `demultiplex_sideband()`, which by default caret-notates every control character in a `remote:` line, so the ESC never crossed the sideband and there was nothing for the relay to flatten. The bytes the U+2028 cases use are untouched by it — U+2028 is not a control character — which is why only the two ESC tests moved. The sandbox now sets `sideband.allowControlCharacters=true`, a key older git does not know and ignores, so the transport is the same on every leg and what is under test is supertool's flattening rather than the runner's git. If a future git drops that key the tests **skip**, naming the git version and what it did, rather than passing: a runner limit rendered as a product verdict is #1205 / #1218. That skip is granted on evidence and never on an absence — git caret-notates (`^[`) what it refuses to forward rather than dropping it, so the skip requires that fingerprint on the relayed line; a receipt with no ESC, no disclosure and no caret means the character went missing in *our* code, which fails. Skipping on the bare absence would have converted the one defect this file exists to catch into a green that blamed somebody's git. The same seam is also pinned unconditionally through a local pre-push hook, whose stdout is inherited by git and never crosses the sideband, so no git release can take that coverage away.

  The relay's ESC flattening is not made redundant by git's sanitiser, on any version. git 2.55's default is `ALLOW_ANSI_COLOR_SEQUENCES`, so an SGR sequence from the remote is still forwarded with a raw ESC in it; only cursor and erase sequences are caret-notated, and only until an operator sets `sideband.allowControlCharacters`. That reading is from git's source rather than measured against 2.55 here, and is recorded as such.

- The same class one file over: `gh-pr`'s `Unresolved threads: UNKNOWN — … (<reason>)` and `gh-pr:N:threads`' `Threads: UNKNOWN — …` render gh's own stderr tail, both fed by the same fetcher. `.splitlines()[-1]` makes the string newline-free by construction so it cannot paint a line, but not ESC-free — and the line above it is the check tally on one render and the branch pair on the other. Both sinks flattened, not one (#1470).
