- **`gl-issue` created the attachment directory the API response chose, and checked containment against that same directory** ([#1484](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1484)). `iid` comes out of the `glab issue view --output json` reply, so the directory `_download_images` writes into was named by the remote host. `os.makedirs` ran before anything validated it, and the per-file guard was anchored to that already-derived directory — a boundary derived from the value it is meant to constrain, which is [#1246](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1246)'s shape one layer down. `_is_inside` itself was correct; it was asked the wrong question.

  Reproduced against the real guard and the real root: an `iid` of `../../../../tmp/audit_pwned` gave `realpath` `/private/tmp/audit_pwned` from an `IMAGE_DIR` of `/tmp/supertool-images`, with `_is_inside(local, out_dir)` answering `True` and `_is_inside(local, IMAGE_DIR)` answering `False`. An absolute `iid` makes `os.path.join` discard the root outright.

  A non-numeric `iid` is now refused **before** any directory exists — a directory created is already a write — and every containment check is anchored to `IMAGE_DIR`, never to the derived path. The tests assert on the filesystem, on what exists under and outside the root after the call, never on a guard having been called: a site can call a guard and write anyway.

  Precondition is a hostile or compromised GitLab host, since `iid` is server-assigned; it is not reachable from an issue author alone.

- **The GitLab error relays let the server choose which line its text landed on** ([#1485](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1485)). `glab` echoes the GitLab API's own error body on stderr, and six renders in `presets/gitlab/` printed it into a line at column 0 with no `_untrusted.flat` — `gl-issue`, `gl-mr`, `gl-pipeline`, `gl-job`, `gl-runners` and `gl-issue-create`. `_untrusted.split_lines` cuts on LF/CR/CRLF alone by design, so a U+2028 survives *inside* what the render treats as one line and puts everything after it back at column 0 for any consumer that splits the way `str.splitlines()` does — ahead of the `[result]` a caller reads as the verdict. Same mechanism as [#1470](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1470), one forge over.

  `gl-api`'s `classify_error` was already correct and is the shape the six adopted rather than a seventh invention. Three more sites in the same subsystem went with them: `gl-mrs`'s list-failure relay, which reaches a receipt because the core appends a failing preset's stderr to it, and `gl-mr`'s `_glab_fail_detail` and merge-tree detail line, where `str.splitlines()` already stopped U+2028 but nothing removed an ESC — a relayed `ESC [2K ESC [1A` deletes the line above it.

  Disclosed, not stripped. Every test asserts on what a `[result]` consumer counts and on the separator having reached the render at all, never on `flat` having been called: a site can call it and print the raw value anyway, and a render that dropped the text would otherwise pass for the wrong reason.

## [0.36.0] - 2026-08-12

### Added

- Every op in every shipped preset is now either mapped to the raw command it supersedes or recorded as a deliberate absence with its reason ([#1384](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1384)). `replaces` reached 22 of 87 ops over four PRs and nothing said which of the rest were decided and which were never looked at; the two render identically. `tests/test_replaces_census_1384.py` partitions the population, asserts it total in both directions, and goes red on an op that belongs to neither.
- Builtin ops (`read`, `grep`, `glob`, `tree`, `wc`) stay outside the guard, and the reasoning is written down rather than left implicit: the matcher scores every pipeline segment, so `cat` and `grep` mappings would fire on a stage of nearly every composed command; the only escape is `raw_command_guard: false`, which is repo-global and would take the forge mappings with it; and the payoff would be round-trips rather than the wrong answers every existing mapping prevents.

- Eleven of the twenty-one GitHub ops now declare what raw `gh` invocation they supersede, up from four, so the shipped `PreToolUse` guard covers the whole `gh` family rather than `gh pr` alone ([#1384](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1384)). `gh issue view` names `gh-issue` (`--comments` / `-c` selects `:full`), `gh issue create` names `gh-issue-create`, `gh pr list` names `gh-prs`, `gh pr checks` names `gh-pr:NUMBER:status`, `gh run view` names `gh-run`, `gh run view --log` / `--log-failed` name `gh-job`, and `gh label list` names `gh-labels`.
- `gh run list --branch` and `gh run list --commit` name `gh-branch`. That pair is the whole `gh run list` mapping: those are the two questions `gh-branch` answers, and `gh run list --branch <default> --limit 1` is the exact command whose wrong answer it exists for — it returns whichever workflow started last, routinely CodeQL, and reports that conclusion as the commit's. A bare `gh run list` is an enumeration no op produces and is left running.
- `gh pr list --json` is excluded too, and asymmetrically: `gh-prs` renders a board with no field-selection vocabulary, and the maintainer skill's branch reap uses `--json headRefName -q` to enumerate merged head branches, which no op produces. `gh issue list --json` stays claimed, because `gh-issues` carries `search=` and `iids` and no documented use of the raw shape survives them. A missed block is the direction this guard may safely be wrong in; a dead end has no per-command way past.
- `--web` and `-w` are excluded from every `gh` mapping that has them, including the four that shipped in v0.34.0. No op opens a browser, so `gh pr view 1 --web`, `gh issue create --web` and their siblings were dead ends with no per-command way past — `raw_command_guard: false` is repo-global. This widens what stays usable; nothing new blocks because of it.

- `gh-branch`'s workflow table names the run: a `Run` column carrying the run id
  and `attempt N`, with the lifecycle word moved to its own `Phase` column. Both
  fields were already fetched, so it costs no extra call, and it is the route
  from the render to `gh-run:<id>` or a re-run that previously needed a raw API
  call. `attempt` prints on attempt 1 too, and an unreadable id or attempt
  renders `?` rather than a default. (#1409)

### Changed

- The repository now runs the raw-command guard it ships. `.claude/settings.json` wires `hooks/pre-bash-guard.sh` as a third `PreToolUse` hook on `Bash`, alongside the two jit-context hooks rather than inside them, so a failure in one is not the other's silence ([#1376](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1376)). Until now the guard reached this checkout only through a plugin release: the install these sessions run is v0.25.0, whose `hooks/` holds `session-start.sh` and no `pre-bash-guard.sh` at all.
- Three hand-written `block` rules under `.claude/jit-context/tools/00-manual/` are retired, markdown and index row together, in the same commit that wires the guard — so nothing is uncovered in between and no command is ever refused twice with two different messages. `gh-pr-view-merge-have-ops.md`, `gh-list-limit.md` and `git-push-has-an-op.md` go; the guard blocks every command each of them forbade, verified per command through `guard:` rather than read off the registry.
- Five rules stay, each because `replaces` cannot reach what it forbids: `supertool-no-cut.md` is about piping an *op's own* output, `harness-tools-blocked.md` fires on non-Bash tools, `op-defaults-that-narrow.md` on an op string rather than a raw command, `merged-is-not-ancestry.md` on `git branch --merged`, which `git-worktrees` answers for a different population, and `git-C-has-cwd.md` on `git -C <path> <sub>`, which no mapping can reach until [#1421](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1421). Each keeper's command is asserted `clean` against the guard, so the day a mapping starts covering one the test goes red and names the rule.

- `gh-prs` gained `merged-since=<ISO date|instant>`, the boundary filter it had no vocabulary for — "what merged since Friday" had no op at all. It takes instants only, never a tag name: resolving a tag has three outcomes and a listing filter has two, and this op follows a `repo:` target while a tag is a read of the local clone. Beside `state=open` (the default) it is refused rather than answered, because `--search merged:>X` cannot match an open PR and the empty board would be a fact about the query, not about the repo ([#1411](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1411)).
- `gh-since-tag` no longer builds its own `gh pr list` argv. It was a third caller of the listing `prs._build_list_cmd` owns — the one that drifted in #1207 and again in #1230, each fix paid for twice — and now calls it with `state=merged,merged-since=INSTANT` and its own field set. The boundary's three states, the local-history reconcile and the `changelog.d` cross-check stay where they are: what must not be duplicated is the judgement, not the render ([#1411](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1411)).
- Every `gh pr list --search` qualifier now composes into one flag. gh binds `--search` to a single string, so `reviewer=@me,merged-since=...` would have emitted two and silently answered half the question — unreachable until this release added the second search key ([#1411](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1411)).
- `gh-prs`'s scope footer names the state it is about. It read "every author's **open** PRs" whatever `state=` asked for, so `gh-prs:state=merged` labelled a merged board as the open one — on the one line whose job is naming the population ([#1411](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1411)).

- **The no-cut jit rule's body is 2,030 bytes instead of 3,884, and the matcher is deliberately unchanged** ([#1433](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1433)). A `tools/` rule is injected in full on every match, false ones included, so the body is the price of every wrong block — one agent reported this one as the largest single input cost of its run. Four wrong blocks in one evening across three callers, against no observed missed cut, so the answer is the cheaper false positive rather than a wider pattern: the env-var prefix and the command-substitution shapes stay disclosed and unmatched. What survives is the table of replacement ops, one line of measurement, and the disclosure; the three-incident write-up moved to the issues that recorded it.

  A ceiling now enforces the "keep it short" rule the notes already stated and nothing checked — `tests/test_jit_rule_body_budget_1433.py` reds any indexed `tools/` rule over 3,200 bytes, and separately asserts the replacement ops and the not-precise disclosure are still present, so a body cannot come in under budget by deleting the half that helps.

### Fixed

- **`unknown operation` listed 44 builtins, none of which was the answer, and withheld the 50 loaded ops that held it** ([#1222](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1222)). `supertool 'worktrees'` printed the builtin roster and then told the reader to make a second call to see the preset ops — one of which was `git-worktrees`. The name was already in the process; only the printing was missing. The refusal now carries a `Did you mean:` line above the roster, produced by three rules and nothing else: a documented synonym, a candidate that is exactly `<prefix>-<typed>` (`worktrees` → `git-worktrees`), and one edit — insert, delete, substitute, or an adjacent swap, so `raed` finds `read` — over names of four characters or more. Under four characters a single edit is noise (`lsx` is one from `ls`) and nothing is offered, because a wrong name costs the reader a round-trip that silence would not have. Candidates are the ops loaded in that process, capped at three; a shipped preset this cwd does not enable is named only when nothing loaded matches, and is labelled `not loaded here`. The roster is never replaced by the suggestion — the guess can still be wrong and the list cannot.
- **A wrong-case op name was answered with its neighbour** ([#1222](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1222), found reviewing the first commit). `Read:x` produced `Did you mean: head` — lowercased, `Read` is distance 0 from `read`, which the "a name is not a suggestion for itself" guard discarded, leaving `head` at distance 1 as the top candidate. An exact case-insensitive match is now the first rule and returns alone, because once the name is known a runner-up is noise. `blame` also survived in `tests/test_parallel.py` and in a `test_parallel_safe_writes_1244.py` docstring that named it as an example of an op absent from `_OP_SAFETY_BUILTIN` — it was absent because it had stopped being an op, which is the one thing that check cannot see.

- **Three registries named `blame`, an op the dispatcher stopped accepting in April** ([#1285](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1285), folding in #1152). `b4099a5` moved `blame` out of the builtins into the `git` preset as `git-blame` and removed it from four places; `_PARALLEL_SAFE_OPS`, `_PATH_ARG_POSITIONS` and `_READ_OP_TARGETS` kept their rows, as did three doc pages. `git log --all -S` settles the question the issue could not: it was **removed**, not left unfinished. The `git blame --line-porcelain` machinery still in the core is `git-investigate`'s blame-hotspot section, not an abandoned op. The risk was nil while nothing dispatched — an op that cannot be invoked cannot misbehave — but two of those tables are containment-adjacent, saying which argument is a path and what may be read, so the row is inert by coincidence: the day a preset or config op is named `blame`, it applies to that. `tests/test_registry_names_dispatch_1285.py` now holds all four op registries against the dispatcher, structurally and by probing `dispatch` itself. PR #1418's equivalent check derives its denominator from the docs, so it did not cover these. There turned out to be a **fifth** registry the issue does not name and the only one anybody copies: `.supertool.example.json` documented `blame` under `builtin-ops` with a syntax, a description and an example, so every project started from that file listed the op in `ops` and produced a full `help:blame` reference for a name answering `unknown operation`. Both config files are checked now, against the op named at the head of each entry's `syntax` rather than against its key — `grep-count` and `read-grep` are deliberately labels for a mode of `grep` and of `read`, and their syntax says so.
- **`_PATH_ARG_POSITIONS` moved from a local literal inside `dispatch` to module scope** ([#1285](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1285)). No behaviour change — it is a constant, rebuilt on every dispatch call until now — but as a local it was unreadable from outside the function, which is why the one table whose rows declare *which argument is a path* had never had its membership checked against anything.

- **`write:@-` got 44 op names in alphabetical order instead of being pointed at `paste`** ([#1303](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1303)). The harness tool is called `Write`, and `.claude/jit-context/tools/00-manual/harness-tools-blocked.md` — which fires on every `Write` attempt in this repo — maps it to `paste`. The tool taught the mapping in one place and forgot it in the other. `write` and `vi` are now the two entries of a synonym table read by the unknown-op message, and additions to it need the same kind of receipt: everything inferable is inferred by the near-miss rules from [#1222](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1222) instead, where the rule can be argued with.
- **The developer agent's own brief prescribed a `git-commit` form that refuses by construction** ([#1303](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1303)). `.claude/agents/opensource-developer.md` spelled the commit step `git-commit:::MESSAGE` with no paths. `git-commit` never stages, so that form is correctly refused — meaning the first commit attempt of every delegated run failed on advice the repo itself handed the agent. The line now names `:::PATHS`, `:::--all` and the `@-` payload route, and `tests/test_developer_brief_commit_form_1303.py` extracts every colon form the brief prescribes and *runs* it against a scratch repo, so a prose rewrite cannot quietly restore a form that does not work. The issue also reports the same line in `CLAUDE.md`; it is not there — `git-commit` appears nowhere in that file.

- **Two JIT rules hard-blocked commands the shipped guard allows** ([#1347](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1347)). `git-push-has-an-op.md` and `gh-pr-view-merge-have-ops.md` predate the registry guard and cover the same two commands with one awk regex, which cannot express *except with these flags* — one-true-awk has no negation. So they refused `git push --dry-run`, `git push -n`, `gh pr create --dry-run` and every `--help`, and the body they injected named `git-push` / `gh-pr-create` as the remedy. Worse than the guard defect of the same shape: the guard prints a suggestion, a `block` prevents the call outright.

  Both drop to `mode: remind`. Enforcement stays with the one gate that honours `unless_flag`, and the reference material the guard's refusal does not carry — the tag route, `git worktree add -b` leaving the branch tracking its base, "a zero exit is not a push" — stays where it was. A new test also pins the `.md` frontmatter `mode:` against the `00-index.tsv` column that actually runs it: they disagree silently everywhere else, which is the same "reads as enforced, never fires" shape #1254 closed for the regex column.

- `gh-branch`'s verdict joins three or more workflow names with `and` instead of
  a trailing comma. `` `CodeQL`, `changelog`, `tests` `` is the shape a truncated
  list has, in the one sentence whose job is to say whether the commit is
  cleared. The list stays uncapped: these names are the verdict's own subject,
  and a shortened subject inside a not-concluded sentence is the
  absence-produced-by-the-tool defect. (#1374)

- `gh-batch-star` and `gh-batch-follow` can now eat `gh-find-starable` /
  `gh-find-followable` output directly. A `#` **preceded by whitespace** ends the
  name and starts an inline annotation; a `#` with no whitespace before it is not
  a comment, so `evil#tool/x` is refused rather than trimmed to `evil`. Nothing
  is silent: the receipt counts the annotations it dropped, names every skipped
  line with its reason, and a run with a skipped line exits 2. (#1387)

- **`gh-branch` printed `concluded success` for a workflow the same render had just refused to clear** ([#1408](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1408)). GitHub closes a run object as `completed / success` while one of its own jobs is still `in_progress` — twice on 2026-08-11, 25 minutes apart, on `pytest (windows-latest, 3.11)` and `pytest (macos-latest, 3.12)`, and neither leg would ever have reported because the run that would have carried its result was already closed. The op read both fields honestly and printed both, so the workflow table said `concluded  success` three lines under a verdict saying that workflow had not concluded, and the natural resolution of that is *the verdict is being pedantic, merge it*. The `Outcome` cell now carries a `⚠` and a sentence under the table names which two sources disagree and which one the verdict acted on. Marked rather than rewritten: `success` is what the run object says, and printing something else would trade a loud disagreement for a quiet one. A run still **running** is untouched — a pending leg under an open run is an ordinary wait — and the leg arithmetic is unchanged, so the tally still sums and no consumer of `summarize()` gains a fifth bucket.

- **Three remote fields reached `gh-branch`'s own lines unflattened, one of them the verdict sentence** ([#1408](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1408)). `presets/github/branch.py` imports `_untrusted` for the #851 convention — a value GitHub returned occupies exactly one line of our render, because a newline in it emits at column 0 and column 0 reads as the tool talking — and applied it to workflow and job names while three neighbours on the same lines went in raw.

  `orphan_lines()` backticked `conclusion` twice in the f-string whose sibling field was already `_untrusted.flat(name)`, inside a two-space-indented block. `_row()` dropped the same field into the fixed-width workflow table, whose own docstring says one extra line is one extra workflow a reader will count as having run. `_names()` rendered the workflow names in the verdict sentence itself — the line `pr_merge` republishes on the merge gate, and the highest-authority line the op writes.

  Flattened at the seam rather than at each call site, so `_names()`'s fifth caller is right too. `conclusion` is an enum in practice and renaming a workflow needs write access to the base repo, so none of the three was a live exploit; the convention is not conditioned on that, because #851 and #981 were both filed after somebody reasoned that way about the field next door.

- The `PreToolUse` hook matched the `Bash` tool alone, so wherever the PowerShell tool is enabled every shell command bypassed the guard and the user saw nothing — which is exactly what a clean pass looks like. The matcher is now `Bash|PowerShell`, and a command routed through a shell this POSIX tokeniser cannot read is disclosed as undecided rather than decided: reading PowerShell quoting with `shlex` would produce false denies, whose only escape is repo-wide. The disclosure is limited to commands naming a binary some op supersedes, so it does not print under every call. It does not reach a native-Windows host with no Git Bash, where the hook command's own `bash` never executes — that is #1378 and is untouched. ([#1413](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1413))

- **#1417's refusal stated a cause that is false when the caller typed `.`** ([#1417](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1417)). `_parse_grep_args` produces `path == "."` from an empty PATH slot *and* from a literal one, and the refusal explained itself with "an empty slot defaults to it" in both — untrue for the second caller, in the one place they go to find out what they typed wrong. It now names the slot and both readings of it. The parser is deliberately not widened to carry the origin: its 6-tuple is unpacked at eleven sites, and the two inputs earn the same refusal for the same reason. `.supertool.json` and `docs/operations/search.md` carried the same half-claim and now say the same thing.
- **A `read` window said which lines came back, never which grammar it took, and the hint that would have caught the commonest mistake was gated behind one that was silent** ([#1417](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1417), folding in #1414 and #1138). `read:PATH:A:B` and `read:PATH:A-B` are one character apart and return different windows; the window line described both in OFFSET/LIMIT terms, so a range call was reported in the vocabulary of the form it did not use. It now names `(OFFSET:LIMIT form)` or `(START-END form)`. The skip-count correction fired only when `LIMIT <= OFFSET`, deferring the rest to the misread-range note, which is itself gated on overshoot-or-`LIMIT < 2*OFFSET` — so `read:PATH:1:40` on a long file tripped neither and got nothing. It now fires on every non-zero OFFSET and names the window that came back — clamped end included, so a call cut short by EOF or the byte cap is not handed a range it never returned. The second range, the one a caller reading `:A:B` as `START:END` was after, is withheld wherever the misread-range note already proposes one, because the two derive different answers from the same numbers. The parse is deliberately unchanged: measured over 5,598 real `read:PATH:N:M` calls, the two parses #1138 proposed would refuse or silently re-aim 5,549 and 3,208 of them.
- **A nested `batch` accepted any single field name and refused the result in the wrong grammar** ([#1417](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1417), folding in #1407). A sub-op with no declared field order places a lone key as an unnamed positional, so `{"op": "batch", "file": "inner.toml"}` ran as `batch:inner.toml` and came back with "batch requires an @file argument, e.g. `batch:@ops.json`" — a command-line example for a caller writing TOML, naming no field. `batch` now declares its one field, so a wrong key is refused by name against `accepted: path`, and the missing-`@` refusal states both spellings including `path = "@ops.toml"`.
- **The editor was told to highlight a `read` window one line above the one that came back, and the range form got no highlight at all** ([#1417](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1417), found reviewing the above). `_read_target_read` returned `OFFSET .. OFFSET+LIMIT-1` for `read:PATH:OFFSET:LIMIT` — OFFSET read as a start line, the same mistake the disclosure fix is about, in the code that decides where the cursor lands. `docs/notifiers.md` documented the off-by-one faithfully, so the doc and the code agreed with each other and neither agreed with the op. `read:PATH:START-END` fell through to no range, so the form the docs tell callers to prefer was the one that never highlighted anything, and `read:PATH:10:0` computed an END before its START and handed `10 .. 9` to an editor.

- The raw-command guard could not see past a program's own global options, so `git -C /tmp/x status` answered `OK: nothing in this command is replaced` while plain `git status` was blocked — one subcommand, two verdicts, and the clean one byte-identical to a command nothing maps. Global options are now normalised away from a per-command table before scoring, and a pre-subcommand option that table has no grammar for is `UNDECIDED` rather than a guess: guessing an option's arity swallows the subcommand, and the resulting wrong block has no per-command escape. Not git-only — `glab --repo O/R mr view 1` was affected too; `gh` was not, because it rejects a pre-subcommand `--repo` outright. Options that *end* the command are a third category rather than ordinary pass-through booleans: `git --version status` prints the version and never runs `status`, and `gh --version pr view 1` is refused by gh itself, so the guard answers `OK` — treating them as skippable scored a command the program does not execute and blocked it. ([#1421](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1421))

- **`supertool-no-cut` stopped firing on the commonest pipe there is** ([#1426](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1426)). Anchoring the pattern to command position also started requiring whitespace before the bar, so `supertool 'grep:x' | head` matched and `supertool 'grep:x'|head` did not — blocked before, silent after. That narrowing is disclosed nowhere: the fragment claimed three and named a different one, so read it as unintentional. The bar may now sit against whitespace **or** a closing quote, which is what a shell leaves there; a bar inside the op's own argument (`gh-job:9:grep:head|tail`) still has a bare letter to its left and is still ignored.

  The suite could not see it. `tests/test_jit_block_match_anchored_1415.py` defines `PIPE = " | "` and all ten fire cases used it, so nothing in 8,400 tests discriminated the space. Four cases now put the bar hard against the quote.

- **A guard refusal whose remedy opens a real pull request** ([#1427](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1427)). `presets/github.json` claimed a bare `gh pr create` with no `unless_flag`, so `gh pr create --dry-run` — the flag whose whole meaning is *print details instead of creating the PR* — was refused and answered with `gh-pr-create:@FILE`, which opens one. That is the `misdirects` class: the named substitute performs the irreversible action the blocked command explicitly declined. #1427 closed the identical shape for `git push` and `git commit`; this is the instance it did not reach.
- **A `--help` is never replaced, by any op, in any registry.** Sweeping that class found it on all twenty-eight shipped mappings at once: `gh pr create --help` was blocked and told to open a pull request, `git push --help` was blocked and told to push. So `--help` and `-h` now un-claim every entry whatever it declares, rather than being a key each mapping has to remember — the direction #1394 was already pushed once, when `glab api -h` blocked with no way past was part of what justified the `*` spelling. Whole tokens only, deliberately unlike `unless_flag`: a short cluster is not expanded, or `-xh` would un-claim the whole repository, and `gh pr create -- --help` is still a file called `--help`.

- **A `-h` anywhere before the `--` un-claimed all 28 `replaces` mappings, including `git push`** ([#1430](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1430)). The help exclusion scanned `_guard_options(argv)` — the argv slice up to a bare `--`, which is *every* token, not only the flag-shaped ones — and returned "no op replaces this" if any of them equalled `-h` or `--help`. So `git commit -m -h` was `clean` and committed with the message `-h`, and `git push origin -o -h main` was `clean` and pushed. `clean` is not `undecided`: it is a positive claim that nothing in the command is replaced.

  Restricting the scan to flag-shaped tokens, the obvious repair, is a no-op — `-h` and `--help` are flag-shaped wherever they stand. The discriminator that matches what the programs actually do is whether the help token was consumed as the value of the option before it. Measured on git 2.46.2 and gh 2.50.0: `git push origin -h`, `git push -h`, `git status -h` and `gh issue list -h` all print usage and run nothing, so their `clean` verdicts were already right; only a help token sitting immediately after another flag is in doubt.

  `_guard_help_state()` now answers in three states — `help` (un-claims every entry, as before), `none`, and `value` for the ambiguous slot. Telling an option's value from a request for help needs per-subcommand option arity this guard deliberately does not carry, so the ambiguous case is scored and blocked with a note saying why, rather than allowed: a wrong block on `git push origin -o -h main` is legible and one flag away from a working `git push -h`, while the other direction is a silent `git push`. The exclusion also moved from `_guard_excluded()` to `guard_command()`, because it is a property of the whole segment rather than of one entry.

  A refusal now prints the guard's notes too, under `Also:`. A `BLOCKED` verdict used to discard them — including "an op's `replaces` entry was dropped" — so a positive match rendered as though nothing in the command had been left unread.

- `gh-issues:nomilestone,iids` returned every open issue: the id feed was
  rendered above the client-side filter block, so `external`, `stale` and
  `nomilestone` were all inert under `iids` and so were the declines they exist
  to produce. The feed is now rendered after the filters, carries their
  narrowing notes as `#` comments, and buys the enrichment call when a filter
  needs one. (#1439)

### Security

- **`radar`'s delivery banner printed a socket path straight out of a `/tmp` state file** ([#1423](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1423)). `_destination_lines` joined the `sock_path` values `transport.emit_destinations()` reads out of the watcher state files into radar's own text, and `SUPERTOOL_WATCH_STATE_DIR` defaults to `/tmp`. A planted state file whose `sock_path` carried a newline printed a whole extra line at column 0 — a fabricated `radar: delivery — all N watcher state file(s) had their last emit accepted by a listener`, which is precisely the false all-clear the banner exists to prevent, authored by anyone who can write to the state directory. `radar.py` imported no `_untrusted` at all, while `dispatcher.list_watchers` and `channel.stranded_watchers` already read the same directory through it.

  Paths are now flattened with `_untrusted.flat` — not `repr`'d, because this line's job is to tell an operator which socket to go and look at — and flattened **before** the de-duplicating set, so two recorded values that render identically are printed once rather than twice. `SOCK_PATH` is flattened at the render too; it is printed by both arms and arrives from the environment. The comparison that decides which watchers disagree still runs on the raw value.

  Radar cannot verify a path it did not write, so flattening alone would have left it asserting one. The arm that prints somebody else's text now carries `_untrusted.flat_note` above it, once, naming the watchers' own state files as the source — and only that arm: a note over a line radar wrote itself would be a claim about the render rather than about the source.

## [0.35.0] - 2026-08-11

### Added

- The GitLab ops declare what raw `glab` invocation they supersede, so the shipped `PreToolUse` guard covers `glab` as well as `gh` ([#1384](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1384)). `glab mr view`, `glab mr list`, `glab issue view`, `glab issue create`, `glab ci trace` and `glab ci get --pipeline-id` are refused in favour of the op that answers them, with `--comments` selecting the `:full` view. `gl-api` and `gl-runners` declare nothing: `glab api` becomes a write under `-X`/`-F`/`--input` and supertool has no route for a GitLab write, so blocking it would dead-end the command `gl-api` itself points writers at.

- Four of the git ops declare what raw `git` invocation they supersede, so the shipped `PreToolUse` guard covers `git` as well as `gh` and `glab` ([#1384](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1384)). `git status`, `git commit`, `git push` and `git worktree list` are refused in favour of the op that answers them, with `--force-with-lease`, `--no-verify` and `-u` selecting which spelling of `git-push` the refusal names. Two of the three commands #1384 measured as allowed-and-silent are now blocked.
- The shapes of those commands that no op answers are left running on purpose, because the only way past a wrong block is `raw_command_guard: false`, which disarms every mapping in the repository: `git push --tags` / `--follow-tags` / `--delete` / `--force`, `git commit --amend` / `--fixup` / `--squash`, and the machine-readable `--porcelain`, `-s`, `-z` forms of `git status` and `git worktree list`.
- Two limits of the mapping schema are documented rather than papered over. `git push origin <tagname>` **is** blocked: it is discriminated by the value of a positional, which no `unless_flag` can express, and `--tags` is the flag-shaped route past it. `git -C <path> <subcommand>` reaches no mapping at all, because `argv` matches a contiguous token prefix and `-C`'s value sits inside it; `cwd:PATH` is the op-side answer. Nine git ops declare nothing, each for a reason recorded in `docs/presets/git.md`.

- `replaces` entries take an `unless_flag`, so an op can declare which shapes of a command it does **not** supersede (#1394). `flag` and `value` only ever added specificity, so an op could say *this argv is mine* and not *this argv is mine except when it carries these flags* — and with the opt-out (`raw_command_guard: false`) repo-global, one over-broad entry disarmed every other mapping in the repository.
- `gl-api` is mapped on the strength of it (#1394): a plain `glab api PATH` read names the op, while `-X`/`-F`/`-f`/`--input` writes — which no supertool op answers at any spelling — stay usable, along with every other flagged shape down to `glab api -h`.
- An exclusion un-claims its own entry and never allows a command outright, a bare `--` ends the option list for the `flag` matcher too, and a malformed `unless_flag` drops the entry and reports `undecided` rather than reading as no exclusion (#1394).

- **`gh-issues` and `gl-mrs` take `search=TEXT`, and the query goes to the forge** ([#1395](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1395)). `gh issue list` and `glab mr list` are both refused by the shipped guard in favour of the board ops, and neither op could search — so *find the issue whose text mentions X* had no route at all, and the honest answer was `"raw_command_guard": false`, which disarms every mapping in the repo. `search=` forwards to `gh issue list --search` / `glab mr list --search`: it narrows the population, not the page. A client-side filter over one `--limit` page answers "which of the first 50 mention X" while disclosing `capped at --limit 50` about the fetch, which on any repo with more than a page of matches is a different question.

- **One key over two engines, and every render says which answered and what it read.** GitHub's issue search covers title, body **and comments**; GitLab's `search=` covers title and description only. The board prints `(search 'X' — GitHub issue search over title, body and comments)` above the rows and in the footer, and the GitLab one names the half it does not cover. A search that quietly scoped to less than the caller meant returns a zero that reads as an absence in the world. `tests/test_board_search_1395.py` asserts the two scope sentences are different and that each names comments, so the day they collapse the suite reds rather than the render going quietly wrong — which is [#628](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/628)'s question answered for this one key rather than in general.

- **The shared spelling is honest for a mechanical reason, not an aesthetic one.** A board's whole grammar is one comma-separated segment and supertool splits an op argument on `:`, so GitHub's qualifier language (`in:title`) is refused by the tokenizer with nothing fetched — it is unreachable from either op. Stripped of qualifiers both engines answer "this text occurs in this thing", and what survives is scope, which is why the scope is printed rather than assumed.

- **Three states, not two.** Rows; an empty result that says *the search ran and matched nothing — an empty result, not a lookup that failed*; and a lookup that could not run, which keeps its non-zero exit and prints no board. `No issues match.` / `No MRs match.` on its own is never printed under a search. The disclosure rides the `iids` number stream too — a leading `#` comment on GitHub, stderr on GitLab — because that shape becomes another tool's input and a shorter list otherwise reads as a quieter tracker.

- **`search=` beside `iids=` is refused on `gh-issues`.** A named population has no listing for GitHub to search, so the query would be dropped and N rows the caller enumerated would read as N rows that matched.

- **`help:OP` prints the `@-` payload route and the field names it derives** ([#1400](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1400)). `help:paste` printed `paste:::PATH:::CONTENT` and stopped, so the payload route every multi-line write needs was discoverable only by guessing — an implementation agent used it and reported that it had guessed `path` and `content`. An entry listing one of two invocation forms is worse than one listing neither, because it reads as complete.

  The block is rendered from the two registries that grant the route, never typed beside them: the `:::` field names are derived from the very `syntax` string printed above it (`_fields_from_syntax`, [#770](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/770)), and the read ops take theirs from `_READ_OP_AT_FIELDS`. So `edit`, `replace`, `replace_dry`, `replace_lines`, `paste`, `append`, `vim`, every preset op with a `:::` syntax, and `read`/`grep`/`grep_around`/`around`/`between`/`validate` all gained it at once, and a syntax reword that silently deletes a route now deletes the documentation with it instead of leaving prose describing a route that is gone.

  An op with no payload route prints no block. That silence is now an answer rather than a gap, because every op that has one prints.

### Changed

- **Documented how Claude Code actually resolves the shipped hook commands, and pinned both as shell form** ([#1401](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1401)). The concern was that `bash "${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/hooks/..."` is resolved by `CreateProcess` searching `PATH`, which on Windows finds System32's `bash.exe` - the WSL launcher, which is not a shell, exits 1 and writes UTF-16 without ever opening the script. That is how this repository's own pytest reached the launcher; it is not how the harness runs a hook.

  A command hook with no `args` is **shell form**: the string is handed to a shell - `sh -c` on macOS and Linux, Git Bash on Windows, or PowerShell when Git Bash is not installed. A hook **with** `args` is exec form, and that is where `command` is resolved on `PATH` and spawned directly - so adding `args` would introduce the defect rather than remove it. The remaining branch, a native Windows host with no Git for Windows, is also the host with no `Bash` tool at all, so a `PreToolUse` hook matched on `Bash` never fires there.

  No behaviour changed. `tests/test_hook_interpreter_windows_1401_1402.py` now refuses `args` on either shipped hook and refuses the two entries drifting apart, so the reasoning survives the next reader not having it.

### Fixed

- `radar`'s delivery banner no longer lets `accepted` be read as *accepted by
  the socket this session reads*. Each watcher has published the path it is
  bound to as `sock_path` since #581 and nothing consumed it, so a second
  session — one that exported `SUPERTOOL_WATCH_SOCK` but left
  `SUPERTOOL_WATCH_STATE_DIR` on the default — got `all N watcher state
  file(s) had their last emit accepted by a listener` while receiving nothing:
  its `radar` had spawned no pollers, because the first session's already held
  every `O_CREAT|O_EXCL` slot in the shared `/tmp` and were writing to the
  first session's socket. The banner now names the count and the other path,
  and says separately when a watcher emitted and recorded no path at all —
  which is not agreement. A fleet that all writes here prints neither line, and
  nothing is stopped, reaped or re-armed on the strength of it.
  `transport.emit_destinations()` is the read-only survey behind it. ([#1309])
- Documented the two-session arrangement that already works, in
  `docs/presets/watch.md` and `presets/watch/README.md`: **both**
  `SUPERTOOL_WATCH_SOCK` and `SUPERTOOL_WATCH_STATE_DIR`, or neither. Both
  files previously described the socket override alone as how a second session
  gets a radar of its own, which is the exact configuration that silently gets
  no pollers. ([#1309])

- **An int-backed setting could not be switched off, and the substitution was silent** ([#1332](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1332)). `_get_op_int` ended in `val if isinstance(val, int) and val > 0 else default`, so a configured `0` in `.supertool.json` was indistinguishable from an absent key and the helper's own default won. `read.elide: 0` shipped documented in three places and inert — a switch that reports back the state it was asked for and does not enter it.

  **A switch now has its own reader.** `_get_op_bool` takes `0`/`1`, `true`/`false` and `yes`/`no`/`on`/`off`, from config or from `SUPERTOOL_<OP>_<KEY>`, and `0` means off whichever way the default points. `read.elide`, `read.abstract` and `read.php_abstract` are read through it; `read.elide`'s inline workaround is gone.

  **The threshold reader still refuses a `0`, but says so.** Honouring `"max_lines": 0` would trade a loud misconfiguration for a silently empty read, which is the worse of the two failures — so `_get_op_int` keeps refusing, and now names the key, the value it discarded and the limit actually in force, the way it has named a bad env value since [#654](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/654). It said nothing at all about a bad *config* value, which is why nobody writing a deliberate `0` could tell it had been ignored.

  **A JSON `true` in a threshold was reading as `1`.** `isinstance(True, int)` is true in Python, so `"max_lines": true` gave a one-line `read` without a word. It is now refused and announced with the rest.

- **`test_parallel`'s three sequential-vs-parallel comparisons asserted an environment condition as if it were a product verdict** ([#1364](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1364)). They compared two independent subprocess runs of the same `read` byte-for-byte, and a `read` receipt's meta line can carry `git?` — the disclosure from [#705](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/705) that the working-tree lookup declined, state unknown rather than clean. One run can trip that while the other does not, and the parallel one spawns four `git status` at once against a 2s timeout, so it is the likelier side. One `pytest (windows-latest, 3.10)` leg went red on a docs-only diff, expecting `crlf git?` and getting `crlf`.

  **The product is right in both forms, and that was checked before the test was touched.** Outside a repository the steady-state answer is no token: git exits non-zero with "not a git repository", `_path_meta_suffix` recognises that and stays silent. The token needs the git call to fail some other way. Both such failures were reproduced against the product on macOS by putting a shim `git` on `PATH` — a `sleep 4` and an `exit 128` with a dubious-ownership message each turn `(1 lines, 10 bytes) crlf` into `(1 lines, 10 bytes) crlf git?`, and an end-to-end run of the test's own five reads with that shim on one side reproduces the CI diff exactly. So neither reading of the receipt is a dropped disclosure; the comparison was over-specific.

  **The token is normalised out of both sides and nothing else is.** Order, headers and content stay byte-exact, which is what those tests exist to check. The Windows trigger itself is not reproducible on macOS and is not claimed to be: what is observed is the mechanism, not the runner condition that fires it.

- **Seven ops the dispatcher accepts were absent from `docs/operations/index.md`** ([#1371](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1371)). `registry` shipped in [#1363](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1363) and reached neither of the page's two listings; the issue was filed as that one op, and enumerating from `_valid_op_names()` rather than from the report found `check`, `diag`, `guard`, `hover`, `ops-compact` and `rename` in the same state. The opening line also said "~40 ops across five categories" against 44.

  Both listings are now held to the product by `tests/test_ops_index_complete_1371.py`: every dispatchable name must appear in the **Categories** table and in the **full op table**, and the stated count must be the real one. The two are separate assertions because they fail for different readers — the full table is what someone who already knows the name greps, and the Categories table is the only route for someone who does not. `workspace` and `resolve` were listed in the full table and in no category, so they were findable by grep and not by reading.

  `diag`, `hover` and `rename` get a new **LSP-backed** category pointing at `docs/mcp-integration.md`, which documented them the whole time.

  **The page also named three ops that do not exist**, found by reviewing the fix rather than by the issue. `blame` had a row with a syntax cell, and `blame:PATH:LINE` answers `unknown operation` — the op is `git-blame`, from the `git` preset. `read-grep` and `grep-count` sat in the Categories table beside real names; they are argument forms of `read` and `grep`, not invocations. Completeness and honesty are separate properties and the first test only had the first, so a second assertion now refuses any name on the page that the dispatcher would not accept, checked against builtins **plus** the loaded preset ops so a legitimate `git-blame` row passes. The `resolve` row also documented only `resolve:SYMBOL`, omitting the `:FILE` argument that a Python relative import needs and without which it is reported `external`.

- **The shipped raw-command guard can now find a Python on a standard Windows install** ([#1402](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1402)). `hooks/pre-bash-guard.sh` probed `python3.9`-`python3.14` and nothing else, and neither python.org's installer nor GitHub's `hostedtoolcache` creates those names - both create `python.exe` and `python3.exe`, and the bare `python3` is permanently banned because on Windows it can resolve to an App Execution Alias stub that blocks rather than errors ([#572](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/572)). So on that whole population the ladder ran out and the guard declined on every `Bash` call - honest, and off, while `raw_command_guard` defaults to on.

  `py -3`, the Windows Python launcher, is added as the **last** rung, after an activated virtualenv and after every versioned name, so a host with a real `python3.12` keeps using it. A candidate still has to print the probe's exact token, which is what rejects a launcher that writes a preamble of its own - such a launcher is skipped and the guard declines in words rather than a verdict being built on an interpreter it could not identify.

  Graded **reasoned, not observed**: nobody on this project has a Windows box. The load-bearing claim is that Windows ships no default App Execution Alias for `py.exe`. Putting the rung last bounds the cost if that is wrong, since any host with a versioned interpreter never reaches it.

  **This reverses a decision [#572](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/572) made deliberately**, and only for this script. That entry recorded `py -3` as "considered and dropped: this is a bash script that only ever runs under Git Bash or WSL, where a Windows launcher shim is the wrong layer to reach for" - a preference about layering, argued without the fact this issue supplies. #572 established that versioned names are not *aliased* on Windows, which is true and is why they are safe to try; it did not establish that they are *present*, and they are not. Under WSL `py` is simply absent and the rung costs one `command -v`. `.githooks/pre-push` keeps the shorter ladder: it refuses the push and lists every name it tried, and documents `PYTHON=` as the way through, so a loud refusal with an escape hatch does not need the rung the way a disclosed allow does.

- **Every regex rule in `.claude/jit-context/tools/00-manual/` is pinned to command position, and the anchor now admits a tab** ([#1415](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1415)). Two `mode: block` rules were tested as a bare substring over the whole command text, with no notion of where a shell would find a command word, so they refused **eleven commands on 2026-08-11** that cut nothing and listed nothing — this repository's own directory name inside a `cd` path, a shell variable, a bar inside an op's own argument, and a quoted payload body seven times, including the filing of the issue, the writing of its test file, a commit message and the verification harness itself. The other six rules were already anchored, but as `(^|[;&|\n] *)`, which admits only spaces: a **tab**-indented continuation line walked through all of them. All eight now open `(^|[;&|\n])[[:space:]]*`.

  **Two defects in opposite directions, and the second one was silent.** A wrong block announces itself; a missed block looks exactly like nothing happening, which is why four `block` rules could fail on tab-indented commands without anyone noticing. Measured against `pre-tool-hook.sh` itself, 23 cases: four rules gain the tab-indented true positive, `op-defaults-that-narrow` stops firing on a mere mention of an op name in prose, `supertool-no-cut` stops firing on the directory name, and every case that must stay allowed — an ordinary `git branch -d`, a `--limit`ed list, a `git -c` carrying no path — is unchanged.

  **Three narrowings on `supertool-no-cut` besides the anchor.** The cutting utility must be a command word after the bar, which stops a bar inside an op's own `grep:` argument; the scan is confined to one line, which stops a payload body joining an earlier invocation; and the tool name must end at whitespace, which stops `supertoolkit` and `supertool-benchmark.sh`. One true positive is newly caught in exchange: a cut behind a second pipe.

  **Narrower is not precise, and the residue is named rather than left to be discovered.** A payload line that *begins* with a command-shaped string still matches: only a tokeniser can tell a body from a command, and the jit matcher lives in `claude-jit-context`, a separate repository. `supertool-no-cut.md`, `CLAUDE.md` and `jit-context.md` all say so.

  Also fixes `git-C-has-cwd.md`, whose frontmatter `match:` had lost the leading `~` its index row carries — inert where it sat, but the `.md` is what a reader copies, and copied as-is it becomes a literal substring rule that can never match.

  `tests/test_jit_block_match_anchored_1415.py` hands each live pattern to `awk` the way the hook does and asserts both directions per rule, plus that no regex row in the index is left unanchored.

- **`grep` declines an empty PATH slot instead of silently scanning the whole tree** ([#1417](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1417)). `grep:_FLAGS|def main:presets/github/issues.py:::40` rejoined to the pattern `_FLAGS|def main:presets/github/issues.py:` with the path `.`, scanned 934 files and returned hits — the house defect in a read op, where the wrong answer is well-formed. Two agents hit it in one day and one acted on the result before noticing. The `|` was incidental: `grep:PATTERN:PATH:` does the same with no alternation in it, because the trigger is the empty PATH token defaulting to the repo root while the real path stays inside the rejoined pattern.

  `_colon_split_hint` already produced the right refusal for this whole family, carrying the `grep:@-` escape that is the remedy — and its first line is `if not path or path == "." or os.path.exists(path): return ""`. Every arm below that keys off "the path does not exist", and `.` always exists, so the one reading in the family that does **not** fail loudly was the one reading the helper declined to diagnose. That line is unchanged — it is correct for the ops that never default a path — and grep's dispatch arm now runs a dedicated check ahead of it.

  It declines rather than auto-correcting, which is where it differs from `around:.supertool.json:232:12` — that one is redirected to `around_line` and disclosed, and is safe precisely because the reading it replaces is a hard failure with nothing to lose. Here the reading it would replace is a successful whole-tree sweep, so a silent redirect swaps one answer nobody typed for another. The gate is narrow: it fires only when the path resolved to `.` and a segment of the rejoined pattern names an existing file or directory, past the first segment. Measured over the 165 distinct `grep:` spellings written down in this repo, 39 hit the rejoin and none is declined. A segment failing cwd containment is skipped rather than named, so the refusal cannot be turned into an existence oracle for paths outside the boundary, and the pattern is re-segmented through `_split_arg` rather than a plain `split(":")` so a Windows drive letter is not torn in half on the only platform where it occurs.

  **`grep` only.** `around` and `between` share the error helper and not the defect: neither defaults a path to `.`, so a `.` there is a value the caller typed, and `between:re:START:END:PATH` carries three caller arguments ahead of the path — `between:re:START:code.py:.` is an ordinary tree-wide range search whose END names a file. Generalising the check to the family produced a false refusal on that call and a printed repair that dropped the `re:` marker selecting the mode.

### Security

- **The GitHub discovery ops printed repository descriptions and logins raw** ([#981](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/981)). `gh-starred`, `gh-following`, `gh-find-starable` and `gh-find-followable` render text from **arbitrary public repositories and accounts**, chosen by a topic search rather than by us — the widest untrusted-input surface in the tool — and every one of those fields reached `print()` with no marker. A newline breaking the alignment is the lesser half: the text after an injected separator is unconstrained, so it can be padded to the block's own shape and read as a row supertool emitted. These ops exist to decide who to follow and what to star, so a forged row is a recommendation the tool did not make. Every remote field now goes through `_untrusted.flat()` and each block carries one `_untrusted.flat_note()` disclosure — the convention [#819](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/819) and [#970](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/970) already established, not a second one. Nothing is fenced and nothing is censored: every word survives, on the one line it was given.

- **The disclosure on the two `find` ops is a `#` comment, because their output is another op's input.** `gh-find-starable` and `gh-find-followable` are written to be redirected into a candidates file and handed to `gh-batch-star` / `gh-batch-follow`, which skip `#` lines and take every other line as a target. `gh-batch-follow` does not require an `OWNER/REPO` shape either, so a bare banner there would be an account it tries to follow — and a login carrying a separator was already an extra follow the reviewer never approved.

- **`gh-find-starable`'s `.replace("\n", " ")` was the shape of a fix rather than one.** It answered one of the ten separators `str.splitlines()` breaks on and none of the escape sequences that can erase a row off the screen, which is worse than nothing there: a site that visibly handles the case is the one nobody re-reads. Flattening now happens **before** the 120-character slice, in that order, for the reason [#970](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/970) gives — a cut made first leaves behind whatever the separator started.

- **Swept the rest of the family rather than the four files the issue named.** `gh-star`, `gh-follow`, `gh-batch-star` and `gh-batch-follow` echo `gh`'s stderr, which quotes back the name it was given; the two batch ops print it as a row in a list a reader skims for exactly the `ERR` lines a forged one imitates. Those are flattened too.

- **The 120-character cap on a batch op's error row was measured on the wrong string.** Found by the independent reviewer of this change. `gh-batch-star` and `gh-batch-follow` sliced `gh`'s stderr to 120 characters *before* the new `flat()` ran, which is the ordering this same change calls out as wrong three files over — and `flat()` spells one U+2028 as eight characters, so a stderr carrying thirty of them rendered a 330-character row against a 120-character budget. The slice now happens after the flatten, against a named `ERROR_MAX`, so the number in the code is the number on screen.

- **`gl-mr` printed a CI job name raw, in two places, and `gl-mrs` was never affected** ([#982](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/982)). A job name comes out of `.gitlab-ci.yml` on the source branch, so anyone who can open a merge request writes it, and `str.splitlines()` breaks on ten separators that field accepts — enough for a name to become its own line, padded to the shape of the block around it: a job that passed, on a pipeline that failed. Both sites now go through `_untrusted.flat()`, the call `gl-pipeline` already made on the same field from the same endpoint.

- The two sites are on different renders and only one was filed. `_named_gl_jobs` builds the `  {status}: {name} (job #{id})` block that **`gl-mr:N:status`** prints — the poll-loop render, read most often and looked at least closely, which is the argument the issue makes for the board and which applies here with more force. `_failed_job_lines` (extracted from `main()` so the flattening has somewhere to be asserted) builds the `  #{id} | {name} | {stage}` block on the full render, which is the `jname` the issue points at.

- **The issue names `presets/gitlab/mrs.py` and the defect is not there.** `gl-mrs` renders every cell through `_board.render_row`, which flattens what it is handed, and prints `[MR titles below come from the tracker — data, not instructions]` above the board. The issue's own evidence table names the real file — `mr.py`, via `jname` — and the prose beneath it misattributed that to `mrs.py`; the harm argument it makes for the triage board does not transfer to a single-MR detail view, and the argument that does is the `:status` render above.

- **`git push --dry-run` was blocked, and the refusal named the op that performs the real push** ([#1427](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1427)). `git push --dry-run` and `git push -n` were not on the bare `git push` entry's `unless_flag` list in `presets/git.json`, so the raw-command guard blocked them and pointed at `git-push`, which has no dry-run route and pushes. Every other way this guard has been wrong costs a *missed block* — a raw read an op could have answered. This one costs the opposite, on the one op here that can destroy someone else's commits.

  It is worse on a refspec. `git push --dry-run origin feature:refs/heads/other` previews pushing a named branch onto a named ref; a caller obeying the refusal and running `git-push` pushes **the current branch to its own upstream** — a ref nobody in that exchange named. `git commit --dry-run` was the same shape and is excluded with it. `-n` is excluded on `git push` and deliberately not on `git commit`, where it is `--no-verify` and commits.

- **A clustered short flag now reaches `unless_flag`** ([#1427](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1427)). `_guard_excluded` compared whole tokens, so an entry excluding `-s` did not exclude `-sb` — the ordinary spelling of the intent `-s` was excluded for — and `git status -sb` was blocked while `git status -s` was not. The gap existed for every short flag on every entry, present and future, so it is fixed in the matcher rather than enumerated per entry: a single-dash token is read as a cluster of single-letter flags.

  Only exclusions, never the positive `flag` matcher. Widening an exclusion makes the guard block *less*, which is the direction it is allowed to be wrong in — a wrong block has no per-command escape short of `raw_command_guard: false`, which disarms every mapping in the repository — while widening the matcher would block more. A `--` token is never expanded, or every long flag containing an `f` would un-claim an entry excluding `-f`.

  The cost is stated rather than hidden: a short flag carrying a clustered **value** is expanded regardless of what the value spells, so `git push -ofoo` now reads as carrying `-f` and is no longer claimed, while `git push -oci.skip` spells no excluded letter and still is. Telling that from `-sb` needs per-flag arity the schema does not carry, and it errs toward allowing.

## [0.34.0] - 2026-08-11

### Added

- `claude-log-cost[:N|:UUID][:raw]` — what tool results actually cost, in bytes,
  measured off the session transcripts already on disk. Per tool and per
  supertool op (split on the render's own `--- op ---` markers), plus the size
  distribution, repeat reads as both a count and a share of total bytes, and the
  byte cost of errors and empty results. Sessions that could not be parsed are
  named as skipped with a reason rather than dropped from the total, results
  with no matching `tool_use` are counted under `?`, non-text result blocks are
  disclosed as a count per kind rather than having their bytes folded in, and a
  marker is only read
  as an op when the command line named that op — an echoed `--- branch ---`
  separator otherwise invents ops that never ran. (#1252)

- `plugin-marketplace[:NAME]` — did this release reach anyone? Per catalogue: whether the plugin is listed at all, the sha it is pinned to, the plugin manifest version at that sha, the commits and releases between that pin and local HEAD, and the catalogue's bump PRs for it with the search that found them. Both hand-rolled routes returned an absence that read like an answer, so this one has three states and never two. The contents API answers HTTP 200 with an **empty body** for the 1.5 MB community manifest (`encoding: none`, no error), which a one-liner renders as "plugin not found"; and a plugin the official catalogue never listed renders identically to one it stopped bumping, which are opposite problems with opposite fixes. A catalogue that could not be read is `skipped` with its reason, never a row saying absent, and the exit status is 1. Measured against the live catalogues on 2026-08-11: supertool's community pin was `dcb574ea` (v0.27.0), 101 commits and 6 releases behind master, with one bump PR ever (#1299).

- `gh-issues:iids=1233,1240,1251` — look up an exact set of issue numbers in one call, for auditing citations. Every requested number gets its own row: the issue, `is a PR` for a number that is a pull request here, `not an issue` for one that resolves to nothing, and `lookup failed` for one the call could not reach — never a silently shorter list, which an audit reads as "these all check out". Filed as a new `gh-titles` op; built as a filter on `gh-issues` instead, so it inherits `per=`, the disclosure machinery and the refusals rather than growing a second render of the same model. `per=` caps it and says how many numbers it did not look up; the `--limit N — more may exist` sentence is never printed, because the population is the one the caller typed. A listing filter beside `iids=` is refused rather than dropped ([#1323](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1323)).
- Board rows now show `[closed]` for a closed issue and `[state:?]` when gh did not say. `state=all` and `iids=` both render closed issues, and one that looked identical to an open one answered "is this citation still live" wrongly.

- `grep` takes `all` in its LIMIT slot — `grep:PATTERN:PATH:all` — for the "find every one" question a capped result answers wrongly even when its `TRUNCATED, N matches total` marker is honest (#1328). The count line reads `limit all` and can never carry a truncation marker, so a completeness sweep cannot be read as a capped one. Works with context (`:all:2`), in `grep_around:PATTERN:PATH:N:all`, and as `limit = "all"` in a payload; refused anywhere but the LIMIT slot rather than re-read as something it could have meant, and never delegated to rtk, whose report cannot count what it did not collect.

- **`read` elides a repeat read of a byte-identical file** ([#1329](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1329)). A second bare `read:PATH` within 15 minutes, when the file's sha256 has not moved **and both reads share the same parent process**, returns one line instead of the content — carrying the sha, the file's size on disk, and the exact command that hands the bytes over. It says "on disk" rather than "withheld" on purpose: a file over `read.max_bytes` is byte-capped on the way out even under `:full`, so the file's size and what the first read actually handed over are different numbers, and naming the former as withheld would overstate it on exactly the files where the cap bites. Off with `read.elide: 0` or `SUPERTOOL_READ_NO_ELIDE=1` — and that first switch is read directly rather than through `_get_op_int`, which is built for positive-integer thresholds and treats a configured `0` as "unset". `read.elide` is the first boolean in this file whose default is on, so through that helper the switch was documented in three places and inert; it is the only site of the class, and every other `_get_op_int` call is a genuine threshold.

- **On this repo the saving is 0.0% of result bytes, and the prose should not borrow anyone else's number.** Measured with `claude-log:cost` over real transcripts: unchanged re-reads are 0.0% of result bytes on the supertool corpus, because batching already prevents the pattern. The 8.7% often quoted is the `Read`-tool-driven corpus — 252,851 B, one `portfolio.json` read sixteen times — and is a statement about a different tool. This is built for what it prevents.

- **What it must not do drove the whole shape.** The op cannot observe whether the caller still holds the first copy, and a re-read after a context compaction is the normal case rather than the edge case: the earlier result was evicted and the model is asking again precisely because it no longer has it. Nothing distinguishes that from a redundant second ask, so the design bounds the damage instead of guessing at it. The elision is always one round-trip from the bytes and names that command in the line, not in the docs. The recency window is measured from the last read that actually **returned** content and is never bumped by an elision, so a file polled every minute is not elided forever. A file whose bytes changed is never elided at any age — repeat reads of files that moved are the ones that carry information. A state file that cannot be read or written returns the content: an unanswered cache is `skipped`, not silence. `read:PATH:full` never elides and re-arms the window. An explicit offset, limit, range or `grep=` filter neither elides nor arms one, because a recorded whole-file read says nothing about a slice request.

- **Keyed on `(session, realpath, sha256)`, where session is `USER | PPID | realpath(cwd)`.** Not mtime, which changes on a no-op rewrite and misses a same-second edit. PPID is the session proxy supertool's call log already uses; the resolved cwd is mixed in because nine worktrees were live on one machine on 2026-08-11 and one agent's read must never suppress another's. The two failure directions are not symmetric — over-keying costs one file returned again, under-keying withholds content the caller never saw — so the key is the narrower one on purpose. One small sidecar per `(session, file)` under `~/.cache/supertool/read-elide/`, never a shared index two concurrent processes would clobber; `gc` reaps the kind after a day, since a PPID in the key makes yesterday's entries unmatchable by construction.

- **Where that fires, measured, because the key is the invoking shell.** `os.getppid()` for `supertool` is the process that ran it, and Claude Code starts a new shell per Bash tool call, so the key changes on every turn: two bare reads of one unchanged file in separate calls both returned 3,840 bytes and left two keys under `~/.cache/supertool/read-elide/`; the same two reads on one command line returned 276 bytes, the elision. It fires for two invocations inside one shell — the case batching already covers — and not for the repeat read after a compaction it was aimed at. Filed as [#1352](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1352). The 0.0% above is unaffected either way: it is a property of the transcript corpus, measured from result bytes, not of the key.

- **The raw-command block belongs to the op, and ships with the tool.** Each op may now declare `replaces` — the raw shell invocations it supersedes — and a `PreToolUse` hook installed with the plugin refuses those commands with **the op's own description** as the message. Before this, the enforcement was hand-written markdown rules living beside the ops they protected, and on 2026-08-11 three of them were failing in three different directions at once: one blocked and did not block the same `gh pr view` minutes apart and reached no subagent at all (20 unblocked raw calls in one triage run), one refused commands that carried the very flag it required whenever a quoted argument preceded it, and one fired on the substring `supertool` — which in this repo is the **directory name**, eight false positives in a day, none of them piping a supertool op. Every one of those is a regex reading a shell command as a string, so the matcher **parses**: the command is tokenised into argv the way a shell would, and the match is on the command word, its subcommands and its flags. A directory name is then not a command word and a heredoc body is not an argv, structurally rather than by another pattern. Flags select *which* op is named rather than whether to block — `gh pr view --json state` points at `gh-pr:N:status`, `--json files` at `gh-pr:N:diff`. The first cut maps `gh pr view`, `gh pr diff`, `gh pr merge`, `gh pr create` and `gh issue list`; a raw call no op supersedes has no entry and is never blocked, which is the whole escape hatch — there is deliberately no environment variable, since one that can be prepended to a command is not a block, and the gate is turned off with `"raw_command_guard": false` in `.supertool.json` where the decision shows up in a diff. A guard that could not answer — a command that did not tokenise, one that hides a substitution inside double quotes or hands a string to `eval`, a registry that could not be enumerated — allows the command and **says so in the transcript**, because failing open silently reproduces the exact defect this closes: a gate that did not run is otherwise indistinguishable from a command that complied. `guard:SHELL COMMAND` asks the same question without running anything. (#1347)

- **`registry` — which ops this project loads, and where each definition came from.** `ops` answers *what can I do*; nothing answered *where did this come from*, and the gap had already cost an audit its subject. A project entry naming an op a preset already defines is a **partial** override — supertool merges it key-by-key, so `{"git-diff": {"red_flags_extra": [...]}}` adds one key and the preset's `cmd`, `syntax` and `timeout` stay in force. Three ops in this repo's own config are that shape (`dashboard`, `radar`, `git-diff`), and every hand-rolled walk over `presets/*.json` plus `.supertool.json` wrote the obvious `ops[name] = entry`, replacing the shipped definition with the stub. The op count is unchanged either way, so nothing looks wrong; the entry simply stops matching every filter downstream. #1350's containment audit lost `git-diff` — the path-naming op it was written about — out of its own population and printed a pass. The merge rule is now one function the loader calls, the loader stamps each op's source during the same walk, and `registry` renders what the loader produced rather than recomputing it; `registry:OP` attributes every key of one entry. A population that could not be fully enumerated prints `INCOMPLETE` in its own body, naming the preset that failed to load, instead of a shorter list — stderr is somewhere else in a batched call, and a short listing and a complete one are otherwise identical. (#1356)

### Changed

- A capped comment list in `gh-issue` and `gh-pr` keeps the first three comments and the last seven, instead of the ten most recent ([#738](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/738)). The budget is unchanged at ten, so no caller pays more context for it.

- The two sides of #738 are right about different comments — the head carries the objection that opened the thread, the tail carries the resolution that closed it — so a cap that takes one end guarantees that on every long thread one of the two load-bearing regions is gone, and the reader cannot tell which. A thread whose opening never mattered rendered identically to one whose opening was the whole point.

- The measurement that would have settled which end is not available, and that is the argument rather than a gap in it: measured across the whole tracker on 2026-08-11 the busiest thread in this repository has six comments and the cap has never fired here, so there is no corpus in which to count where the load-bearing comment sits. With no evidence for either end, the design that does not require choosing one is the answer. It is also not a new convention — `gl-mr` has kept a head and a recency tail with an inline gap marker since it was written.

- The disclosure moved with the cut. The header reads `10 of 25 shown, 15 hidden from the middle` rather than `15 earlier truncated`, which was true of a tail-only cap and would be false of this one; and the seam itself now carries `...[15 comments hidden here — use :full to fetch all]`, because a header alone leaves the reader unable to see that two adjacent comments are not consecutive.

- **A changelog fragment must now name its own issue, and the release check refuses one that does not** ([#1251](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1251)). `changelog.d/<issue>.<section>.md` holds the issue number in exactly one structural place — the filename — and assembly writes the *body* into `CHANGELOG.md` and deletes the file. So the number survived a release only when the author happened to type it into the prose, which made findability a property of author habit rather than of the release process.

  Measured on the fragment bodies as they stood at each release commit: **8 of the 20 entries in v0.32.0** and **6 of the 28 in v0.33.0** named every issue but their own, several citing three or four neighbours. Only two of the twenty had a `test_the_change_is_findable` to say so, and the two that did are why the defect was found at all — the other six would have shipped in silence. One of the eight, #1197, was findable only because a *different* fragment in the same release happened to mention it.

  `collect()` gains a `self_reference_finding` stage and the `changelog-fragment` validator mirrors it, so `paste` and `edit` refuse the fragment at write time and `--check` refuses it in the PR. `(#1251)` anywhere in the body satisfies it, as does a link whose URL ends in the number; the `- **Bold summary** ([#1251](link)).` opening `changelog.d/README.md` has always prescribed does both. A bare `1251` does not, deliberately: v0.32.0's #1130 was findable only because it cited `tests/test_preset_git_splitlines_register_1130.py`, which no reader would aim at and no author could be told to produce.

  The alternative was to have the assembler append the reference itself. It was refused on two grounds: it would rewrite an authored entry, and `changelog.d/README.md` promises that nothing is reformatted; and its unavoidable "is it already there?" test cannot distinguish a self-citation from the #1197 coincidence.

  The stage sits ahead of the body scan because it needs no parser — a definite refusal must not be lost behind the `CannotValidate` raised when `markdown-it-py` is absent — but it does not stop the scan, so a fragment that is both malformed and silent about its issue gets both findings in one run.

### Fixed
