- `gh-branch`'s verdict sentence now agrees with the number of workflows it is talking about ([#841](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/841)). It read "nothing has failed, but CodeQL, tests **has** not concluded on d6cf7a4, so **they are** neither a pass nor a fail" — a singular verb and a plural pronoun over one subject, in the line a maintainer reads at every merge gate. The pronoun half was already count-aware and the verb half was left hardcoded, so the two disagreed on every commit with more than one workflow moving.

- The sibling sentences #841 asked to be checked were wrong the same way, and are fixed with it: "the job list for A, B did not come back" is now "the job lists", and "A, B ran on the previous head and has no run" is now "have no run". Every count-dependent word in the verdict now comes from one helper instead of its own inline conditional — two independent conditionals over one count is a disagreement waiting to be written.
- Found while reviewing the above, in the clause appended onto that same rendered line: `scope_clause`'s UNESTABLISHED arm read "so whether these 1 are all of them is UNKNOWN" whenever a single workflow had produced a run on the commit, which is an ordinary case rather than an edge one. It now names the noun as well as the count — "whether this 1 workflow is all of them" — because fixing the agreement alone would still have left the reader guessing what was being counted.

- **One implementation of "is this url on GitHub", parsed rather than counted, and a `None` that says which of four things it means** ([#907](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/907)). The lookalike-host hole itself closed in [#1212](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/pull/1212), but it closed twice — `gh-issue` and `gh-issues` each grew their own hand-rolled check over `url.split("/")` — and the two disagreed. `gh-issues` stripped userinfo and port off the authority before comparing; `gh-issue` compared the whole thing, so `https://user@github.com/o/r` and `https://github.com:443/o/r`, both perfectly ordinary URLs, resolved on the board and were refused by the single-issue op. Both read `o#x` as the owner of `https://github.com/o#x/r`, because a `#` ends a path and slash-counting does not know that. There is now one predicate in `presets/_repo_target.py` — `is_github_host`, `url_host`, `github_owner_repo` — built on `urlsplit`, and both ops call it.

  GitHub Enterprise Server is now decided rather than assumed, which was the open question the issue left. It is **not** supported here, and the reason is written where the next reader will loosen the literal: a GHES install lives on an operator-chosen host and is not a subdomain of `github.com`, so the `.github.com` arm never reached it. That arm admits GitHub's own `www.`, `api.` and `gist.` subdomains — two comments and a test docstring called them "Enterprise" and were wrong. If GHES is ever wanted it belongs in configuration, next to `SUPERTOOL_IMAGE_HOSTS`, not in a widened constant.

  `gh-issues` no longer answers a bare `None` to four different questions. An empty listing, rows carrying no url, rows whose urls are on some other host, and a `github.com` url too short to hold an owner and a name were one answer, and that answer is rendered into the decline a reader is meant to act on. Each now names itself, by count — never by quoting a url back, because a row url is tracker content and the error line is ours.

- **Bare `#N` citations in the maintainer skill resolved to unrelated issues in this repo** ([#1233](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1233)). When the sibling repo's name was removed from `.claude/skills/opensource-manager/SKILL.md`, the qualified citations (`claude-remember#253`) broke loudly and the bare ones (`#255`) broke silently — each now a well-formed reference to a real, unrelated `claude-supertool` issue, indistinguishable from a correct one by any textual check.

  All 124 distinct numbers and 191 occurrences in the file were re-derived against what each sentence claims, not against the cited issue's state. Twelve occurrences across nine numbers were the sibling repo's and are now qualified `claude-remember#N`: the stale-clone anecdote, the untrusted-input example, the destroys/fails-to-preserve/misreports ranking table and its lead-in, the last-mile delivery passage, and the manifest-updater claim. The ranking table's header said "Example from this repo" while all four of its examples were the other repo's; it now says which repo they are.

  `#263` appeared four times meaning two different issues — three times this repo's phpstan scope defect, once the sibling's silent-backup one — and only the fourth moved.

- **`repo:OWNER/NAME` was a shipped op that no registry admitted exists** ([#1240](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1240)). It has been implemented since [#673](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/673) and is documented in prose in four places, but it was absent from `_MAIN_LEVEL_OPS`, from `_OP_SAFETY_BUILTIN` and from `.supertool.json` — so `ops` did not list it, `help:repo` denied it, the unknown-op message left it out of "Valid operations", and `claims` reported every document citing it as *unchecked* rather than holding. The op that exists to reach another repo could not be discovered from the tool.

  There was no new category to invent: `cwd` is the other leading pseudo-op, `_MAIN_LEVEL_OPS` exists for exactly that class, and its own comment already says they belong in any list a caller reads. `repo` was simply never added to it. Its safety class is declared `read-only` rather than left to the `acts` fallback, which renders `!`.

- **The maintainer skill cited `presets/_pr_board.py` as settled precedent for a module that does not exist** ([#1240](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1240)). It is the name [#958](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/958) proposes and that issue is still open, so the line was quoted at an agent as an existing pattern to follow. It now reads as the work item it is, and names what *is* already shared for that argument — the judgement, `presets/github/pr.py`'s `_reconcile_checks`, which `dashboard` and radar's `gh_prs` tier both call rather than re-derive.

- **`gh-pr-merge` now says how far the base has moved since the checks ran** ([#1257](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1257)). The preview opens with a `## Base` block: `BEHIND` by N with the base branch's head sha and date, a stated level, or `UNKNOWN` naming why the compare call did not answer. Three states, because an absent warning and an unasked question rendered identically.

  On 2026-08-10 `master` failed 13 of 15 legs from two PRs that were each 22/22 green, merged four minutes apart — one adding a preset op with no `safety` key, the other adding the whole-tree test requiring one. Disjoint files, so nothing conflict-shaped fired, and the tally was correct: it is a statement about the PR's merge-base, and nothing asked whether that was still the default branch head.

  It discloses and never blocks. A `strict` arm was considered and declined: an opt-in refusal is only typed by somebody who has already decided to be careful, so it adds nothing over reading the line. The distance is asked about `headRefOid`, never `headRefName` — the tally belongs to a commit.

- **Four ops accepted the `force` bypass and did not say so in the registry** ([#1269](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1269)). `bluesky_like`, `bluesky_follow`, `devto_publish` and `hashnode_publish` all read a `force` token out of their argument, and none of them named it in the `syntax` string that `supertool 'ops'` prints. `force` is the bypass for the publish confirmation gate and for the fail-closed pre-flight duplicate checks ([#562](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/562), [#601](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/601)) — the refusal tells the caller to use it, and the registry did not tell them it exists. All four declared it in the opening line of their own module docstring, and all four in the prose of `docs/presets/*.md`; the registry was the one surface that omitted it, and it is the one an agent reads.

  A new guard sweeps every op in every manifest, decides by AST whether the script *evaluates* the string `force` (a docstring or an error message mentioning `|force` does not count, or the sweep would be about prose), and requires the `syntax` string to name it as a whole word — `git-push:force-with-lease` is a different token. **10 ops read it; 4 did not declare it.** An op whose `cmd` cannot be resolved to a script raises rather than dropping out of the sweep.

  The guard is deliberately one token wide, and says why in its own docstring. The other two routes #1269 proposed were measured against this registry first: deriving tokens from the parse yields 199 candidates of which 4 are real, 2% precision; round-tripping every token the `syntax` names finds 0 drifts across 34 ops and 56 tokens, and executing that check for real would mean invoking the confirmation-bypass token on the write ops it most matters for.

- **`map` on the entry-point shim now says the surface is next door** ([#1272](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1272)). `map:supertool.py` returns the shim's two real symbols — small, correct, positive, and read as supertool's own surface. [#1259](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1259) disclosed the facade only where the result was already empty, on the argument that an absence is read as an absence in the world; an answer-shaped answer is the harder half of the same defect, because nothing about it prompts the second call.

  The note is worded as disclosure and not as a correction: the listed symbols really are the shim's and the map really is complete for that file, so it affirms the result and then offers `map:_supertool.py` as a call to add, never a re-run to replace. Same gate as #1259 — the named pair, both files on disk side by side. A map of the *directory* stays silent, because it already enumerates `_supertool.py` on the next line.

- **The suite's symlink-capability line reported a floor as a total** ([#1274](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1274)). `conftest` printed `N symlink-dependent tests did NOT run on this platform`, counting only skips carrying the `symlink-capability(#1143)` token. Three of the five mechanisms that keep a symlink call site off a privilege-less runner produce no such skip, and the register counted 27 sites under them, not the 20 the issue estimated -- 12 hand-rolled probes and 8 unrelated platform markers, which skip without the token, plus 7 `except OSError` arms, which do not skip at all -- so `N` was a subset presented as a total. [#1232](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1232) had fixed the loud version of this, where the line read `0` while four tests were failing for exactly that reason; a plausible non-zero number is quieter and prompts nobody to check it. Twelve of those sites were removable and are removed: the three `watch` hostile-file suites each hand-rolled a `_can_symlink()` probe with their own `pytest.skip` wording, and now call the shared `require_symlink()`, so their skips are counted. The other two mechanisms are kept deliberately -- a `needs_nofollow` marker fires at collection on every Windows runner whether or not the privilege is present, and a symlink call inside an `except OSError` arm is not a skip at all -- so stamping the token onto them would assert a reason nothing measured. Instead the line now carries its own population: `N of M skipped tests did NOT run for this reason`, followed by which mechanisms are not in `N` and where the full list lives. Observed under a forced-absent privilege in a child pytest; `windows-latest` has the privilege today, so the privilege-less runner remains unobserved from here.

- **A live containment check took its exemption list from a documentation table** ([#1277](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1277)). `test_every_core_only_key_read_by_a_decision_is_stripped` fails when one of the core's own decisions consults a result key an adapter is free to write. It needs a list of keys that are legitimately adapter-owned, and it used this repo's transcription of `validators/SCHEMA.md`'s adapter table — so the boundary moved whenever that table did.

  Emitting a field and consulting a field are two permissions and only the second is a containment property. They are now two lists: `SCHEMA_ADAPTER_KEYS` stays the doc transcription, pinned to `SCHEMA.md` by #1042's drift guard, and `DECISION_READABLE_KEYS` is what a core decision may read. The relation asserted between them is containment, not equality — deliberately narrower is the legitimate state, and it is the state that was already true.

  The count is the finding: **four** of the nine documented adapter fields — `diff`, `duration_ms`, `file`, `metrics` — were exempt from the check and are consulted by nothing, so the exemption ran four keys wider than the property it stood for. Two guards keep it that way: one fails on any key exempted that no decision reads, one pins the withheld set so that adding a row to `SCHEMA.md` reddens the test instead of silently pre-authorising the next key a decision starts reading.

- **The exit code was decided by re-reading text formatted for a human, and it was wrong in both directions** ([#1291](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1291), [#1279](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1279)). A dispatch receipt is `--- {arg} ---` followed by the op's answer, and `{arg}` is whatever the caller typed — so locating the boundary in the rendered string made the verdict a function of the argument.

  A **successful** op could exit `1`: the failure scan searched the whole body for a `---` line followed by an error-shaped one, and an argument spanning lines supplied both. `supertool 'grep:zzz ---<newline>ERROR: nope:README.md'` found nothing, said so, and exited `1` — after which the batch tally added in v0.33.0 printed `1 refused` in words, an explicit false sentence built on a false bit.

  A **failing** op could exit `0`: the header's close was taken to be the first ` ---` in the body, which an argument can contain. A `git-commit` refusal whose message quotes an op receipt — the shape this repo's own commit convention asks for — exited `0`, which is the defect fixed in v0.33.0 returning on a different input.

  The verdict is now taken where the receipt is assembled, from the string the op returned, before a header is prepended to it. Preset ops are not a second population: their exit status is already recorded at the subprocess and the `FAIL` line is rendered from it. Eighteen early-return gates inside dispatch now go through one assembly point, `_receipt(header, body)`, rather than each building a string for something else to parse back; two more sit ahead of it and mark the refusal directly.

  It is also no longer a function of receipt size. Measured on a diff-shaped body of 3000 `--- a/path` hunk headers: **0.15 microseconds against 0.85 milliseconds**, and unchanged at 6000 hunks where the scan doubles to 1.68 ms.

- **The printed cleanup command had no "default branch could not be read" state, so it handed over the DELETE the cleanup arm would have refused** ([#1292](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1292)). `run_cleanup` refuses all three items when this repository's default branch is unestablished — one of the four facts #1281 established a delete needs. The **command-printing** path, which is the default one and the one a human actually pastes, tested only whether the head was cross-repository or equal to the default branch. An **empty** default branch satisfies neither: `""` is not the head. So it fell straight through and printed a ready-to-paste `gh api -X DELETE .../refs/heads/<head>` having never established that the head is not the branch it was about to delete.

  Empty is a reachable answer rather than an impossible one. `_repo_identity` returns it whenever the API reply lacks `defaultBranchRef.name`, `main()` bails only on the repository half, and the section header three lines above already renders `default_branch or '?'` — the file elsewhere knows the value can be missing.

  The printed arm now tests the same three conditions as `run_cleanup`, **in the same order**, and picks its stated reason in that order too, so the two arms cannot report different grounds for one refusal. The file's own comment already called a printed delete "the same decision made by the reader"; it is now the same decision in code as well. Quoting makes a wrong command safe to paste — it does not make it right.

- **A file outside `changelog.d/` can no longer name a fragment the next tag will delete** ([#1293](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1293)). The release *consumes* fragments, so any reference keyed to `changelog.d/<n>.<section>.md` is green for exactly the window between the PR that writes it and the release that consumes it, and red on that release and every one after — and the window is invisible from inside the PR that adds it, because the file is present the whole time that PR's CI runs.

  It has shipped four times. #941 took five legs on v0.26.0, #953 thirteen of twenty on v0.27.0, and #1231 thirteen of twenty-two on v0.33.0 — that last one was not an assertion at all, just a filename in a tuple of paths a test swept and resolved with a `read_text`, which the #1053 AST detector is blind to by construction. So the class was never a syntax.

  `tests/test_changelog_findable_1293.py` asks which fragments are on disk *now* and refuses any tracked text file that names one, in any language and by any shape. Keying it to the directory's contents rather than to a filename pattern is what makes it precise: a reference to an **already consumed** fragment names nothing the next tag can delete, and 185 lines across 19 tracked files are exactly that — doc examples, comments, `tmp_path` fixtures — every one correct and every one left alone. Swept for live-keyed references at the same time: **zero**, `tests/test_ops_roster_1231.py` having been the last. When nothing is pending, or when git cannot list the checkout, it skips rather than passing, because a scan that looked at nothing must not read as a clean sheet.

  The rule is now stated where fragment authors meet it — `changelog.d/README.md` and `docs/contributing.md` — with `CHANGELOG.md` and `assert_change_is_findable(<issue>)` named as the two permanent things to point at instead.

- **Three `git status` gates inherited the display setting that decides whether git mentions untracked files at all** ([#1295](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1295)). `status.showUntrackedFiles=no` is an ordinary user or repo preference. A consumer reading `git status --porcelain` with inherited config gets an **empty list from a dirty tree** and cannot tell "nothing there" from "not looked" — the mechanism that disarmed #1290's gate. Each of these now pins `-c status.showUntrackedFiles=normal` on the command line, where it outranks config files **and** `GIT_CONFIG_*` both:

  - `git-push`'s pre-push "you forgot to commit X" catch. It had three states for a status that *failed* and none for one that succeeded after being configured not to look — which renders as silence, which reads as "nothing was left behind", on the run right after a push landed.
  - `oss_train`'s pre-rebase guard, whose own comment already read *"A status this op could not read is not a clean tree"*. That was written about a non-zero exit; a suppressed read exits **zero**, so the principle was stated and the code did not cover the case that arises. The guard opened and the op went on to fetch, rebase and force-push a worktree an agent was working in.
  - `git-commit`'s `--all` resolution. #1295 filed this one as a render; it is the strongest gate of the three. `_worktree_changes` feeds the list that gets **staged and committed**, so a suppressed untracked half does not merely print short — `--all` commits the tracked half only, under a receipt naming that subset as the answer to `--all`.

- **`normal`, not `all`.** The flag is there so the command line has the last word on whether untracked files are mentioned; `all` would additionally defeat git's own directory collapse and turn an untracked `venv/` into thousands of lines. Every gate here only needs to establish that the tree is not empty.

- **The remaining `git status` readers are deliberately left alone, and a register says so.** `git-status` and `git-checkout` render their working-tree section for a human and branch on nothing, and pinning a *render* overrides a display preference in the one place it is meant to take effect. That split is the whole judgment, so it is recorded per site in `tests/test_git_status_display_config_gates_1295.py` rather than left for the next reader to re-derive: a new `git status` under `presets/git/`, `presets/github/` or `scripts/` is a red build until someone writes down which kind it is. A shared helper was rejected for the reason it usually wins — it would make the pinning invisible at the call site, which is exactly where the decision has to be made, and it cannot express an answer that differs per site. The register also asserts that every site marked as a gate *actually carries the pin*, because a table of intentions is the inert-gate shape this repo keeps filing.

  Not swept: the three consumers in `_supertool.py`, left untouched because that file was under concurrent rewrite. They are named in the register so the zero reads as "out of scope" rather than "none exist". `git clean` has no consumers in these trees; the `git ls-files` and `git diff` readers were checked and take explicit pathspecs or plumbing flags with no equivalent display suppression.

- **A `node --check` that never answered was rendered as a broken dashboard** ([#1296](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1296)). `html-check` gives `node --check` 30 seconds per inline `<script>` block and, on blowing that, reports the refusal by name — the three-state contract working. `tests/test_html_check.py` then asserted a pinned source line against it, so the correct refusal arrived as a failing test that read as a defect in the validator. Observed twice on `pytest (windows-latest, 3.11)`, both cleared on a re-run.

  The gate #794 built for tests asserting a file is *clean* now also covers tests asserting a file is *broken*, where a stall is `ok: false` with `count: 1` and therefore slips past `assert_declined` before failing on the line number. `_adapter_verdict.skip_if_stalled()` runs the same four-clause predicate and declines; every spawn in `test_html_check.py` goes through it. The timeout is unchanged at 30s, and nothing else about the assertions moved — a clean verdict on a broken page, a finding on the wrong line, an absent `node`, and a `timeout` reported in 12ms all still fail.

- **A `~/` path was refused as not found, and the receipt named a path that had never been stat-ed** ([#1300](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1300)). `_safe_path` — the containment gate — has expanded `~` before checking since [#146](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/146), but it returned only a verdict, so every op then opened the caller's literal `~/x`. `os.path.abspath` turns that into `<cwd>/~/x`, which never exists: the gate approved one path and the op tried a different one. Measured before the fix across the thirteen read ops that take a path — `read`, `head`, `tail`, `wc`, `stat`, `ls`, `tree`, `map`, `grep`, `grep_around`, `around`, `around_line`, `between` — and every one of them failed, while `cwd:~/dir` had expanded correctly all along in the CLI pre-pass, so the tool disagreed with itself about what a tilde meant.

- **The containment boundary did not move.** `_gate_paths` returns the check *and* the string the caller must use, in one call, so a route cannot clear one path and open another. The expansion it hands back is the same `os.path.expanduser` the check already applied, written back only after the check passed — a `~` resolving outside the boundary is still refused with `path escapes cwd`, and `tests/test_tilde_path_1300.py::TestContainmentIsNotWidened` pins both halves. Deliberately narrower than the gate's own normalisation: no `realpath`, which would silently redirect a write through a symlink, and no `expandvars`, because `$` is a legal filename character and expanding it would break files that read fine today.

- **The preset/custom-op chokepoint had the same shape and the same defect.** [#1287](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1287)'s `"paths": {"args": [...], "root": ...}` gate checked the expanded path and then let `_resolve_custom_op` substitute the literal one into the op's `cmd` template — which runs argv-form through `shlex.split`, so no shell expanded it either: a declared op reading `{file}` answered `cat: ~/t.txt: No such file or directory`. It now gets the gate's own expansion, on the declared branch only. An op grandfathered in `_UNDECLARED_PATH_OPS` reaches no check at all, so it keeps the literal for the same reason `glob` does. The same one-line write-back went into the two internal chokepoints, `render_file` and `_atomic_write`, and into the `around`/`between` misordering-recovery hints, which stat the slot they promote and so had been declining to recognise a tilde file that exists.

- **`glob` is the deliberate exception, and now says so instead of answering `(0 files)`.** It is not in `_PATH_ARG_POSITIONS` and resolves its own pattern, so there is no containment gate for an expansion to sit behind — expanding `~` there would widen what the op can reach rather than fix what it can say. It refuses with `unsupported path form: glob does not expand ~`, naming the absolute spelling that works. The zero it used to return was the house defect in miniature: an absence the tool manufactured, reading exactly like an empty directory.

- **`tried:` now prints the string that was actually opened.** `_path_not_found` ran its own `expanduser` purely for display, so the receipt named an expanded path that existed — one the reader had listed seconds earlier — while the tool had touched a different one. That line is `os.path.abspath(path)` and nothing else. A `~user` that cannot expand keeps its literal spelling in the receipt and gets a hint saying `~` was not expanded, in place of the `wrong CWD?` advice that provably cannot fix it (same reasoning as [#734](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/734) and [#921](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/921)).

- **Three tests were reaching the live internet, and all three passed on whatever came back** ([#1312](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1312)). `test_hashnode.py::test_comment_main_aborts_on_dupe` stubbed the op's `gql` and left `gql_safe` — which is the one the pre-flight actually calls — so every leg of every PR opened a real HTTPS connection to `gql.hashnode.com`. It went red on PR #1302, a diff of one test file and one markdown table, when Hashnode began answering 301: the redirect guard refused the off-origin hop and said no credentials were sent, correctly, in a message with no `ABORT` in it. The product was right and the harness rendered it as a product defect.

  Two more in `test_security_error_echo_691.py` had the same shape one layer along. They patched `MODULE.urllib.request.urlopen`, but every preset routes through `_http.urlopen`, which calls `_http._OPEN` — bound to the opener at import and never looked up on `urllib.request` again. The stub replaced a name nothing calls, so `bsky.social` and `dev.to` were contacted for real. The bluesky one is the sharp case: it exists to prove that a password echoed back by a remote is redacted, and the echo it injects had never once been delivered.

  All three are stubbed now, at the seam the product reads, and each assertion was tightened so it can only be satisfied by the injected body — `main()` has three `ABORT` arms, and the hashnode test had spent its life green on the wrong one.

  `tests/_netblock.py` is the guard: `block_outbound(monkeypatch)` refuses any non-loopback `connect` or `getaddrinfo` and names the host and what to stub, so a missing stub fails at the socket instead of being answered by the internet. Armed in both touched modules. Loopback and `AF_UNIX` stay open — `test_http_bounds.py` and the `claude-channel` suites bind real servers and are hermetic.

  The count is measured, not grepped: the whole suite was run under a socket observer that recorded every outbound attempt (`10186 passed`, 285s). Three tests, three hosts, and nothing else across 559 test modules.

  `OutboundBlocked` derives from `BaseException` on purpose. Presets catch broadly by design -- `gql_safe` swallows every `OSError` to return `None`, and `hashnode/comment.py::main` renders a bare `except Exception` into an `ABORT -- pre-flight failed` line. An ordinary `Exception` would be absorbed there and printed as a plausible ABORT, so the guard's own refusal would arrive as a product verdict. That is the same defect one layer up.

- `grep` and `around` now refuse any top-level alternation branch that matches every line, not just an empty one (#1314). The #1120 guard tested for `b == ""`, so `grep:^\|def op_:PATH` — the bash-BRE rewrite turning `\|` into a top-level `|` with `^` to its left — sailed through and reported 5 of "1000+ matches" for a pattern matching every line of the file. A branch is saturating when it matches the empty string, which is what `^`, `$`, `.*` and `z*` have in common; the refusal now names the offending branch. `^$|alpha`, `(^|,)alpha`, `colo(u|)r` and `[|]b` are all still searches and still run.

- **`claude-log` answered with another directory's sessions when the cwd had none** ([#1317](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1317)). `project_dir()` fell back to the store whose encoded name shared the longest common *prefix* with the cwd's, and a prefix walks sideways. Measured from `~/Documents/st-wt/1317`, with 89 stores present and none of them this worktree's: it returned `-Users-floriandavid-Documents-st-wt-1024`, and `claude-log-list` and `claude-log-cost` rendered a normal, plausible board about a different worktree's work with nothing in the output naming the substitution. Worktrees are the normal shape here — nine were live the day it was filed — so this was the default state of a delegated run, not an edge case.

  Resolution is now **upward only**: the cwd's own store, else the nearest ancestor's, else nothing. A sibling is never an answer to "what happened in this directory". The resolver returns three states rather than a bare path — `direct`, `ancestor` and `missing` — because a `Path` cannot tell a hit from a substitution, which is the whole of the defect.

  `missing` declines by name, quoting the directory asked about, the store that would hold its sessions, and how many stores exist, so "none of them is yours" cannot be read as "there are none" and neither can be read as an empty board. `ancestor` is legitimate — a subdirectory belongs to its project — and is still not the directory the caller stood in, so it prints `Source: ancestor store — no sessions recorded for X; showing Y, which is not the same directory` rather than leaving the reader to diff a `Project:` path against their own cwd.

  Ancestors are derived from the path string, not from `pathlib`: on POSIX a backslash-separated Windows path is a single component with no parents, so a `.parents` walk would have resolved on Windows and declined on macOS for the same input.

  `claude-log-tail` and `claude-log-summary` take an explicit UUID and were never affected — `session_path()` identifies a session by name, not by neighbourhood.

  Not closed, and named where it lives: `encode_cwd` is Claude Code's own naming scheme and maps `/`, `-` and `:` all to `-`, so `/Users/foo/bar` and `/Users/foo-bar` write the same store name and nothing on disk says which. A `direct` hit is ambiguous in exactly that way too, so no resolution order over these names can decide it. Pinned by `TestKnownLimit` so a future disambiguator has a failing test to turn green.

- **A create a validator refused, and no validator rolled back, is now disclosed as still on disk** ([#1320](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1320)). `paste` of a malformed `changelog.d/` fragment printed the refusal and `[result] 1 op run, 1 write` — the same footer a fragment that passed prints — and left the artefact in the tree for `git status`, test collection and every later read to find.
  - **The issue's stated mechanism was wrong, and re-deriving it changed the fix.** It reported that a create "has no baseline, so the comparison cannot fire". #1088 already built the create arm: `_rollback_action(False, None)` is `unlink`, and a new `.json` that does not parse really is removed. `? → N ✗ (baseline not measured)` is a statement about the delta, not about whether rollback can fire. The only discriminator is per-validator `rollback_on_fail`.
  - **So the fix is not rollback, and not flipping the flags.** Four of this repo's eight validators set `rollback_on_fail: false` deliberately — `ruff` and `lsp-diag` are advisory, `git-status` is not about the file's content, and `changelog-fragment` refuses shapes an author iterates on. Unlinking there would trade a misreport for the destruction of a write the caller asked for.
  - **`[left on disk]` is the mirror of `[rolled back]`**, built the same way: it quotes the receipt's own `created …` line back, so a filter that caught the claim catches its qualification adjacent to it. It confirms rather than retracts — the path is real and the next action is to delete or fix it.
  - **The `[result]` line carries it**, because that is the part that survives a pipe: `1 op run, 1 write, 1 left on disk — 1 created file a validator refused was NOT removed and is still on disk`. `nothing changed on disk` is suppressed when it fires, so a batch that both reverted a write and kept a refused create cannot net to a footer that is false about the one path the reader must act on.
  - **The exit code does not move**, and that is the one place the mirror of `[rolled back]` stops. A rollback exits 1 because the write did not land; here it landed exactly as asked. Gating would make `rollback_on_fail: false` mean "advisory, unless you created the file" — the identical finding exits 0 on an edit — so a repo whose new file trips an advisory linter would break its `&&` chain over a checker its own config declared non-blocking.
  - **Four boundaries stay silent**: a clean create, a `skipped` (a checker that declined refused nothing), an overwrite (the `edited` line above already states it truthfully), and a create a rollback already removed or already reported on.

- `read`'s inline `grep=` filter now goes through the same pattern gate as `grep`, `grep_around` and `around` (#1344). It had been wired to neither half of it: `read:probe.txt:::grep=^|x` returned every line of the file under an ordinary `(2 lines, 8 bytes)` header — nothing looks impossible, and what the caller takes away is that every one of those lines matched the pattern they typed. A saturating filter is now refused on this route too, rather than disclosed: the whole file already has a spelling (`read:PATH`), so the refusal removes no call anyone meant. bash-grep BRE alternation is rewritten here as well, so `read:PATH:::grep=alpha\|gamma` filters on either branch instead of searching for a literal `alpha|gamma` — and the rewrite is disclosed, never silent, which is the trap #1344 was filed to avoid. Both decisions live in one function (`_pattern_gate`), pinned by a test, so a fifth route cannot inherit a third behaviour.

- **`gh-pr` refuses a mode word it does not have, and `:threads` now exists** ([#1346](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1346)). `gh-pr:1331:notamode` rendered the default dashboard at exit 0, and so did `:threads`, `:reviews` and `:comments` — while that same dashboard's header printed `Unresolved threads: 1 / 1`. The op advertised a thing, accepted a request for it, and returned something else. An unrecognised mode is now refused naming the ones that exist, exit 1, before anything is fetched, matching `gh-job`/`gl-job`.

  `gh-pr:N:threads` prints the review threads the header only counted: `path:line`, resolved state, outdated marker, every comment body, unresolved first. One op's render, not a new op — the count and the bodies come off the same `reviewThreads` selection. It declines with `UNKNOWN` when the GraphQL call fails rather than reporting none, which the header's own count cannot tell apart.

  The agent that reported this could not read a review comment on its own PR and fell back to `gh api repos/.../pulls/1331/comments`.

- **`gl-api` declares a containment boundary for real, instead of being the grandfathered op the guard cited as declared** ([#1351](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1351)).

  `_syntax_names_a_path`'s docstring held `gl-api` up as the worked example of the safe pattern — "that op answers with `"paths": {"args": []}`, a declaration that someone made rather than a default nobody noticed". It carried no `paths` key and sat in `_UNDECLARED_PATH_OPS`, the grandfather register the same docstring describes emptying. The sentence the next author reads when deciding whether their op needs a declaration was pointing at an ungated one.

  Fixed by making the claim true rather than accurate: `gl-api:PATH` is an API route, it now declares `"paths": {"args": []}`, and the register shrinks from 20 to 19. The empty form carries no `root` — there is nothing for a boundary to bound, and inventing one would read as a choice somebody made.

- **The docs described `read`'s elision as a live saving; measured, it never fires between two Bash tool calls** ([#1352](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1352)). `_read_elide_session_key()` carries `os.getppid()`, which for `supertool` is the shell that ran it — and Claude Code starts a new shell per tool call, so the key changes every turn. Re-derived here rather than taken on trust: two bare reads of one unchanged file in separate calls both returned 3,840 bytes and left two keys under `~/.cache/supertool/read-elide/`; the same two reads on one command line returned 276 bytes, the elision line. It fires inside one shell, which is the case batching already covers, and not for the repeat read after a compaction it was built for. `README.md`, `docs/operations/reads.md`, `docs/configuration.md`, `.supertool.example.json` and the pending [#1329](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1329) fragment all now name the condition instead of implying it always holds. **No behaviour changed** — the key is a separate decision and stays open, because the reasoning behind it is still right and only lacked this measurement.

- **The condition is pinned by a test, not only by prose.** `tests/test_read_elide_session_boundary_1352.py` runs `supertool` under two different parent processes and asserts the second read returns content, with a same-parent arm as the positive control — without which "content came back" is equally consistent with the feature being off, the cache unwritable, or the test spawning wrongly. Whoever changes the session key gets a red test naming the boundary rather than a paragraph they have to notice. Written against the shipped claim first, where it failed on `assert "elided" in second`.

- **A call's exit code could be the previous call's verdict** ([#1359](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1359)). `dispatch_verdict` returned `_call_failed()`, a pure read of the thread-local `_DISPATCH_STATE.call_failed`, whose only reset lived inside `dispatch` at depth 0 — a function `dispatch_verdict`'s own docstring records as one callers replace ("both the tests and the MCP layer monkeypatch it"). Under that documented contract the reset never ran and the bit carried over from whatever last refused on the thread. It now establishes the flag immediately before the call it is about to judge. Before the call, never after: a sub-op that refuses at any depth must still reach its parent's verdict, so the depth-0 clear inside `dispatch` is unchanged.

- **The tally said "all 2 refused" about two ops that had not.** Reproduced on macOS with no pytest involved: a real refusing `read`, then `main(["edit:@-", "@-"])` over a replaced `dispatch`, printed `[batch] 2 ops ran — all 2 refused.` and exited 1. The exit code was the visible half; [#1284](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1284)'s tally turned the same stale bit into an explicit false sentence. The sibling counters beside it — `_SKIP_COUNT`, `_ROLLBACK_COUNT`, `_NOT_CHECKED` — are all read as per-call deltas for exactly this reason ([#680](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/680)); this bit was the one member of the group with neither a delta nor a reset.

- **It is what turned `master` red on macOS only, and the platform was never the cause.** At `df34db5`, `tests/test_stdin_clash_341.py::test_bare_dash_arg_is_not_treated_as_stdin` failed `assert 1 == 0` on macOS 3.10/3.11/3.12 with ubuntu and windows green. xdist `--dist load` schedules individual tests, so which test follows a real refusing dispatch inside one worker is decided by core count — the same mechanism recorded in `tests/conftest.py` for the [#689](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/689) macOS red. `tests/test_repo_target_673.py` stubs `dispatch` from the same shape and was exposed to the identical leak; both files were in the unexplained `8 failed` set reported and deliberately not cleared during [#1329](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1329).

### Security

- **Preset ops sat outside the core's path chokepoint entirely, and the next one written reproduced that by default** ([#1287](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1287)). `_PATH_ARG_POSITIONS` is the core's per-op table of which argument is a path, gating every builtin since [#146](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/146). **No preset op was ever in it.** So a preset op with a path argument enforced containment itself or not at all, and "not at all" was the default for anything newly written. [#1283](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1283) — `claims:/etc/hosts` reading the file in the same call that `read:/etc/hosts` refused it — was one instance, fixed inside that op, and nothing about the fix made the next preset op safe.

  Every preset and custom op now passes through one gate in `_resolve_custom_op`, above the subprocess. What the core cannot supply is the **boundary**: `claims` resolves a relative argument against the repository root, so imposing the core's cwd would refuse `claims:docs/x.md` run from `docs/` — a call that works today and should. So the op declares both and the core enforces both:

  ```
  "paths": { "args": [1], "root": "repo" }
  ```

  `args` are argument positions counting the op name as `0`; `root` is `"cwd"` (the core's boundary) or `"repo"` (the repository root). `"args": []` declares that no argument here is a filesystem path — `gl-api:PATH` is an API route, and that is now a claim someone made rather than a default nobody noticed.

  **An op whose `syntax` names a path and declares nothing is refused**, not skipped. A path argument that reaches no check is not a check that could not run; it is an unchecked read, and it renders identically to a checked one.

  Four ops declare today: `claims` (`repo`, the boundary [#1283](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1283) established) and `xml` / `xml_attr` / `xml_count` (`cwd`, which closes a real hole — `xml:/etc/passwd:...` parsed and reported on the file). **Twenty of the twenty-four shipped ops that name a path are grandfathered by name** in `_UNDECLARED_PATH_OPS`, because refusing them in the release that introduced the rule would break every one of them. That set only shrinks, and `tests/test_preset_path_chokepoint_1287.py` goes red if a name is added to it or if a new op with a path argument skips the declaration — which is the point: a convention a careful author misses on the day they read it is not a convention, it is a trap, and this one now fails the build instead.

  Several of the twenty cannot be expressed as an argument position at all — the publish ops carry their file inside a `|`-separated blob, `git-commit` takes a `:::`-separated tail, `git-resolve` a comma list. Draining that register is per-op work and is filed, not done here.

  A declaration the core cannot honour is refused rather than ignored. `{"args": [-1]}` — a plausible spelling of "the last argument" — passed the shape check in the first cut of this change and was then silently dropped by the range filter, so the op ran completely unchecked while looking exactly like a gated one. That is this repo's standing defect, an absence produced by the tool read as an absence in the world, reintroduced inside the fix for it; found in review and pinned. Negative indices are refused because `parts[-1]` on a bare call is the op name, so the core cannot resolve the slot the author meant.

  The core's opt-outs (`SUPERTOOL_ALLOW_OUTSIDE_CWD=1`, `"allow_outside_cwd": true`) are honoured at **every** boundary and the refusal names them. `_safe_path` grew a `root` parameter rather than a repo-root twin: [#882](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/882) and [#889](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/889) are what a second copy of this rule costs. `presets/claims/check.py` keeps its own check underneath as defence in depth, since the script is also runnable directly.

  **A correction to the write-up, not only to the code.** The maintainer skill's containment section said read-side containment has one universal boundary and one chokepoint, and that only write-side needs a domain-specific one. That half was wrong, and [#1283](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1283)'s agent said so from a call that would break. The chokepoint is universal; the boundary never was.

- **The path chokepoint's own detector read `syntax` and nothing else, so an op whose `cmd` uses `{file}` was never asked to declare a boundary** ([#1350](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1350)).

  [#1287](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1287)'s rule is that an op naming a path and declaring nothing is **refused, not skipped** — a path argument reaching no check is an unchecked read, not a check that could not run. Its detector inverted that for one input shape: an op whose `syntax` names no path, or which carries no `syntax` key at all, took the `return None` arm. No declaration demanded, no check run, and a verdict indistinguishable from declared-clean. Two states inside the guard that exists to insist on three.

  **The detector now reads the `cmd` template too, and the two are OR'd rather than ranked.** `{file}` and `{dir}` are the core's own placeholders, so an op writing one has already said which argument it means a filesystem path to be. The ordering was measured, not assumed: of the 24 shipped ops the `syntax` detector finds, **zero** carry either placeholder, so letting `cmd` supersede `syntax` would have disarmed the gate for every one of them. Going the other way, exactly **one** shipped op is found by `cmd` alone — `oss_train`, in this repo's own `.supertool.json`, which now declares `"paths": {"args": []}` because its argument is a worktree name bounded by `wt_root` inside the script ([#1246](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1246)), a boundary neither `cwd` nor `repo` can express.

  **`{arg}` is deliberately not a signal**, though it substitutes the very same argument `{file}` does. Sixteen shipped ops pass a handle, a ref, a tag, an ID or a repo slug through it and none takes a path; promoting it would refuse all sixteen and gate nothing.

  The refusal now names the signal that fired. An op with no `syntax` was being told it "names a path in its syntax ()", which reads as a bug in the guard rather than a demand on the op.

- **`glob` was outside the cwd containment boundary entirely** ([#1366](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1366)). From a directory with no opt-out, `read:/tmp/x/f.txt` refused and `glob:/tmp/x/*.txt` answered — same target, same call, two verdicts. What crossed was not file contents but an **existence oracle**: directory layout, project names, file naming, whether a given path is there at all (same family as [#1135](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1135) and [#1142](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1142)). `glob` resolves its own pattern and was absent from `_PATH_ARG_POSITIONS` with no note beside it — the only unexplained absence in a table where `grep`, `around` and `between` each say why — so it reached neither the dispatch gate nor [#1287](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1287)'s declaration gate, which only ever sees preset ops. It was an oversight, not a decision, and the table now says so.

- **A glob pattern is not a path, so it is gated in two halves and neither one narrows a result.** The two obvious single answers both fail: the literal prefix before the first magic character is *empty* in `*/../../etc/*`, so a prefix gate clears it; and filtering the expanded matches turns a refusal into a shorter list, which is this repo's house defect wearing a clean receipt. Instead, before disk is touched the pattern's **reach** is checked — every magic component read as one ordinary name, which loses nothing, because no glob metacharacter can invent a `/` (`*`, `?` and `[...]` stay inside a component, `**` spans them but only downward), so the traversal is fully determined by the separators and `..` already written. Brace groups are expanded first and each branch checked on its own: `_expand_braces` runs *inside* `_glob_files`, so `{.,/etc}/host*` used to read as one contained component and fan out into a pattern the gate never saw. After expansion the matches are checked too, for the one escape a pattern cannot predict — a wildcard landing on a symlink pointing out of the tree — and that refuses the **whole call**, naming no file: dropping the entries would report a population it had silently narrowed, and printing them would disclose the very paths the refusal is about.

- **A refusal is never `(0 files)`.** Both halves say `path escapes cwd`, with the same opt-out sentence as every other containment refusal — now a single `_ALLOW_OUTSIDE_HINT` constant rather than a second copy of the remedy. A manufactured zero is indistinguishable from an empty directory, which is exactly what `glob` said about `~` until [#1300](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1300). `glob` still does not expand `~`, for the same reason as before: the gate here reads a pattern, not a path, so there is nothing for an expansion to sit behind.

- **`glob` patterns resolve from the cwd, and three places said "repo root".** Found by the independent reviewer of this change, reading around the diff. `glob.glob` and the `os.walk` branch both resolve against `os.getcwd()`, so from a subdirectory `glob:*.txt` sees that subdirectory — but `docs/operations/reads.md`, the comment above the mid-path retry, and the retry's own user-visible note (`no match at repo root for …`) all claimed otherwise. The note now says `no match under cwd`. It mattered next to this change specifically: the new boundary is the cwd, and a doc row one clause away calling the same directory the repo root leaves a reader unable to tell which one the refusal is about.

- **The raw-command guard is no longer blinded by a `#` comment, a wrapper word, an absolute path, a brace group or a line continuation** ([#1389](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1389)). Six shapes each hid a raw command from the gate that ships enabled by default, and every one returned `clean` — so the hook stayed silent and the command ran, which is the sentence the guard was built to make impossible, true of the guard itself.

  Every one was the matcher disagreeing with the shell about **where a command starts**, so the fix is one answer rather than six patches. Comments are now stripped line by line inside the quote-aware scan that already rewrites newlines — `shlex`'s own `commenters` runs to the end of its input, and since that input is the whole command, one `#` on line one hid every line under it. A backslash before a newline is deleted as the line continuation it is, instead of reaching the lexer as an escape that glued the next line's command word onto the previous token. `{` and `}` are separators, so a grouping construct no longer pushes the real command word to index 1. The command word is compared by the name a shell would run, on either path separator and with a Windows executable suffix removed, so `/opt/homebrew/bin/gh` is the `gh` the registry declares.

  And the wrapper words: `env`, `timeout`, `nice`, `ionice`, `stdbuf`, `setsid` and `doas` join the prefix list, but the list is not the fix. Each of those takes options of its own before the command word, and writing down seven option grammars is case work that goes stale one utility at a time — each gap a silent bypass. What is true of every wrapper is weaker and enough: the command word is somewhere further along the same segment. So inside a wrapper-led segment every suffix is offered to the registry, which catches `env -u FOO gh …`, `timeout -k 5 60 gh …` and `sudo -u somebody gh …` without knowing anything about `env`, `timeout` or `sudo`. Outside one, nothing changes: `echo gh pr view 1` runs nothing and is not blocked.

  The suffix scan buys that at a stated price: inside a wrapper-led segment, positional arguments that coincidentally spell a registry argv are blocked — `timeout 30 tar -cf - gh pr view`, over three files named `gh`, `pr` and `view`, is refused. That direction is a message the caller can read and work around; the alternative direction is what #1389 is a report of.

  **A command word the shell computes is now `undecided`, never `clean`.** `$'gh' pr view 1`, `${x:-gh} …`, `X=gh; $X …`, `$(printf gh) …`, `gh$IFS""pr$IFS""view` and `` `printf gh` pr view 1 `` all run `gh pr view 1` under bash — verified with a shell function, not reasoned about — and all tokenised to something matching nothing. Expansion cannot be implemented here, so the verdict is the third state the matcher already uses for `eval` and `sh -c`: the command runs, and the transcript says the command word was unreadable. Only the command word: `ls -la $HOME` stays `clean`, because a disclosure printed under most commands anyone writes is one nobody reads.

  `tests/test_guard_command_word_1389.py` is a table of shapes rather than a test per fix, in three directions — sixteen commands the shell would run and the guard must block, six whose command word it must decline to read, and four it must stay out of the way of. The next bypass is the shape nobody listed, so it costs one row.

- **`SUPERTOOL_PYTHON` was a silent off-switch for the raw-command guard, and the hook no longer reads it** ([#1390](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1390)). `hooks/pre-bash-guard.sh` put the variable at the head of its interpreter ladder and `exec`d the first candidate that survived `-c pass`. Every binary that exits 0 survives that, so `SUPERTOOL_PYTHON=/usr/bin/true` produced rc 0, no stdout and no disclosure — the gate off, from one environment variable, which is exactly the hatch `guard_command`'s own docstring says was refused on purpose. `/bin/echo` was worse: its output landed in the slot the hook's JSON verdict occupies.

  Three things changed. A candidate must now identify itself as a Python 3 rather than merely exit 0. `SUPERTOOL_PYTHON` does not participate in this ladder at all — it exists for supertool's own op subprocesses, and a gate deciding whether a command may run is a different trust context; `VIRTUAL_ENV` stays because on some hosts it is the only interpreter there is, and is required to look like a venv (`pyvenv.cfg`) rather than merely to be set. That narrows the exec-before-every-Bash-call primitive rather than closing it, and the wrapper says so in a comment instead of implying otherwise: the ladder cannot be made environment-free, because `PATH` is an environment variable too.

  Third, **"could not run" is now reachable when a candidate ran and produced nothing.** Previously only an empty ladder disclosed, so an interpreter that started and said nothing rendered byte-identically to a clean verdict — the three-state contract present in `guard_command`, present in `pre_bash_guard.py`, and lost at the shell layer under both. `pre_bash_guard.py` therefore writes an envelope on every path, including the one where nothing is replaced, so silence from the interpreter is now a fact the wrapper can act on.

- **A cloned repository's `.supertool.json` could write lines into the guard's system-authored denial** ([#1391](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1391)). `guard_command` walks up from the cwd for config, so any op in a repo you cloned could declare `replaces[].argv` — `"git status"` is enough — and the refusal then rendered that op's `use` and `description` verbatim into `permissionDecisionReason`. Both are newline-bearing, the description cap was per match while the number of matches was uncapped, and the whole thing reached the model unsolicited on any `Bash` call. The direction is inbound: untrusted repository bytes acquiring the authority of the tool's own refusal channel.

  The refusal still quotes the op's own description, and that is a decision rather than an omission. It is the feature the guard is built on — the refusal text cannot describe a flag the op no longer has — and replacing it with "run `help:OP`" would charge a second command on every legitimate block, forever, to disarm a case the three measures below already disarm. A gate that makes the common path more expensive is a gate that gets switched off.

  So: registry text is flattened through `presets/_untrusted.flat` before it is interpolated, which is the repo's one implementation of "this value occupies exactly one line" and covers the ten separators `str.splitlines()` folds on rather than the newline alone. The cap is one budget for the whole message plus a limit on how many matches are detailed, not a per-match cap multiplied by an uncapped number of matches. And a refusal that quotes an op defined in the project's own `.supertool.json` now says so, so a stranger's prose is never read as supertool's; a preset-defined op is not attributed to the project, because a disclosure that fires on everything is wallpaper.

  Reproduced against a real file on disk, not in-process: the audit that filed this was read-only and said its file leg was inferred. `tests/test_guard_refusal_injection_1391.py` plants the config and drives `hooks/pre_bash_guard.py` end to end.

- **`glob` answered questions about directories outside the boundary, as counts** ([#1392](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1392)). Two mechanisms, one class.

  `_glob_reach` modelled `**` as exactly one component. The expander treats it as zero-or-more, so a `..` written after a `**` climbed one level further than the gate believed and a pattern carrying one `**` per `..` cleared the pattern gate before walking out. The reach is now checked at both ends of that range — every magic component as one level down, and every `**` expanded to zero. Zero is the only other extreme that needs checking: dropping a downward component can only move the cursor up, so the all-zero expansion climbs at least as far as any expansion in between.

  And the exclude-paths filter ran **before** the containment check, so an outside directory whose contents are excluded had every match filtered away and the check then saw an empty list. `glob:**/../.ssh/*` rendered as `(0 files, 6 files hidden by exclude-paths)` while a directory that does not exist rendered as `(0 files)` — a refusal converted into exact cardinality, and two distinguishable answers about a directory the caller may not read. The check now runs over the excluded entries too: being excluded is a reason not to print a file, never a reason not to gate it.

  The refusal itself no longer reports how many matched. The reasoning that shipped with the gate says dropping entries hands back a shorter list under an honest header and printing them discloses the paths; the count is the third form of the same disclosure, and `51 match(es)` next to `2 match(es)` is the whole oracle in one number.

  Not a regression: before the gate landed, inside this same release delta, `glob` had no containment check at all and would have printed the names. This is a narrowing that left a residue.

## [0.33.0] - 2026-08-11

### Added

- **`claims:PATH` — does a document's references still hold?** `.claude/skills/opensource-manager/SKILL.md` told the maintainer, under a bullet headed "Two genuine gaps", that no op rendered a commit's run list and nothing tallied label distribution; `gh-branch:COMMIT_SHA` (#1083) and `gh-labels:tally=PREFIX` (#1084) had both shipped, and the second is the cohort burn-down that file orders reported every tick. A doc that is loaded rather than read does not merely risk being wrong, it produces the behaviour it describes. `.claude/jit-context/*.md` is the sharp end — injected at the moment of a tool call — and on the day this shipped it listed five issues under "Open defects" headings, all five closed.
- **It checks references, never reasoning, and the boundary is measured rather than argued.** Flagging `#NNNN` citations by issue state plus an absence-marker word list scored 15 flagged, 2 real — 13% — because past-tense narration of a fixed bug is lexically identical to a present-tense claim that a hole exists. Three narrower lexical anchors were measured against this repo's whole doc corpus and scored 14%, 11% and 20%. None beat the number already rejected, so there is no lexical lens in the op at all and the render says so. Over 22 documents here: 11 contradicted, 11 real; none of the original 15.
- **Three lenses.** Backticked `name:...` tokens against the live registry — `key=` flags only, because a bare segment is a value in a placeholder slot, and a head resolving to nothing is `couldn't check` rather than a finding (19 such tokens here were skill ids and label filters, none a stale op name). Paths, `:LINE` numbers, quoted lines and section headings against the tree — a quotation beside a line number is checked against that line, since a number alone only proves the file is long enough. And issues cited under a heading that *declares* them open defects, which carries a verdict where prose cannot because it reads the document's own annotation instead of guessing at its grammar.
- **Three states, and the third never collapses.** A doc with nothing contradicted but something unchecked prints `NOT A CLEAN DOC`. A sibling repo's path, an ambiguous basename, a placeholder in a naming convention, a citation into another tracker and an unreadable tracker are all `couldn't check` — and the sibling-repo rule refuses to sweep prose for `owner/name` slugs, because doing so read `dependabot/outside-contributor` as a repository and ate two real findings.

- **`ops:roster` — every op name plus a safety class, and nothing else** ([#1231](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1231)). No descriptive listing form fits the SessionStart hook's ~7,168-byte cap: `ops` is 47,254 bytes in this checkout and `ops-compact` 9,067, so the startup listing was truncated on **every** session and everything alphabetically after `grep` was hidden — the whole `gh-*` and `git-*` families, `radar`, `watch`, `read`, `paste`, `tree`. `ops-compact` disclosed the truncation honestly and that did not help, because what was hidden was *existence*: in one session a maintainer reached for `worktrees` while `git-worktrees` existed, hand-rolled four `gh pr create` calls past `gh-pr-create` and its closing-reference check, and hand-rolled a cohort tally past `gh-labels:tally=`. Three agents independently reported `write:` is not an op, none having been told `paste:` is. The roster is ~1.7KB and the whole hook payload ~2.7KB, against the ~7.2KB cap. It is now what `hooks/session-start.sh` prints.

  **The class is the reason names alone were not enough.** Most ops teach their own signature on contact — `between:FILE:747:820` answers *"'820' was read as the path"* and names the op that does take a range — so roster → call → error is a complete learning loop. It is not available for an op that acts on the world: `oss_train` force-pushes a merge train, `gh-pr-merge` merges, `watch` spawns a poller, `git-push` publishes. Unmarked is a positive **read-only** claim, `*` writes files in this tree, `!` changes something outside it or starts something that outlives the call. The class is consequence, not mechanism: `bluesky_status_since` reads a feed and writes `~/.config/bluesky/last_check`, so probing it silently eats the window the next real briefing would have reported — it and its two twins are `acts`.

  **Declared, never inferred, and the fallback is the loud one.** Preset and project ops carry a new `"safety"` key beside their `cmd`; built-ins take theirs from `_OP_SAFETY_BUILTIN` in the binary, which a project's `.supertool.json` cannot downgrade — the class is a property of this build and the config may be absent or somebody else's. An op with no class, or an unrecognised one, renders `!`: an `acts` op mis-shown as probe-safe invites someone to probe `oss_train`, while the reverse costs one `help:OP`. Tests fail if any shipped preset op omits the key, so the next op cannot ship unclassed. `_PARALLEL_SAFE_OPS` was rejected as a derivation source despite being documented as the read-only set — it carries `format_staged`, which writes every staged file.

  Flat and alphabetical rather than grouped by family: every miss above was a neighbour miss, and one alphabetical sweep finds `gh-pr-create` beside `gh-pr` where a family grouping asks the reader to already know the family. A test pins the roster under half the cap, so adding ops cannot quietly reintroduce the truncation.

- **`ops` refuses an unrecognised argument instead of discarding it** ([#1231](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1231)). `ops:gh-labels` printed the entire 47KB listing and said nothing about the token it dropped — an argument ignored without a word, in the op whose subject is which arguments exist, in a tool whose rule is that an unrecognised token is refused. It now names the alternative: `help:gh-labels` for that op's full entry, which carries more than the listing row ever did, or `ops:roster` for every name. Deliberately *not* made into an `ops:PATTERN` filter: `help:OP` already answers what a filter would and answers it with more, and a filter would rebuild this issue in miniature, since `ops:gh-labl` matching nothing renders identically to an op that does not exist.

- **`jit-index` — a jit-context rule whose regex the matcher cannot honour is refused at write time** ([#1254](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1254)). A `**/00-manual/00-index.tsv` row is an ordinary `paste` or `edit`, so nothing in the write path ever looked at its `match` column, which is compiled by **awk** rather than PCRE (`pre-tool-hook.sh:80`, `pre-path-hook.sh:105`). The one-true-awk that macOS ships drops an escape it does not define, so `gh\s+pr` compiles to `ghs+pr` and matches nothing. Two `block` rules were dead this way on 2026-08-10, one of which had never fired since the day it was written, and nothing anywhere said so.

  **The check is structural, not a compile, and that is the decision the issue left open.** awk does not *fail* to compile `\s` — it compiles it, silently, into the wrong thing and exits 0, so an adapter that hands each pattern to the local awk and reads the exit status returns a clean verdict on the exact row that produced the issue. The load-bearing half is therefore a property of the pattern text: an escaped ASCII letter or digit that awk does not define is dropped and the pattern matches the bare character. That catches `\s`, `\d`, `\w` and the construct nobody has listed, and it answers the same on ubuntu, macos and windows — which is the point, since the verdict must not become a statement about the runner. A pattern has to survive the most conservative POSIX awk, because compiling under gawk is not a licence to write `\s` for a hook that fires on somebody's Mac.

  A compile pass against the installed awk still runs, for the failure only a real engine can report: a malformed pattern such as `gh[a` is a **fatal** awk error, and both hooks are invoked as `bash "$S" || true`, so one unbalanced bracket does not disable one row — it silences every rule in the file. Two further dead constructs are refused on the same grounds: `\b` is a backspace to awk rather than PCRE's word boundary, and the tools matcher lowercases the command before matching, so an uppercase literal outside a bracket expression can never match.

  Three states. `skipped` when the file is not a jit-context index, or when awk is absent *and* the structural half found nothing — a half-run check is not a pass. A structural *finding* is still published without awk, because declining to answer must never suppress an answer already in hand.

- **`gh-pr-merge:N:squash|force|cleanup` now runs the cleanup it used to print for you to retype** ([#1256](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1256)). Measured on this repo: 96 of 99 remote branches were merged and undeleted, and 10 worktrees on merged branches survived one day. Cleanup was skipped because it was a second decision after the interesting one had ended.
- It runs **only** after `MERGED` is read back off the remote. The rule it replaces — cleanup is a separate command — was written when nothing verified the merge; the read-back gate is now exactly that verification, and it sits upstream of this arm. A merge that is not confirmed skips all three items and issues no command at all.
- Three items, three states each, never two: `done`, `refused: <reason>`, `skipped: <reason>`, with a `[cleanup] N done, N refused, N skipped` tally. A cleanup that could not run never renders as a cleanup that had nothing to do.
- The remote branch goes through `gh api -X DELETE`, never `git push --delete`: the pre-push hook runs the entire suite per deletion, so 96 branches that way is about three hours of pytest whose output looks like progress.
- A worktree is removed only when `git-worktrees` says `idle`, read off that op's own `[result]` tally rather than re-derived here; `cannot tell` is treated as occupied and refused by name. The tree is then read — by two commands with different failure modes, see #1290 — and refused if it holds anything git is not tracking — `--force` governs modified and untracked files only, never ignored ones ([#1280](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1280)). Immediately after your own merge the honest answer is usually `refused: cannot tell` — the litter this exists for is day-old trees, which are the ones that pass.
- The local branch is deleted with `git branch -d`, never `-D`. `-d` cannot confirm a squash merge and declines — observed on `fix/1207`, whose PR had merged — and that decline is printed as a finding rather than forced past or skipped in silence.
- Nothing is deleted until the head branch is established to be in **this** repository and the remote ref reads back at the PR's own `headRefOid` ([#1281](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1281)). A head that is cross-repository, unestablished, or named after the default branch refuses all three items.
- Local items are skipped outright when a `repo:OWNER/NAME` target is set: the checkout is then not that PR's repository, and a branch of the same name here is a different branch.
- The exit code stays a statement about the merge. A refused cleanup is not a failed merge.

### Fixed

- **`git-commit`'s receipt no longer replays the whole message once the commit has landed** ([#946](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/946), [#1235](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1235)). The op header is `--- <the argument you sent> ---`, and for this op the argument is the commit message — so a twelve-line message was printed in full above a nine-line receipt, once to send and once to read back. On success the header is now `git-commit: "<subject>" +N more message lines → M path(s): …`, because `git log -1` already holds the message and the receipt underneath is what proves the commit landed.

  **On a refusal it stays verbatim, and that is the point.** Nothing was committed, so the header is the only surviving copy of a message the caller composed; eliding it there would cause the loss #1235 was filed about rather than fix it. The summary is gated on the op having succeeded, and arguments under 160 characters keep their verbatim header either way.

  The second half of #946 — `git-status` opening with a preceding command's output — was **not** reproducible: every op's output opens with its own `--- <op> ---` header, which is the unambiguous delimiter the issue asks for, and anything printed by an earlier process lands above it.

- **A `git-commit` refusal no longer suggests a repair that corrupts the message it is repairing** ([#946](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/946)). `git-commit:::MSG:::PATH` splits on `:::`, so a `:::` inside MSG makes the tail of the message arrive as a PATH — which the op correctly refuses. The suggested repair then rebuilt the message by rejoining on a single `:`, whatever had actually split it, so the `:::` came back as a `:` with nothing saying so. Both offered routes carried the rewrite; pasting either committed bytes the caller never wrote, under a refusal that was otherwise right.

  The refusal now leads with the `@-` payload route carrying the message byte for byte, and offers the single-colon reading below it, stating that the separator changes. Both readings are named; neither is guessed at.

  On the payload route the same check can fire, and there the refusal no longer claims the message "was split on ':'" — nothing was split, the fields arrived structured. It names the entries that are not paths, leaves the message intact, and declines to guess where the stray text belongs.

- `validators/SCHEMA.md` and the core's `_VALIDATOR_CORE_ONLY_KEYS` were two hand-maintained copies of one contract and nothing compared them. `tests/test_schema_contract_drift_1042.py` now does, in **both** directions: a key the core strips that the doc does not declare core-only, and a field the doc advertises as adapter-writable that the core silently drops before any decision reads it. The second direction had never been checked anywhere — it reads as a product bug rather than as stale prose, because the documented field simply does nothing and reports nothing.
- The core-only keys were enumerated in prose and nowhere machine-readable, so the doc carried a second copy of its own claim. They are now a "Core-only fields" table in `validators/SCHEMA.md`, and the prose points at it instead of re-listing them.
- `diff` and `skipped` had rendered outside the field table since #411. A blank line after the `metrics` row ends a Markdown table, so both appeared as a paragraph of literal pipe characters — including `skipped`, the third state and the most-cited field in the whole contract. Closed up, and the guard now fails on any field row that falls outside its table.

- **`html-check` matches `*.htm`, and every bundled adapter is now in `.supertool.example.json`** ([#1159](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1159)). `.htm` is the same document with a shorter suffix — identical content, identical checker — and a page saved that way got no inline-JS check at all. One entry covers both, in this repo's own config and in the catalogue, rather than a second `html-check-htm` row: unlike the `yaml-check` / `tsc-check` pairs there is no second tool and no second decision to record.

  `docs/validators.md` tells the reader to "enable any of these by copying the relevant entry from `.supertool.example.json`". **Eight adapters had no entry there**, not the seven the issue counted, and the list differs as well as the number: `changelog-fragment`, `lsp-diag`, `phpmd`, `phpmd-mcp`, `phpstan`, `phpstan-mcp`, `phpunit-mcp`, `rector-mcp`. The issue named five of those plus `common/`, which is a library the adapters import and not an adapter at all; it missed `changelog-fragment`, `phpstan` and `rector-mcp`. Counting the directories rather than copying the number is what turned that up, and the guard below now produces the list rather than a person doing it.

  With the violations gone the guard is buildable and is landed with them: every directory under `validators/` must be reachable from a `cmd` in the catalogue, and every catalogue `cmd` must point at a directory that exists. `common/` is excluded by name, so a future non-adapter directory is a visible decision rather than a pattern that happens not to match it. This asserts nothing about this repo's own `.supertool.json`, deliberately — it is correct for a Python repo not to run `phplint` on itself.

  Each new entry's `timeout` is set **above** the adapter's own internal budget, not equal to it. `docs/validators.md` already states the rule on the `html-check` row — when the two match, the core's timer always wins the race and the row reads `NOT CHECKED` with nothing naming what hung, where with headroom the adapter's own arm fires first and reports a cause. All seven of the new entries with a readable budget were written wrong first and caught by review: `phpstan-mcp` allows itself 60s to spawn plus 180s per call and had been given 120. A guard reads each adapter's own budget out of its source and fails on any of the seven that does not clear it, with a second test asserting the reader still finds all seven — a sweep that quietly stops reading must not pass as a clean sweep.
