  A file **no** validator's `match` glob selected counts towards `not checked`, not towards the clean total: "we own no checker for this type" and "every checker passed" must not be the same number on the one line whose job is telling them apart. And a `validate:` bundled into a batch that also mutated something appends `validated N files (M with findings, K not checked)` to the mutating footer — an inner op is at dispatch depth > 1 and renders no footer of its own, so its counts had nowhere to go.

  `presets/git/resolve.py`, which folds `validate:` output into per-file blocks by splitting on the headers, now drops `[result]` and `[branch: …]` explicitly instead of relying on its row regexes failing to match a line that opens with `[`. That was already true of the #979 decline path; making the footer unconditional made an accident load-bearing.

  It does not make `| tail -1` a verdict. #381 requires `[branch: …]` to be the last line whenever a footer prints, so inside a repo `tail -1` lands there, and that was already true of the decline path. The footer is owed on its own merits: a run whose final line is one file's row has no line describing the run at all, wherever the reader looks.

- **`gh-run:N` states which branch a run came from instead of prescribing a checkout** ([#1056](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1056)). The line under `Branch:` used to read `⚠ MISMATCH — switch with: ./supertool 'git-checkout:<branch>'` for any run not from the cwd's branch. Reading a run is not a claim about wanting its branch: runs are read when something is red, and the run you most need to read is routinely one you are not on and must not switch to. It was printed to an agent standing in a branch worktree with uncommitted work in it. It now reads:

  ```
  You are on: fix/1014 — this run is from master; reading a run needs no checkout
  ```

  `⚠ MISMATCH` goes with it — being on a different branch from a run you are inspecting is the ordinary case, not an error to correct. No `git-checkout`, and no `./supertool`, which need not exist in the cwd (#905).

  The line is not deleted. A field that simply vanished would read as "you are on the right branch" (#531), and the branch a run came from is useful context when the run is red. `gh-pr`, `gh-job`, `gl-mr` and `gl-job` keep the prescription: #850 governs all five together and is still open, and this is the one op whose premise was wrong.

- **`grep`'s `TRUNCATED` marker now states how truncated** ([#1073](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1073)). `— TRUNCATED, more matches exist` disclosed that an answer was partial without disclosing its scope, so 21 matches and 500 matches produced identical bytes while warranting opposite next actions. A truncated result now reads `— TRUNCATED, 137 matches total`.

  Three states, kept apart: a counted total, a total that hit the counting ceiling (`1000+ matches total (count capped at 1000)`), and the delegated rtk path, which has no candidate list to count over and says `more matches exist (total not counted)` rather than borrowing the shape of a real count. A complete answer still prints no marker and no total, so the marker's absence remains a positive statement that the count is exact.

  The ceiling was measured, not guessed: over a 67,855-file tree a dense pattern's walk went from 0.01s to 10.3s when counting everything, and stopping at 1000 cost 0.05s. Tunable via `grep.count_ceiling` / `SUPERTOOL_GREP_COUNT_CEILING`, never applied below the caller's own `LIMIT`.

### Fixed

- **`gl-runners`' live count can no longer be reordered onto an unannotated fleet** ([#807](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/807)). `radar_report` skips `annotate_recent_work` when nothing is queued, and `_is_responsive` — which reads that annotation and raises without it — is called in the live count further down. It was correct only because the skip and the count sat on mutually exclusive branches, with nothing stating the invariant and nothing testing it. One reordering, hoisting the count or merging the arms, crashes a live radar run.

  No behaviour changed. What changed is that the arrangement is now enforced by a test rather than by luck: the existing suite drove `radar_report` with fixtures that already carried both annotation marks, so it stayed green under exactly the reordering the issue describes.

- **`flatten_remote` walks every container, not just strings and lists** ([#825](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/825)). The single door every watch event leaves through walked `str` and `list` and dropped everything else — a `dict` value, or a string inside a list of dicts — into an `else` arm that reached the socket unflattened. A source sending `payload={"jobs": [{"name": ..., "error": ...}]}`, a shape nothing forbids, got no flattening at all, and the failure was silent: no raise, no log, and the consumer dropped the field rather than complaining. The guarantee held by two accidents downstream rather than at the door claiming to provide it.

  Naming types is how the next poller's field gets missed, exactly as naming keys is — which is what the function's own docstring already argued. It now recurses over `str` / `list` / `tuple` / `dict`, values only, to a stated bound of six levels. Past the bound the value is **refused** and replaced by the tool's own one-line words rather than passed through: a pass-through past the bound is the same hole one level deeper, and a cyclic payload has to terminate somewhere regardless.

- **The `gh-prs` radar tier checks filter values, not just filter keys** ([#973](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/973)). `radar:state=opne` passed the key check — `state` is a known filter — reached no command line, and rendered the default board as though it were the filtered one. The quieter half of #939's defect: the token *is* recognised, so every vocabulary check passes, and only the argv builder knows the request was dropped. #961 built this check for the `gl-mrs` tier and left the GitHub side uncovered.

  The domain is the op's own `_STATES` rather than a second hand-written copy, since two lists of GitHub's PR states is how they disagree. Every accepted filter key is now pinned to the argv it produces, so a key accepted here and ignored by `_build_list_cmd` fails a test rather than a board.

- **The delegated `grep` no longer answers a POSIX BRE reading of the pattern** ([#987](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/987)). With rtk delegation on — the default everywhere except this repo's own `.supertool.json` — the pattern was handed to the system grep with no `-E`, so `|`, `+`, `?`, `(` and `{` were ordinary characters there and not in the native walker. `ab+c` matched the line containing a literal plus instead of `abbc`.

  It only ever showed when the BRE reading happened to match something: a BRE that matches nothing exits non-zero and falls through to the native walker, where the answer is right. So the wrong answers were intermittent, data-dependent, smaller than the truth, and indistinguishable from correct ones.

  `-E` is now passed, and delegation is whitelisted rather than blacklisted: only patterns whose ERE and Python readings coincide by construction go to rtk. Any backslash escape outside the punctuation both dialects share, lookaround and inline flags (`(?...)`), non-greedy quantifiers, and POSIX bracket classes all run on the native walker. The whitelist is why GNU's `\<`/`\>` word boundaries — which anchor in ERE and are the literal characters `<` and `>` in Python — are covered without having been enumerated.

- **`docs/validators.md` no longer reads as if `$SUPERTOOL_REQUIRE_VALIDATORS` were the only switch on a non-verdict** ([#989](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/989)). #979 corrected the one sentence that was flatly wrong; the section around it was still organised as though that variable decided every case, so a reader concluded they could suppress escalation by leaving it unset — and then read the non-zero exit as the tool ignoring their configuration.

  The section now says what the variable *does* control (a checker the operator named that the core watched break down) and tabulates the two absences that escalate whatever it says: an adapter that ran and reported only `code: "adapter"` errors, and a core timeout. Both are recorded through `_validator_no_verdict`, which never consults the variable. Every row of that table is pinned by `tests/test_require_validators_core_975.py`.

  This file is the canonical write-up of the three-state contract for this repo and is cited in briefs, so a stale claim in it propagates into behaviour, which is the more expensive half of the harm.

- **A PR or MR wedged in `running` comes back onto the delta board** ([#1025](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1025)). After the first tick a board is a delta, and `running` is correctly not a standing problem — a pipeline in progress is the ordinary state of something that was just pushed. It is also the only state that can persist indefinitely *while being wrong*: a wedged leg, a runner that never picks the job up, a workflow waiting on an approval nobody will give. None of those ever changes, so the snapshot never mismatches and the row is suppressed on every tick after the first. #1022 made that visible in a `NOTE` line; it did not make it actionable.

  The elision is kept and given an expiry. A row whose reported facts have not moved for `stale_running_minutes` (default 240, `0` off, per tier) prints again carrying the state it was observed in and how long it held — `[running 5h unchanged]`, or `[pending 5h unchanged]` for a GitLab pipeline a runner never picked up, since a pipeline that never started is not running. The signal is time since the entry's own facts last changed, stored as `_since` on the snapshot and **excluded from the delta comparison** — a timestamp inside the compared facts would make every row differ every tick, which is the delta collapsing rather than a staleness signal. It is deliberately not time since the last *leg* state change, which is truer and is the one fact a tier does not store; that limit is stated in the docs rather than papered over.

  Three states, not two: an entry with no `_since` — a snapshot written before this landed, or a corrupted one — is **unknown**, never zero, and unknown is not flagged. The next write stamps it, so a run already wedged at upgrade time is first named one threshold later, once, rather than never. `gl-mrs` covers `pending` alongside `running`, since a runner that never picks the job up leaves the pipeline there.

- **The validator cache key now carries a meaning version, so a change to what a cached field *means* misses instead of being replayed** ([#1048](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1048)). The key was `content ‖ name ‖ cmd ‖ tool-fingerprint` — what was analysed, and by which build of the analyser. Nothing in it described how the core interprets the result it reads back, so when the core changed its own reading of a field it owns (a `count` that starts excluding a category, an `ok` that starts implying something narrower, a key that becomes core-only), entries written under the previous meaning verified, sat inside the TTL, and were read under the new rules. Nothing was forged: the bytes were correct when written and wrong when read, which is why nothing in the suite noticed.

  The component is derived rather than declared — a hash of `validators/SCHEMA.md`'s content plus the sorted core-only key set. A hand-bumped revision constant is the guard this repo distrusts on sight, and #1042 is a filed instance of exactly it. Putting the release version here instead is correct and blunt: it cold-invalidates every validator cache for every user on every release, whether or not any meaning moved, which is the trade #1044 refused.

  Hashed by content and not by `stat`, so a fresh clone or a reinstall of the same bytes still hits the cache. An install where `validators/SCHEMA.md` cannot be read gets its own key space rather than defaulting into the readable one — it cannot say which meaning its entries were written under, which is the three-state contract applied to the key itself.

  `tests/test_validator_cache_meaning_version_1048.py` pins the property the issue asked for: an entry written under one meaning is a miss under another.

- **`grep` names the pattern it actually ran when the pattern contains a `:`** ([#1065](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1065)). `grep:re:Checks|failed:PATH` rejoins to the pattern `re:Checks|failed`, and `|` binds looser than concatenation — so the first alternation branch is the literal `re:Checks`, which matches nothing. The op returned three confident results for a question nobody asked, with `scanned 1 files` true and useless: it did look, at someone else's pattern.

  The tokenization is not ambiguous, so nothing is refused; what was missing was the disclosure. A `:` in the pattern is exactly the condition under which the rejoin happened, so that is when the effective pattern is echoed above the report line. A leading `re:` additionally says that `grep` has no such prefix — `between:re:START:END:PATH` is the op that does, which is where the spelling came from.

- **`gl-job` and `gh-job` now word an elision identically, and `gl-job` stopped inventing one** ([#1066](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1066)). `gl-job:N:grep:PATTERN` printed a bare `...` above the log's first line whenever the first hit sat at index 0 — a marker covering nothing at all. That is the same off-by-one the GitHub twin fixed in #1050; the two files are private twins for this renderer and nothing compared them, so the fix sat unmirrored for 640 issues.

  The two ops also described the same concept with two strings. `gl-job` now uses the GitHub wording verbatim:

  ```
  ... (44 lines elided by this op — no error pattern matched them; the log itself is intact)
  ```

  The longer form won because its extra clause is the one being misread: a bare `...` does not distinguish *this op elided lines* from *the log itself was truncated*. The cost is a longer line when a render carries several markers.

  `gl-job:N:fail` also accounts for the lines after its last shown block, so every withheld line is now covered by exactly one marker on both ops. That trailing marker is deliberately not printed in the default view, which follows the blocks with `## Tail (last N lines)` — most of the lines it would declare elided are printed three lines later.

  `tests/test_gl_job_gap_marker_twins_1066.py` compares the twins directly, so the next divergence fails there rather than being found by a reviewer reading git log.

- **`git-commit`'s left-behind receipt accounted for untracked files and then dropped them** ([#1070](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1070)). Two shapes, both reading as "nothing was left". The pasteable `Intentional? If not:` line named only the modified tracked paths, one line below a header that had just counted the untracked ones — pasted, it commits a strict subset and prints its own green tick over that. And when the *only* thing left behind was untracked, the whole block was absent: a brand-new test file, never committed, under `Files committed: N ✓` with no mention of it anywhere, invisible until CI runs a file that is not in the tree.

  The remedy now states that untracked files are not in it, and the untracked-only case prints its own line. Still counted, never listed — the scratch-file-dump decision of #1016 stands, because the fix is disclosure, not a listing.

- **`replace_lines` no longer turns a uniform file mixed in silence** ([#1075](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1075)). The line-endings receipt was asked about the file *before* the write, so the branch that exists for a mixed file could only fire on a file that was already mixed — an all-CRLF file plus an LF replacement block came back mixed with nothing said. Every byte the caller typed was on disk; the receipt was what was wrong.

  The census now describes the bytes on disk, at both call sites, and `replace_lines` reports the endings of the block it actually wrote rather than only the trailing one it had to invent — a block that already ended a line invented nothing, short-circuited the note before the census, and hid the same defect behind the first.

  A write that leaves the file uniform still says nothing, so the marker keeps meaning that something was decided.

- **`gl-job:N:fail` claimed completeness on a job that never failed** ([#1095](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1095)). `All error blocks (N lines matched, no tail truncation)` makes two claims — the selector found everything, nothing was cut — and both are true of the selector and false of the log on a job stopped before it produced a failure. The op already knew: `Status: canceled` is printed from the same value nine lines above. On any status other than `failed` the header now degrades to `Error blocks (N lines matched) — but see below` and the render names `:raw:-80` and `:grep:PATTERN` as the reads that can answer. Keyed on the complement, so a status GitLab adds later lands on the disclosure rather than on the overclaim; the `failed` path is unchanged.

  This is the GitLab half of [#916](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/916), which fixed `gh-job` and said so — the twin drift went one release unpinned. A shared helper was considered and rejected: two of the four disclosure lines are forge-specific, and what drifted was a missing call, which sharing cannot prevent. One test now drives both presets through a non-fitting status instead.

- **`gl-job:N:fail` headlined six lines of teardown as the error blocks** ([#1097](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1097)). The default patterns contain the bare substring `ERROR`, and GitLab ends every failed job with `ERROR: Job failed: exit code N` — one contentless line, enough on its own to produce a block, with the section markers and the cleanup line drawn in around it by `error_context`. On job 7021139 that produced `All error blocks (6 lines matched, no tail truncation)` while a Playwright assertion, the actual cause, never appeared. `:fail` and the default view now look at what the selector anchored on rather than at the window it drew: a selection whose every anchor is boilerplate is reported as the gap it is, with the discounted lines printed rather than hidden. `ERROR: Job failed (system failure)` and the timeout form are deliberately not treated as boilerplate — they do say why the job died.

  Nothing was added to a pattern set to fix this. Adding GitLab's terminal line as a pattern would have flipped every honest refusal into a confident, useless block.

- **Two holes in the cause-marker floor** ([#1097](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1097)). Cause markers run in addition to whatever patterns are in play, so that a per-job `job_patterns` table can narrow one tool's noise without being able to hide the reason a job died. The `…Error: ` marker required at least one word character in front of it — the FQCN shape, not node's or Playwright's, so a line opening `Error: JS errors detected:` fell straight through the floor. And the MySQL client's `ERROR 2026 (HY000):`, the cause on line 108 of job 7125000, matched nothing at all. Both are now markers.

- **The README version badge said 0.14.1, fifteen releases after that was true.** It links to `.claude-plugin/plugin.json`, so the badge and the file it points at disagreed on the front page of the repository. It drifted because it was the one published version site with no test behind it — `plugin.json`, `VERSION` and `pyproject.toml` are each pinned, and none of them has ever drifted. The release sweep could not see it either: that sweep greps for the version being replaced, and a site frozen at a *different* wrong version matches nothing and reads exactly like a site that was already correct. `test_readme_version_badge_matches_code` now pins it to `supertool.VERSION`, and an unmatched badge pattern fails rather than passing, since a regex that found nothing has not checked the badge — it has failed to look at it.

### Security

- **`git-push` rendered the MR/PR target branch unflattened at three sites, and the guard for that certified all three** ([#1038](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1038)). The target of a request is a refname chosen by whoever opened it, and git accepts characters `str.splitlines()` breaks on, so the MR/PR receipt line, the mergeability warning and the stale-base advisory could each carry forged extra lines. `presets/git/push.py` imported `_untrusted` for the first time here. The stale-base advisory is flattened on the **echo only** — `git rev-list` still counts against the real ref, because flattening the value would change which ref is measured and trade a loud forgery for a quiet wrong answer about how stale the base is.

  The scan that exists to catch exactly this passed on the file, and said so, for three independent reasons: `_git_common` normalises `target_branch` / `baseRefName` into a key named `target`, which the scanner's field-name set had never heard of; the read is a subscript where it matched `.get(...)`; and the line is *returned* where it matched `print(...)`. Any one alone was enough. All three are closed, and the taint tracking is per function scope now rather than per file, so widening the set to a common local name adds no false findings — a scanner with false findings is one that gets an allowlist, which is the failure this scan exists to avoid.

  It still misses the stale-base site, and structurally: the value leaves as a call argument rather than a print or a return, and there is no interprocedural tracking. That one was found by review, not by the guard, and the honest limit of the scan is now written down in `docs/presets/git.md`.

- **`gh-pr-merge`'s zero-checks refusal offered a `gh-branch:` command built from the head branch** ([#1038](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1038)). Same attacker-chosen field, and a convenience command rather than a deliverable, so flattening it would only have made it safe and wrong — a command the reader runs on the tool's authority that answers about a branch which does not exist. It is gated on `_refname.ordinary()` now, exactly as this op already gated the head-branch delete command: ordinary names get the op, unordinary ones get the name in full and a sentence saying no command is offered and why. The CONFLICTING refusal's base branch is prose, not a command, and is flattened.

- **A U+2028 in a diff line forged a file boundary in `gh-pr:N:diff`, silently dropping every added line after it** ([#1081](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1081)). `_pr_diff.parse` split the fetched patch with `str.splitlines()`, which breaks on eight separators a unified diff does not recognise. A separator inside an added line produced a fragment at column 0, the `diff --git ` branch opened a new file record from it, and the rest of the file's additions vanished — a phantom second file listed as changed, and the real added lines gone, inside the merge gate's own reading tool. Reachable by any contributor who controls one added line; the likelier victim is a legitimate contributor whose file happens to contain one.

  `presets/_untrusted` now owns both directions of the line question. `visible()` already covered every separator a *consumer* might split on, because anything in that set can forge a line in text we print. The new `split_lines()` is the opposite set — LF, CR and CRLF, the separators a line-oriented protocol actually defines — and it is what `parse()` and `_hunk_signature()` use. It restates `_supertool._LINE_BREAK_PATTERN` because a preset runs with `presets/` on `sys.path` and cannot import the core, and a test pins the two equal so they cannot drift.

  **No disclosure was added to the parse, and that was the decision.** `_untrusted.fence()` already renders the separator as a Control Picture glyph or as `[U+2028]` in the hunk body, so once the line is one line the reader sees the forged header in full, on the line it was smuggled into, named. A second announcement at the parse layer would be noise about something already said. The flattener could not save this on its own — it protects the *display* of a field and the structural parse had already run — but it does finish the job once the parse is right.

  **The `diff --git ` branch was deliberately left ungated.** The issue proposed also refusing a header found mid-hunk; that is wrong. Git emits the next file's header immediately after the previous file's last hunk line with no terminator, so firing mid-hunk is the ordinary multi-file case, and gating it on `hunk is None` would break every diff containing two files. The forgery was the fragment, not the branch, and a regression test pins the two-file case.

  CRLF patches are unaffected: CRLF is a line ending in the conservative definition and is consumed like LF, so no `\r` survives into a hunk body to be disclosed on every rendered line — which a bare `split("\n")` would have caused.
## [0.28.0] - 2026-08-08

### Added

- **`gh-labels` — the repo's label vocabulary, with usage** ([#998](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/998)). Before applying a label you have to know which labels exist, and `gh issue edit --add-label` offers nothing useful when you guess wrong. With no op for it the answer came from a hand-rolled `gh label list --json name -q '.[].name' | grep` pipeline — the surface [#454](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/454) exists because of — paid on the *first* call of every triage or release-planning run, by every fresh agent, forever. The spelling is not portable either: this repo uses `priority-high`, `claude-remember` uses `priority:high` and has no `lane-*` family at all, so an agent carrying one repo's spelling into the other mislabels or silently no-ops.

  The op prints names, descriptions and how many **open** issues carry each, grouped by name prefix. The grouping is declared as inferred, because a prefix is a convention of whoever created the labels rather than a GitHub field, and a family of one is not rendered as a family.

  A count has three states and never two: exact when every open issue was read — pull requests are not counted, since `gh issue list` excludes them, so `0` means "on no open issue" rather than "unused" and a label carried only by open PRs reads zero; a floor rendered `>=N` when the read hit `GH_LABELS_ISSUE_CAP` (default 400), naming the cap and the knob, because a label used only by the four-hundred-and-first issue would otherwise read as unused and "unused" is the input to deleting it; and `?` when the issue list could not be read at all — never `0`, since "I did not look" and "nobody uses it" are opposite facts that print as the same character. An unreadable label list is an error and a nonzero exit rather than an empty list, while a repo with genuinely no labels says that in its own words. The read paginates, so a repo past a hundred labels is not silently truncated into a vocabulary an agent then invents around.

- **`git-status:brief`** ([#1028](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1028)). Drops the local-branch inventory and the last-5-commits log, so the working tree and the MR/PR block — what the op is usually called for — sit near the top instead of below a dozen lines about other branches. That verbosity is what creates the incentive to pipe the op through `tail`, which is a documented mistake here because these ops put the meaning first; a flag removes the incentive rather than the symptom.

  The default is deliberately untouched: somebody depends on the branch list, and changing what a bare `git-status` prints is a behaviour change for every existing caller. Brevity drops only sections that were **answered** — a working tree or stash list that could not be read still renders its `UNKNOWN` marker, and the `git-status INCOMPLETE` footer still appears, because dropping those would be the absence-as-answer defect wearing a flag.

### Fixed

- **Four radar tests asserted on a board that may never have been printed** ([#800](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/800)). `test_no_drift_when_event_and_source_agree`, `test_pruned_state_file_does_not_report_drift`, `test_a_healthy_feed_produces_no_warning` and `test_no_other_scope_note_when_the_only_live_feed_is_this_one` each carried exactly one assertion, and each of those was an absence — no drift mark, no `WARNING`, no other-scope note. Stubbing `render` to return nothing at all left all four green, which is the same shape as the filter that did nothing behind 3758 passing tests: an absence the tool produced, read as an absence in the world.

  Each site now pins the board before reading its content. The pruning case takes two, because its absence had two innocent explanations — a board that never rendered, and a state file that was never read — and only the second is what the test claims, so `1 pruned` is asserted alongside the row.

  No blanket skip, deliberately. A test that declines whenever the board is missing also declines when radar is genuinely broken and prints nothing, which trades the loud failure for the quiet one.

- **`gh-branch`'s green now states what it covers, and names the workflows it does not** ([#846](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/846)). Every source in the leg reconciliation from [#804](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/804)/[#837](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/837) is read off the runs on the commit, so a workflow that produced no run appears on neither side of the arithmetic and cancels out exactly. The tally sums, every term is accounted for, and it describes a strictly smaller universe than the reader believes they are looking at. On the morning of the v0.27.0 tag `Verdict: GREEN — every workflow on dcb574e concluded and every leg passed (19 legs across 3 workflows)` was that sentence: `slow tests` was the fourth, `schedule`-triggered, declared in `.github/workflows`, never dispatched on that commit, and it started four minutes later. A release was tagged on it.

  The workflow directory is now read **at the head SHA** — not off the checkout, which is a different ref — and the names declared there are compared against the names that produced a run. The verdict state is deliberately unchanged: a `paths` filter, a `branches` filter, a job-level `if:`, a workflow disabled in repository settings and a matrix computed at runtime are each a legitimate reason for a declared workflow to produce no run, and every one is either invisible from here or costs more calls than the answer is worth, so concluding a shortfall from an absence would trade a silent miss for a false alarm on a merge gate. What changed is that the clearance states its own scope on the line people read, and the uncovered workflows are named beneath it.

  The clause names the un-covered workflows itself rather than pointing at a block below it. Every surface republishing this verdict quotes lines out of it and not the same ones — `pr_merge._default_branch_report` filtered for four prefixes, so a clause ending "named below" arrived on the merge gate with nothing below it, and #846's own reproduction was a `Verdict:` line read on its own. The names now ride on the sentence, capped with `+N more`, and the merge gate additionally carries the detail block as a blank-line-terminated region. `presets/dashboard/dashboard.py` calls the same new `scope_for` seam, because the dashboard's default-branch line is the board a human reads immediately before tagging and it was publishing the unscoped green that motivated this issue. `presets/watch/tiers/gh_prs.py` makes the same call and is deliberately not touched here.

  Two parses had to agree or the check manufactured the false alarm it exists to refuse. `parse_triggers` stripped a trailing YAML comment and `parse_name` did not, so `name: tests # the matrix` never matched GitHub's `workflowName` of `tests` and a workflow that had run and passed was reported as not covered; a comment now starts at a `#` after whitespace, so `build#3` keeps its hash and a quoted `release # 1` keeps its spaces. A flow sequence spread across lines — `on: [pull_request,` / `push]` — was truncated at the first line, which answered `is_push_triggered` as False and routed a genuinely undispatched **push** workflow into the quiet summary: the loud line this issue exists to print, silenced by the parser. It is read whole now, and an unterminated bracket declines rather than returning the part that was read.

  The enrichment is bounded by construction rather than by a projection: one directory read plus `ceil(12 / 6)` waves at a 10s per-call ceiling is a 30s absolute worst case, against `gh-branch`'s budget raised to 90s and `pr_merge`'s wrapper raised to 120s. A projected-cost refusal was tried first and rejected — it declined a ten-file repository that would in practice have answered in about three seconds, turning a working check into a permanent non-answer.

  The two absences read differently because they are different questions. A workflow with no push-family trigger producing no run on a pushed commit is expected, so those collapse into one summary line — naming them individually on every call is how a disclosure gets tuned out. One that **does** declare a push trigger and produced no run gets its own line, stating that the question is open rather than answering it, and a workflow whose `on:` block could not be parsed is in that same loud group, because "I could not tell" is not "no". The declared set itself has a third state: an unreadable `.github/workflows`, or one wider than the twelve files this op will fetch in a render, prints `UNESTABLISHED` with the reason instead of claiming complete coverage; a genuine 404 is the opposite answer and is treated as one, since a commit with no workflow directory declares nothing there and needs no caveat.

- **`git-commit:::amend` made a commit whose subject was the word `amend`** ([#962](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/962)). There is no amend route in this op, so a word that is unambiguously an *instruction* in git's vocabulary was silently reinterpreted as *content* — and the receipt printed a green tick over it, with nothing distinguishing "you asked to amend and I did" from "you asked to amend and I named a commit after your request". The recovery is `git reset --soft HEAD~1`, which is the git operation people most reliably get wrong under time pressure. `amend` and `--amend`, as the whole message, are now refused before anything is staged: nothing is added, nothing is committed, and the refusal names the gap it is standing in for.

  **It refuses under [#692](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/692)'s contract, after the `Repo:` / `HEAD before:` stamp rather than before it.** Every other refusal path in this op names the repository and branch it refused you in, and this is the one that hands the reader a raw `git commit --amend` to run — so which checkout and which branch is the first thing they need, and the one thing the op knows and they may not. Nothing is staged either way, so the earlier position bought nothing.

  **The refusal is an exact match on the whole message, not a heuristic.** "This message looks like a git subcommand" drifts — the first thing it takes down is `revert the revert`, and every later widening of it is invisible until it refuses somebody's real subject. Exactly `amend` or `--amend`, stripped and lowercased, with nothing else in the message, cannot drift.

  **And it is not a dead end, because `amend` is a legal English word.** The refusal names `SUPERTOOL_ALLOW_LITERAL_AMEND=1` and prints the exact call to re-run with it, using the same off-vocabulary as the co-author trailer beside it. It also names the two raw-git forms (`git commit --amend --no-edit` / `-m 'NEW SUBJECT'`) and says plainly not to amend a commit that is already pushed — *and that this op has no way to tell you whether it was*, which is the reason an amend route was deliberately **not** added here. That route needs its own refusal for published history and is a feature, not something to grow out of the side of a bugfix.

- **`git-commit`'s refusals listed fifteen paths and then offered a remedy naming three of them** ([#963](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/963)). Both `ERROR: nothing staged` and the post-commit left-behind warning printed the full list of candidate files and followed it with `git-commit:::MESSAGE:::` carrying the first three. Pasted, that stages three, commits, and prints a success receipt; nothing in the line says the other twelve were dropped. A remedy that produces the wrong outcome is worse than no remedy, because it carries the authority a refusal lends the tool — it is read by someone who has just been told they were wrong, in the state of mind where they paste what they are handed. The remedy now names **every** path it listed.

  **Past the display cap it names none of them, on purpose.** A refusal that dumps 200 pathspecs into a suggestion is its own defect, and dumping the first 20 of 200 is the original one wearing a bigger number. Over 20 the line becomes a visible placeholder — `git-commit:::MESSAGE:::PATH[:::PATH...]` — with `N paths in all, 20 shown and N-20 not shown — name the ones you mean`. Three states, and the third one declines rather than guessing.

  **The left-behind hint also glued a literal `…` onto its last pathspec.** `…:::f12.txt…` is not a path, so the remedy for "you left files behind" failed on paste even when it was otherwise right.

  **The counts are measured against what was printed, not re-derived from the cap.** `ERROR: nothing staged` prints modified and untracked as two lists capped *independently*, so a tree with 15 of each shows the reader all 30 — and a remedy computing `min(cap, 15 + 15)` announced `20 shown and 10 not shown`, which is false twice over, in the one line whose whole purpose is not to be. Both remedies now take the list that was actually printed plus the true total. Found by the independent review of [#1062](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/pull/1062), in the first version of this fix: the defect survived inside its own repair, under a docstring asserting the guarantee it broke.

  **And a path containing a quote pastes now.** The `:::` suggestion is a single-quoted shell word, so `it's.txt` closed it early and the pasted line was a syntax error; the payload array wrapped each path in raw `"`, so a `"` or a backslash in a filename produced TOML the payload route cannot parse. Paths reach these lines unquoted on purpose — `git status -z` is read precisely so spaces and non-ASCII survive ([#1003](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1003)) — and quotes were the case that was not carried through. Shell-quoting is unconditional rather than `shlex.quote`, which leaves ordinary words bare and would have re-written every line that was already correct.

  **The third `_colon_remedy` call site was still uncapped, and that one had never been capped at all.** The comma-guess remedy behind `git add failed` — `A ',' above is not a separator here. Did you mean:` — builds its list by splitting the caller's own argument on `,`, which is unbounded: one argument can hold any number of commas. When the remedy grew its `shown`/`total` pair, the two sites named in the review were updated and this one kept calling it with a single argument, which defaults `total` to `len(shown)` and makes the placeholder branch unreachable there by construction. Twenty-five guessed pathspecs went into one pasteable line with nothing saying anything had been left out, three lines below the docstring asserting that cannot happen. It now takes the same cap and the same placeholder as the other two, and past the cap it lists the guesses as well, because the count line claims what the reader saw and nothing above it had shown them. Found by the second independent review of [#1062](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/pull/1062) — the same shape as the first finding, one call site along.

  **The `:`-split refusal quoted its own payload example by hand, and still does not.** Its `paths = [...]` array wrapped each path in a raw `"` — the exact defect fixed above for the other payload example, in a sibling function that predates it, so a path holding a `"` produced TOML the payload route cannot parse and a path holding a backslash produced TOML that parses as a *different* path. `src\new\tab.py` is the quiet half of that: both escapes are legal TOML, so the payload loads without complaint and would stage something the reader never named — which is a Windows path shape, not an exotic one. Its `./supertool '...'` line was hand-quoted too, and the subject it reconstructs is the caller's own prose, so an ordinary apostrophe closed the shell word early. Both now go through the helpers rather than through `%s`.

  **The two defects the issue actually reported do not exist and did not when it was filed.** The `:`-split refusal's `@-` example has emitted a separate `paths = [...]` key since it landed in [#751](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/751)/#771, never a file list inside `message`; and its single-colon suggestion commits the intended subject and stages the intended path, because `:::` is the outer separator and survives the tokenizer. Both are now pinned end-to-end — the second by executing the suggested line and asserting the resulting subject — so the claim is settled by a test rather than by reading.

- `gh-prs`, `gh-issues` and `gl-mrs` refuse a filter key given with no value (`author=`, `label=`) instead of dropping it and answering with a wider board ([#974](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/974)). The key is known, so [#939](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/939)'s unrecognised-token refusal never fired; the query was then built with `if not val: continue`, so the flag vanished. On `gh-prs` that widened the board rather than merely un-narrowing it — the role-key test `any(k in filters for k in ("author", "assignee", "reviewer"))` is satisfied by an empty value, so `--author @me` was suppressed too and `gh-prs:author=` returned everyone's PRs while the scope line still named a filter. The refusal names the key, says the value is missing rather than misspelled, and states the widening.
- The `gh-prs` radar tier and the `gitlab-mr-feed` poller inherit the same refusal, because the check lives in the tokenizer they share. The poller's existing `unknown` guard returns `None` — "population not established" — so an empty scope no longer spawns a watcher per stranger's MR, and does not crash the long-lived process either.

- **`git-commit`'s `nothing staged` refusal pointed only at the route the caller had already rejected** ([#986](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/986)). A caller on `git-commit:@-` is usually there *because* their message will not survive `:`-tokenization, and being answered with `git-commit:::MESSAGE:::PATHS` reads as "you used the wrong form" when the accurate statement is "here is how this form stages". The refusal now names both routes, and spells the payload one out with its `paths` key pre-filled from the list it just printed.

- **A pathspec that failed to add never said what the separator was** ([#986](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/986)). `git add` answering `fatal: pathspec 'a.txt,b.txt' did not match any files` tells a caller who guessed `,` only that their guess was wrong. The failure now states `Paths are separated by ':::' — not by commas, not by spaces`, and where a comma-joined token is **not** something git already knows, offers the split form as a question (`A ',' above is not a separator here. Did you mean:`). A token git recognises is never taken apart, because `a,b.txt` is a legal filename and re-splitting it would trade a loud failure for a quiet wrong one.

  **The issue's headline claim — that `git-commit:@payload` has no way to stage — is false, and this is its third airing.** The `paths` key has worked since [#340](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/pull/340), the field registry is derived from the op's own `syntax` string, and `tests/test_git_commit_payload_route.py` has pinned the committed bytes since [#415](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/pull/415). [#400](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/400) claimed it, [#1003](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1003) claimed it again, and both were already refuted in the tree when they were written. A further pin asserts the staged file list rather than only the message, so "it cannot stage" is now false against a test that reads on staging specifically. What made the claim keep coming back is the `nothing staged` remedy above: two agents reached the payload route, got an error naming the *other* route, and concluded the key did not exist.

- **`git-status` omitted its working-tree and stash sections entirely when git did not answer** ([#1002](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1002)). Both sections were guarded by `returncode == 0` with no other arm, so a held index lock, a corrupt index or a `git status` that outran its 5s budget produced a report with nothing at all where the working tree belongs. The only disclosure was the `git-status INCOMPLETE` footer at the very bottom, which says that *some* section is missing without saying which — and it arrives after the reader has already scrolled past an empty space that is byte-for-byte the render of a clean tree. Each section now has three states rather than two: `## Working tree: clean`, `## Working tree (N changes)`, and `## Working tree: UNKNOWN — …` quoting git's own words at the place the section belongs. The footer is kept as well: the marker is where the eye is, the footer is what survives a `| tail` and what a script greps. A run in which every call answered gains neither.

  **The issue as filed does not reproduce, and that is on the record in the tests.** It reported the section vanishing in a linked worktree with six dirty files. It does not: with a `git status` that answers, the files are listed — in a linked worktree, on a branch with no commits of its own, in a repository with fifty-nine other branches, all of which were tried. `test_a_dirty_tree_still_lists_its_files` pins that render so the report is not re-filed a third time. What is real is the half the issue's own "fix shape" paragraph asked for, and that half was reachable and silent.

- **`git-commit`'s refusals named the fault and not the remedy** ([#1003](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1003)). A payload that would not load — the plain message file that is the obvious thing to write, a mistyped key, an `@` reference left in the colon slot — produced either a bare TOML line-and-column or `takes the @reference as the only argument`. Three agents in one evening met one of those, each guessed `message` and `paths` from scratch, and one mangled its own commit message past the shell instead, which is permanent in that history. Every such refusal now ends with the keys the op actually wants and a call that would work, derived from the same registry that drives the `@payload` route, so it cannot drift into describing a shape the loader would reject. This applies to every op with an `@payload` route, not only `git-commit`.

  **A refusal on an unstaged tree now names what is unstaged.** `ERROR: nothing staged.` was correct and unhelpful: the op had just read the working tree, and the caller's only remaining move was a raw `git add -A` — the command this op exists to replace, and one the repo's own hook flags. The refusal stays, because committing files the caller did not name is not a default anyone wants; it now lists the modified tracked and the untracked paths separately and hands back a `git-commit:::MESSAGE:::…` call naming the first few. Three states again: a genuinely clean tree says it is clean, and a `git status` that did not answer says *that*, rather than printing two empty lists that read as clean.

  **The first claim in the report is false and is pinned as false.** `git-commit` has had an `@payload` route since [#340](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/340); [#400](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/400) reported it missing once already. What was missing was any way to find out it existed from the error you were looking at, which is what the change above is.

- **Printed remedies prescribed `./supertool`, which does not resolve where they are printed** ([#1012](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1012)). `./supertool` is a gitignored symlink: absent in a linked worktree, and inside a `claude-supertool` worktree actively wrong, because the global `supertool` on `PATH` then resolves to a different checkout and runs *that* tree's core against *this* tree's presets — the mixed tree [#678](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/678) discloses after the fact. `git-conflicts` closed its output with `Resolve: ./supertool 'git-resolve:::ours:::PATH'` and `git-push`'s watch advisory with `Run it yourself: ./supertool 'watch:…'`, both at the moment the reader is mid-conflict or mid-recovery and least likely to second-guess a copy-pasteable command. A rule in a docs page is consulted; a command in an error is pasted.

  `push.py` already carried the answer for one line of its own output, from [#879](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/879). It is now shared as `_git_common.st_hint` and applied to every printed follow-up in `git-conflicts` and `git-push`: `./supertool 'op'` where the wrapper exists and is executable, `python3 supertool.py 'op'` where only the entry point does, and a stated `(no runnable supertool found in <dir> …)` where neither does — a hint invented for an install nobody found is a remedy that cannot be run, which is the same defect one layer down.

  Printed `./supertool` follow-ups remain in `git-merge`, `git-resolve`, `git-diverge`, `git-commit` and in the `gitlab/`, `github/` and `watch/` presets. They are the same class and the helper is now in place for them, but they are outside what this issue names.

- **A conflicted `_supertool.py` took the whole tool down with a traceback** ([#1015](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1015)). A rebase that touches the core leaves it holding live `<<<<<<<` markers, which is not valid Python, and `supertool.py` is a thin entry point that imports it ([#931](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/931)) — so the failure was a `SyntaxError` pointing at a conflict marker, and it took out **every** op rather than one, for exactly as long as the conflict existed. A traceback there reads as *the tool is broken* rather than *the tool cannot describe this state*, and what it cost in practice was a fall back to `git diff --name-only --diff-filter=U` plus `awk` on the marker range: the hand-rolled resolver `git-conflicts` exists to replace. The entry point now refuses by name — which file, which lines carry markers, that no op can run, and that this is not a report of what is conflicted — and prints a recovery that does not go through the module under conflict, because `presets/git/conflicts.py` and `presets/git/resolve.py` import only `_git_common` and `_env` and run standalone against the tree you are standing in. A syntax error with no markers in it keeps its own diagnosis rather than being reported as a merge conflict.

  **The issue as filed is wrong about the mechanism, and the title is narrower than the defect.** It reports `git-conflicts` "parsing its own conflict markers as Python". It does not parse anything: `_all_conflict_blocks` reads the file as text and already survives a file it cannot read. The crash is at `import _supertool`, before dispatch — which the issue's own comment worked out independently, and which is why the fix is in the entry point and not in the preset.

- **`git-commit` printed a green tick over a partial commit** ([#1016](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1016)). `Files committed: 5` under a `✓` does not distinguish "these five are what you asked for" from "these five are all that made it", and the tick above actively argues nothing was left out. The failure mode is a branch pushed and a PR opened believing the change is complete, silent until CI fails on a half-change — or worse, passes, because the files left behind were the tests. The op now names the modified tracked files that are still uncommitted after the commit lands, with a `git-commit:::MESSAGE:::…` call for them. Named rather than counted: "2 not included" costs a second call to find out which, and a reader who has to make that call usually does not.

  **Untracked files are counted and not listed, on purpose.** Nearly every worktree carries some, and a list of them under every commit is a list nobody reads on the commit that needed it. A *modified tracked* file is the one that means "you edited this and did not commit it". A run that left nothing behind prints none of this at all.

  **And the check itself has three states.** A `git status` that does not answer renders `⚠ Left-behind check SKIPPED` with git's own reason, never silence — silence there is byte-for-byte the receipt of a complete commit, which is the same defect one layer along. The scan reads `--porcelain=v1 -z` rather than the newline-terminated form, because git *quotes* a path containing a space or a non-ASCII byte in the latter, and a quoted path pasted back into a `git-commit:::MSG:::PATH` call is not that path; the `-z` stream also lets a rename's second record be consumed rather than parsed as a status line of its own, which would have invented a modified file out of a path that no longer exists.

- **`radar` no longer reports a PR that left the filter as one that stopped being open** ([#1024](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1024)). Both delta tiers computed the departed set as "in the previous snapshot, not in the live population", and the live population is filter-scoped — `author=@me` by default. Merged, closed unmerged, reassigned to somebody else, stripped of the label the filter selects on, and "the filter itself changed between runs" all arrived as the same absence and all rendered as `N no longer open`. Three of those five are still open and still need work, so a maintainer who read that line and stopped tracking the PR had been told the opposite of the truth by a footer doing exactly what it was written to do.

  The board now says what it can support: `N left this board` in the footer, and a `radar: NOTE` naming the departed identifiers, listing the histories it cannot tell apart, and giving the op that answers which — `gh-pr:<number>` or `gl-mr:<iid>`. Deciding merged-versus-reassigned from the board would cost one live lookup per departure, and that lookup can itself fail, so it would need this three-state sentence anyway; the sentence alone costs no call and cannot be wrong. Absent departures the line is absent, so its absence stays the positive claim.

  On the GitLab tier the departed set is computed against the whole open population rather than the board, so an excluded MR is never counted as departed — an exclusion removes a row, not a member, and counting one would report the operator's own standing decision back to them as a merge.

  **On a full page the board declines the word "departure" entirely.** The live fetch is a single page with no pagination loop, so an entry pushed past the page limit by newer ones is missing from the live population while being open and still matching the filter — a fourth history none of the three offered covers. Calling it a departure sends the reader to a lookup that shows it open, from which the only remaining conclusion is also wrong. When the population reaches the page size the footer reads `N off this page` and the disclosure becomes a WARNING naming the page limit alongside the other three. A departure also makes the tier report unhealthy, because `healthy` feeds `quiet_when_healthy`, which drops the tier's whole output — and a departure-only tick is elided rows plus one summary line, so a healthy verdict there suppressed the notice completely.

  A tick whose only event is a departure now reads `radar: no rows changed` rather than `radar: no change`. The departed entry has no row left to print and every survivor legitimately elides, so the summary line used to announce that nothing had happened on the one tick where something fell off the board. The named identifiers are sorted, too: the cap at twelve makes which ones get named load-bearing, and the snapshot is written in the order the upstream page returned.

- **`git-status` reported a cleanly rebased branch as `ahead 5, behind 1`, which reads as lost work** ([#1028](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1028)). The count is arithmetically true and its ordinary meaning is the opposite of what happened: `ahead N, behind M` is the render for two histories that have genuinely diverged, while after a rebase nothing was lost and the remote merely holds the pre-rebase originals of commits the branch already carries. Two agents stopped mid-task on separate lanes the same night to work out which of the two they were in. Class: a reader acting reasonably concludes "I have diverged and may lose commits" where the truth is "I am ahead cleanly and the remote is behind".

  The count is **not** suppressed — that would trade a confusing render for a quiet one, and lose the fact that the remote differs at all. A two-sided count now carries a `Diverged:` line saying which kind it is, decided by `git rev-list --count --right-only --cherry-pick HEAD...@{upstream}`: `--cherry-pick` drops every upstream commit whose patch already exists on this side, so what remains is exactly the commits the remote has and this branch does not. Zero is a rebase or any other replay (`REBASED — … nothing is lost and the remote is stale`, with the force-with-lease push); non-zero names how many remote commits are genuinely absent from this history and says a force push would discard them. A check that did not answer renders as neither verdict, in the `UNKNOWN — … did not answer` vocabulary [#1002](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1002) established for this file. The extra call is made only when both sides are non-zero, which is the only ambiguous render.

  An unrecognised mode is now reported instead of silently rendering the default ([#647](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/647)'s class): `git-status:breif` used to look exactly like the render you asked for.

- **`tests/test_op_workspace.py` failed ~10 of its 16 tests on one full-suite run and passed on the next, and passed in isolation either way** ([#1030](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1030)). `_load_config()` parses the optional `mcp` block into the module-level `_mcp_specs` dict **in place**, and nothing ever cleared it. `tests/conftest.py` hands every test `_CONFIG = {}` and restores `_CONFIG`, `_CONFIG_CHECKED` and `_CONFIG_PATH` around it, but `_mcp_specs` — derived from exactly that config — was not in `RESET_GLOBALS`, so one test that forces a real config load left this repository's own `py-lsp` spec (`match: "*.py"`, tools `refs`/`diag`) in the table for the rest of that xdist worker's life. `tests/test_at_file_route.py::TestPayloadRoutePin` is that test, legitimately: it chdirs to the repo root and rebuilds the `@payload` registry, which is the only way to pin the shipped routes. Ten of the sixteen `op_workspace` tests drive a `.py` file, so every one of them then routed References and Diagnostics to an LSP no test had configured. `--dist load` decides run by run whether the leaker and the victims share a worker, which is the whole of the intermittency — nothing about the file itself is order-sensitive. Reproduced deterministically as `pytest -n0 tests/test_at_file_route.py::TestPayloadRoutePin tests/test_op_workspace.py`: 10 failed, 7 passed.

  **The guard that exists to catch precisely this could not see it.** `test_every_mutable_global_in_supertool_py_is_reset_or_deliberately_exempt` ([#397](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/397)) selected candidates with `name == name.upper()`, so the one lowercase mutable global in `supertool.py` was never a candidate: the assertion passed on an empty difference and read as "every mutable global is accounted for" while the only unaccounted one was structurally invisible to it. Case is not the contract, mutability is; the filter is `not name.startswith("__")` now, and `_mcp_specs` is per-run scratch like the other config-derived state.

  **A second, product-side defect on the same code path.** `op_workspace`'s References renderer split each hit with `str.index(":")` twice, which is safe only for the heuristic grep path that produces `file:line:content` by construction. An MCP `refs` server answers in its own shape — cclsp, the server this repository's own `.supertool.json` routes `*.py` to, leads with a prose header and bullet lines — so the first line carries one colon and no second one and `ValueError` escaped `op_workspace` entirely, reaching the user as `ERROR: argument parsing: substring not found`, which names neither the argument nor the problem. That is what turned the leak from a wrong References section into ten hard errors. A line that is not `file:line:content` is now rendered as the server wrote it: dropping it would trade a loud failure for a quiet one, and inventing a line number for it would be worse than either. Reachable in production by anyone who configures `mcp.tools.refs`, independently of the test leak.

- **`cargo-check` asks cargo which file a diagnostic names instead of guessing from the path's tail** ([#1045](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1045)). A package at the workspace root is printed by cargo as `src/lib.rs`, and every workspace member's absolute path ends with those same two segments — so the root package's pre-existing error was charged to the member file under validation, keeping its real rustc code, and `rollback_on_fail` reverted a correct edit over it. Raising the two-segment floor from [#1037](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1037) again could not have fixed it: the two strings are identical and what tells them apart is the workspace layout, not the path.

  So the layout is read rather than inferred. Cargo prints a relative diagnostic path relative to the **workspace root** — to that root whichever directory it was invoked from — and prints anything outside that root as an absolute path; `cargo metadata --no-deps` reports the root without resolving the dependency graph, so it touches no network and pays for no build, and it is only called when a run has diagnostics to attribute. Anchoring the relative case to that root resolves every diagnostic path to exactly one absolute file and the comparison becomes equality, with no suffix, no floor, and no tie to break. The two-segment floor's accepted cost goes with it: `build.rs` and other files at a crate root were always non-verdicts and are now simply decidable.

  Attribution has three outcomes, and the new one is the point. "This file" is a finding; "another file" is reported in full by its own path, unplaced, as before; and **"the workspace root could not be read" is now a distinct non-verdict that says so** — naming the path cargo gave and why the root is missing, rather than claiming the diagnostic belongs to some other file. A relative path with no root under it is a real path in every package in the tree, so declining to name one is the only honest answer. Every way the lookup can fail is a reason rather than a crash, including a spawn failure that only Windows raises.

- **`edit`, `replace` and `replace_lines` rewrote every line ending in a CRLF file to LF** ([#1049](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1049)). All three opened the target without `newline=""`, so Python's universal-newline translation flattened every `\r\n` to `\n` in memory and `_atomic_write` put those bytes back. A one-line edit produced a whole-file diff, under a receipt that named a single line — true about intent, false about effect. `op_append` has opened with `newline=""` since it was written, with a comment stating the contract; the other three never adopted it. Nothing on POSIX authors a CRLF file in the ordinary course of work, so no local run and no macOS or ubuntu CI leg ever exercised it.

  **The obvious fix on its own would have swapped one bug for another.** A caller composing a payload types LF, so an `old` string describing lines of a CRLF file arrives LF-terminated and, once the read stops flattening the file, matches nothing. Preserving endings alone would turn a silently damaging edit into a hard `old string not found`. The literal text is therefore matched first — a file that matches exactly is never reinterpreted — and only on a miss are the re-terminated forms tried, with the replacement re-terminated to match. The receipt says which convention was used.

  **Mixed-ending files have no single right answer, so `replace_lines` does not invent one.** Lines the op did not name come back out byte for byte, each keeping its own ending. The block it writes takes the ending of the line it replaces, or for an insert the line above it — not a file-wide majority vote, because on a mixed file a majority rewrites the caller's own line to the other convention, which is the same silent normalisation one line wide. Whenever the file is not plain LF the receipt says so, including the census: `line endings: file is mixed (2 CRLF / 2 LF / 0 CR) — every line this op did not touch kept its own`.

  Every test in the new suite asserts **bytes**. A text post-condition decodes `\r\n` to `\n` and would call a CRLF file equal to an LF one, so the same green would sit over a write of the wrong bytes.

  **Not fixed here, and deliberately: `vim`.** It reads with the same gap, but it is a line-oriented editor whose every motion, `o`/`O` and `dd` assumes `\n`; adding `newline=""` under that without reworking the model would trade whole-file normalisation for scattered mixed endings, which is harder to see and harder to review. Filed rather than half-done.

- **`edit` spliced LF into a CRLF file, and two other receipts miscounted what they had done** ([#1049](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1049)). Review of the three passes above, each finding checked against `master` rather than against the previous commit on the branch — all three are regressions this work introduced, and all three were invisible while the read still flattened every file to LF before this code saw it.

  `edit` re-terminated the text you supplied only when your `old` had needed re-terminating to match. A single-line `old` matches literally, so a multi-line `new` went in verbatim and left a CRLF file mixed, silently. The bug is the inconsistency more than the silence: `old` spanning a line boundary and `old` on one line produced *different bytes for the same intent*, decided by an accident of how much text you happened to quote. `edit` now matches the convention of any file that uses one throughout and discloses it, exactly as the multi-line path already did; a mixed file still takes your bytes as typed, and says so.

  The other two are receipts describing work correctly done. On a CR-only file every line number came out as 1, because the arithmetic counted `\n` characters and a CR-only file has none — correct only while the read was translating `\r` to `\n` first. And `replace_lines` stripped `\n` but not `\r` from its preview, shipping a stray carriage return into the terminal on every context line of a CRLF file.

- **The first cut of the CRLF fix left `replace` reporting replacements it had not written** ([#1049](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1049)). `op_replace` reads the file twice — once to count matches, once to write — and only the write pass was given `newline=""`. On a CRLF file the counting pass saw universal-newline-translated content and found an LF `old`; the write pass saw the real bytes and found nothing. `content.replace()` returned the file unchanged, `_atomic_write` wrote it back, and the receipt printed the *counting* pass's number: `(2 replacements in 2 files)` over two files that had not moved a byte. A fix for an absence-read-as-presence defect had produced a fresh one, in the same op, one function apart.

  Both passes read the same way now, and the convention is resolved once during the scan and carried to the write rather than re-derived. The receipt's count comes from the bytes about to be written, never from the scan. A file that matched during the scan and no longer matches when the write reads it back — it changed on disk in between — is named as **not modified** rather than counted or silently dropped.

  **`replace_lines` was re-terminating content the caller had written deliberately.** Giving the inserted block the file's local ending is right for a newline the op has to *invent*, and wrong for the endings inside a block the caller typed: `test_mixed_line_endings_preserved` has stated that contract since before this issue, and the first cut broke it. Caller content now passes through verbatim, mixed endings and all; the local convention is consulted only for the trailing newline, and only when the block does not end a line at all.

  **And the line-ending receipt fired where nothing had been decided.** A clean edit of a uniform CRLF file, matched literally, every byte outside the match unchanged — and the receipt said so at length, under the `↳` marker that means "something here needs your attention". On Windows every file is CRLF, so that note appeared on every edit ever made; it also collided with `test_successful_edit_has_no_diagnostic`, which reads `↳` as "a diagnostic was emitted" and was right to. The note is now emitted only where the ending used had more than one defensible answer: a mixed file, or the caller's own text re-terminated to match. Silence is the correct receipt for a choice that was never made.

  **All four were caught only by the Windows legs, and only because those fixtures use `write_text`.** `Path.write_text` translates `\n` to `os.linesep`, so every such fixture is CRLF on Windows and LF everywhere else — which is why the tests are worth leaving exactly as they are. Converting them to `write_bytes` would make them deterministic and would delete the only CRLF coverage in the suite. The new pins alongside them write bytes explicitly, so the same ground is covered on every platform without giving up the accidental coverage the matrix provides.

- **`replace` re-terminated your line endings and never said so** ([#1049](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1049)). `_newline_note` states the invariant in its own docstring — *"re-writing the caller's own endings is always disclosed"* — and `edit` and `replace_lines` call it. `replace` did the same `_newline_variants` re-termination and called nothing: a multi-line `replace` against a CRLF file rewrote the block you typed from LF to CRLF, correctly, under a receipt that mentioned only a count. The bytes were right; the invariant was stated and not held, which is the same absence-read-as-presence shape the rest of this issue is about, pointed at the receipt instead of at the write.

  The disclosure is not `edit`'s line copied across. `replace` is multi-file and the answer differs per file — one CRLF file re-terminated and one LF file matched literally, in the same call — so a single summary sentence would be true of the run and false of every file it did not apply to. The convention is marked on each file's own line (`src/win.rs (1) [CRLF]`) and the explanation is said once beneath the list. A file that matched byte for byte carries no marker, and a call where nothing was re-terminated prints no line at all: the narrowing that removed this note from every clean edit of a uniform CRLF file is preserved, because on Windows every file is CRLF and a disclosure that fires on every call is noise before it is information.

- **`gh-job:N:fail` says when it elided something and how much, and the count that settles legs-versus-tests is printed** ([#1050](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1050)). The gap between two matched error blocks was rendered as a bare `...`, which is the *log's* own vocabulary — a truncated `AssertionError: ...`, a pytest diff elision, a `gh` field cut short. Reading PR #1047's Windows red, that `...` covered a `[validators]` block whose single line, `fake : ok (no new errors)`, was the entire discriminator between three candidate causes; it read as part of the assertion above it, was never looked for, and recovering it cost a second call with `:grep:`. The op was not truncating at the end — it said `no tail truncation` — it was eliding the middle, which is the harder case to notice because the output looks complete. Markers now name the cause and the size, and every withheld line, including any past the last shown block, is accounted for by exactly one of them.

  Two more defects were on the same lines. A phantom marker was emitted before the very first block whenever the first match was line 1, claiming an elision over nothing at all — an absence the op invented, printed directly above the log's own first line. The same off-by-one sat in `:grep:`.

  The trailing marker is `:fail`-only. The default `gh-job:N` render prints these same sections and then `## Tail (last 80 lines)` immediately below it, which contains most of the lines a trailing marker would have declared elided — on a 500-line log whose last match sits at 400 it claimed ninety-nine were not shown and eighty of them appeared three lines later. Only a render that prints blocks and nothing else can truthfully make that claim.

  The summary reported is the **failing** one, not the last one. A job running pytest twice — a second suite step, a `--lf` retry, tox — writes two, and taking the trailing one turned `6 failed, 100 passed` followed by `7 passed` into `Suite: 7 passed` on a job with six real failures, which is this issue's own defect reintroduced by its own fix. The last invocation reporting a failure or an error wins, only when none did does the trailing one stand, and the count is disclosed when there is more than one. The match is anchored at column 0 so a nested run reprinted indented under `-s` or inside captured subprocess output cannot displace the job's own, and a `2 warnings in 0.30s` summary counts zero tests and is declined rather than printed under a header reading "these count TESTS".

  Separately, `checks: 20 total: 16 passed, 4 failed` counts **legs** and nothing said so. Read as four *tests*, with three names visible past the elision, it looked like some legs passed where their structurally identical twins failed — which points at ordering or shared state, a completely different investigation. It was six-of-six uniform across all four legs, which points at the fixture, and the agent handed that diagnosis had to correct the premise before it could work. `gh-job` now prints the job's own terminal summary as a `Suite:` line — the only number in the render that counts tests — and `gh-pr` adds a one-line unit note under a tally that has something in the failed bucket, and only then. A log that states no summary prints no line rather than a zero. The line is matched by its shape rather than by pytest's `=` rule, because GitHub Actions is not a tty and writes none: a first version required the fences, passed against a fixture built from the issue's quote, and would have matched nothing in any real CI log.

- **`read:PATH:::grep=PATTERN` answered `(no lines matching 'PATTERN')` about a file that contains it** ([#1052](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1052)). The filter was never the problem — the window was. `op_read` applied the `read.max_lines` default (300) before handing off to `render_file`, and the filter ran inside that window, so on a 351-line file the inline filter looked at lines 1-300, never saw the match at line 328, and reported its zero in the tool's own voice. The standalone `grep` op found the same string in the same file in the same session, which is the only reason it was caught. It cost a wrong step: the zero was read as "this checkout does not have that test" and the next few minutes went into branch divergence.

  A filter is not a window. `read.max_lines` bounds how much a read **emits**; it never had a reason to bound how much a filter **searches**, and a filtered read emits only the lines that matched. `grep=` with no explicit LIMIT now searches the whole file — the 20 KB byte cap still bounds the output, and still discloses itself when it fires.

  **And the zero has three states now, not two.** Whenever the scan did not cover the file — an explicit `read:PATH:0:10:grep=X`, an offset, a byte cap — the answer names the range it searched and the number of lines it did not: `(no lines matching 'X' in lines 1-10 of 340 — the other 330 lines were NOT searched, so this is not an answer about the whole file)`. A filter that matched something but stopped short says so too. The sibling `grep` op's zero has always carried `scanned N files`, which is what makes it trustworthy; this one carried nothing at all.

  **A third state on the same code path, one layer up.** A `grep=` value that does not compile as a regex falls back to `re.escape` and a literal search. The fallback is right — an unusable pattern should not fail a read — but it was silent, so a rejected pattern's zero was spelled exactly like a real absence. The receipt now names the `re.error` and says the search was literal.

- **The new three-state zero printed a backwards line range** ([#1052](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1052)). Reading with a `grep=` filter at an offset past the end of the file produced `no lines matching 'x' in lines 1001-1000` — a span whose start is after its end. The counter naming the scanned range only advances inside the scan loop, and when the offset is past EOF that loop never runs. The count of unsearched lines was right all along; the range naming them was not, and a disclosure that reads as nonsense is not read at all.
