That case now says the offset is past the end and that nothing was searched.

- **A filtered read that matched and then hit the byte cap never said the rest of the file was unread, and every `grep=` note arrived below the content it qualified** ([#1052](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1052)). Two review findings on the fix above.

  The three-state zero was guarded on the scan *not* having been truncated, so the combination that matters most — a large file, matches found, output stopped at the 20 KB cap — fell through to the older wording: `truncated at 20000 bytes — showed lines 1-92 of 400 (308 more lines)`. The byte cap breaks the scan loop, not just the emission, so those 308 lines were never looked at; `(308 more lines)` can only be read as 308 lines that did not match. That is the same absence-read-as-presence this issue was filed to remove, left standing in exactly the case where the file is big enough for it to cost something. The capped scan now names the cap, the range it did search, the count it did not, and where to resume.

  All of these notes are also now rendered directly under the count header rather than appended after the matches, which is where the same disclosure for windowed reads has been since [#955](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/pull/955): a correction that arrives after the reader has already paid for the wrong window is barely a correction.

- **`vim` destroyed every non-UTF-8 byte in the file, including bytes the edit never touched** ([#1059](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1059)). `op_vim` read with `errors="replace"`, which turns each such byte into U+FFFD in memory, and `vim` writes the whole buffer back. A single `cc` on line 1 therefore rewrote a stray latin-1 byte on line 40 — unrecoverably, with nothing in the receipt saying anything had happened. `edit`, `replace` and `replace_lines` have read with `surrogateescape` since #1049 and carry a comment saying exactly why; `vim` was the one that did not get it. Now it does.

  **Three reads, not one.** The entry read was the obvious one. `:r FILE` splices a *second* file's text into the buffer that gets written, and `:norm` re-reads the file from disk twice per range. All three had the same `errors="replace"`, so fixing only the entry read would have left two live paths to the same destruction.

  **Refusing to open such files was considered and rejected.** That trades destruction for an outage on files that work today — the loud-for-quiet trade pointed the wrong way.

  **The receipt had to move with it.** A `surrogateescape` buffer holds lone surrogates, and receipts echo the buffer back as context lines and a diff hunk. No UTF-8 stream can encode a lone surrogate, so the fixed op wrote the correct bytes and then died with `UnicodeEncodeError` on the way to saying so: a traceback, no receipt, over a file that had changed. `edit`, `replace` and `replace_lines` have carried that same latent crash since #1049 and nobody had hit it. Sanitised once at `dispatch`, the outermost frame every consumer shares — display only, U+FFFD on screen, exact bytes on disk.

  **Still no `newline=""` on `vim`, deliberately** (#1049's reasoning, unchanged): every motion, `o`/`O` and `dd` assumes `\n`, so adding it underneath converts one whole-file normalisation into scattered mixed endings. That is a separate design job, and the byte destruction was not blocked by it. Shipping half is worth more than waiting for the whole.

- **`read` and `replace_lines` disagreed about what a line is, so editing line N could edit a different line** ([#1060](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1060)). `render_file` split the file's bytes; `op_replace_lines` split the decoded string, and `str.splitlines()` additionally breaks on U+000B, U+000C, U+001C, U+001D, U+001E, U+0085, U+2028 and U+2029. A file holding any of those had two line numberings, with the ops that read on one side and the ops that write on the other: you read your target at line N, asked for line N, and the write landed elsewhere. The edit succeeded, the receipt named line N, and the content at line N was not what the reader saw there. The overwritten content is gone.

  **One function owns the definition and every line-numbering op uses it.** Two independent splits is how this happened; fixing one side to match the other by hand would have left the next author free to reintroduce it. `read`, `replace_lines`, and the receipt line-lists of `edit` and `append` all route through it.

  **The definition chosen is the conservative one — LF, CR and CRLF only.** That is what a caller counting lines in an editor, in `wc -l`, or in any line-oriented CLI will have counted; `str.splitlines()` is arguably more correct about Unicode and is definitely more surprising. This is a contract change for `replace_lines` on files containing those eight characters, stated here rather than picked by whichever function was easier to edit.

  **Where the two definitions differ, the read discloses it** instead of silently picking one: a file holding any of the eight gets a `note:` line under its header naming which, and saying that other tools will number it differently while supertool's own reads and line-addressed edits agree with each other. An ordinary file says nothing. The disclosure also survives delegation to `rtk`, which renders the body but knows nothing about supertool's contract.

- `gh-issues:iids` and `gh-prs:iids` now disclose the page cap. Both return before any footer is built, so the bare number list — the shape whose output becomes another tool's input — was the one consumer told nothing, and a truncated list was byte-identical to a complete one. The note rides on **stdout** as a leading `#` comment rather than on stderr, because `_run_custom_op` returns a successful op's stdout and drops its stderr (#654): a note there is a note nobody receives. The number list stays parseable and the exit code stays 0.
- `gh-issues` client-side flags now name what they removed. `gh-issues:external` over an all-internal queue printed `No issues match.` and `0 issue(s)` — true about the filter, read as a statement about the queue. The footer carries `external excluded 2 of 2 fetched`, and the same for `stale` and `nomilestone`. Chained flags all measure against the fetch: `gh-issues:external,stale` reports both counts `of N fetched` where N is what came back, not what survived the previous filter — the same invariant the page-cap note holds (#864).
- Not reproduced, and worth recording: the issue reports `gh-issues:per=100,iids` returning 48 of 78 open issues. It returns all 78, from a branch worktree and from the live clone, and the rendered board's `capped at --limit` footer has been in `_footer` since the op was born.

- `gh-pr:N:diff:PATH` now serves the **net** diff for the path instead of the first commit that touched it. The fetch asked `gh pr diff N --patch`, which is format-patch — one section per commit — so a file touched by three commits arrived three times and the hunks route rendered the first and stopped, with no truncation notice of any kind. The file list one level up was built from the same records and printed one file as several rows. On PR #1057 (five commits) the op showed `op_replace`'s first-pass `newline=""` addition as the current code and a test assertion that a later commit had already replaced; a review agent produced two confident findings about code that did not exist. Output was 14429 bytes against a 65536-byte cap, so no cap was involved. `gh pr diff N` with no flag is the merge-base-to-head diff GitHub already computes, which is the thing being merged and therefore the thing under review — nothing is reassembled here (#1068).
- `gh-pr:N:diff` records are now coalesced per path before either render, so serving a first-of-N is structurally impossible rather than merely unlikely. A path that still arrives more than once — any future source that replays a file per commit — has **all** its entries shown, oldest first, under `Assembled from N entries for this path in the fetched diff … the LAST occurrence is the current one`. The file list sums such entries into one row rather than counting one file as `2 files`.

- `gh-prs` no longer states an absence it did not establish. The `author=@me` default is kept — `gh-prs` means "my PRs" — but it is now **disclosed** on every board, and an empty one names how many rows the filter excluded and how to see them, instead of printing `No PRs match.` / `0 PR(s)` over an outside contributor's open PR. Four states, never two: rows found, rows excluded by the filter (with the count), genuinely nothing open, and `UNKNOWN` when the check itself could not run — a probe that failed to spawn is never rendered as `excluded none`. The excluded count costs one extra `gh pr list`, fired only when the board came back empty under the *implicit* default.
- **New flag `gh-prs:anyauthor`** — every author's open PRs. Before it there was no spelling of that question at all: `author=` is refused for carrying no value and `label=`/`state=` are not role keys, so the default survived every attempt to widen it. Combining `anyauthor` with an explicit `author=`/`assignee=`/`reviewer=` is refused rather than resolved by precedence.
- `gh-prs` gained the `capped at --limit N — more may exist, raise with per=N` disclosure that `gh-issues` has had since birth, measured against the fetch rather than against what survived `failed`; and an empty `failed` board now says how many not-failing rows it dropped. Both boards now state the cap **above** the table as well as in the footer — a footer is lost by exactly the consumer that truncates (#633/#635/#657), and the cap fires precisely when the board is at its longest. Only the absences the caller did not ask for get a header line; a board that was not cut still prints nothing above the table.

- **`gh-job`'s `Suite:` line no longer presents the log author's number as the job's own count** ([#1076](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1076)). The count is read out of the job log with a regex anchored at column 0, after timestamps and ANSI have been stripped — so the anchor is satisfied by ordinary program output, and on a pull request the code writing that output is the pull request's code. `flat()` was doing its job throughout: no forged *line* reached the render. What it cannot do is make the number authoritative, and the wording called it "the job's own summary line" under a header reading "These count TESTS". The provenance caveat was also conditional on there being two or more summaries, so a job that ran no suite at all and emitted one stray matching line got the number with nothing attached at all.

  The line now states unconditionally that it is what the log claims rather than a count supertool made, and it is cross-checked against the job's conclusion as the Actions API reports it — the one fact in this render the log does not write. `Suite: 0 failed, 9999 passed` on a job the API calls `failure`, or failures on a job it calls `success`, prints that the two do not agree. Agreement is not narrated, because a cross-check that speaks on every render is one nobody reads, and a conclusion that is not yet an answer (`cancelled`, `timed_out`, `skipped`, `in_progress`, empty) manufactures no contradiction — reading "not success" as "the suite failed" would be the same over-claim pointed the other way.

  Reading the count from `junit.xml` instead was the audit's suggestion and the better source, and it is **not reachable from this op**: `.github/scripts/junit_summary.py` writes that file to the runner's working directory, nothing uploads it as an artifact, and `gh-job` reads `gh run view --log` and only that. Its *output* is log text like everything else, and a workflow file is part of a pull request's diff in any case. Hardening the regex was declined for the same reason it always is here — a pattern set cannot be complete, and a tighter one that still matched would produce a more confident-looking wrong answer.

  One bug found on the same line while fixing it: the "did this invocation report a problem" test was `"failed" in body`, which is true of `0 failed, 9999 passed`. It now reads the counts as numbers, so a summary reporting zero failures is no longer selected over a later clean one as though it had failed.

- **`branch.verdict()` can no longer be called without a scope, and radar's default-branch row states the scope it cannot account for** ([#1077](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1077)). [#846](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/846) built `scope_for` as a seam and said why in its own docstring — `presets/dashboard/dashboard.py` and `presets/watch/tiers/gh_prs.py` both call `verdict()` directly, and "a caller that has to remember to compute this will not". The dashboard was wired; the radar tier was not, by the same change. So the disclosure that exists because v0.27.0 was tagged on a commit whose declared workflows had not all run was unreachable from the board that reports the default branch on every tick.

  `scope` is now a keyword-only argument with **no default**. A caller that omits it raises rather than publishing an unscoped green — a default is a reminder, a required argument is a mechanism, and the difference is the whole content of this issue.

  The tier's blank-on-GREEN is where the disclosure was actually being dropped, and it was not simply removed. `scope_for` now returns a third value saying whether the green is bounded, and the tier speaks on a green only when it is not: a declared workflow set that could not be read, or a workflow declaring a **push** trigger that produced no run on the head commit. A `schedule`- or `pull_request`-only workflow producing no run on a push is expected, and on this repo `slow tests` and `changelog` are permanently in that state — so a board that spoke whenever the clause was non-empty would print the same two lines on every tick forever, which is precisely the habituation `scope_clause`'s own docstring says this repo has already paid for twice. The loud/quiet split reuses `_declared_workflows.is_push_triggered`, the predicate the named block already renders on, so the two cannot drift, and an `on:` block that could not be read counts as loud on both sides.

  The tier's `could_tell` moves with it, and that is the part that makes the lines reachable at all: radar's `quiet_when_healthy` discards a healthy tier's entire output, so un-blanking the lines while still reporting healthy would have looked fixed and disclosed nothing to an operator running quiet. It is dropped only against the green — every other state here is a finding, and a finding is something the tier could tell; a green is a clearance, and a clearance over a set of unknown size is not one.

  `gh-branch` itself and the dashboard section are unchanged in behaviour: both still print the full clause and the named block unconditionally, the dashboard being the board a human reads immediately before tagging.
## [0.27.0] - 2026-08-08

### Added

- **`gh-pr`'s pending count carries an age, so a progressing run and a wedged one no longer render byte-identically** ([#801](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/801)). `checks: 18 total: 14 passed, 0 failed, 4 pending`, printed twice seven minutes apart, was the same line whether four macOS legs were queued behind runner availability and merging in five minutes, or the run had wedged an hour earlier and nothing further was arriving. Eight PRs sat on that line for the better part of an hour on 2026-08-07 and each one was resolved by hand, in the web UI, for a timestamp. `gh-pr:N` and `gh-pr:N:status` now close the line with `— oldest pending 41m`.

  **The age is the oldest still-pending leg, and the other two candidates were rejected for stated reasons.** The *run's* age is diluted by every leg that already finished. *Time since the last leg changed state* is the tempting one and is wrong in exactly the case this issue was filed from: sixteen legs finish, two stay queued behind a busy pool, and the last observable state change is as old as the sixteenth completion — so a normal queue renders identically to a dead run, and renders as dead. Trading an ambiguous line for a confidently misleading one is not a fix. The oldest pending leg is scoped to the thing the reader is waiting for and nothing else.

  **It is not a staleness alarm.** Nothing prints `STALLED`. A runner with nothing to do is indistinguishable from a runner that cannot work and this repository went 0-for-12 on that inference ([#750](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/750)). The clock is reported; the conclusion is the reader's.

  **A pending leg with no readable start time is disclosed, never dropped.** `gh` spells an unset timestamp `0001-01-01T00:00:00Z` rather than null — it parses cleanly and yields an age of about two thousand years — so it is refused alongside an absent or unparseable one, and the count of refused legs is printed on a disclosure line beneath the tally, saying that the age above is a *floor* rather than the answer. When no pending leg is readable at all the line ends `— oldest pending age UNKNOWN` and the reason is stated underneath. Dropping such legs from the maximum would make the reported age *younger*, which is the reassuring direction and therefore the dangerous one.

  **No new request.** `startedAt` was already in the payload `gh pr view --json statusCheckRollup` returns. `_checks.summarize` appends the note after the whole line, deliberately outside the comma-separated term list: spliced into the pending term it put prose where `tests/test_check_tally_454.py` parses counts back out, which lost the `pending` term entirely and would have let a `2 of 4` be read as a term worth 2. That test caught it, the decoration moved rather than the parser, and the promise that every term sums to `N total` is untouched. The boards that render one tally per row (`gh-prs`, `dashboard`) stay one line wide — the age is opt-in via `summarize_github(..., with_age=True)`.

- **`gh-issue` and `gl-issue` say whether the linked work is green, not only that it exists** ([#815](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/815)). `gh-issue:803` printed `#808 (OPEN)` at a moment when #808 had a failed leg. `OPEN` is true and it was the whole story the op told: a reader on a triage tick concludes "the fix is in flight" and moves on, when the fix is in flight *and currently red* — one of those says wait and the other says go look. The linked-PR block now carries `checks: 18 total: 13 passed, 1 failed, 4 pending ⚠ NOT ALL GREEN`, in the vocabulary `gh-pr:N:status` already uses, from `_checks.summarize` rather than a second hand-rolled sum ([#454](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/454)).

  **The cost question the issue asks to be answered: it is zero, so there is no opt-in gate.** The obvious objection is one extra API call per linked PR, on a tracker where most issues have one. There is none — `closedByPullRequestsReferences` is already fetched over GraphQL and `commits(last: 1) { commit { statusCheckRollup } }` hangs off the same selection set. Measured against the live API on 2026-08-07: issues 1007, 803 and 969 returned 20, 18 and 20 contexts respectively, one request each. Gating a free field behind `:full` would only hide it.

  **Three states, because a PR with no run must not read like one that is waiting.** A null `statusCheckRollup` renders `no check runs on this commit — whether one is still coming is UNKNOWN`, never a zero tally (`0 passed, 0 failed, 0 pending` reads as "accounted for, nothing outstanding", which is [#452](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/452)'s exact wrong reading) and never as pending. Classifying *whether a run is coming* needs the head commit's age and mergeable state, so the line names `gh-pr:N` rather than re-fetching its evidence. A tally the response did not carry says `UNKNOWN`, because an omitted tally reads as "nothing to report". A matrix wider than the 100-leg page size is disclosed with `⚠ INCOMPLETE — 100 of 137 legs read`.

  **`gl-issue` lands in the same change**, which is what the issue's own comment asks for — a fix on one family only would become the parity gap it was meant to close. Each related MR now carries `pipeline: failed (#154290) ⚠ NOT ALL GREEN` from `head_pipeline`, already in the payload, so no extra call there either. It is a **status, not a leg tally**, and the asymmetry is deliberate: GitLab puts no per-job breakdown in an MR, so matching the GitHub shape would mean `projects/:id/pipelines/N/jobs` once per related MR — a real, uncapped, per-MR request on a list that holds up to ten. A missing or null `head_pipeline` declines with the sentence `gl-mr` already prints for that state rather than asserting there is no pipeline.

- **`gl-api:PATH[?query][:full]` — a GET-only read of any GitLab REST path** ([#831](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/831)). The `gl-*` family is specialised — MR, MRs, pipeline, job, runners, issue — and everything else in the API had no op at all, so an access-review session went out as raw `glab api` eight times and tripped the `use-supertool` reminder eight times. A guard that fires on correct behaviour is one that stops being read, including on the calls where it is right; this op is what lets the reminder be honest.

  It is not the thin wrapper the issue proposed, in three places.

  **The method is pinned rather than defaulted, and no caller flag is forwarded.** `glab api` switches to POST on its own the moment a `-f`/`-F` is present, so "supertool passed no method" would not have meant "supertool sent a read". The op takes one thing, a path, sends `--method GET`, and refuses a path that is flag-shaped, contains whitespace, or is `graphql` — naming `glab api -X POST PATH -f key=value` in the refusal rather than guessing. A passthrough that accepted `-X POST` would not be a larger read op; it would be a write surface reachable from every alias and batch that can spell `gl-api`, with no validator, no rollback and no confirmation in front of it. The guarantee is about what supertool sends, not a claim that GitLab treats every GET as free of side effects.

  **A full page is not a complete list.** `projects/:id/members/all` returns twenty rows whether the project has twenty members or a hundred and thirty-seven, and nothing in the body tells them apart — this repo's own defect class, an absence produced by the tool read as an absence in the world, landing on an access review where it is the failure that matters most. Three states, never two: fewer rows than `per_page` says `complete`, exactly `per_page` says `INCOMPLETE` with the count and the boundary it compared against, and `:full` follows every page and says that instead. The boundary is `min(per_page, 100)` because GitLab silently caps `per_page` at 100 — `?per_page=200` returning 100 rows is a *full* page, and comparing against the 200 that was asked for would call it complete, which is the same defect one layer down. A `page=` above 1 discloses that the earlier pages were never fetched. An object response carries no completeness line at all: it was never paged.

  **The whole body is remote text.** Every other op here knows which of its fields a stranger wrote; a generic passthrough cannot, so nothing is exempt — the body is fenced, control characters are disclosed and fence glyphs are neutralised. Inside JSON the encoder does most of that, but `ensure_ascii=False` (kept, so a non-ASCII name stays readable) leaves U+2028 and U+2029 raw, and a non-JSON body has no encoder in front of it at all. A body that is not JSON is labelled `NOT JSON` and shown verbatim rather than parsed with a shrug.

  Emission is budgeted by `GL_API_MAX_BYTES` (default 65536), and the two shapes are cut differently on purpose: an array is cut **by item** so what prints is still a valid JSON array (`CAPPED: 41 of 4820 items shown`), and anything else is cut by characters and says `the JSON above is cut and does not parse` rather than letting the reader find out in a decoder.

  Not shipped: the `gh-api` half of the issue. `presets/github/` is under active change on another branch, and the GitHub pagination contract is a different one (`Link` headers, no `per_page` echo), so it is a separate change rather than a copy of this one.

- **`gh-pr-create:@FILE` — open a PR from a payload, and never guess the base** ([#950](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/950)). The payload route, for the same reason `gh-issue-create` has one: a PR body is long markdown with colons, fences and quotes, and none of that survives `:`-tokenisation.

  `repo` defaults to the origin remote and `head` to the current branch, because both are unambiguous facts about where you are standing — a detached HEAD is refused rather than substituted. `base` is required and is never defaulted: `master` and a release branch are equally plausible from one cwd, and a wrong base does not fail, it opens a PR that reviews clean, merges clean, and lands the change where nobody was reviewing. The refusal names the repository's default branch without using it. Both refs are echoed back with the source each came from, so a wrong one is visible at creation instead of after the merge.

  The receipt answers what the second call always was. **Zero checks is not "pending"** — an empty rollup renders identically to one nobody has filled in yet, so the receipt states which of the two it is, with GitHub's own ~15min run-creation window as the boundary and a stated `UNKNOWN` past it; waiting for a run that will never exist is what cost a PR its first life. The body's closing references are parsed with the same reader `gh-pr` uses and echoed back, so a malformed `Closes` line is caught here rather than discovered after the merge. Ends on a one-line `[result]` verdict that survives a pipe.

- **`gh-pr-merge:NUMBER` — merge a PR, then prove it landed** ([#950](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/950)). Replaces four hand-rolled calls, one of which was a hand-written `jq` expression sitting in the middle of the maintainer's merge path — and a hand-rolled `jq` over check states is what produced [#454](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/454), where a `CANCELLED` leg counted as neither a pass nor a pending and very nearly merged a run that had already concluded `failure`.

  **This is the first op in the family that writes, so the refusal surface is the design.** It refuses a PR that is not `OPEN`, a draft, one GitHub reports `CONFLICTING`, one whose `mergeable` is `UNKNOWN`, one whose merge state is not `CLEAN`, one with `CHANGES_REQUESTED`, one with zero check runs, one whose rollup could not be read, and one whose legs are not all green — where green is #454's arithmetic and `CANCELLED`, `SKIPPED`, `TIMED_OUT`, `NEUTRAL` and `ACTION_REQUIRED` are each named and none is permission. A tally it could not reconcile against what the runs declare is a refusal too: every leg *read* passing is not the claim that every leg passed, which is the call `gh-branch`'s own verdict already makes. Pending legs are named here even though the shared disclosure helper drops them — that exclusion is right for a status board and wrong for a gate, where which legs you are waiting on is the entire question. There is no green-bypass; a refusal names the raw command instead. Without `|force` the op prints the gate and merges nothing, through the same confirmation gate the publish ops use.

  **Nothing is inferred from an exit code.** `gh pr merge` can print nothing at all on success, so `state`, `mergedAt` and `mergeCommit.oid` are read back off the remote and all three must arrive before the merge is called verified.

  **Then every linked issue, named individually, with its verified state.** The body's own closing references are reconciled against GitHub's `closingIssuesReferences`, and the disagreement between them is the finding: read against the API on 2026-08-07, eleven of the last twelve merged PRs here had their declared reference bound and PR #908 did not — its body said `Closes #899`, GitHub bound nothing, and no error was raised anywhere. Every issue that did not close carries the exact command to close it by hand; a lookup that failed renders as `unknown` with its reason, never as closed and never omitted. A merge that lands while an issue stays open is rendered as both facts at once, implies no rollback, and does not exit 0.

  The default branch's state after the squash is reported separately via `gh-branch`, because a green PR is a statement about its merge-base and that gap has left `master` red for hours with the board reading clean. Branch cleanup is named and never run — chaining a delete onto a merge once deleted the branch and auto-closed the PR when the merge had failed on a conflict.

  **And a head branch that is not an ordinary refname gets no delete command at all**, which is a third state rather than a quieter second one. A fork PR's head branch is named by whoever opened it, and neither treatment makes a printed command both correct and safe: shell-quoting stops the shell acting on the name but leaves a U+2028 inside the quotes, so the line still renders as three ([#965](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/965)); flattening fixes the render and re-points the delete at a branch that does not exist. `presets/_refname.py` already draws that line — quote where the command is the deliverable, withhold where it is a convenience — and deleting a merged branch is the convenience case, since it has a button on the PR page. The name is still printed in full, flattened onto one line, with the reason no command accompanies it.

- **`dashboard` — "what do I do next", in one read-only call** ([#953](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/953)). Four reads used to answer the maintainer's standing question and none of them answered it: clone currency, the default branch's CI, the open-PR board and worktree occupancy, joined by hand six times in one session. `dashboard` performs the join and returns the two facts none of the four carried — which PRs are mergeable right now, and which lanes are free.

  The verdict column is the value and the risk, so `MERGE` is the last branch reached and the only one that asserts anything. It is derived from the shared `_checks` tally and from `gh-pr`'s own leg reconciliation, not a second copy of either: **a tally that does not sum to the legs the run declares renders `UNKNOWN`** — never `WAITING`, which would assert the missing legs are still coming, and never `MERGE`. `MERGE` requires every leg in the passed bucket rather than the absence of a failure, so `CANCELLED`, `SKIPPED`, `TIMED_OUT`, `NEUTRAL`, `ACTION_REQUIRED` and any state added after this shipped fall out as `UNKNOWN` by construction instead of by enumeration.

  Lane occupancy is inferred, and `git-worktrees`' three states are carried all the way up. An open PR or an `occupied` tree makes a lane `occupied`; a lane whose only signal is a tree the occupancy check could not decide is `unknown`, because `cannot tell` is not `idle` one layer up either; and `free` additionally requires that every live worktree in the repository was attributable to some lane, so one stray occupancy nobody could place degrades every otherwise-free lane to `unknown` and names it. Reporting a lane free while an agent works in it is how two agents end up editing one file. The labels themselves live on issues, not on PRs — measured on this repository, seven lanes existed, 54 of 65 open issues carried one, and no open PR carried one at all, so a lane board read off PR labels would have printed all seven free while six PRs and thirteen worktrees were live.

  A section that could not be fetched prints its heading, says `!! unread` with the reason and is counted in the footer, because a dashboard missing its board must not read as a dashboard with an empty board; `next:` declines outright rather than advising from data it never got. Read-only permanently — clone currency uses `git ls-remote`, which reads the remote's ref without writing yours, and every command `next:` can name is a read op. GitHub only; GitLab equivalence is stated as out of scope in `docs/presets/dashboard.md` rather than half-built.

### Changed

- **Every invocation was recompiling 17,380 lines; the entry point is a shim now** ([#931](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/931)). CPython writes and reuses `__pycache__/*.pyc` for modules it *imports*, and never for the script named on the command line — `__main__` is compiled from source on every run, by design. The whole tool *was* that script, so every call re-parsed and re-compiled all of it. `supertool.py` is now ~80 lines that import `_supertool.py`, which is the same file under a new name.

  Measured with the harness from the issue, macOS/py3.14, 15 samples, `min`: `python3 supertool.py version` went from 199.4ms to 89.0ms, and the recompile term specifically from 109.2ms to 1.3ms. On GitHub runners the term was 143.0ms (ubuntu), 144.8ms (windows) and 100.0ms (macOS), so this is not the Windows-specific cost the issue was originally filed as — it is paid on every platform, by every user, on every call, and roughly 900 times per CI leg.

  Nothing about the invocation contract moves. `python3 supertool.py 'op'`, `python3 -m supertool`, the `supertool` console script and the `~/.local/bin/supertool` / `dvsi/supertool` symlinks all behave exactly as before, and `import supertool` still yields the module that holds the code — the shim rebinds its own `sys.modules` entry rather than re-exporting, so a name patched on `supertool` is the same object the implementation reads.

  An install that copies `supertool.py` alone now refuses with exit 2, naming the missing file and the directory it looked in, instead of raising `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named '_supertool'` at whoever inherited it. That verdict is taken from what is on disk beside the shim and never from whether `import _supertool` succeeds — wherever the tool is installed as a package the name resolves from anywhere, so the naive version ran a *different* tree and printed a convincing version banner. For the same reason the shim checks which file actually loaded, since `sys.path` does not outrank the `sys.meta_path` finder an editable install puts there, and warns on stderr if it was not the one beside it. And `_supertool.py` is still runnable as a script — anything spawning `[sys.executable, supertool.__file__, ...]` lands there, and without that it would have printed nothing and exited 0.

  Three things quietly stopped looking at the code when it changed name, and all three moved with it rather than being discovered later: the coverage floor (a 89% floor over 17k lines would have become a 89% floor over an 80-line shim, still green), the `changelog.yml` path filter that decides whether a PR owes a fragment, and the mixed-tree guard, which compared the invoked file against the project's `supertool.py` by identity and now compares install directories — file identity could never hold again and it would have warned on every invocation made from inside a checkout.

### Fixed

- **`cargo-check` blamed the file you edited for a sibling module's compile error** ([#754](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/754)). `cargo check` analyses the whole crate, and the adapter matched every short-format diagnostic in the output without once comparing the path cargo printed to the path it was asked about. Editing a healthy `src/main.rs` in a crate whose `src/sibling.rs` does not type-check produced `ok: false` with `file` naming main.rs, `line: 1, col: 29` — a location in sibling.rs — and an empty `source_context`, because the crate-relative path was resolved against wherever the adapter happened to be running rather than against the crate. Three false statements about a file that compiled fine, and with `rollback_on_fail` set, grounds to revert an edit that was never the problem.

  Split out of [#753](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/753), which fixed the misclassification and left this deliberately open, because the answer is a schema decision rather than a regex change: what should a clean file in a crate that does not compile report?

  **The diagnostic is kept and only the attribution changes.** A crate error caused by another file is real; what was wrong is the claim about which file caused it. Filtering it out would leave the caller with a clean-looking file in a crate that does not build — a misreport traded for a silent loss, the worse of the two. A diagnostic naming another file now reports `code: "adapter"`, `line: null` and `col: null`, carries no `source_context`, and names the real `path:line:col` plus the rustc code in its message, so it can still be read and acted on but never mistaken for a line of this file. `ok` stays `false` and no error is dropped. A diagnostic that does name this file is untouched and keeps its own line, column and rustc code.

  `adapter` rather than a new code because every guarantee it already carries is the one wanted: the result is never cached, since a whole-crate verdict is not a function of this file's content while the cache key is a content hash, and it never triggers rollback. `skipped` was rejected for the reason a tool fault is — it omits `errors` entirely, and the crate error would disappear.

  **Paths are compared by suffix on segment boundaries, not by joining onto the crate root.** The obvious fix is wrong for any crate in a workspace: verified on cargo 1.97.1, running from `ws/member` makes cargo print `member/src/sib.rs`, relative to the workspace root and not to the crate root it was invoked in, so `crate_root / src_file` yields `ws/member/member/src/sib.rs` and matches nothing — every genuine finding about the file under validation would have been demoted to a non-verdict, the same defect pointing the other way and the quieter of the two. A suffix match needs no base and touches no disk, so one rule covers crate-relative, workspace-relative and absolute paths alike, and the separator boundary keeps `src/xmain.rs` from matching `src/main.rs`.

  **Case is folded before separators are normalised, never after.** `os.path.normcase` is the only stdlib call that knows whether a platform is case-insensitive, and on Windows it also rewrites every `/` into `\\` — so normalising separators first and folding second un-normalises them, and the suffix rule went on testing for a `/` boundary against two backslash-separated strings. Every diagnostic failed to match, including the file's own, which is the exact regression this fix was written to prevent, and it reached CI: three `windows-latest` legs red, one of them the pre-existing `test_cargo_check_source_context_on_error`. The fold is now injectable the way `refusal.daemon_transport_reason` takes `has_uds`, so `ntpath.normcase` reproduces Windows semantics on every runner and the rule is pinned from any platform rather than only from the one that has the behaviour. Nothing in the comparison rests on two `resolve()` calls agreeing character for character either: `os.path.abspath` joins onto the working directory while `Path.resolve()` goes through `_getfinalpathname`, so an absolute diagnostic path is now matched against the raw target as well as the resolved one.

  `source_context` for a diagnostic about this file is now read from the target the adapter was handed rather than from a path reconstructed out of cargo's output, which is what was returning empty. The rule is written up in `validators/SCHEMA.md`, and `tests/test_cargo_sibling_attribution_754.py` drives it in process on every platform and against a real two-file crate wherever cargo is installed — the attribution depends on cargo's own relative paths, which a stub would have to guess at.

- **A missing dev.to CSRF token no longer blames a redesign that did not happen, and the encoding scan no longer reads `open(timeout=...)` as a file open** ([#766](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/766)). Two reports about conditions neither check had actually looked at.

  `devto`'s session-cookie path scrapes an `authenticity_token` out of `/settings`. When it found none, it had exactly one thing to say — `authenticity_token not found in /settings HTML — Dev.to layout may have changed` — and the common cause is the other one: `dev.to` answers `/settings` with a same-origin 302 to `/enter` once the session cookie expires, the redirect is legitimate and is followed, and the login page carries no token. Every noun in that message was then wrong: the HTML was `/enter`, the layout was fine, the cookie was dead. [#761](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/761) added a `NOTE:` line disclosing the hop, but the line an operator acts on still pointed at a dev.to redesign.

  There are three outcomes now rather than two, and the difference between them is a fact the op already had — the URL that answered. Token found; token absent from a page that answered under a *different* URL, which names the expired cookie and tells you to re-copy it; token absent from `/settings` itself, which says so, states that no redirect happened and therefore that the session is live, and only then says the layout may have changed. The unknown case stays unknown: replacing one confident wrong cause with a different confident wrong cause is the same defect facing the other way.

  Separately, `tests/test_encoding_seam.py`'s AST scan treated every `X.open(...)` as `Path.open` — one carve-out for `os.open`, nothing else — so `presets/_http.py`'s `OpenerDirector.open(req, timeout=timeout)`, which touches no file and decodes nothing, was reported as `open() without encoding=` and failed the build. #761 worked around it by binding the method to a plain name, a contortion of shipped source to satisfy a false positive that would have bitten the next author calling `.open()` on something that is not a path.

  The scan now declines a call that names a keyword neither `open` nor `Path.open` declares. That is a fact about two signatures rather than a guess about a receiver, so it cannot be widened by accident: every keyword they *do* declare still flags, and `**kwargs` — where the names are unknown at parse time — still flags too, on the rule the scan already used for a non-literal `mode`. The plain-name binding in `_http.py` stays, but as the deliberate patch seam the redirect tests need, and its comment now says that instead of citing a false positive that no longer exists.

- **A failed related-MR lookup no longer vanishes `gl-issue`'s whole section** (found while building [#815](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/815), and worse than what it reported). `if mr_result.returncode == 0:` had no `else`, and the enclosing `except (subprocess.TimeoutExpired, json.JSONDecodeError): pass` swallowed the rest — so a query that failed printed **no `Related MRs` line at all**. A missing section reads as "this issue has no MRs", which is the signal that an issue is unclaimed, and the action that invites is delegating work that has already been done. That is [#780](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/780) item 1, fixed on the GitHub side and still live here; `gh-issue` at least printed `Linked PRs: unknown`.

  #815's own comment states that neither family omits the section. That is true at *zero* — both print an explicit `none`, which is what was verified there — and it was not true on failure.

  The section now prints `Related MRs: unknown — could not query (...)` on a non-zero exit, a timeout, unparseable output, and an unexpected JSON shape. `Related MRs: none` still means an answered zero, and nothing else does.

  **Including the spawn failure, which escaped the old handler entirely.** `glab` missing from `PATH` raises `FileNotFoundError` from `subprocess.run` — `[WinError 2] The system cannot find the file specified` on Windows — and `PermissionError` where POSIX raises `IsADirectoryError` ([#618](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/618)/[#627](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/627)). Neither was in `except (TimeoutExpired, JSONDecodeError)`, so the op raised through the code whose entire job is to say "I could not ask" — [#997](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/997)'s mechanism. `OSError` is caught, not one platform's spelling of it.

  The same arm was missing from `gh-issue`'s `_print_linked_prs`, whose `main()` guards its own `gh` call with `except FileNotFoundError` while the linked-PR lookup did not. Both are covered now, and both are pinned by tests that raise `FileNotFoundError` and `PermissionError` explicitly rather than relying on a platform to produce one.

- **A baseline nothing measured is no longer printed as a baseline that measured zero.** `phpunit-mcp` reported `0 → 7  (+7) ✗` after an edit that introduced nothing — all seven tests were already failing because the local test database was missing a table — and the reporter nearly reverted a correct fix on the strength of that `0 →`. The mechanism is not phpunit's: `_drain_validator_queue` calls `_validator_render_diff(None, data)`, because the **slow tier by design runs no baseline pass at all**, and `before.get("count", 0) if before else 0` turned that `None` into a literal zero. So every `"tier": "slow"` validator reported every pre-existing failure in the repo as a regression the current edit had caused, on every run. Same arithmetic as [#969](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/969), one caller over: an absence given a number and subtracted as though it were a measurement.
- **The row now reads `? → 7   ✗ (baseline not measured)`.** Three states on the left of the arrow, not two: measured, measured-and-non-zero, and not measured.
- **The delta and the `+` prefix went with it, because they are the same subtraction in two more columns.** Seven minus an unmeasured baseline is not `+7`, so no `(+N)` is printed; and the per-error `+ ` prefix means "introduced by this op", which every finding qualifies for when the set it is diffed against is empty. Fixing only the arrow would have moved the false number rather than removed it.
- **The quiet half: a clean slow-tier run claimed `(no new errors)`.** Zero equalled the fabricated zero, so it took the equal-counts branch and asserted a comparison that never happened. It reads `? → 0` too. This is the one that would have survived a fix aimed only at the loud case.
- **The marker is deliberately unchanged.** The file does have those errors now, and nothing measured whether it did before — so the row states what it knows and softens nothing. Turning `✗` into a shrug because the baseline is unknown would trade this bug for the one where a real regression reads as pre-existing, which is the trade the whole "three states" rule exists to refuse. Rollback semantics are untouched; the slow tier does not roll back at all.
- **A measured baseline still gets real arithmetic.** The fast tier runs a genuine pre-op pass, and `0 → 7`, `(pre-existing — not from this edit)` and `(no new errors)` all still mean exactly what they say there.

- **`git-resolve` no longer prints `markers: clean` for a file whose syntax validator declined to run** ([#880](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/880)). `_digest_block` condensed each file's validator rows and matched only two shapes, `tool : ok` and `tool : N err`. A validator that matched the file and then declined emits a third — `phplint : skipped — php not installed` — which set neither counter, so the file condensed to `None`: the value meaning "the validators ran and none handles this file type", which the receipt deliberately prints as nothing. A `.php` conflict staged on a machine without php therefore reported `markers: clean`, byte-identical to a file whose parser ran and passed.

  This is one layer in from the four routes #883 fixed. Those are failures of the *batch* — the child crashed, timed out, was never found, folded to the wrong block count — and every one is caught before a single row is read. Here the child ran fine and emitted a well-formed block, and the decline is a row inside it. It is also the likeliest of the five to be met, because it needs no crash at all, only a missing interpreter.

  A decline beside a pass costs a word rather than the whole verdict: `validate: ok | ⚠ not checked by phpstan (php not installed)`. The reader takes this line as the verdict for the file, and half-checked may not render as checked. A block with no rows at all is still `None` and still silent — that is the one state which really is an answer about the world, and widening it would put a warning under every `.md` in every resolve.

  Two of the three routes named in the issue were already fixed by #883; the third — a path excluded for containing `:` or `,` — stopped existing when #878's sender-side filter was replaced by the `@payload` route, so nothing is excluded any more. The route fixed here is a fourth the issue did not name.

- **`gh-job:N:fail` claimed a complete answer on a job that never failed** ([#916](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/916)). `:fail` selects error blocks, which is right for a job GitHub calls `failure` and close to the worst possible filter for one it calls `cancelled`: a cancellation writes exactly one error line, `##[error]The operation was canceled.`, and puts everything diagnostic outside it. The render nevertheless headlined its selection `All error blocks (11 lines matched, no tail truncation)` — two claims that are true of the *selector* and false of the *log*. On the job in the issue, thirty lines further down in teardown output carrying no error marker of any kind, sat six `Terminate orphan process: pid (…) (python)` lines: the difference between "the suite is slow" and "the process tree was still populated when the runner pulled the plug", and the strongest available evidence on a hang whose cause was still open ([#914](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/914)). It cost a day, and an issue body asserting "the log says nothing" as though that were a property of the log.
- **The op already knew.** `Status: cancelled` is printed two lines above, from the same value the selection branch reads — so it held, at selection time, the fact that error blocks were the wrong selector, and applied it anyway. It now drops the completeness claim (`## Error blocks (N lines matched) — but see below`) and appends a note naming the conclusion, saying error-block selection is a poor fit for it, and giving two ops that do reach the evidence: `gh-job:N:raw:-80` and `gh-job:N:grep:orphan`. Both verified against the live job — `:grep:orphan` returns all six `Terminate orphan process` lines.
- **Disclosure rather than a wider pattern set, deliberately.** Teaching the patterns to match `Terminate orphan process` would fix that one log and trade a loud wrong answer for a quiet one: the next cancelled job's tell is some other unmarked line, and a larger set that still misses it produces a longer and more confident-looking block. A pattern set cannot be complete, so the honest output is that these N lines matched *and* that this selector is not where the cause lives here. It is the three-state move of `docs/validators.md` §"Declining instead of guessing" applied to a selector rather than a checker.
- **Not suppression either.** Every matched line is still printed in full. Answering nothing, or clamping the selection down to a tail, would be the same defect pointed the other way — trading "it told me the wrong thing loudly" for "it quietly gave me something else".
- Keyed on the complement — `display_status != "failure"` — rather than on a list of the other conclusions, so a state GitHub adds later, or an in-progress job whose display status is `queued`, lands on the disclosure instead of on the silent overclaim. The `failure` path is byte-identical and pinned by its own test.
- **The sibling is deliberately untouched.** `gl-job:N:fail`'s pattern set does not match Playwright's `Error: JS errors detected:`, and on one e2e job it reported `All error blocks (6 lines matched)` where all six were teardown boilerplate. Same symptom — but there the conclusion *is* `failure`, so no signal exists to key a disclosure on, and extending this fix's claim to cover it would be the same overclaim one repo over. Filed as its own problem rather than folded into this one.

- **`CHANGELOG.md`'s link refs are audited on every pull request, and the two releases that shipped without one are backfilled** ([#918](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/918)). `## [0.24.0]` and `## [0.25.0]` had no link-reference definition, so both rendered as literal bracketed text rather than as links to the release, and `[Unreleased]` had twice been left comparing from a tag two releases behind — a link that resolves, returns a real diff, and shows shipped work as pending. The assembler has written one definition per cut since #906, which keeps the *next* release honest and says nothing about the state it inherited, so `--check-links` now reads the whole table and `.github/workflows/changelog.yml` runs it repo-wide on every PR: the run that finds the refs stale must not be the run cutting the tag.
- **A version that was never tagged is declared, not guessed at.** `0.11.0` and `0.14.0`–`0.19.0` have sections in the file and no tag anywhere, and a `releases/tag/vX.Y.Z` invented for one is a 404 that renders as a working link — `[0.11.0]` already carried exactly that and is now removed rather than left resolving to nothing. Those versions are listed in `UNTAGGED_RELEASES`, the list is audited itself (a declared version that *has* a definition, or that is not in the file at all, is a finding), and nothing from 0.20.0 on may be added to it, so the third state cannot become a place a real regression is filed away.
- **The changelog is now pinned to the version that ships.** `plugin.json` and `pyproject.toml` were already tied to `supertool.VERSION`; the newest `## [x.y.z]` section was tied to nothing, so a release could bump three of its four files and describe a different version in the one users read.

- **`grep` handed a comma-separated path list no longer blames the CWD** ([#921](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/921)). `grep:mark.slow:tests/a.py,tests/b.py,tests/c.py` joined the list into one filename, failed, and offered `wrong CWD? Prefix the call with cwd:PATH` — the one remedy that provably could not apply, since all three files resolved from the current directory. Following it produces the same error a second time, and the working fallback is to grep the parent directory instead: 391 files scanned to answer a question about three.

  The list is still refused — `git-resolve` accepts `PATH[,PATH...]` and `grep` does not, and quietly making it work here would be a second spelling to remember rather than one fewer. What changed is that the refusal names the cause and states what it checked: `a comma-separated list is not accepted here — grep takes ONE path, and the whole list was read as a single filename (all 3 of its entries exist, so the cwd is not the problem)`. When only some entries resolve it says `2 of 3` rather than implying all; when none of them do it stays silent and the ordinary CWD advice stands, because a path with a literal comma that is simply absent is a typo, and inventing a list there would trade one misreport for another.

- **`read` now states the window it returned, and `grep` refuses `LIMIT 0`** ([#945](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/945)). Two numeric arguments were accepted, produced confident output, and meant something other than what the caller typed.

  `read:PATH:OFFSET:LIMIT` takes OFFSET as a skip count, so `read:file.py:19:1` renders line 20 and line 19 is absent from the output entirely. Nothing in the render distinguished "here is line 19" from "here is a line near 19", so anyone quoting the result into a brief, a commit message or an issue quoted the wrong line with full confidence. Every read with a non-zero OFFSET now carries one line — after the count header, before the content — naming the window asked for, the window returned, and why the window ended: `window: offset 19 + limit 1 = lines 20-20; returning lines 20-20 of 403, stopping at line 20: the limit was reached`, plus a pointer to the 1-based `read:PATH:19-19` range form. The semantics are unchanged: re-basing OFFSET would have broken every caller who already had it right, trading a visible wrong answer for an invisible one.

  A window ends for one of three reasons and the note names which of them it was: the LIMIT was reached, the file ended, or the 20 KB byte cap cut the render short. Only two of those were ever distinguished, so a capped read announced `stopping at line 54, the end of the file` at the top of a body whose own footer, 20 KB further down, said 146 lines remained — the false claim first, and the one a caller quotes. When two reasons land on the same line the note says they coincide instead of picking one, and a read that ends for a reason it cannot attribute says that rather than inventing one.

  Every count in the render is now taken from the last line the read actually *looked at*, not the number of lines it printed. The two differ under compact mode, which skips blanks and comments without counting them: a `read:mix.py:10:50` whose body visibly ended at line 60 was headed `returning lines 11-35 of 200, stopping at line 35, the end of the file` — a window that was not returned, a stop that did not happen, and an end-of-file 140 lines early. The same miscount drove the `... (N more lines)` footer, which reported 165 where 140 remained; it predates the window note, but leaving two disagreeing counts in one render is worse than either alone, so both now come from the same number. A note over a compacted window also states how many of the lines in its span were suppressed, because a range that reads as contiguous when it is not is the same defect one level down.

  The same render used to sign off a windowed read with `[complete file — no more lines]` — false, because lines 1 to OFFSET were never emitted, and outright backwards when OFFSET sat past EOF, where *zero* lines were emitted and the output still said the whole file had been shown. A windowed read that reaches EOF now closes with `[end of file — lines 1-OFFSET not shown]`, and a window past EOF says `returning nothing — the file has N lines`.

  `grep:PATTERN:PATH:0` used to accept the `0`, ignore it, and quietly substitute the default limit; the filed case spent about 18 KB of the caller's context before that was visible. `0` is now refused by name. Honouring it as unlimited would hand a caller who typed one character an unbounded dump into a shared output budget, and substituting the default means the LIMIT that ran was never the LIMIT that was typed — so neither is guessed. `grep_around` and the `grep:@payload` route refuse it on the same terms.

- **`git-push` no longer reports a tracker it could not reach as a branch with no MR** ([#948](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/948)). The shared branch→MR lookup returned `None` for *there is no open MR/PR* and for *the lookup did not happen*, and swallowed every exception on the way — on the op a person reads immediately before and after the one irreversible thing supertool does. It now returns an `MrLookup`: a fact, or the reason there is no fact.

  Three consumers read that `None` and all three took it as an absence. The MR line went missing, which reads as "no MR yet, open one". The mergeability warning and the stale-base check were skipped silently, so a conflicting MR raised nothing. And `:watch` printed *"there is no open MR/PR for this branch yet — nothing to watch. Open one"* about a request that may well exist. That last one is a positive claim about the world, manufactured out of a lookup that timed out.

  The push is never blocked. This runs after the ref has moved, and a tracker that cannot be reached is not a reason to withhold work already on the remote — refusing there would trade a quiet wrong answer for a loud one that is worse. The receipt degrades to a stated unknown naming the CLI and its own words.

  The healthy path is byte-identical: a lookup that answered prints what it always printed, and a branch that genuinely has no MR still says nothing. Three cases are answers rather than failures, two of them on the reading `git-status` already used — a CLI saying *no open merge request* / *no pull request*, and the other host's CLI saying *none of the git remotes … point to a known GitHub host*. The second is structural and permanent, so declining on it would put a warning on every push in every GitLab repo with `gh` installed. An answer already given is never downgraded by the fallback: `glab` reporting "no MR" on a GitLab repo stands, whatever `gh` does a moment later.

  The phrase list `git-status` used to keep privately now lives beside the lookup and is imported, split into "this host has no such request" and "this is not this host's repo" — the two need different treatment and one copy.

  Reading those phrases is not enough on its own, because both CLIs check their own credentials **before** they look at the repository. An unauthenticated `gh` exits `4` saying so and never reaches *none of the git remotes … point to a known GitHub host*, so a repo with no forge remote at all — a sandbox whose `origin` is a path under `/tmp`, a clone from a colleague's disk — was reported as an unknown rather than as the plain absence it is. That fact was local the whole time, so the lookup now asks `git remote -v` first: if git answers and no remote names a host, there is no tracker for a request to be open on, and no CLI is consulted. A repo whose remote *is* on a forge is unchanged — it still probes, and still declines out loud when the probe cannot answer. Only a positively-local remote counts as local; a shape the check does not recognise is probed rather than assumed, because a wrong "no MR" is the expensive direction.

  Two things about that local check are worth stating, because both were got wrong once. A Windows checkout puts its remote at `C:/Users/…/remote.git`, which has a colon before its first slash — the scp-style shape — so a drive letter reads as a hostname and a temp directory reads as a forge; one character before the colon is what tells them apart. And `git` itself may not be on PATH, in which case `_git` raises rather than returning: that is the "git did not answer" state, so it is caught and degrades to `unknown` instead of taking the receipt of an already-successful push down with it. The reason then names git rather than the CLI, so the reader is not sent to fix the wrong tool.

  The reason attached to an unauthenticated CLI is now legible. `gh` says what it needs across four lines, none of which contains an error keyword, so the salient-line picker fell through to the *last* one — and inside GitHub Actions that is `GH_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }}`, a fragment of an example block offered to the reader as the reason their lookup did not run. The disclosure was correct and unreadable, which is half a disclosure.

  **The disclosure found a second defect on its first run, which is the argument for having built it.** `glab mr list --state opened` is rejected by glab 1.86 — `Unknown flag: --state.`, exit 1 — so the GitLab arm has been failing at argument parsing on every call for as long as the flag has been there, falling through to `gh`, which cannot answer on a GitLab repo either. Nobody found out, because both failures were swallowed. Open is `mr list`'s default (`--closed` is the opt-out), so the flag was unnecessary as well as wrong; it is gone, and the argv is pinned by a test.

  `git-status` was **not** affected, contrary to the issue: it has had its own three-state `_hosted_request` since #705 and never called this function. The consumers were `git-push` and `git-commit`'s post-commit hint.

- **A rolled-back edit is now named as one, in the footer and next to the claim it retracts** ([#952](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/952)). A validator with `rollback_on_fail` rejects an edit, the previous bytes are restored — and the receipt still said `edited src/Foo.php (line 40-44)`, a positive claim about a mutation that no longer existed. Two agents reported it independently on the same day, which is what said this is the normal shape of a failed edit on the payload route rather than a corner.

  Both of the ways this output is actually read agreed with the claim. `grep -E 'edited|ERROR'` returned the `edited` line and nothing else, because the `[rolled back]` marker below it shared no token with it. And `| tail -1` returned `[result] 3 ops run, 2 writes` — `M writes` had correctly excluded the retracted write since #621, but only the single-op case rendered that exclusion as a sentence (`0 writes — nothing changed on disk`). In a batch where other ops did write, a reverted edit became an arithmetic mismatch the reader has to notice before they can explain it.

  A rollback is now its own state, counted where it is decided and rendered as a word: `[result] 3 ops run, 2 writes, 1 rolled back — 1 edit was reverted after validation and did NOT land`. It is deliberately not `skipped` — a skipped op declined and left the disk alone, a rolled-back one wrote and had the write undone, and the remedies differ — and it is not folded into `— nothing changed on disk`, because a plain no-match prints exactly that too. Those were the two most confusable outcomes on this path and they now render differently.

  The `edited` line is **not** suppressed. Printing nothing on a rollback would make "written, then reverted" indistinguishable from "never ran", which is the same absence-read-as-fact defect wearing different clothes. The claim stays and is retracted in place, in a line that quotes it back and names the file:

  ```text
  [rolled back] phplint regressed; src/Foo.php restored — retracts "edited src/Foo.php (line 40-44)"; the file was NOT edited
  ```

  Any filter that caught the claim now catches the undo, adjacent to it. The old wording — `[rolled back] phplint regressed; file restored` — named no file at all, so in a batch it could not say which of several ops had been reverted.

  A rollback also makes the call exit non-zero, on the same grounds as #680's skip: `batch:@ops && git commit` committed a set with one edit reverted and exited `0`. The counter is bumped inside `_retract_write`, the single chokepoint both rollback paths already pass through, so a third path added later cannot be silently invisible; it is read as a per-call delta so one reverted edit cannot poison the exit code of every later call in a warm daemon process.

- **`radar` no longer stops pollers on a run that spawned nothing** ([#957](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/957)). The duplicate-poller reap from [#749](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/749) sat in `main()`, above every tier, so it ran on every `radar:*` invocation — including the ones that established no coverage at all. A tier that raised before it could spawn (live GitLab unreachable: exit 1, no board, nothing healed) had already stopped somebody's process on the way in, and so had a radar configured with only a fleet tier like `gl-runners`, which keeps no watchers to begin with. Those runs cannot have contributed a duplicate, so they now remove none.
- The reap moved onto the spawn path rather than being made opt-out. A flag would have put the same fusion one layer up and needed remembering at the exact moment nobody is thinking about it; the honest bound is already in the code — a call that spawns nothing has nothing of its own making to reap. It now fires from radar's `_watch`, once per run, immediately before the run's first spawn. Ordering is unchanged and still pinned: reaping *after* a spawn would judge the poller this run just started.
- Nothing changes for the tick you actually run. `radar` heals, healing spawns, so it reaps first and names every PID it stopped at the top of the board, exactly as before. A run that reaped nothing is still silent — "reaped nothing" and "did not reap" are the same fact for a reader (no process of theirs was stopped), and a disclosure line on every board is the furniture the Windows scan decline was already trimmed back for.
- `radar:--state` was never affected: it returns before `main()` reached the reap, and it never spawned. That is now covered by a test, so the read-only contract survives the reap moving rather than being an accident of an early `return`.
- Also fixed, from the same edit: the radar test fixture in `tests/test_watch_radar.py` spawns for real through radar's spawner, so an unpatched suite run could reach the machine's own `ps` and signal a developer's live pollers. It stubs the reap now; the reap's own behaviour stays pinned against the fake fleet in `tests/test_watch_radar_reap_749.py`.

- **radar's GitLab tier refuses a filter token it cannot apply, instead of widening the population it watches** ([#961](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/961)). [#939](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/939) rewired `gh-prs`, `gl-mrs` and radar's **GitHub** tier onto the shared tokenizer in `presets/_filter_tokens.py`; the **GitLab** tier still read `mrs._parse_multi(arg)[0]`, discarding the third element — the tokens it could not place. `radar:milestne=v19` therefore fell through to the default filter and rendered every open MR of yours, exit 0, no warning; `radar:author=@me,milestne=v19` dropped the typo and labelled the board `scope author=@me`, which is true about the query and false about the question. Half of radar refused an unrecognised token and half did not, so testing a typo against the GitHub tier concluded the class was closed.
- **Why this is worse than the op-level version:** a board is printed, a scope is _watched_. Radar heals a per-MR watcher onto every iid the scope resolves and names the discovery feed after it, so a silently widened scope starts firing `mr_opened` for strangers' MRs. The mr-feed poller already declined exactly this (#939); the tier is the same shape and did not get it.
- The tier **refuses** rather than declining. `fetch_population` returns `None` because it has no reader — it runs in a loop and its only channel is the events it emits. A tier has a reader, and `tier_reports` already isolates one, so a `RadarError` reaches the operator on stderr with exit 1 while every other registered tier still renders its board. `radar:--state` is the exception: it prints `filter : REFUSED — …` in place, because a read-only view that raises is the view you cannot open.
- The tier's vocabulary is its own, and both directions are pinned by tests. **Narrower than the op:** `iids` and `failed` are board _shapes_ — a radar board silently reduced to a bare id list, or to only the failing rows, is the same lie as a widened one — and `per=` is a page size the tier reads from config, so accepting it in the arg would drop it one level down. **Wider than the GitHub tier:** `glab mr list` has `--milestone`, `--source-branch` and `--target-branch` where `gh pr list` has none of them, and copying `gh_prs.KNOWN_FILTERS` would have refused three filters this tier can actually apply.
- The second defect on the same line: a **known** key whose value maps to nothing. `state=mergd` passes the key check, then `_build_list_cmd` finds no entry in `_STATE_FLAG` and emits no flag, so glab answers with its default `opened` — the merged board renders as the open one and radar heals watchers onto it. Refused, with the accepted values named. A value the backend simply does not match (`milestone=nosuchmilestone`) is still forwarded: an empty board there is the truth.

- **A board op's filter split by the `:` tokenizer was dropped, and the board printed as the answer** ([#964](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/964)). `gh-issues`, `gh-prs` and `gl-mrs` take their filters as one comma-separated segment, and supertool hands every `:`-segment to the preset as its own argv entry — but each `main()` read `sys.argv[1]` and nothing else. So `gh-issues:state=open:oops` reached the op as `['state=open', 'oops']`, the second half was discarded in silence, and the board rendered from a partly-applied filter at exit 0 with no warning. All three now refuse, naming the segments that were never applied and the single-segment form that survives the tokenizer.
- **This is [#864](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/864) one layer up, and the layer is why it survived it.** #864 taught the *tokenizer* in `presets/_filter_tokens.py` to refuse a token it could not place, and #939 put all three boards behind that one refusal. Nothing guarded the argv the tokenizer is handed. So the refusal was not bypassed by a token mangled into something that looks valid — it was bypassed by never being shown the token at all, which is why every value-level check kept passing. The new guard is in the same module for the same reason: two independently written refusal paths in one preset family is how they disagree again in three months.
- **The colon-in-a-value case, which has no fix and now says so.** `label=lane:tracker-ops` splits into a perfectly valid `label=lane` plus an orphan, so the key is known, the value is a string the backend might match, and nothing anywhere objects — `gh issue list --label lane` is queried instead. There is no escape: `label=lane\:x` splits identically, and [#806](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/806) declined to promote `\:` into a supported contract. Rather than invent a grammar, the refusal states that such a value cannot be expressed to a board op at all, so a reader stops looking. A payload route (`gh-issues:@file`) remains open to be designed later; GitLab's scoped `scope::value` labels are the real candidate for it, not GitHub's.
- **The issue's own premise did not survive checking, and the finding is larger than it.** It was filed reporting that this repo's labels are namespaced with a colon — `lane:tracker-ops`, `priority:medium` — and that every lane query was therefore returning a silently empty board hiding fifty issues. Verified live against the tracker on 2026-08-07: `gh label list` returns `lane-tracker-ops`, `lane-validators`, `priority-medium` — every one spelled with a **hyphen**, and no label containing a colon has ever existed here. `gh-issues:label=lane-tracker-ops,state=open` returned its sixteen rows before this change and returns them after. No lane query anyone could actually run was ever empty. What *is* real is the general case the colon example is one instance of: any trailing segment, on any of the three boards, was discarded without a word, and `gh-issues:state=open:COMPLETEGARBAGE` returned the entire open board as a filtered one.
- Ops whose grammar is genuinely positional — `gh-job:ID:raw:START:END`, `gh-job:ID:grep:PATTERN` — are deliberately not covered, and the helper's docstring says so.

- **A `rollback_on_fail` validator that could not run reverted a good edit** ([#969](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/969)). `_validator_regressed` compares an error count before an edit with the count after it, and an absence of information carries `count: 1` — that is the only channel `SCHEMA.md` gives it. So a checker that answered before the edit and could not answer after it scored `0 → 1`, read as a regression, and rewrote the file with its pre-edit bytes. The edit was fine, nothing had checked it, and the work was gone. Every other open finding misinforms; this one destroyed.

  **#967 had already won this argument one commit earlier and the rollback path did not hear it.** It established that a result whose errors are all `code: "adapter"` is a non-verdict rather than a finding, and taught the renderer, the `[result]` line and the exit code to say so. `_validator_regressed`'s own docstring promises that "the red the caller sees and the revert it triggers can never disagree" — after #967 they disagreed exactly: the row printed `NOT CHECKED` while the file was reverted underneath it.

  **The core's own timeout was the same absence and the likelier trigger.** `code: "orchestrator"`, `ok: false`, `count: 1`, from the `TimeoutExpired` arm — reachable with no exotic configuration at all, just a loaded machine and `jsonlint`'s 10s budget, on a validator this repo ships with `rollback_on_fail: true`. It now renders `NOT CHECKED (timed out — no verdict about this file)` instead of `1 err (timeout)`, is excluded from the delta, and exits non-zero. A count about a file the checker never finished reading is a measurement nobody took.

  **The `before` side was the same defect pointing the other way, and it was the quiet one.** A baseline that produced no verdict also carries `count: 1`, so a real finding introduced by the edit cancelled against it: the row read `1 err (pre-existing — not from this edit)` about an error that edit had just created, no rollback fired, and the call exited 0. A baseline nothing measured is not a clean baseline and is not a zero — it is the absence of a baseline, now folded into the case that already existed for one. Those rows show `? → 1`, never `0 → 1`.

  **The judgment, stated so it can be argued with: keep the edit, disclose loudly, exit non-zero.** The alternative was to refuse the write so nothing lands unverified, which is defensible for a gate whose point is that the file must not change unchecked — and it is the trade #665 already declined, for a reason that is stronger here. The pre-edit bytes a revert restores were never checked either. Reverting buys no safety over disclosing; it only deletes.

  **A core timeout now escalates with `$SUPERTOOL_REQUIRE_VALIDATORS` unset, which narrows #975.** That release grouped the timeout with four adapter breakdowns and pinned all five to a quiet exit 0 when the variable is unset, on #665's rationale: an optional checker nobody installed must not redden unrelated edits. The rationale covers the four — they become a `skipped`, which is what a missing tool produces — and cannot produce the fifth, because reaching a timeout needs the adapter present, spawned, and still running when the budget expired. So the checker that could not be vouched for is one the operator configured and expects. Its parametrized case is now asserted separately, in the opposite direction, with that reason written next to it; the other four are untouched, and `skipped` is still deliberately not folded in. The two rendering paths were also spelling one failure two ways — a required timeout read `(no verdict about this file)` and an unrequired one `(timed out — …)` — so they now agree; the variable changes the exit code, not what went wrong.
