  **`validate:` gained the `[result]` footer it never had.** It mutates nothing, so the footer was gated out entirely and its non-verdict reached the reader in the row and the exit code but not in the summary line the docs tell them to trust. The line now appears for a read-only op precisely when a checker declined, naming it, and carries no op or write counts — there was no op to count.

- **`$SUPERTOOL_REQUIRE_VALIDATORS` exited 0 on five ways a required validator did not run.** [#967](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/pull/967) fixed the one case an adapter can report about itself — it ran, `refusal.required()` found the binary missing, and it emitted an `adapter` error. Every way the adapter is too broken to reach that code went elsewhere: an adapter that prints nothing, prints non-JSON, crashes, or replies without a verdict key all land in `_validator_unusable_reply` and become a `skipped`, and one that hangs lands in the core's own `TimeoutExpired` arm and rendered `1 err (timeout)`. `_note_not_checked` recorded none of them, so `supertool 'edit:...' && git commit` proceeded past an ungated edit in all five — the entire failure mode the variable exists to prevent, guarding a secret scanner among others. The row text was already honest in every case; only the exit code lied, and the exit code is the half a `&&` reads.
- **The core now answers the question instead of asking the adapter.** `_validator_gate_did_not_run` keys on the two things the core constructed itself — the `no_verdict` marker on a `_validator_unusable_reply`, and `timeout` — and consults `$SUPERTOOL_REQUIRE_VALIDATORS` through the core's own `_validator_required`. The core watched each of these five happen; it does not need the cooperation of the process that failed in order to know that it did. The row reads `NOT CHECKED  (no verdict about this file)` with an `adapter` or `orchestrator` reason line, the validator is named on the `[result]` line, and the call exits 1.
- **Scope is the breakdowns the core observed, not every skip.** `warm_unsafe` ([#345](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/345)), an out-of-scope path ([#263](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/263)) and a resolver that maps a file to nothing are a healthy adapter declining on its own terms, and nothing in the reason string distinguishes them from a broken one — hence the core-internal `no_verdict` key rather than prose matching. Escalating those under `'*'` would fire on ordinary edits nobody meant to gate, which is a gate that cries wolf: the quiet bug traded for a louder one rather than fixed. An adapter that is genuinely absent still escalates through `refusal.required()`, as before.
- **Still an exit code, still not a refusal, still not a rollback.** The write lands, and an edit is never reverted by a checker that formed no opinion about it — [#967](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/pull/967)'s judgment call and [#969](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/969)'s, unchanged. Unset the variable and none of this is reachable: every one of the five is the honest `skipped` it always was and exit stays 0.
- **The core's reader of the variable is a deliberate second implementation of `refusal.required()`**, because that twin lives in the package adapters import inside their own subprocess, and a gate that stops working when a `sys.path` resolution does is not a gate. `tests/test_require_validators_core_975.py` executes `validators/common/refusal.py` and pins the two to the same answers across thirteen env-var shapes plus the `os.pathsep` form, so the copy cannot drift into a second rule.

- **A line range handed to `between` now names the op that answers it, and a correct range read is no longer told it was wrong** ([#983](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/983)). Two halves of the same defect: the op that cannot do ranges pointed nowhere, and the op that can do them called its own caller mistaken.

  `between` is `SYMBOL:PATH`, so `between:file.py:12420:12700` tokenized `12700` as the path and failed with `ERROR: path not found: '12700'` — a filesystem complaint about a number, which is the tokenizer's own mis-split wearing the shape of an absence on disk. Since the path token held a colon it then reached the payload hint and advised a `between:@-` TOML body, which cannot fix a line range either. Three agents in one evening read that as "supertool cannot do this" and fell back to `sed` or the harness `Read`. The error now says `between does not take line ranges` and names `read:PATH:START-END` with the caller's own numbers substituted in; the single-token case, `between:file.py:12420`, names `around_line:PATH:LINE[:N]` as well. No new op and no new form: `between` still does exactly one thing, and the redirect only fires when the numeric token is not itself a real path and the path in front of it resolves — otherwise this would be guessing at an ordinary typo.

  The range form it points at, `read:PATH:START-END`, has shipped since 0.19.0 and was being actively discouraged by the tool. A successful `read:supertool.py:16116-16120` closed with `OFFSET is a skip count, not a start line — for lines 16115-16119 use read:supertool.py:16115-16119`: a lecture about a form the caller did not use, naming a span one line off from the one they asked for. The window note only ever sees the OFFSET the range was already converted into, so it could not tell the two spellings apart; it is now told which one was typed. The disclosure itself is unchanged — a range read still states the window it returned — and the offset form still gets the correction it was written for.

- **Re-running an applied payload now says the replacement is already in the file, instead of printing what a broken anchor prints** ([#984](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/984)). Two states a caller most needs to tell apart — "this already applied" and "this anchor never matched" — shared one message, `ERROR: old string not found`, and the reader could not recover which from it. The remedies are opposite: one means stop, the other means find a new anchor.

  `edit` now checks whether the text it was going to write is present, and says where:

  ```text
  ERROR: old string not found in a.py
    ↳ the replacement text is ALREADY present at line 12 — this looks like a re-run of an edit that already applied, not a broken anchor
  ```

  A located fact, not a verdict. The `ERROR` stands, the op is still counted in `K skipped`, and the call still exits non-zero — downgrading a failure because it is probably benign is how a loud bug becomes a quiet one.

  This is the half of the re-run problem that `re-applied` (#701) does not reach. That signal fires when `new` contains `old`, so the anchor survives its own edit and the payload applies a second time. When `new` does not contain `old`, the second run matches nothing and there was no signal at all. The other two halves the issue reported had already shipped and were verified against the tracker before this was written: the batch footer has carried `K skipped` at the very bottom, below the validators and surviving `| tail -1`, since #680, and the re-apply disclosure since #701.

- **The coverage gate no longer exempts itself from the coverage gate** ([#991](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/991)). `.github/scripts/` was measured on every run, printed in the report, and floored by nothing — it could go to zero without reddening a build. It now carries two floors: 92% on `.github/scripts/coverage_gate.py` by name, and 92% on the rest of the directory.

  Two entries and not one because the measurement is what decided it. The bucket read 82.65%, made of `assemble_changelog.py` at 93.95%, `junit_summary.py` at 94.12%, and **the gate itself at 46.43%** — the least covered thing the gate measured was the gate. A single floor on the bucket average is the arrangement in which the two tested files pay for the untested one, which is the argument `coverage_gate.py` already makes for giving `_supertool.py` and `presets/` separate floors, applied one level down.

  What the 46% was hiding matters more than the number: `report()` had no test at all. The function that decides pass from fail, the branch that turns "nothing was measured" into a failure rather than a 0% that clears a floor of 0, and the stale-floor advisory were all uncovered, along with `measure()` and `main()`'s reporting path. `report()` could have been changed to `return 0` unconditionally and all twelve pytest legs would have stayed green. The refusal branches added in #877 were, by contrast, the covered part.

  `tests/test_coverage_gate_floor_991.py` covers the verdict function — a below-floor bucket returns 1, each floor fires on its own bucket with the others at 100%, an unmeasured bucket fails rather than passing, the advisory fires past `_SLACK` and stays quiet inside it — and the floors above were measured after those tests existed rather than pinning the accident of the day.

  The floor found something on its first real run against master, which is the argument for it in one line: `.github/scripts/` measured 91.07% because `check_links()` — the `--check-links` arm added days earlier, the function that turns the link-ref audit into a receipt and one of three exit statuses — had no test at all. The audit beneath it was covered thoroughly; the arm that reports it was not, so it could have returned `ok` for every input and the suite would not have noticed. Covered now in `tests/test_changelog_link_refs_918.py`, rather than by lowering the floor to accommodate it.

  Prefix matching is longest-match now rather than first-match, in `classify()` and `_bucket_key()` alike. With a file entry and the directory containing it both declared, first-match made the verdict depend on dict insertion order: reordering the literal for readability would have moved the gate onto the directory floor and printed a number that looked just as convincing.

- **`dashboard`'s lane board matched a prefix no label in this repository uses, so every lane was unplaced and the section was inert** ([#1007](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1007)). `LANE_PREFIX` was hardcoded to `lane:`, read out of the *title* of [#964](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/964) — an issue whose entire subject is a colon that appears in no label name. The seven labels here are `lane-watch`, `lane-release`, … so the universe came back empty, every row rendered `lane ?`, and the footer read `0 lanes free, 0 occupied, 0 unknown` beside six open PRs and thirteen live worktrees.

  **The vocabulary is configuration now, and unconfigured refuses.** `ops.dashboard.lane_prefix` in `.supertool.json`, with no default and deliberately so — `claude-supertool` spells lanes `lane-watch` while `claude-remember` spells priorities `priority:high`, same organisation and opposite convention, so a literal that is right here is wrong one repository away. Absent, the lanes section prints `!! unread`, names the key, and the footer reads `lanes UNCONFIGURED`: the property `radar_tiers` was given in [#528](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/528), because a prefix nobody chose selects zero labels and zero labels reads exactly like a repository with nothing in flight.

  **An empty lane universe is its own state, which is the part that would have caught this on the first run.** A configured prefix matching nothing and a repository that genuinely declares no lanes rendered identically as a tally of zeroes; the first is a defect and the second is fine. The section is now `!! degraded` and says `no label matches 'lane:', so the lane universe is empty and no lane can be reported free`, names the labels sharing its stem behind a different separator, and suggests the spelling — as a suggestion the reader applies, never a fallback the op applies for them, since silently retrying the other separator would rebuild the guess this removes. The footer has four shapes and none is `0, 0, 0`: a real tally, `lanes UNREAD`, `lanes UNCONFIGURED`, `lane universe EMPTY`.

  **What already worked was kept and is now pinned.** Under the total failure the op never reported a lane free: it said `unplaced`, printed `'unknown' is NOT 'free'`, and declined in `next:`. That is why this was a `priority-high` bug and not a two-agents-one-file incident, and a test now fails if it is traded away for a tidier board.

  **The false measurement is gone.** `dashboard.py` and `docs/presets/dashboard.md` both asserted "Measured on this repository on 2026-08-07: 7 `lane:*` labels exist". Seven lane labels do exist; not one is spelled that way. Both now cite the spelling the tracker actually returns, and a test fails on any re-appearance of `lane:*` in either file.

- **`git-push:watch` reported "Watching →" for a watcher that had refused to start** ([#1010](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1010)). `_spawn_watch` was fire-and-forget: `Popen` with stdout *and* stderr on `DEVNULL`, and `True` returned the instant the call did not raise. The `watch` op names its own refusals — an unknown source, a pid-file slot it could not claim, and on Windows an `os.fork` that does not exist — by exiting non-zero and saying so on stdout, and every one of those went into `DEVNULL` underneath a receipt line announcing coverage that had never been established. It now waits for the spawned op to exit (bounded, and cheap: the process being waited on is not the poller — `watch` claims the slot, detaches a grandchild and returns) and has **three outcomes, not two**: started, *not* started with the child's own reason quoted, or `UNKNOWN` when the op outlived the budget. The timed-out child is left running rather than killed, because it may already have detached a working poller, and the receipt says plainly that it is neither claiming one exists nor claiming one does not.

  **This is also the red Windows leg.** `test_watch_spawns_through_supertool_py_when_the_wrapper_is_missing` failed as `assert '' == 'watch:gitlab-mr:42'` on `windows-latest, 3.12` and nowhere else, on two open PRs that share no files. Neither branch caused it and neither did the entry-point shim: the test file and `presets/git/push.py` are byte-identical across commits where that leg is green and commits where it is red, and the shim is not an ancestor of either branch. The spawn was asynchronous, so the test waited for the sentinel file to *exist* and then read it — and on Windows a file exists from `CreateFile`, before a byte of its payload lands. The empty read was the tool's own race arriving as if it were the watcher's answer. With the spawn waiting for its child there is no window to lose, and the test now reads the sentinel with no polling at all, so a return to fire-and-forget fails it immediately on every platform.

- **`radar` printed 3 PR rows under a footer reading `6 open | 2 failing | 4 running`, and nothing said the other three had been elided** ([#1022](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1022)). `gh-prs`, run from the same directory seconds later, returned all six. Nothing was lost in the fetch: both tiers render a *delta* board after the first tick — rows that moved since the previous snapshot, plus standing problems — while the footer tallies the whole open population. `running` is not a standing problem, so three ordinary open PRs that had simply not changed since the previous tick dropped off a board that still counted them. A partial board is strictly harder to notice than an empty one, because it looks like a working board.

  **Rendered rows plus elided rows now equal the population the footer prints.** Every open PR or MR lands in exactly one of `shown` and `elided`; the footer carries an `N unchanged not shown` token so the arithmetic can be checked against the rows above it, and a partial board names the rows it held back:

  ```
  radar: NOTE — 3 of 6 open PRs are not on the board: unchanged since the previous
  run and not a standing problem (#1004, #956, #1018). The footer counts all 6, so
  rows plus 'unchanged not shown' is the whole population; `gh-prs` prints every row.
  ```

  A count a reader cannot resolve back to a PR is not a disclosure, so the identifiers are named and not merely tallied — capped at twelve, with the remainder counted.

  **The elision itself is kept.** A running PR that has not moved since the last tick is genuinely no news, and re-printing it every tick is how a board trains its reader to skim — which is the failure mode standing exclusions already exist to prevent. What was wrong was the silence, not the choice.

  **Both tiers had it, so both are fixed.** `gl-mrs` carries the identical construct and elided identically; the disclosure lives once, in `tiers/_snapshot.py`, next to the delta store whose consequence it is. The `gl-mrs` footer gained the same token, which changes one exact-match line: `radar: no change | … | 1 watched | 1 unchanged not shown | feed ok`.

  **Three existing tests asserted the defect.** They checked that a suppressed row's identifier appeared nowhere in the output at all, which makes "this row was suppressed" and "this row was suppressed silently" the same assertion. They now assert the row is absent from the printed rows *and* named in the disclosure.

- **A payload whose ''' literal block carries `\\` is now named before the ops run, instead of landing bytes nobody wrote and reporting `edited`** ([#1027](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1027)). TOML triple-single-quoted literals process no escapes, so `\\d` in a payload is backslash-backslash-d. When the doubling is in `old` the anchor cannot match and the runner reports the skip — that half was already safe. When it is in `new`, the anchor matches, the write lands, the receipt says `edited`, and every validator agrees, because two backslashes are legal in nearly every language this tool edits. The wrong bytes reached disk and nothing anywhere said so.

  ```text
  ⚠ payload: a ''' literal block carries `\\`. A literal block processes NO escapes, so each pair reaches the file as TWO backslashes -- if you meant one, write one.
    ↳ `new` (1 occurrence): PAT = re.compile("\\d+")
  ```

  **It warns and never rewrites.** Collapsing `\\` to `\` would guess at intent, and some payloads want two characters; a wrong guess in the write path is worse than the bug, because the caller loses even the ability to read the bytes back and see what they asked for. The message says so in as many words, so the receipt cannot be read as a correction.

  **It warns rather than refusing**, which is where it parts from #834 and #835. Those fire at a fixed position — immediately before the closing quotes, at the end of a shell line — and there every reading has a second spelling, so a refusal strands nothing. This pattern has no position at all: a payload that legitimately writes a pair does so at an arbitrary offset, and refusing would make that unwritable everywhere.

  The line between signal and noise sits at exactly two places. A `"""basic"""` block is never flagged, because there `\\` *is* one backslash and is the correct spelling — a guard that fired on it would fire on its own remedy. A run of three or more is never flagged, because it was counted rather than produced by reflex. It is deliberately **not** narrowed to escape-looking sequences: the reported cases were `\\d`, `\\302` and `\\n`, and `\d` and `\302` are not TOML escapes, so the reflex is generic rather than TOML-specific and any escape set narrow enough to filter would miss the report it was written for. Measured instead — 710 of 208854 lines in this repository carry a `\\`, 0.34%, in the pathological corpus whose densest files are tests about backslash handling.

- **`batch:` now prints its `[result]` count above the first op as well as below the validators** ([#1027](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1027)). The footer is separated from the per-op results by a validators block long enough that `| tail` ends on `git-status : ok`, which reads as success — so a non-zero `K skipped` was the one number a reader was most likely to miss. The footer is unchanged and `[branch: X]` still ends the output; the leading copy costs one line and makes the count visible with no filter. Scoped to `batch:`, because a single op's receipt is three lines with the footer already adjacent to them. This is the half of #984 that #1018 marked `Part of` and left unbuilt; #1018 itself shipped the rollback wording and the already-applied hint, both verified against the tracker before this was written.

- **`gl-api` sent your GitLab token to any host the path named** ([#1035](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/1035)). `path_refusal()` refused four shapes — empty, flag-shaped, whitespace, `graphql` — and the value then went to `glab api --method GET` verbatim. `glab api` accepts an absolute URL as its endpoint and attaches the instance's `Private-Token` header to it, so `gl-api:http://127.0.0.1:8765/leak` handed a live personal access token to a listener the *input* chose, rendered the listener's reply as an ordinary result and printed `PASS` over it. `:full` repeated the request on every page. The input is not hypothetically remote: a path can arrive out of an issue body, an MR description or a CI job name, all of which this repo already treats as text a stranger wrote.

  **A path may not name a host**, and that is now an allowlist of what a GitLab API path may contain rather than a denylist of schemes — a denylist has to enumerate every spelling of `http` and is one new scheme, one casing and one encoder behind forever. Refused: a scheme at the front in any casing and with or without the `//` after it (`http:host` is opaque-but-absolute and glab takes it too); a `//` anywhere in the path portion, which is what a protocol-relative `//evil.host/x` and a userinfo `//gitlab.com@evil.host/x` both need; a backslash, which the parsers that disagree fold into `/`; and any character outside RFC 3986's `pchar` plus `/`, which is what takes out control bytes, `#` and `<`. All three structural checks run a second time against the percent-decoded value, so `http%3A%2F%2Fevil.host` and `%2F%2Fevil.host` do not smuggle past the first pass. Because nothing can name a host, every request still resolves against the instance glab is configured for, without supertool having to read glab's config to find out which one that is.

  **Refused, never sanitised** — the same argument the op's docstring already made about `-X POST`. Stripping the scheme would send *a* request, and its answer would read as the one the caller asked for. The refusal names the value and which of the four structural facts it tripped, in the shape the existing refusals use.

  The breakage budget is pinned too, because a rule this shape is only worth having if real paths survive it: `projects/:id/members/all` and every other glab `:placeholder`, a leading `/`, percent-encoded group paths (`projects/group%2Fsub%2Fproj/issues`), query strings including GitLab's own bracket filters (`?not[labels]=bug`), ISO timestamps with their colons, npm scoped packages (`packages/npm/@scope/name`) and percent-encoded `@` in a search value all still go through unchanged.

  **What this does not cover, stated rather than implied.** A GitLab-hosted path that answers with a redirect, or a `Link` header under `--paginate`, is followed by glab and not by supertool — Go's client strips `Authorization` across hosts but not a custom `Private-Token` — so the guarantee is about the host supertool asks for, not about every host glab may end up talking to.

  Swept the siblings for the same shape: `gl-api` was the only op putting a caller-supplied string in an endpoint position with no fixed prefix in front of it. `gl-mr`, `gl-job`, `gl-pipeline`, `gl-runners`, `gl-issue`, `gl-mrs`, `gh-star`, `gh-follow`, `gh-check`, `gh-job`, `gh-branch` and `_declared_legs` all interpolate into a path that begins with a literal segment (`projects/:id/…`, `repos/{owner}/{repo}/…`, `user/starred/…`), where a scheme cannot reach column zero.

- An adapter could switch off `rollback_on_fail` by printing `"timeout": true`
  in its own result. The core reads that flag to mean "the checker never
  answered", which since #969 correctly suppresses rollback — but the flag is
  the core's own, stamped by the arm that watched a subprocess exceed its
  budget, and nothing stopped an adapter from setting it. A real finding wearing
  it rendered as `NOT CHECKED` and the bad write stood. Every key the core owns
  (`timeout`, `no_verdict`, `elapsed_s`, `resolved_to`) is now dropped from an
  adapter's payload at the one point it enters the core, and the adapter's own
  `ok` / `count` / `errors` are left untouched. Its message also no longer
  prints under the `orchestrator` provenance column, which exists to mark text
  the core wrote.

- `cargo-check` charged another crate's compile error to the file under
  validation, which on a `rollback_on_fail` validator reverted a correct edit
  over a defect it never touched. The path-suffix match #754 introduced had no
  floor: a one-segment target matched any file of that basename anywhere in the
  tree, and the raw `{file}` argument was compared in whatever relative form the
  caller typed, so `vendor/crates/foo/src/main.rs` and `crates/foo/src/main.rs`
  were "the same file". A suffix now has to be at least two segments, and every
  form of the target is anchored to the working directory before comparison.
  cargo's own path stays a free tail — it is relative to the workspace root, and
  joining it onto the crate root is the demotion #754 exists to prevent.

- The validator cache was a second way into #1036. `_validator_run_one` returns
  a cache hit before it reaches the point where an adapter's payload is stripped
  of the keys the core owns, so an entry written by any build from before that
  fix carried the adapter's `"timeout": true` verbatim. Nothing retired those
  entries: the cache is signed with this machine's own secret, so a stale entry
  verifies, and its key is `content ‖ name ‖ cmd ‖ tool-fingerprint` with no
  supertool version in it, so upgrading does not miss it. Inside
  `validator_cache_ttl_hours` (default 24, `0` meaning forever) a real finding
  came back out of the cache wearing a timeout the core never observed, the row
  read `NOT CHECKED`, `rollback_on_fail` did not run and the bad edit stood. The
  cache read now strips the same keys the fresh path does, and re-stamps the two
  the core owns for the run in hand — `elapsed_s` is the lookup that just
  happened, `resolved_to` is the target just resolved — rather than replaying a
  cached copy of either.

### Security

- The coverage gate no longer keeps its scratch data at a fixed, world-guessable
  path in the system temp directory. `.github/scripts/coverage_gate.py` wrote
  `coverage_gate.ini` to `<tmp>/supertool-coverage-gate/` with
  `mkdir(exist_ok=True)` and no ownership, symlink or mode check, then ran
  `coverage run --rcfile=` against it and exported it as
  `COVERAGE_PROCESS_START` to every child process. A coverage rcfile can declare
  `plugins =`, which coverage imports — so on a shared-`/tmp` machine another
  local process could pre-create or symlink that path and have its own code run
  inside the gate that decides whether the release's coverage floors pass. The
  directory is now `<repo>/.coverage-gate/`, created at mode 0700 with the
  rcfile at 0600, which keeps `--report` working (the path is still stable) and
  makes it per-checkout rather than shared by every worktree on the machine. Not
  exploitable on the single-tenant GitHub runner; the gate is documented as
  locally runnable, which is where it mattered.
- The coverage gate refuses instead of degrading when it cannot write that
  config. A symlinked or uncreatable scratch directory, or a failed write, now
  prints `coverage gate: REFUSED` and exits 2 without reaching the report — a
  third state alongside pass (0) and floor-failure (1). With no config there is
  no coverage data, every bucket totals zero statements, and a zero prints the
  same as a directory that genuinely holds no code.
- `.github/workflows/tests.yml` declares `permissions: contents: read`. It
  checks out, installs and runs tests, and publishes nothing; with no block the
  token got whatever the repository default happened to be, and that default is
  a settings page that can widen without touching this file.

- **A runner description or a job ref can no longer become a line `gl-runners` appears to have written.** Same mechanism as #965 — an API-supplied string reaching `print()` without `_untrusted.flat`, and `str.splitlines()` breaking on one of the ten separators #886 widened `flat()` to cover — on the three hand-padded blocks this op renders: the fleet table (`{description[:22]:<22}`, `{tags[:34]}`), the queue view (`{name:<44} {ref:<24} on {runner}`), and the STARVED / UNKNOWN diagnosis, where a description is interpolated into the sentence naming which hosts a reader should go and check. A GitLab runner description is set by whoever registered the runner and a job's `ref` and `tag_list` by whoever can push a branch, so all three are a stranger's text. Twenty renders across `_print_fleet`, `_owner_names`, `_print_diagnosis`, `_print_queue`, `_print_full` and `radar_report` now flatten.
- **What the payload could forge here is a row, not just a line.** None of these blocks goes through `_board.render_row`, which flattens every cell it is handed — they pad with f-string field widths, which is why the defect exists at all. The text after the separator is unconstrained, so it can be spaced to the widths of the block it lands in and read as something the tool emitted: a runner that is not in the fleet, a `3 live runner(s)` verdict against a tag that has none, or — the case in the test — the `Queue: 1 pending, all have a responsive runner` all-clear rendered underneath a queue the op had just reported `## STARVED`. Nothing in this op feeds a merge decision, which is why #968 left it out of a release blocker; it feeds an operational one, and this tracker already records a misleading process view getting two live watchers killed, one of them the one that was needed.
- **Flatten, then truncate — the order is the fix, not an implementation detail.** The fleet table slices its cells to the column width. `flat()` can *widen* a field, because a stream that cannot carry U+2028 spells it `[U+2028]`, eight characters for one (#863), so flattening a cell already cut to 22 trades a row that splits for a row that overflows into the next column. Slicing last keeps `:<22` a width rather than a floor. The queue view has no such slice and is deliberately not given one: cutting a job name to 44 characters to protect an alignment shows the reader a different job's name while they are deciding which job is stuck, which is a visibly ragged row traded for a quietly wrong one. A long job name already pushes that column with no hostile input involved, and the rows around it are independent `print()` calls that are unaffected.
- **The #965 scanner now answers for `ref`, and still for nothing that is not a refname.** `presets/gitlab/runners.py` was already inside `test_no_preset_prints_a_refname_raw`'s three scanned trees; what it was outside of was the key set, so the build was green. `ref` was added on the test the set was built to pass rather than on it sounding like a refname: it names exactly the two `gl-runners:queue` sites and nothing else in those trees, so the set still needs no exemption. `name` was not added and the `title`/`name`/`login` widening **rejected** in #968 stays rejected — `name` alone adds an `mr.py` hit that is a CI job name, and keeping the scan green past it would take the per-field allowlist that is the failure mode the scanner exists to avoid. The remaining fields here are pinned by `tests/test_forged_runner_line_970.py`, which asserts the post-condition per mode: no forged line, and the render is the same height as the same fleet with the separator replaced by a space.
## [0.26.0] - 2026-08-07

### Added

- **`tests.yml` caches pip and bun installs instead of pip-installing from cold on every one of its 15+ legs** ([#890](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/890)). Every `actions/setup-python` step now sets `cache: pip` with `cache-dependency-path: pyproject.toml`. A bare `cache: 'pip'` was tried and rejected: the action's default dependency-file glob is `**/requirements.txt`, this repo ships none, and the step fails outright with "No file matched" — redding the whole board. `pyproject.toml` only works as the cache key because every job's install step was rewritten from a hand-typed `pip install pytest pytest-cov ...` list to `pip install -e .[dev]`, so the hash actually tracks what gets installed; hashing it against the old hand-typed list would have been a stale-cache bug wearing a fix's clothes. The notifiers job's separate `bun install --frozen-lockfile` gets its own `actions/cache` step keyed on `hashFiles('notifiers/claude-channel/bun.lock')`, honest the same way since that lockfile is real and committed.

  Pinned by `tests/test_ci_pip_cache_890.py`, which reads the workflow structurally (`tests/_workflow_parse.py`, extended here with a `with:` field on `Step` alongside the existing `env`) rather than by substring, for the same reason `test_ci_job_timeouts_722.py` and `test_ci_non_python_coverage_557.py` already do (#731): a comment can say anything and move no assertion.

- **`map` reads markdown: `.md` and `.markdown` render their heading tree** ([#887](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/887)). `# Title` becomes `h1 Title  [1]` and each level indents one step further, so `map:CHANGELOG.md` now answers with the section list and line numbers a caller needs before reaching for `between:`. It is a `_TS_LANG_MAP` entry plus a heading walker over the tree-sitter `markdown` grammar `tree_sitter_language_pack` already ships — not a fourth hand-written regex tier, which would have been a second implementation of something the grammar knows and would have counted `#` inside fenced code blocks as headings. Setext headings (`Title` over `=====`) are covered by the same grammar.

  **`read:` is deliberately unaffected.** Giving `.md` a grammar would otherwise have enrolled markdown in abstract read, so a large `README.md` would come back as its table of contents. A signature list stands in for the function body it heads; a heading does not stand in for the prose it heads. `_ABSTRACT_READ_SKIP_LANGS` states that exemption in one place, and a test pins that code is still abstracted.

  **Directory maps now include markdown**, since `.md` joins the extension set `map` walks — a repo map shows `README.md` and `docs/*.md` alongside code. On docs-heavy trees this consumes more of the 100-file cap than before.

  **The walker is tested where no grammar exists, against a recording rather than an invention.** CI installs no tree-sitter package, so every test that parses real markdown skips there and the new extraction logic would have shipped on local greens alone — the coverage floor in `.github/scripts/coverage_gate.py` is what turned that from invisible into a red job. `_ts_extract_markdown` only touches `.type`, `.children`, `.start_point` and the byte offsets, so it runs against a replay object; the tuple it replays was **recorded from the real grammar's output**, not composed by hand, and three guards re-derive it from the real parser wherever the grammar is present — full tree-shape equality, identical extraction from replay and parser, and a check that the recording invents no node type the grammar never emits. A hand-built tree that quietly stopped describing the grammar would be a test asserting its author's fiction, which is worse than the gap it closes.

- **A `shellcheck` validator — shell semantics, where `bash -n` only ever answered "does this parse"** ([#665](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/665)). `shellcheck -f json`, ruleset resolved from the project's own `.shellcheckrc`, `rollback_on_fail: false`. `bash-check` stays: it is in-process-cheap and it is what still runs where shellcheck is not installed. An absent `shellcheck` reports `skipped` with the install hint, never `ok`.

  **The receipt in the issue does not hold, and the docs now say so.** #665 justifies the validator with `claude-remember#251` and calls it "SC2015 verbatim". Measured against ShellCheck 0.11.0, SC2015 does not fire on that line at any severity, with every optional check enabled — the rule carries a deliberate carve-out for an `|| echo`/`|| printf` branch, and the redirect on that `echo` is what made the bug destructive. So this validator would not have caught the bug it was filed for. `tests/test_validators_shellcheck_665.py::test_the_issues_own_receipt_is_not_caught` pins the gap, so a future ShellCheck that closes the carve-out fails the test and corrects the documentation in the same pull request.

  What does fire, and is exercised on real files rather than assumed: SC2164 (`cd` without `|| exit`), SC2086 (unquoted expansion), SC2181 (`$?` instead of testing directly) and SC2155 (`local x=$(cmd)` masking an exit code).

- **`SUPERTOOL_REQUIRE_VALIDATORS` — a skip that CI can refuse to accept** ([#665](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/665)). The three new validators all wrap external binaries most machines lack, and `skipped` on every run of every job is how a validator becomes decorative. Naming one in this variable turns "the tool is not installed" from a third state into a loud `adapter` error whose message names the variable, so the reader is sent to the CI image rather than to the file. Comma- or `os.pathsep`-separated, case-insensitive, `*` for all. It only ever turns quiet into loud — there is deliberately no value that turns a finding into a skip.

- **An `eslint` validator — JavaScript semantics were entirely unchecked** ([#667](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/667)). `eslint -f json`, global binary or `npx --no-install`, `rollback_on_fail: false`. Before this, a plain `.js` file got syntax (`node-check`), formatting (`prettier-check`) and nothing else: no unused variables, no `==` versus `===`, no unreachable code, no shadowed declarations.

  **Three ways eslint says nothing, and all three used to read as a clean file.** The tool not installed; the tool installed with no resolvable config, which exits 2 with an *empty stdout* and the explanation on stderr; and — the one the issue does not mention, verified against eslint 10.8.0 — a file matching an ignore pattern, which exits **zero** and returns a single `ruleId: null` message saying it was ignored. All three now report `skipped` with the reason.

  **No fallback configuration is shipped, and that is the decision rather than an omission.** Inventing one would have the validator enforce rules the project never adopted, and the first thing anyone does about findings they did not opt into is switch the validator off. It would also be misleading for the case that motivated the issue: the "never `var`" rule mostly governs JavaScript inside XML templates and inline handlers, which eslint cannot reach at all, so a fallback would produce a green that says nothing about the rule it was configured for. A repository that wants JavaScript linted adds `eslint.config.js`; until then the row states on every edit that nobody checked.

- **A `gitleaks` secret-scanning validator — thirty validators and none of them looked for a credential** ([#668](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/668)). `gitleaks detect --no-git --redact` on the edited file, no `match` glob because a credential is not a property of a file type. This is the one check whose absence is a disclosure problem rather than a quality one: a pushed secret is a rotated secret.

  **The finding never carries the value, and neither does anything written on the way to it.** gitleaks' report holds the secret in cleartext and `--report-path` is the only route to JSON, so the naive adapter writes the credential to disk before deciding not to print it. Three layers: `--redact`, so the value never reaches the report; a `mkdtemp` at mode `0700` removed in a `finally`, so no report survives a crash; and no `source_context` on the error, because the source line *is* the secret and a validator receipt is a terminal, a log and an agent transcript at once. The rule id, line and description are what a reader needs to act. `tests/test_validators_gitleaks_668.py` asserts this against the whole serialised payload, so a future field cannot reintroduce it quietly.

  **`rollback_on_fail` is `false`, against the issue's own suggestion.** Reverting does not unpublish anything — the value reached the edit from a payload, a paste or a context window, all of which still hold it — while it does destroy everything else the edit contained. And a `--no-git` scan of this repository returns 12 findings of which 12 are test fixtures, so rollback would have reverted real work over fake keys, which is the fastest route to the validator being switched off. The finding stays fully loud; only the destructive auto-revert is off.

  **False positives are suppressed per line, never per directory.** A trailing `gitleaks:allow` comment is one line, lands in the diff and says nothing about the next line. The lever deliberately not shipped is an `exclude` glob over `tests/` or `docs/`: it turns the check off invisibly and permanently for exactly the paths most likely to grow a real credential, and a silenced scanner looks identical to one finding nothing. A test pins the absence of that glob.

- **radar can watch a GitHub PR board** ([#859](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/859)). `presets/watch/tiers/` held exactly one tier and it spoke GitLab, so the board this repository is actually merged from was the one population radar could not see. Register `gh-prs` like any other tier:

  ```json
  { "ops": { "radar": { "radar_tiers": { "gh-prs": {} } } } }
  ```

  One `gh pr list` call builds the board — GitHub returns the check rollup and the review decision on the list response, so there is no per-PR enrichment wave — and the rows are `gh-prs` rows, so the board, the op and `gl-mrs` cannot drift apart.

  **The repository's default branch is a board member.** A green PR is a statement about its merge base, and nothing watches `master` after a squash lands; the row composes `gh-branch`'s own four states (`GREEN` / `NOT GREEN` / `NO RUN` / `UNKNOWN`) rather than a second, weaker verdict. `default_branch` names the ref, `""` switches the member off, and absent resolves the repo's own.

  **It is a parallel tier rather than `gl-mrs` generalised**, because three of the four things that tier does do not transfer: there is no `github-pr-feed` source, so new PRs are found on the next radar tick and the footer says `discovery: radar ticks only`; drift has no analogue, since a PR's identity under a re-push is its head SHA and not a pipeline id; and watch state is keyed by PR number with no repository. What does transfer is the snapshot, which moved to `presets/watch/tiers/_snapshot.py` and is now read by both tiers — keeping a previous board keyed by the population it describes is not a GitLab argument, and a second copy of it is how a fixed defect comes back.

  **The one-filter invariant gains a clause on GitHub.** Board and watcher fleet still come from one resolved filter, and that filter must describe one repository: under a repo target a live poller for `#12` cannot be told apart from `#12` of the clone it was started in ([#673](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/673)), so coverage renders as `watch coverage UNKNOWN` and nothing is healed. Zero watched would be a number a reader acts on, and healing on it would be an action taken on a misidentification.

  **Every route by which the board could narrow itself says so.** A filter token the tier cannot honour is refused before any call, because `gh pr list` silently ignores an unrecognised key and would otherwise return the whole unfiltered board reading as "everything matched". An auth failure or rate limit raises, exits non-zero and snapshots nothing. A filter that matched nothing is reported with its scope rather than as "no open PRs". A PR with an empty check rollup is counted `unchecked`, never green. And a PR the board calls green — the only claim that can be wrong in the expensive direction — is reconciled against the legs its runs declare through `gh-pr`'s own machinery ([#724](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/724), [#804](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/804), [#837](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/837)), consumed and never re-implemented; a shortfall marks the row `[legs UNVERIFIED]` and counts as unchecked. The tier prints no leg count of its own.

- **`radar:--state` looks at the tiers without spawning anything** ([#859](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/859)). `radar` heals, and healing forks pollers, so inspecting this subsystem used to cost the same as acting on it — and the result was hours of not inspecting it. The read-only view reports which module each registered name resolved to, the options it accepted, the ones it did not recognise, and, for a tier exposing the new optional `radar_state(options)` hook, its resolved scope, its snapshot file and its live pollers. Both shipped tiers implement it; everything comes from files already on disk and no API is called.

  It is an argument rather than its own op deliberately: `ops.radar.radar_tiers` merges into the op it is keyed by, so a second op name would need a second copy of the tier list — and a read-only view describing a different tier set from the one radar runs is precisely the defect it exists to remove. A tier with no `radar_state()` says so, rather than rendering as an empty block that reads as healthy.

- **`gh-prs` now fetches `headRefOid`** ([#859](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/859)). Not rendered; it is what the radar tier keys its delta on. A push that lands a new head commit re-runs everything, and without the SHA a `failed → failed` transition across two different commits reads as "no change" — a missed event on a board a maintainer merges from. One extra field on a response already being fetched.

- **`gh-issues` carries the milestone, and can ask for its absence** ([#864](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/864)). Every release tick starts with a milestone query, and the board could answer neither half of it — so each one paid for a raw `gh issue list --json … --jq` fallback plus a second call to re-acquire the labels the op gives for free.

  **The milestone is a flag, not a column.** A column costs its width on every row of every board, and most issues on most repos carry no milestone, so a reserved cell would be mostly blank space taken from the title. It rides in the flags slot beside `[stale]` instead — `[m:v0.26.0]` when there is one, nothing at all when there is not. `[m:?]` is the third state and is load-bearing rather than decorative: `gh issue list --json milestone` returns an explicit null for an unmilestoned issue, so a missing key means the field did not come back, and rendering that as blank would assert "unscheduled" about an issue nobody asked GitHub about.

  **`nomilestone` is the gap query, and it declines rather than guessing.** `gh issue list` can name a milestone; it cannot ask for the absence of one, so the filter runs client-side over the fetched rows. That makes a row whose milestone did not come back unplaceable — keeping it reports a scheduled issue as unscheduled, dropping it hides exactly the kind of gap the query exists to find — so the op declines and names the field, the way `external` and `stale` already do.

- **`gh-pr:N:diff` and `gh-pr:N:diff:PATH` — a PR's diff in the shape a reviewer walks it** ([#875](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/875)). Every read a PR supports was covered — state, tally, mergeability, branch, linked issues, job logs — except the one the merge decision actually rests on, so every review fell back to raw `gh pr diff` piped through a hand-written filter. `gh-pr:N:status` reports that the suite is green, and a green suite is exactly what the review rule says proves nothing: the op surface covered the check you are told not to trust and omitted the check you are told to do yourself.

  **The raw command is also the wrong shape.** An eighty-file mechanical sweep carries four files of judgment, and reading it whole is not a review, it is a context burn. `:diff` returns the file list with per-file line deltas, heaviest first; `:diff:PATH` returns that one file's hunks, fenced as the stranger's text a branch diff is. Same two-step walk `gh-job` already models with `:fail` / `:raw:-N` / `:grep:PATTERN`, in the same preset family.

  **Heaviest first rather than grouped by kind, deliberately.** `git-diff` groups its file list with a path classifier private to its own preset; copying that here would create the second definition that lets the two drift, which is the failure the shared check-tally and board-layout modules exist to prevent. Churn-descending needs no shared vocabulary and is the order a reviewer takes anyway.

  **`[same edit xN]` is a note and never a filter.** A file whose every hunk is byte-identical after stripping whitespace is flagged so attention goes elsewhere; it is never removed from the list and never shortened. The test is exact equality rather than similarity, because under-flagging costs a reviewer nothing and a wrong "mechanical" verdict is an invitation to skim the file that needed reading.

  **Three states, because this renders inside the merge gate.** A diff nobody could fetch prints a named refusal and exits 1, never an empty file list — "this PR changes nothing" is the worst available lie at the moment someone is deciding whether to merge it. A PR that genuinely changes no files gets a different sentence saying the diff was read and is empty. A path not in the diff is a refusal too, naming the paths that are, because "not in this PR" and "in this PR and unchanged" are otherwise the same silence and the first is usually a typo or the wrong number. Both caps disclose what they withheld in the render they truncated, the file cap keeping the real total in the header, the byte cap naming the counts above and below the hunks. The route goes through the shared `gh` wrapper, so it honours `repo:OWNER/NAME` — a raw `gh pr diff` from the wrong directory answers about the wrong repository, silently and well-formedly.

- **`git-push:set-upstream` and `git-push:to-upstream` — the two intents behind the ambiguous-upstream refusal, said in this op's own vocabulary** ([#879](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/879)). When `@{upstream}` resolves to a branch that is not this one, the op still refuses to guess. These are how the caller answers it without leaving the op:

  ```bash
  ./supertool 'git-push:set-upstream'   # push <branch> under its own name, retargeting tracking to <remote>/<branch>
  ./supertool 'git-push:to-upstream'    # push onto the tracked ref on purpose, explicit HEAD:<ref> refspec
  ```

  `:set-upstream` is the usual first push for a worktree branch. Its receipt names what it retargeted away from rather than rendering the branch as if it had never had an upstream — saying `Upstream: none` there would hide the exact thing the flag authorised.

  `:to-upstream` never issues a bare push: a bare push is precisely the input `push.default=simple` refuses, so the refspec is explicit and the header names the destination, since that destination is routinely a shared base branch. The rebase-recovery re-push carries the same refspec, or a non-fast-forward would silently turn a deliberate target back into the bare push git already rejects.

  **Asking for both is refused** (exit 2, nothing pushed) naming the two refs. They are different destinations; resolving the contradiction by precedence would be exactly the guess the refusal exists to prevent, and on the `:to-upstream` side the wrong choice writes to a branch everyone shares. Neither flag has a default and neither is implied — the caller still has to say which one they meant, which is the whole value of the decline.

- **Four heavy local tests marked `slow`, and a scheduled workflow to keep
  them running somewhere** ([#891](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/891)).
  Three tests that cost 95s of CPU in the local suite —
  `test_fetch_timeout_gives_a_verdict_not_a_traceback`,
  `test_rebase_timeout_fixture_survives_a_slow_helper_spawn`,
  `test_batch_at_cap_runs_to_completion` — are now `@pytest.mark.slow`.
  A fourth candidate, `test_a_network_failure_is_not_reported_as_a_refusal`,
  is deliberately left unmarked: #922 (open, not merged) is expected to cut
  its cost from ~20s to ~0.5s, and marking it now would need revisiting the
  moment that lands. Excluding `slow` from CI's main matrix would otherwise
  mean these tests — timeout/hang/network-failure disclosure tests, this
  repo's most-filed defect class — run nowhere at all, so
  `.github/workflows/slow-tests.yml` runs `pytest -m slow` daily on
  `ubuntu-latest` instead.
- **`--durations=25` on the main CI pytest leg** ([#891](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/891)).
  Roughly 7 of the ~10.5 minutes a Windows leg takes are spent between 98%
  and 99% of the progress bar (see [#917](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/917)),
  and until now nothing in the log said which test was running there. The
  flag makes the tail name itself instead of being guessed at.

- **`changelog.d/` — one fragment file per change, assembled at release** ([#906](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/906)). 55 of the last 60 merged PRs touched `CHANGELOG.md`, every one of them appending to the top of the same 2,670-line file. That makes conflicts quadratic rather than occasional: with N open PRs, each merge re-conflicts the other N-1, and `oss_train` exists to automate exactly that churn — a tool built to survive the problem rather than remove it. A PR now adds `changelog.d/<issue>.<section>[.<slug>].md` and never opens `CHANGELOG.md` at all, so two PRs never touch the same path and the conflict class disappears instead of being merged around. `python3 .github/scripts/assemble_changelog.py --version x.y.z` folds the fragments into a new release section at release time and deletes them.

  **`merge=union` was the one-line alternative and this repo already proved it wrong.** `tests/test_git_resolve_heading_dup_839.py` exists because a line-level union on a document whose meaning comes from structure emits a duplicated `## [x.y.z]` heading and silently reparents every unreleased line between the two copies under a tagged release. A correctness bug in the changelog dressed as a convenience.

  **Three states, never two.** The assembler reports `ok`, a finding, or `skipped`, every run. Zero fragments is `skipped` with a stated reason and a non-zero exit rather than an empty release section and a green exit — the defect class this tracker is fullest of is an absence produced by a tool being read as an absence in the world. A filename that does not parse is **refused by name**, not skipped, because a file the release tool passed over quietly is an entry that never ships and nobody is told. Findings are gathered before refusing, so one bad name does not turn a release cut into a queue.

  **Whatever sits under `## [Unreleased]` at release time is folded into the release being cut**, above the fragment-derived entries, with same-named `###` subsections merged into one heading rather than emitted twice — the duplicate-heading failure is live in this repo (#911) and #839 is the precedent for what it costs. `[Unreleased]` means "goes out in the next release", so it goes out in it; the heading itself stays as the anchor the compare link needs, with an empty body. Not folding was tried first and it produces exactly the stranding it was meant to prevent: a tag that ships silently omitting nine real changes, which then still read as pending. **The merge is checked by arithmetic, not trusted**: entries in plus entries produced must balance, and a mismatch refuses the write rather than reporting a clean run over a dropped line. The assembler also rewrites the `[Unreleased]` compare link and adds the new tag's link ref, removing a step from a release checklist that already edits four files.

  **The CI check is its own workflow** (`.github/workflows/changelog.yml`), not a job in `tests.yml`: "did this PR add a fragment" is a policy read of a diff, not a test. It validates every fragment name repo-wide, then requires a fragment from any PR touching `supertool.py`, `presets/`, `validators/`, `formatters/`, `notifiers/` or the plugin manifest. Docs- and tests-only PRs are exempt, and a `no-changelog` label is the stated way out — requiring a fragment for a typo fix is how the discipline decays into a reflex-added empty file.

  **No new dependency.** `towncrier` and `scriv` both solve this and both are dependencies; the assembler is 250 lines of stdlib in `.github/scripts/`.

- **`git-worktrees` names each tree's open PR, in four states** ([#941](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/941)). The board answered *is anyone working in this tree* and never *is that tree's work published, and is it green* — so choosing where to act next meant running `git-worktrees`, then `gh-prs`, then `gh-pr:N:status` per PR, and joining branch → path → PR number → check tally by hand. Both halves of that join were already held by the tool. Each row now ends in a tracker token and carries its reasoning as one more evidence line.

  **Four answers, and they do not collapse.** `PR #N` with the check tally summed by `_checks.summarize()` — the same arithmetic `gh-pr:N:status` prints, so a `CANCELLED` leg is a named term rather than a silent zero. `no open PR` when GitHub answered and nothing tracks a branch that is pushed. `no remote ref` when there is no remote-tracking ref here. And `PR unknown` when the lookup did not run — offline, unauthenticated, rate-limited, a non-GitHub remote — which is the pair that matters: `unknown` and `no open PR` are the tool's absence and the world's absence, and merged into one they read *this work is unpublished, take the tree*, in the op whose whole job is deciding which tree to take, at exactly the moment you are least able to check. The failed lookup is therefore consulted before any local fact, and it names which failure it was.

  **One call for N worktrees — and a full page is `unknown`, not `no PR`.** A single `gh pr list --limit 100`, keyed by head branch, serves every row. But a page that comes back *at* its cap is authoritative only for the branches it named; a branch missing from it is `PR unknown`, because a partially-answered batch is the same defect wearing state 2's clothes.

  **"Never pushed" is not claimed, because it cannot be observed.** The first live run called four `[merged]` worktrees "never pushed"; all four had been pushed, merged and deleted on the remote. A deleted remote branch and an unpublished one leave an identical local trace, and `branch.<name>.merge` does not separate them either — `git worktree add -b X … master` writes an upstream of `origin/master` for a branch that has never left the machine. The row reports what it saw and names both histories.

  **On by default, which is a cost this op did not previously carry.** It made no network call at all before; it now makes exactly one, on an 8s budget, adding about a second. Opt-in behind a suffix was the alternative and was rejected: the friction being fixed is a join done in the reader's head, and a suffix only helps a reader who already knows it exists. `nopr`, or `SUPERTOOL_WORKTREE_PR=0`, restores the fully offline op. The `[result]` line counts the rows whose tracker did not answer, so a missing answer survives `| tail -1`, and the exit code stays a statement about occupancy alone — a tracker nobody could read says nothing about whether a tree is safe to enter.

### Changed

- **The pre-push hook runs the suite for `master`, not for feature branches** ([#893](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/893)). It ran the full suite on every push — measured at **176.66s** on a real push — and that cost is serial and blocking, while the PR's 19 checks run in parallel on somebody else's machine and cost the author no waiting at all. CI being slower in wall-clock is not the comparison that matters. The hook now reads the refs git hands it on stdin and gates on the destination: `master`/`main` still pay for the suite, where a red default branch is a shared cost nobody opted into; a feature branch does not, because a red PR branch is what PRs are for. `PREPUSH_FULL=1 git push` forces it.

  **The skip is announced, and an unreadable stdin runs the suite rather than skipping it.** Three states, not two: some callers invoke a hook with stdin closed, and "the question was never answered" must not render as "feature branch, skip it" — the cost of being wrong that way is three minutes, and the other way is master. Both paths say which one they took.

  **What was rejected, and why it is written down.** Dropping the hook's `-m 'not benchmark'` override was considered and refused: the comment above it argues that the default `not slow` filter lets a slow test CI runs slip through, and that reasoning holds. It would also have bought nothing today — only 7 tests carry `@pytest.mark.slow` and none of them are the four that own the suite's cost ([#891](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/891)). `-x` was refused too: on a three-minute suite it converts one run showing every failure into one run per failure, which is why `--tb=short` is there.

- **CI no longer runs `slow`-marked tests on every push** ([#891](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/891)).
  `tests.yml`'s pytest job used to override `pyproject.toml`'s
  `-m 'not slow and not benchmark'` default with `-m 'not benchmark'`, so
  marking a test `slow` changed only the local inner loop — the twelve-leg
  matrix ran it at full duration on every push regardless. CI's `-m` filter
  now matches the local default, and the pre-push hook (which mirrors CI)
  follows the same change.

### Fixed

- **`map` reported `(no symbols)` for every file type no tier can parse, stating a missing parser as a missing structure** ([#887](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/887)). `map:CHANGELOG.md` on a 2,616-line file carrying ~70 headings answered `(no symbols)`. That is a claim about the document, and it is false; the true statement was about the tool, which had no markdown patterns and never said so. The cost was concrete: the reporter, told the file had no structure, hand-rolled a counter against `## Unreleased` — the file spells it `## [Unreleased]` — and published `0` unreleased entries for a release with twelve.

  **Three states, not two.** Symbols found; a tier parsed the file and it defines nothing (`(no symbols)`, unchanged); and **no tier has a grammar or pattern set for this extension**, which now renders `(no symbol parser for .ext - tree-sitter and the regex tier have no .ext grammar)`. The disclosure names the extension and what was available when it declined, so a reader learns whether installing a package would change the answer — the same three-state contract `docs/validators.md` §"Declining instead of guessing" applies elsewhere, and the shape [#790](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/790) already used for an unloadable grammar.

  **The loud failure was not traded for the quiet one.** A file a tier genuinely parsed and found nothing in still reads `(no symbols)`; the two facts render differently and a test asserts they do, in both directions. `tier: none` replaces `tier: regex` in the report line only when nothing in the run was parseable — naming a tier that never had a pattern to try would tell the same lie one line higher, and a mixed directory keeps the tier that actually produced symbols.

  **The class, not the instance.** The disclosure is computed from whether any tier claims the extension, not from a list of known-bad ones, so it covers `.rst`, `.txt`, `.yml`, `.sql`, `.css`, `.vue` and every extension nobody has thought of yet. Directory walks only visit extensions some tier claims, so the state is reached by naming a file directly — which is how the issue was filed. Fixing markdown alone would have left the next unparsed type silently structureless.

- **`gh-pr`, `gh-job`, `gh-run`, `gl-mr` and `gl-job` reported `⚠ MISMATCH` for a branch that IS checked out — in a sibling worktree — and prescribed a checkout `git-checkout` itself refuses** ([#850](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/850)). Run from the live clone on `master` with `fix/900` held by `~/Documents/st-wt/900`, `gh-pr:fix/900` printed `You are on: master ⚠ MISMATCH — switch with: ./supertool 'git-checkout:fix/900'`. Both halves of that line fail the standing test. `MISMATCH` was true of the current directory and reads as a claim about the repository, so a reader concludes the branch is checked out nowhere. And the remedy is an action git rejects outright — `fatal: 'fix/900' is already used by worktree at '/…/st-wt/900'` — which `git-checkout` already knew, because it catches exactly that stderr and answers `Switch with: cd <path>`. The knowledge existed one op over and none of the five call sites had adopted it, the same shape as [#263](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/263).

  **Three states, not two.** `presets/_branch_locale.py` answers *where is this branch* and the render follows: `✓` here; **the worktree path** when a linked worktree holds it, with `cd` as the remedy; `⚠ MISMATCH` plus the checkout hint only when the branch is held nowhere — the one case where switching is an action git will accept. A fourth line covers a `git worktree list` that did not answer: it says the location is UNKNOWN and suggests nothing, because "checked out nowhere" is a positive claim and a failed probe is not evidence for it.

  **A detached worktree parked on the same commit does not count.** Only the porcelain `branch` field matches. Conflating the two would reintroduce the ambiguity the change exists to remove, and it is pinned by its own test.

  **The path is printed exactly as git wrote it, separators included — that is a decision, not an oversight.** `git worktree list --porcelain` emits POSIX separators on every platform, so a Windows render reads `C:/Users/.../st-wt/900` rather than the native `C:` backslash form. Normalising it would make two ops print the same path two different ways: `presets/git/checkout.py` answers this same situation with `Switch with: cd <path>` taken straight from git's stderr, and Git Bash — the shell on those runners — takes the forward-slash form. It is stated here because it is the shape most likely to be quietly undone: the render looks wrong to anyone who has not read git's porcelain contract, and normalising it would pass every test except `test_the_rendered_path_is_the_one_git_itself_printed`, whose whole job is to compare the render against the bytes git emitted rather than against a path `pathlib` built.

  **The warning was not deleted.** Deleting it would have made the symptom vanish and taken a real signal with it — the ordinary single-worktree case is still the common one, and there `MISMATCH` is both true and actionable. It is unchanged there.

  **It costs one extra local subprocess, in the mismatch path only** — and #804's cost test is what surfaced it, before any human read the diff. `check()` returns at the `✓` branch before the lookup, so standing on the branch spends nothing; only the path that previously rendered a wrong line now pays a `git worktree list --porcelain`, measured at **29 ms** against a render whose other calls are network `gh`/`glab` round trips. It is already lazy, and memoisation would buy nothing: every op calls `check()` at most once per process (`gitlab/job.py`'s two call sites are the arms of one `if`/`else`). The lookup also runs *after* the caller's own fetch, so no API ordering changed. `tests/test_gh_run_matrix_reconcile_804.py`'s fixture recorded it as the run-view call because its fall-through both answered every unrecognised command with the run payload and recorded it as `view_argv`; the fixture now names the commands it answers and raises on one it has not been taught, so the next new subprocess is a failure rather than a wrong answer.

  **Five hand-built copies became one helper.** The line was copy-pasted across both families (`github/pr.py`, `github/job.py`, `github/run.py`, `gitlab/mr.py`, `gitlab/job.py`), so fixing one would have left the four everyone else reads — and the GitLab side was latent rather than absent: identical code, one worktree in the project it targets today. `#531`'s `actionable=False` behaviour is preserved exactly and still governs only the imperative; `cd` is exempt from it, since it moves you rather than HEAD, which is precisely what a session that must not move HEAD wants to hear. Both names on the line now go through the [#851](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/851) boundary — a branch name is API text and a worktree path is a filename, and a newline in either forges a line in a header the reader takes as the tool's.


- **`git-checkout`'s "Rebase in progress" warned on the debris a finished rebase leaves behind, permanently and with no remedy** ([#900](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/900)). The check fired when any of `REBASE_HEAD`, `rebase-merge/` or `rebase-apply/` existed in the git dir. `REBASE_HEAD` is not a state marker — it is a ref git writes while replaying a commit — and on the conflict → `--continue` → completion path git never unlinks it. So after one conflicted rebase the repo carried the ref forever: both state directories gone, `git status` reporting nothing, `git rebase --abort` answering `fatal: no rebase in progress`, and the warning on every subsequent checkout with nothing a user could type to clear it. The condition is now the two directories alone. Reproduced identically on git 2.39.5 and 2.46.2.

  **Only that one ending leaves the ref, which is why the report was hard to confirm.** Measured per ending rather than assumed: a rebase that never conflicts leaves nothing, `--abort` cleans up `REBASE_HEAD` too — contrary to the issue's account of it — and only conflict-then-`--continue` leaves it. A repo that has since been rebased cleanly or aborted shows no trace, so the same repo can and does stop reproducing between filing and reading.

  **Dropping the term costs no detection, and that is the part that had to be checked before narrowing it.** A missed rebase is worse than a noisy one, so every stopped shape was run: merge backend, am backend (`--apply`), `--rebase-merges`, and the interactive `break` and `edit` stops. All of them hold one of the two directories — they are what git's own status reads to decide it is mid-rebase. The `break` stop settles it in the other direction: it carries **no** `REBASE_HEAD` at all, so the ref was never what this check stood on, and a version leaning on it would go blind exactly where a rebase really is in progress. The reasoning is in the code as well as here, because the term looks plausible enough to be re-added by the next reader.

  **`MERGE_HEAD` on the line above is inert, not fine.** The issue passes it through as correct because git deletes it when the merge commit lands. It does — and it also deletes it on *any* checkout, including a no-op switch to the branch already checked out. Combined with the op's own dirty-tree guard, which returns before the warnings whenever the index is still unmerged, there is no state in which that line can render. It is harmless and left alone, but it is not load-bearing and should not be cited as the precedent for how these checks work. Pinned by a test so a future git that keeps `MERGE_HEAD` turns it back into a real case. Rebase state is the opposite — `rebase-merge/` outlives the switch — which is why the rebase warning is worth having at all.

  **`CHERRY_PICK_HEAD`, `REVERT_HEAD` and `BISECT_LOG` are equally worth warning about and equally absent**, and deliberately not bundled here: a stopped cherry-pick is exactly as dangerous to walk away from as a stopped rebase, but adding detections is a scope decision to argue on its own rather than smuggle into a fix that removes one.
- **`git-resolve` never read the exit code of the validator it shelled out to, so a child that died reported the same as a child with nothing to say** ([#883](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/883)). The post-resolve syntax digest in `presets/git/resolve.py` folds the `validate` op's `validate: PATH` blocks back onto files and read **only stdout**: `res.returncode` was never inspected and `res.stderr` was dropped. `None` in that map means "the validators ran and none of them handles this file type", which the receipt prints as nothing on purpose — and four other outcomes were arriving as that same nothing, or as something worse than nothing.

  **The case that forges a pass is a child killed *after* a complete reply.** #881's block-count guard already caught the common shape of a dead child by accident — zero blocks for N files — so a crash was visible, but attributed to the fold (`not checked (validator output had 0 block(s) for 1 file(s))`) and stripped of the one line of stderr that says what broke. A child killed once its last block was flushed passes that guard with the right block count and every row reading `ok`, and the digest then renders `validate: ok` about a process that did not survive its own run: the strongest claim this tool can make, about a run that did not finish. `returncode` separates the two and the function already had it. Non-zero now maps every path in the batch to `not checked`, naming `exited N` or `killed by signal N` and the child's first stderr line — and does **not** retry on the second filter pass, because a non-zero exit is not "that filter selected nothing".

  **`no validators configured` and "neither filter pass selected anything" are not errors, and are still not silence.** The child ran fine and said it had nothing to run. That is a different fact from "none of these validators handles `.txt`", and the two rendered identically — so a config with no validators reported every resolved conflict as `markers: clean`, including, in the test that asserted this behaviour, a file that does not compile. Both now decline. Three tests asserted the old silence and all three fed `no validators configured` under a docstring describing the *per-file* answer; they are retargeted at the shape that actually means it — an emitted block with no rows — which stays `None` and stays quiet, so an ordinary `.txt` in an ordinary config prints `markers: clean` and nothing more. The noise this trades against is bounded to configs where the digest column was meaningless anyway.

  **The reason line is bounded and flattened.** It lands in `markers: clean | {digest}`, a line the tool owns at column 0, and a failed child's stderr is untrusted text that can carry any of the ten separators `str.splitlines()` splits on plus the erase-line/cursor-up pair that removes a line rather than adding one (#851). It goes through `presets/_untrusted.flat` — the call, not a second copy of the rule established by `_flat_cell` in #895 — first non-empty line only, cut to 120 characters. The wording has to distinguish *could not run* from *nothing to say*; it does not have to diagnose.

  **Scope.** [#880](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/issues/880) covers the render-side silence of the genuine `None` and stays open and untouched: the `else` branch it proposes is a separate decision, and the one absence that is a real answer is deliberately left absent here.

  **Method.** TDD, red before green. RED, on unmodified `master`: `escapes cwd` absent from `not checked (validator output had 0 block(s) for 1 file(s))`; `validate: ok` returned for a child killed by signal 9; `markers: clean` alone for both zero-validator replies — **4 failed, 4 passed**. GREEN: **7152 passed, 79 skipped** across the suite. The post-conditions are asserted on the rendered receipt through `resolve.main()`, never on a helper being called — that assertion passes on the broken version. Two counter-tests hold the line the fix must not cross: a block with no rows still digests to `None`, and a first filter pass that selects nothing still falls back to the name list.
- **`read`'s compact mode kept one spelling of an HTML comment close it meant to drop** ([alert 5](https://github.com/Digital-Process-Tools/claude-supertool/security/code-scanning/5)). `_COMPACT_SKIP` lists the blank-and-comment-only line shapes that compact mode elides from `read` output. Its XML/HTML branch matched `-->` and not `--!>`, which closes a comment just as `-->` does — Python's own spec-compliant `html.parser` tokenises `<!-- x --!>` and `<!-- x -->` identically, one comment and no stray data. So a comment-only line ending the `--!>` way rendered where its twin did not. **Impact is one wasted line of output in compact mode**, on a file spelling its comment closes an uncommon but legal way.

  **This is not a security fix and the entry will not be written as one.** The alert is CodeQL's `py/bad-tag-filter`, whose premise is that the regexp filters HTML *for safety* — that something downstream is protected by what the pattern removes. `_COMPACT_SKIP` has exactly one consumer, `if compact and _COMPACT_SKIP.match(line): continue` in `op_read`, and it decides whether a line is **printed**. Nothing is sanitised, no output is re-parsed as HTML, and a line that survives the filter is displayed rather than trusted. Under-matching costs a line of context; it cannot grant anything. The rule's severity does not transfer to this call site, and a CHANGELOG claiming a vulnerability was closed here would be a false claim outliving everyone able to correct it. **The alert is fixed on its factual half only** — the pattern did miss a real comment close, and now does not.

  **Scope: the one branch, argued rather than inherited.** The neighbouring branches were checked for the same class of gap and have none. `<!--` already covers HTML's abrupt-close forms (`<!-->`, `<!--->`) because they open with it. `/*` and `*/` are C-family, where no alternative spelling exists. `--!>` was the only miss. The widened `--!?>` is also checked for overshoot in the other direction: it must not become "any line starting with two dashes", since a YAML document marker carries content the reader asked for.
